book: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning

questions.q: In the Preface to Make It Stick, how do the three authors describe the division of roles among themselves?
options: All three are cognitive scientists who split the research by topic
Roediger is a storyteller and Brown and McDaniel are cognitive scientists
Roediger and McDaniel are cognitive scientists and Brown is a storyteller
Brown and Roediger are educators and McDaniel is the researcher
questions.explain: The Preface says Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel have dedicated their careers to studying learning and memory, while Peter Brown is a storyteller. Together they explain the science mainly by telling stories of people who have mastered complex knowledge and skills rather than by reciting research.

questions.q: A reader of Make It Stick notices that retrieval practice is explained early in the book, then comes up again in later chapters in new contexts. According to the Preface, what explains this?
options: The authors deliberately apply spaced repetition and interleaving to the book's own key ideas
The chapters were written by different authors who did not coordinate their topics
The authors treat each topic serially and only summarise earlier material in the final chapter
The publisher asked for repetition so that chapters could be read in any order
questions.explain: The Preface says that, unlike most books that cover one topic and move on, this book applies two of its own principles, spaced repetition of key ideas and interleaving of related topics, so that “we unabashedly cover key ideas more than once”. Readers who return to an idea periodically remember it better.

questions.q: A medical student tries the study strategies recommended in Make It Stick and finds that they feel wrong and less productive than her usual habits. According to the Preface, what does this reaction illustrate?
options: That the strategies work only for students in the humanities, not in medicine
That she has not yet read enough of the research to apply the strategies correctly
That the strategies must be combined with reform of the school system to be effective
That the most effective learning strategies are not intuitive, which is the catch the authors warn about
questions.explain: The Preface states the catch directly: “the most effective learning strategies are not intuitive”. It also notes that even college and medical students, whose main job is learning, rely on study techniques that are far from optimal, so a feeling of wrongness is expected rather than a sign the strategies have failed.

questions.q: In the Preface to Make It Stick, what is the catch the authors identify about the science of learning, and why does it matter for how people study?
questions.a: The catch is that the most effective learning strategies are not intuitive. Research into how we learn and remember shows that much of what people take for gospel about learning is largely wasted effort, and even college and medical students rely on techniques that are far from optimal. Widely accepted practices are rooted in theory, lore and intuition, so people need evidence-based strategies to replace them, and those strategies will feel unfamiliar.

questions.q: The Preface to Make It Stick promises that the book will repeat its key principles in different contexts and names the audiences it is written for. Using the table of contents, explain how Chapter 8, Make It Stick, carries out those two promises.
questions.a: The Preface says the book is written for students, teachers, trainers in business, industry and the military, coaches, and lifelong learners, and that it deliberately returns to key ideas across the book so readers remember them better. Chapter 8 is organised by exactly those audiences, with sections of tips for students, lifelong learners, teachers and trainers. Each set of tips revisits retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving, which were first explained in Chapters 2 and 3, so the closing chapter is itself the spaced repetition the Preface announced.

questions.q: In 2002 the James S. McDonnell Foundation awarded a research grant to Roediger, McDaniel and nine other cognitive psychologists, with ____ as the principal investigator.
questions.explain: The Preface says the grant, titled Applying Cognitive Psychology to Enhance Educational Practice, was awarded to Roediger and McDaniel and nine others, with Roediger as the principal investigator. The team collaborated for ten years on translating cognitive science into educational science.

questions.q: The Preface says the book applies two of its own primary learning principles to its structure: spaced repetition of key ideas, and the ____ of different but related topics.
questions.explain: The authors explain that learners who interleave the study of different topics learn each better than if they had studied them one at a time in sequence, so the book mixes related topics rather than covering each one once and moving on.

questions.q: Which of these audiences does the Preface to Make It Stick explicitly say the book is written for?
options: Trainers in business, industry and the military
Lifelong learners nearing middle age or older who want to stay in the game
Policymakers seeking to reform the school system
Coaches
Neuroscientists mapping the neural underpinnings of learning
Publishers of textbooks and study guides
questions.explain: The Preface lists students and teachers, trainers in business, industry and the military, leaders of professional associations offering in-service training, coaches, and lifelong learners nearing middle age or older. It explicitly says the book is not about reforming education policy or the school system, and it says much remains unknown about the neural underpinnings of learning rather than addressing neuroscientists.

questions.q: Which of these claims does the Preface to Make It Stick make about the research on how people learn and remember?
options: The field goes back 125 years
It has been particularly fruitful in recent years
It confirms that the study techniques most students already use are close to optimal
It has fully explained the neural underpinnings of learning
Its principles and strategies can be put to work immediately, at no cost
questions.explain: The Preface describes a field that goes back 125 years, has been especially productive recently, and has yielded strategies that can be applied right away at no cost and to great effect. It says the opposite about student habits, which are far from optimal, and admits that much remains to be known about learning and its neural underpinnings.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Preface, the team of cognitive psychologists funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation collaborated for five years on research to translate cognitive science into educational science.
questions.explain: The Preface says the team collaborated for ten years, not five, and that the book is in many respects a direct result of that work. The grant was awarded in 2002.

questions.q: Put these points from the Preface to Make It Stick in the order in which the authors make them.
items: People generally go about learning in the wrong ways
Two cognitive scientists and a storyteller team up to tell stories of mastery
A McDonnell Foundation grant brings eleven cognitive psychologists together
The book repeats key ideas using spaced repetition and interleaving
The book is written for students, teachers, trainers, coaches and lifelong learners
questions.explain: The Preface opens with the claim that people learn in the wrong ways, then introduces the three authors and their approach, explains the 2002 McDonnell Foundation collaboration that the book grew out of, describes the book's own use of spacing and interleaving, and closes by naming its readers and stressing that the strategies can be used right now.

questions.q: Match each person or organisation named in the Preface to Make It Stick with the role the Preface gives them.
pairs: Principal investigator of the 2002 research grant on applying cognitive psychology to education
Co-director of Washington University’s Center for Integrative Research in Learning and Memory
The storyteller among the three authors
St. Louis funder that awarded the grant to eleven cognitive psychologists
questions.explain: The Preface identifies Roediger and McDaniel as cognitive scientists, with Roediger leading the grant and McDaniel co-directing the Washington University centre, Brown as the storyteller, and the McDonnell Foundation of St. Louis as the funder that sought to bridge the gap between research on learning and its application in education.

questions.q: According to the Preface, sort each item by whether it is something Make It Stick is about or something the authors say the book is not about.
groups: What the book is not about

items.t: What people can do for themselves right now to learn better and remember longer
How education policy ought to be reformed
How teachers and coaches can design learning principles into the learning experience
How the school system should be restructured
Stories of people who have found their way to mastery of complex knowledge and skills
A complete account of the neural underpinnings of learning

questions.explain: The Preface says the book is about what individuals can do right now, since “The responsibility for learning rests with every individual”, and about how teachers and coaches can help, told through stories of mastery. It explicitly says it is not about reforming education policy or the school system, and it acknowledges that much remains to be known about the neural basis of learning.

questions.q: In Make It Stick, what do the authors mean by learning?
options: Acquiring knowledge and skills and keeping them readily available from memory to make sense of future problems
Absorbing as much information as possible during a single intensive period of study
Understanding a subject well enough to pass an exam shortly after studying it
Developing creative abilities that depend less on facts than on insight
questions.explain: The authors define learning as acquiring knowledge and skills and having them available from memory later. Passing a test soon after study or sheer volume of information does not capture the lasting availability they stress.

questions.q: Why did pilot Matt Brown make his landing approach in a wide left-hand turn after shutting down his right engine?
options: The runway at his Louisiana fuel stop could only be approached from the left side
Without right-side power, only a left turn still gave enough lift to level out
A left turn burned less fuel than a right turn while the oil pressure kept falling
Turning left stopped the failing engine from losing any more of its remaining oil
questions.explain: Matt used what he knew from memory about flying on one engine: with the right engine dead, a left-hand turn was the only way to keep enough lift to level out. The reason was aerodynamic, not about runways or fuel.

questions.q: In the opening story, Matt Brown shut down his ____ engine after the oil pressure kept falling.
questions.explain: The oil pressure dropped in his right engine, so he shut that one down, feathered the prop, and flew on the left engine.

questions.q: The authors say learning is an acquired ____, and that its most effective strategies are often counterintuitive.
questions.explain: The third immutable aspect of learning they list is that learning is an acquired skill rather than something fixed.

questions.q: True or false: The authors argue that the most effective learning strategies are usually the intuitive ones.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: learning is an acquired skill and the most effective strategies are often counterintuitive.

questions.q: Which of these are immutable aspects of learning that the authors say we can all agree on?
options: To be useful, learning requires memory so that what we learned is still there later
We need to keep learning and remembering all our lives
Learning is an acquired skill
Learning ability is fixed at birth by our genes
Learning that feels easy is the most durable
questions.explain: The three points are that learning needs memory, that it continues across life, and that it is an acquired skill. The book argues against the idea that ability is hardwired and says effortful learning is more durable than easy learning.

questions.q: In the opening story, in what order did Matt Brown carry out his actions once he decided to deal with the failing engine?
items: Shut down the ailing right engine
Feather the propeller to reduce drag
Increase power on the left engine
Fly with opposite rudder
questions.explain: He shut down the right engine, feathered the prop, added left power, and flew with opposite rudder to limp the last miles.

questions.q: What is the order of the three aspects of learning the authors say we can probably all agree on?
items: Learning requires memory so it is available later
We must keep learning and remembering throughout life
Learning is an acquired skill whose best strategies are counterintuitive
questions.explain: The passage lists memory first, lifelong learning second, and learning as an acquired skill third.

questions.q: Why does the authors' definition of learning make memory essential, and how does Matt Brown's engine emergency show this?
questions.a: They define learning as acquiring knowledge and skills and having them readily available from memory so you can make sense of future problems. Matt faced an engine failure alone at night and had to recall from memory the tolerances of his Cessna and the procedures for flying on one engine. Knowledge that is not there when needed is of no use, which is why learning requires memory.

questions.q: In the authors' claim about effortful learning, what does the comparison of easy learning to writing in sand convey?
options: Easy learning is simple to correct because mistakes can be smoothed over
Easy learning is unreliable at first but becomes permanent with repetition
Easy learning is quickly lost, here today and gone tomorrow
Easy learning is fast to acquire and so the best use of study time
questions.explain: The authors say learning is deeper and more durable when it is effortful, and easy learning is “like writing in sand, here today and gone tomorrow.” The image is about impermanence.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: What do the authors mean by massed practice?
options: Practicing several related skills mixed together within one session
Practicing a skill with gaps of days between the sessions
Practicing a skill together with a large group of other learners
Single-minded, rapid-fire repetition of something you are trying to burn into memory
questions.explain: Massed practice is the practice-practice-practice of conventional wisdom, such as cramming. Mixing skills is interleaving and leaving gaps is spacing, both of which the authors favor.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: According to the authors, why do rereading and massed practice get taken as signs of mastery?
options: They give rise to feelings of fluency that learners mistake for mastery
They produce the best results on delayed tests, as the research shows
They are the most effortful strategies, so learners credit them with the most gain
Teachers are trained to recommend them above every other strategy
questions.explain: Rereading and massed practice create fluency, and that feeling is read as mastery even though the strategies are largely a waste of time for real mastery or durability.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: How do the authors describe the relationship between exercise and the brain in learning?
options: The brain works like a muscle that grows bigger with every hour you study
The brain is not a muscle, but the neural pathways of learning get stronger when retrieved and practiced
Neural pathways stay fixed once formed, so practice helps only bodily skills
Neural pathways get stronger simply through exposure, whether or not retrieved
questions.explain: They explicitly say the brain is not a muscle that gets stronger with exercise, yet the pathways making up a body of learning strengthen when the memory is retrieved and the learning is practiced.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: What do the authors say happens when you space out practice or interleave the practice of two or more subjects?
options: Retrieval feels easier and more productive, and learning lasts longer as a result
Retrieval is harder and feels less productive, and learning fades sooner than before
Retrieval is harder and feels less productive, but learning lasts longer and can be applied more versatilely
Retrieval feels much the same as with massed practice, with no difference in durability
questions.explain: The effort of spaced and interleaved practice makes it feel less productive, yet it produces longer lasting and more versatile learning. The feeling of ease belongs to massed practice.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: What do the authors say about the popular idea that you learn better when taught in your preferred style, such as auditory or visual?
options: It holds for visual learners but not for auditory learners
It holds only when the style has been identified by a formal test
It is supported, but only for adults studying alone
It is not supported by the empirical research
questions.explain: They state the notion is not supported by empirical research, and add that people learn better when they go wide and draw on all their aptitudes instead of one favored style.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Why does the book say interleaving practice at computing the volumes of different geometric solids is useful?
options: It makes you better at picking the right solution when a later test presents a random solid
It lets you memorize each solid's procedure faster within a single session
It removes the need to understand how the solids differ from one another
It makes each practice session feel smoother and more fluent
questions.explain: Interleaved and varied practice helps you extract the underlying rules that differentiate problem types, so you pick the right solution in an unfamiliar situation.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: How do the authors define elaboration?
options: Repeating new material in the same words until it becomes fully automatic
Expressing new material in your own words and linking it to what you know
Breaking new material into the smallest pieces and studying each piece in turn
Adding extra detail to your notes so they look more complete and thorough
questions.explain: Elaboration is about meaning and connection to prior knowledge, which is why the authors say there is no known limit to how much you can learn this way, unlike mechanical repetition.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: A student is struggling to grasp the abstract principle of angular momentum. Which approach fits the authors' advice?
options: Reread the textbook definition until it feels familiar and fluent
Memorize the textbook definition word for word before looking for any examples
Tie it to something concrete she already knows, such as a skater spinning faster as she draws in her arms
Put the topic aside until she feels a natural interest in physics
questions.explain: The authors say an abstraction is easier to learn when grounded in something concrete you already know, and they use the skater example for angular momentum.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Cramming for exams is an example of ____ practice.
questions.explain: Massed practice is the single-minded, rapid-fire repetition of material you are trying to burn into memory, and cramming is the authors' example.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Recalling facts, concepts, or events from memory is called ____ practice.
questions.explain: Retrieval practice, such as using flashcards, strengthens memory and interrupts forgetting, and is more effective than review by rereading.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Giving new material meaning by expressing it in your own words and connecting it with what you know is called ____.
questions.explain: Elaboration is the process the authors say has no known limit, in contrast to mechanical repetition.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: A ____ is a mental representation of some external reality, such as a batter's picture of how a curveball looks.
questions.explain: The authors define a mental model as a mental representation of some external reality and use the baseball batter to illustrate it.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: All new learning requires a foundation of ____ knowledge, as when trigonometry depends on remembered algebra and geometry.
questions.explain: New learning builds on what you already know, so the foundation of prior knowledge must be in place first.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: The authors say the popular idea that people learn best when taught in their preferred ____, such as auditory or visual, is not supported by research.
questions.explain: Matching instruction to a preferred learning style is the notion the authors say is not supported by empirical research.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, rereading text is one of the learners' preferred study strategies but among the least productive.
questions.explain: Rereading and massed practice are by far the preferred strategies of learners of all stripes, yet they are among the least productive.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim that a single simple quiz after reading a text produces learning no better than rereading the text.
questions.explain: They claim the opposite: one simple quiz after reading or a lecture produces better learning and remembering than rereading or reviewing notes.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that trying to solve a problem before being taught the solution leads to better learning, even when errors are made in the attempt.
questions.explain: This is one of their principal claims: attempting the problem first improves learning, errors included.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Which of these does the book say about retrieval practice?
options: It strengthens the memory
It interrupts forgetting
A single quiz can beat rereading the text
It removes the need for any prior knowledge
It works for facts but not for concepts or events
questions.explain: Retrieval strengthens memory, interrupts forgetting, and a single quiz beats rereading. The authors describe it as recalling facts, concepts, or events, and say all new learning still needs prior knowledge.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Which of these does the book give as examples of interleaved practice improving later categorizing or choice of solution?
options: Computing the volumes of different geometric solids
Identifying types of birds
Identifying the works of different oil painters
Repeating a phone number while dialing it
Rereading a chapter in close succession
questions.explain: The solids, birds, and oil painters are the book's three examples of interleaving. Repeating a phone number and close rereading are not interleaving.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Which of these does the book give as examples of prior knowledge needed before new learning?
options: Knowing how to land a twin-engine plane on two engines before landing it on one
Remembering algebra and geometry to learn trigonometry
Mastering the properties of wood and how to join boards before cabinetmaking
Being fluent with a lecturer's wording before understanding the lecture
Highlighting a text before reviewing the notes
questions.explain: The plane, trigonometry, and cabinetmaking examples all show new learning resting on a foundation. Fluent wording and highlighting are not offered as prior knowledge.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Which of these does the book list as cues a batter can use to tell what kind of pitch is coming?
options: The way the pitcher winds up
The way the pitcher throws
The spin of the ball's seams
The noise of the crowd
The umpire's stance
questions.explain: The wind-up, the throw, and the spin of the seams are the subtle signals named for each kind of pitch. The batter winnows out extraneous distractions such as crowd noise.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: In the baseball example, in what order do the batter's mental models build outward from the narrowest to the broadest connections?
items: Telling pitch types apart from cues like the wind-up and seam spin
Linking those pitch models to knowledge of stance, strike zone, and swinging
Linking them to models of player positions and base runners
Linking those to models of the opposition and signals from the dugout
questions.explain: The batter forms a model for each pitch, connects it to batting mechanics, then to player positions, and finally to the opposition and dugout signals.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Match each term to the authors' meaning.
pairs: Single-minded, rapid-fire repetition of material you want to burn into memory
Recalling facts, concepts, or events from memory, as with flashcards
Giving new material meaning by putting it in your own words and linking it to what you know
A mental representation of some external reality
questions.explain: Each pairing follows the authors' own definitions in their list of claims.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Match each idea in the heat-transfer and weather examples to the everyday experience the authors use.
pairs: Warming your hands around a hot cup of cocoa
The way the sun pools in the den on a wintry day
A blast of air conditioning on a hot day in Atlanta
Warm air holds more moisture than cold air
Water dripping from the back of an air conditioner
questions.explain: The authors use these everyday experiences as examples of elaboration, linking new principles to what you already know.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Match each principle to the example the authors use for it.
pairs: New learning needs a foundation of prior knowledge
Landing a twin-engine plane on two engines before learning to land on one
Ground an abstraction in something concrete
A figure skater spinning faster as she draws her arms to her chest
Testing calibrates your judgment of what you know
A pilot discovering in a hydraulic-failure simulator whether he is on top of the procedures
Put new knowledge in a larger context
The more of the story of history you know, the more of it you can learn
questions.explain: Each principle appears in the claims list with the example paired here.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Sort each strategy by how the authors rate it.
groups: Preferred but among the least productive

items.t: Rereading text
Massed practice
Cramming for exams
Retrieval practice with a quiz
Spacing out practice
Interleaving different subjects
Using flashcards

questions.explain: Rereading, massed practice, and cramming give fluency but little durable learning, while retrieval, spacing, and interleaving are harder but longer lasting.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Sort each activity by whether it is elaboration or mechanical repetition.

items.t: Explaining new material in your own words
Connecting a new idea to your own experience
Describing how new learning relates to what you already know
Going over the same material again and again without adding meaning
Quickly hitting the limit of what you can keep in mind

questions.explain: Elaboration gives material meaning and has no known limit, whereas mechanical repetition quickly reaches the limit of what you can keep in mind.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Sort each example by the idea it illustrates in the authors' claims.

items.t: Algebra and geometry needed for trigonometry
Wood properties and joinery needed for cabinetmaking
Landing on two engines before landing on one
Telling a curveball from a changeup by its cues
Linking pitch models to player-position models
Linking models to the opposition and dugout signals

questions.explain: The first three show new learning resting on earlier learning. The last three show a batter building and connecting mental models.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Sort each statement by whose view of intellectual ability it reflects.

items.t: Learning something new changes the brain
Failure is a source of useful information
Mental models you develop let you reason, solve, and create
Intellectual ability is hardwired from birth
Failing a challenge is an indictment of your native ability

questions.explain: The authors say the elements shaping your abilities lie to a surprising extent within your control, so failure is information rather than a verdict.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Why do the authors say we are poor judges of when we are learning well?
questions.a: When learning is harder and slower and does not feel productive, we are drawn to strategies that feel more fruitful, such as rereading and massed practice. These produce feelings of fluency that we take as signs of mastery, but the gains are often temporary. Testing helps calibrate our judgment.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: According to the claims, how does retrieval practice differ from rereading as a way to study, and why does it work?
questions.a: Retrieval practice means recalling facts, concepts, or events from memory, for example with flashcards, rather than going over the text again. It strengthens the memory and interrupts forgetting, and even a single quiz beats rereading the text or reviewing notes. Periodic practice strengthens the retrieval routes of the learning.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: Why do the authors recommend spacing and interleaving practice even though they feel less productive?
questions.a: When you space practice and get a little rusty, or interleave two or more subjects, retrieval is harder and feels less productive. That effort produces longer lasting learning and makes it possible to apply it more versatilely in later settings. Interleaved and varied practice also helps you extract the underlying rules that tell problem types apart.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: What is elaboration, and why do the authors say there is no known limit to how much you can learn when you practice it?
questions.a: Elaboration is giving new material meaning by expressing it in your own words and connecting it with what you already know. Mere mechanical repetition quickly hits the limit of what you can keep in mind, as in the Far Side cartoon of the student whose brain is full. The more connections you create to prior knowledge, the stronger your grasp and the easier later recall.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: How does the baseball batter illustrate a mental model, and why does it give an expert an advantage?
questions.a: A great batter culls out distractions and attends to the cues that mark each kind of pitch, forming a distinct mental model for each. He connects those models to batting stance and strike zone, to player positions, and to the opposition and dugout signals. Because he has distilled the key elements and linked them, he can make sense of the changing information better than a less experienced player.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: How do the authors argue that intellectual ability lies within your own control, and how should this change the way you see failure?
questions.a: Although we start with the gift of our genes, every time you learn something new you change the brain and become capable through developing mental models. So ability is not simply hardwired, and failure is not an indictment of native ability. Failure becomes a source of useful information, a sign you need to dig deeper or try another strategy, and making and correcting mistakes builds the bridges to advanced learning.
questions.section: Claims We Make in This Book

questions.q: What is cognitive psychology, as the authors describe it?
options: The study of learning theories handed down through teaching traditions and personal experience
The use of new imaging techniques to find the brain mechanisms that underlie learning
The design of testing regimes and instructional organizers for gifted and remedial groups
The basic science of understanding how the mind works through empirical research on how people perceive, remember, and think
questions.explain: Cognitive psychology is the basic science of how the mind works. The other options describe lore, neuroscience, and educational psychology.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: What do the authors say neuroscience can currently tell us about how to improve education?
options: We are still a very long way from knowing what neuroscience will tell us about improving education
Imaging has already shown which study strategies work best in classrooms
Brain research has replaced cognitive psychology as the best guide to teaching
Neuroscience has largely settled how tests and instructional organizers should be designed
questions.explain: Neuroscientists are advancing understanding of brain mechanisms, but the authors say it is far too early to know what this means for education.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: A website offers study tips and says they are scientifically proven. By the authors' standards, which check is the most reliable?
options: Whether it matches what teachers and coaches have long believed
Whether it rests on controlled experiments that passed peer review
Whether many other popular websites repeat the very same advice
Whether it feels right given your own experience as a student
questions.explain: The authors urge skepticism and say good evidence comes from experimental studies with appropriate controls that stood up under scientific review. Lore and intuition are what they warn against.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: The basic science of how the mind works, which uses empirical research to study how people perceive, remember, and think, is cognitive ____.
questions.explain: Cognitive psychologists have spent over forty years building a body of evidence on what works in learning.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: The best empirical studies are ____ in nature: the researcher develops a hypothesis and tests it through experiments.
questions.explain: Such studies must meet rigorous criteria for design and objectivity.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: True or false: The authors say they conducted most of the studies they describe in the book themselves.
questions.explain: They say they collaborated in some of the studies but not the lion's share; most come from the wider scientific literature.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: Which of these does the book say the authors do in presenting their evidence?
options: Distill findings from studies that stood up under review before publication in professional journals
Say so where they are offering theory rather than scientifically validated results
Use anecdotes from people whose work requires mastery of complex knowledge and skills
Discuss each research study at length in the main text
Rely mainly on their own unpublished experiments
questions.explain: They keep discussion of studies to a minimum, citing them in the notes, and label theory as theory. They draw on published studies, not mainly on unpublished work of their own.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: Why do the authors advise being skeptical about advice on how to learn, and what standard do they offer for judging it?
questions.a: Advice is easy to find, but not all of it is grounded in research, and not everything that passes as research meets scientific standards such as appropriate control conditions. The best studies are experimental: a researcher states a hypothesis and tests it under rigorous criteria for design and objectivity. The authors rely on studies that stood up under review before being published in professional journals.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: How, according to the authors, is much teaching and studying structured today, and what have cognitive psychologists been doing about it?
questions.a: Much of how we structure training and schooling rests on a mix of theory, lore, and intuition drawn from personal experience as teachers, coaches, and students. For over forty years cognitive psychologists have worked to build a body of empirical evidence about which strategies actually get results.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: In what order does a finding pass through the process the authors describe before it earns a place in their book?
items: A researcher develops a hypothesis
The hypothesis is tested in experiments meeting rigorous design standards
The results stand up under review by the scientific community
The results are published in professional journals
questions.explain: The authors draw on studies that tested a hypothesis experimentally, survived scientific review, and were published in professional journals.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: Match each group of researchers to what the book says they are concerned with.
pairs: Empirical research into how people perceive, remember, and think
Theories of human development and the tools of education, such as testing regimes
Brain mechanisms underlying learning, studied with new imaging techniques
questions.explain: The authors list these groups as having a hand in the puzzle of learning.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is empirical research or theory, lore, and intuition.

items.t: Experiments with appropriate control conditions
A hypothesis tested for objectivity and generalizability
Findings reviewed before publication in professional journals
Methods handed down from earlier generations of teachers
A coach's sense of what works from personal experience
Teaching habits shaped by what feels right to us

questions.explain: The authors contrast evidence-based findings with the mix of theory, lore, and intuition that much of schooling is built on.
questions.section: Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition

questions.q: Why do the authors say our faith in massed practice runs so deep?
options: Research has consistently shown that massed practice builds durable memory
Massed practice forces learners to retrieve the material from memory each time
Most of us see fast gains during the learning phase of massed practice
Its gains stay stable for weeks and months after the practice ends
questions.explain: The fast gains are real but, the research shows, transitory and quick to melt away.

questions.q: What are the three strikes the authors say count against rereading?
options: It is tiring, it distorts memory, and it works only with short texts
It is expensive, it gives no feedback, and it favors high-ability readers
It is slow, it forces cramming, and it discourages any self-quizzing
It takes time, it does not last, and familiarity is mistaken for mastery
questions.explain: Familiarity with a text comes to feel like mastery, which is the self-deception, and the time spent is no measure of mastery.

questions.q: What do the penny memory test and the UCLA fire extinguisher study show?
options: Repeated exposure over many years does not by itself produce durable learning of details
Learning details requires a deliberate intention to remember them
People remember objects they use every day better than rare ones
Faculty retain safety information better than students do
questions.explain: Even people who had seen pennies often or walked past an extinguisher for years could not identify them, showing that repetition alone does not build lasting memory.

questions.q: A student plans to learn a list of biology terms by silently reading it ten times tonight. What does the authors' argument predict?
options: He will retain the terms for months because repeated exposure burns them in
It will feel increasingly familiar, but the gains will be transitory and melt away quickly
He will retain the terms well provided he concentrates on them single-mindedly
He will remember best the terms he finds hardest to read
questions.explain: The authors say people commonly believe repetition burns material into memory, but gains from massed repetition melt away and growing familiarity is mistaken for mastery.

questions.q: Rereading is the number ____ study strategy of most people, including more than 80 percent of college students in some surveys.
questions.explain: The authors call this finding a chill for educators because rereading is often “labor in vain.”

questions.q: Matt Brown called his employer's eighteen days of ten-hour lecture-heavy training the ____ method of instruction.
questions.explain: The “fire hose” method is an example of a training system that leans on the belief that mere exposure leads to learning.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the simulator phase of Matt Brown's training provided retrieval practice that was spaced, interleaved, and varied.
questions.explain: They describe the simulator as retrieval practice involving the same mental processes he will use at altitude, and as a series of tests that help calibrate his judgment.

questions.q: True or false: The UCLA professor who had worked there for twenty-five years found his nearest fire extinguisher down the hall, far from his office door.
questions.explain: It was right next to his office door, inches from the doorknob he turned every day, yet he had never learned where it was.

questions.q: Which of these does the book quote as examples of study advice that is plain wrong?
options: The key to learning is repetition; the more times you go over material the better you store it
If you intend to remember something, you probably will
Repeat, repeat, repeat to burn what you must remember into memory
Quiz yourself after studying to find what you do not know
Wait some days before rereading the material
questions.explain: The George Mason, Dartmouth, and St. Louis Post-Dispatch tips all rest on repetition or intention. The book's own advice favors self-quizzing and spacing.

questions.q: Which of these does the book say about Matt Brown's business-jet training?
options: The first seven days were classroom instruction on the plane's systems
He must have about eighty memory action items at his immediate command
A pilot's story of a fuel filter bypass light made a dry schematic come alive
The whole course was flight simulator work
The training lasted thirty days in total
questions.explain: The course lasted eighteen days: seven of classroom lecture, then eleven mixing classroom and simulator. A story from a pilot on about day five made the fuel schematic stick.

questions.q: Why does rereading feel as though it works even though the authors say it does not?
questions.a: With rereading, growing familiarity with the text comes to feel like mastery of the content, which is a kind of unwitting self-deception. The hours spent can seem like due diligence, but the amount of study time is no measure of mastery. Rereading is also time consuming and does not result in durable memory.

questions.q: What happened on about the fifth day of Matt Brown's training, and what lesson do the authors draw from it?
questions.a: While the pilots struggled to stay focused on a fuel-system schematic, an instructor asked if anyone had seen the fuel filter bypass light go on in flight, and one pilot told how ice nearly cost him both engines. That story made the schematic come to life and stick. The authors conclude that learning is stronger when it matters, when the abstract is made concrete and personal.

questions.q: How did the second phase of Matt Brown's training differ from the first, and why was it more effective?
questions.a: The first phase was a fire hose of lectures and PowerPoint, relying on exposure. The next eleven days mixed classroom with flight simulator training, which required active engagement: grappling with the aircraft, responding to unexpected situations, and drilling the movements. The simulator gave retrieval practice that was spaced, interleaved, and varied, and acted as a series of tests that helped Matt and his instructors calibrate where he needed to focus.

questions.q: In what order did the main phases of Matt Brown's business-jet training unfold?
items: Hours of PowerPoint lectures on the plane's systems
The day-five story of a fuel filter bypass light
Eleven days of mixed classroom and flight simulator work
questions.explain: He began with lectures, the fuel story came about the middle of day five, and the final eleven days mixed classroom and simulator.

questions.q: Match each example to what the book says it shows or claims.
pairs: People who have seen a penny countless times cannot pick the correct image
Most faculty and students failed to identify the extinguisher nearest their office
Claims that repetition is the key to storing material permanently
Claims that if you intend to remember something, you probably will
questions.explain: The first two are examples that exposure does not build memory; the other two are examples of bad advice the authors quote.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is a belief the book challenges or what the research shows.

items.t: Exposing yourself to material enough times burns it into memory
Making learning easier and faster makes it better
Practicing single-mindedly over and over is the best way to master a skill
Harder learning is stronger and lasts longer
Gains from massed practice are transitory and melt away quickly
The amount of study time is no measure of mastery

questions.explain: The authors say much of what teachers and students do is not serving them well, and that research turns the easier-is-better belief on its head.

questions.q: Chapter 1 is titled Learning Is Misunderstood. What does this title signal about the chapter's job in the book?
options: It lays out the full evidence for each strategy before describing any misunderstandings
It begins with the neuroscience of memory before turning to study advice
It shows that common beliefs and study habits are wrong, before later chapters describe better strategies
It reviews the history of education theories in the order they arose
questions.explain: The chapter makes claims, contrasts evidence with lore, and shows how people misunderstand learning, with later chapters developing the remedies in depth.

questions.q: How does Chapter 1 point forward to Chapter 2, To Learn, Retrieve?
options: It says Chapter 2 will describe spacing and interleaving of practice
It says Chapter 2 will treat illusions of knowing in detail
It says Chapter 2 will give tips for teachers and trainers
It says the power of active retrieval is the topic of Chapter 2
questions.explain: Chapter 1 previews the claims and then hands off the topic of retrieval to Chapter 2, while mixing up practice is the subject of Chapter 3.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 1 ends by saying Chapter 8 will pull the book's strategies together with specific tips and examples.
questions.explain: The authors say they circle through the topics several times and at the end, in Chapter 8, pull it all together with specific tips and examples.

questions.q: Why do the authors open Chapter 1 with the story of pilot Matt Brown, and how does it connect to the claims that follow?
questions.a: Matt's night-time engine emergency illustrates what the authors mean by learning: knowledge and skills held in memory and available to solve future problems. It sets up the claims about memory, prior knowledge, and effortful practice, and Matt returns later as an example of training that works and training that does not.

questions.q: In what order do these sections appear in Chapter 1?
items: Claims We Make in This Book
Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition
People Misunderstand Learning
Illusions of Knowing
Testing: Dipstick versus Learning Tool
The Takeaway
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the claims to the evidence standard, then to how people misunderstand learning and the illusions of knowing, then testing, and finally the takeaway.

questions.q: Match each claim made in Chapter 1 to the later chapter whose title develops it.
pairs: Learning styles are not supported by the research
We are all susceptible to illusions of knowing
Spacing and interleaving make learning last
Intellectual ability lies within your own control
questions.explain: Chapter 1 gives its claims in brief and says they are set out more fully in the chapters that follow; the later chapter titles show where each is developed.

questions.q: Who began the mid-1960s experiments, cited as early evidence against repetitive exposure, that tested people on their memory for lists of common English nouns?
options: Endel Tulving at the University of Toronto
Robert Sternberg and two colleagues
Washington University scientists in St. Louis
Safety researchers in the Psychology Building at UCLA
questions.explain: The authors trace the finding back to Endel Tulving at the University of Toronto, who tested recall of noun lists. Sternberg is quoted later about knowledge, the Washington University studies came decades after, and the UCLA fire extinguisher study is a separate example of exposure failing.

questions.q: Put the phases of Endel Tulving's noun experiment in the order they happened.
items: Participants read a list of paired items such as chair—9 six times, expecting no memory test
Participants were told they would be given a list of nouns to remember
One group got the same nouns they had already read; another group got different nouns
The two groups turned out to learn the nouns equally well
questions.explain: Tulving first had everyone read the pairs six times without warning of a test, then announced a list to learn, gave one group familiar nouns and the other new ones, and found that prior exposure made no difference.

questions.q: In Tulving's experiment, the learning curves of the group that had already read the nouns and the group that had not were statistically ____.
questions.explain: The authors report that the two groups’ learning did not differ: the learning curves were statistically indistinguishable, so six prior readings gave no head start.

questions.q: True or false: According to Tulving's finding, a student who has already skimmed a vocabulary list six times should learn it noticeably faster than a classmate seeing the words for the first time.
questions.explain: Tulving found the opposite of what intuition suggests: prior exposure did not aid later recall, and “Mere repetition did not enhance learning.” The two groups learned at the same rate.

questions.q: What do the authors say Tulving's noun experiment and the many studies that followed it established?
options: Unexpected memory tests disrupt learning that would otherwise have lasted
Nouns are remembered more easily than numbers paired with them
Repetition by itself does not lead to good long-term memory
Six readings are too few; durable memory needs many more exposures
questions.explain: The point of the series of investigations is that repeated exposure or holding an idea in mind longer does not, on its own, produce durable memory. The studies said nothing about adding more readings helping, and the surprise test was not the cause of the result.

questions.q: Describe the 2008 article in Contemporary Educational Psychology on rereading: who reported it, what it studied, and what earlier work it built on.
questions.a: Washington University scientists reported a series of studies, run at their own school and at the University of New Mexico, on rereading as a strategy for improving understanding and memory of prose. Like most research it stood on earlier work: some studies had shown that reading the same text several times produces the same inferences and connections each time, and others had suggested modest benefits from rereading. Those modest benefits had appeared only in specific situations, which the new studies set out to tease apart.

questions.q: In the earlier rereading studies the 2008 article built on, in which situation did rereading a text produce a lasting benefit?
options: Students who reread immediately and were tested right away
Students who reread immediately and were tested after a delay
Students who waited some days before rereading the material
Students who read the material once and highlighted it heavily
questions.explain: The spaced readers, who reread after a lapse of some days, outperformed those who did not reread. Immediate rereading gave only a slight edge on an immediate test, and that edge had worn off by a delayed test.

questions.q: Which of these describe what the earlier studies found about reading a text and immediately rereading it?
options: On an immediate test the rereaders did a bit better than one-time readers
On a delayed test the benefit had worn off and the groups performed alike
Each reading produced the same inferences and the same connections between topics
Rereaders formed richer and different inferences on each pass through the text
Immediate rereading made delayed test performance worse than a single reading
questions.explain: Immediate rereading gave a small, short-lived advantage that disappeared on a delayed test, and repeated readings produced the same inferences rather than new ones. The studies found no benefit from immediate rereading, but they also did not find that it harmed later recall.

questions.q: Match each detail of the Washington University rereading experiment to its value.
pairs: Number of students who took part
Where the five passages came from
High-ability and low-ability readers at two universities
Reading once versus reading twice in close succession
None, for either group, at either school, in any condition
questions.explain: The experiment put 148 students of differing ability at two universities through five passages from textbooks and Scientific American, read once or twice in succession, and found no rereading benefit at all under those conditions.

questions.q: True or false: In the Washington University experiment with 148 students, rereading in close succession helped the low-ability readers even though it did nothing for the high-ability readers.
questions.explain: The researchers found no rereading benefit for either ability group, at either school, in any of the conditions tested. The finding was not limited to strong readers.

questions.q: What conclusion do the authors draw from the rereading research about when, if ever, to reread a text?
options: Reread once after a meaningful lapse of time, but avoid several readings in close succession
Reread as many times as it takes for the text to feel fluent and familiar
Never reread; a single careful reading is the only reading that is useful
Reread immediately after the first reading, while the material is still fresh
questions.explain: The authors say a single rereading makes sense once a meaningful lapse of time has passed since the first reading. Multiple readings in close succession are time-consuming and yield negligible benefits compared with more effective strategies that take less time.

questions.q: Surveys of college students confirm that highlighting, underlining, and sustained poring over notes and texts are the ____ study strategies, by far.
questions.explain: Despite the evidence that close-succession rereading yields negligible benefits, surveys show these passive review strategies remain by far the most-used, which is what professors have long observed.

questions.q: Priya reads a chapter three times in a row the night before a quiz and feels confident. Based on the rereading research in Early Evidence, what should she expect on a test given a week later?
options: She will do markedly better than classmates who read the chapter only once
Her score will be about the same as a classmate who read the chapter once
She will do worse than a one-time reader because the extra readings caused fatigue
She will gain from the extra readings only if she is a high-ability reader
questions.explain: Multiple readings in close succession gave no advantage on delayed tests in the studies described, for readers of any ability. The research does not say the extra readings hurt; it says they waste time that better strategies could use.

questions.q: Besides bad study advice, what subtler reason do the authors give for why students favor rereading?
options: Rereading is the fastest way to get through assigned material
Rising familiarity and fluency with a text create an illusion of mastery
Professors reward students who can repeat lecture phrases verbatim
Rereading is less stressful than being tested on the material
questions.explain: The authors say rising familiarity with a text and fluency in reading it make students feel they have mastered the ideas, which pushes them toward rereading. Speed, stress and grading practices are not the explanation they give.

questions.q: Students work hard to capture the precise wording of lecture phrases, laboring under the misapprehension that the essence of the subject lies in the ____ in which it is described.
questions.explain: The authors warn that mastering the syntax of a lecture or text is not the same as mastering the ideas behind it; being able to repeat the phrases says nothing about understanding their significance.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' view, a student who can repeat the phrases of his lecture notes word for word has shown only familiarity with the wording, not that he understands the ideas or how they apply.
questions.explain: The authors state that being able to repeat the phrases in a text or your notes is no indication that you understand their significance, their application, or how they relate to what you already know.

questions.q: Describe how the first-year psychology student who got a D had studied, and why the authors say he does not know how to study effectively.
questions.a: He attended every lecture, took diligent notes, read the text and highlighted the critical passages, then went back, highlighted his notes, and reviewed the highlighted notes and text several times until it all felt thoroughly familiar. When his professor asked whether he had tested himself on the key concepts, turned main points into questions to answer later, rephrased ideas in his own words, related them to what he knew, or looked for outside examples, the answer was no every time. His diligence produced familiarity, which he mistook for mastery; he never did the retrieval and elaboration that produce real learning.

questions.q: Which of these did the professor ask the D student whether he had done, to which he answered no in every case?
options: Define a key concept such as conditioned stimulus and use it in a paragraph
Convert the main points of the text into questions and later try to answer them
Rephrase the main ideas in his own words as he read
Reread the whole textbook chapter a final time the night before the exam
Copy his highlighted passages into a separate notebook
questions.explain: The professor asked about self-testing on key concepts, turning main points into questions, rephrasing ideas, relating them to prior knowledge, and finding outside examples. Rereading and recopying highlights are the kind of passive review he had already done; she did not ask about them.

questions.q: The illusion of mastery is an example of poor ____, which the authors define as what we know about what we know.
questions.explain: The authors call the illusion of mastery an example of poor metacognition: being accurate about what you know and do not know is critical for decision making, and rereading to fluency undermines that accuracy.

questions.q: Of the categories in Donald Rumsfeld's 2002 statement, which one do the authors emphasize to make their point about students who do not quiz themselves?
options: Known knowns
Known unknowns
Unknown unknowns
Knowable unknowns
questions.explain: The authors add their own emphasis to the unknown unknowns, the things we do not know we do not know. Students who skip self-quizzing tend not to know what they do not know, so they overestimate their mastery.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, do students who hear a lecture or read a text that is a paragon of clarity tend to overestimate how well they know the material?
options: Clear texts contain less information, so there is less to learn
Teachers tend to grade more leniently on clearly presented material
Clarity makes the material easier to retrieve later, so they really do know it
The ease of following the argument gives them the feeling they already know it
questions.explain: The ease of following a clear argument feels like knowing it, so students conclude they need not study it; when tested they cannot recall or apply the critical ideas. Clarity does not make the material stick on its own.

questions.q: Sort each of these into real learning as the authors describe it, or an illusion of knowing.

items.t: Being able to recall the critical ideas when put to the test
Applying the ideas in a new context
Fluency gained from rereading lecture notes
Feeling you already know it because the lecture was easy to follow
Accurately judging where your knowledge is weak
Confidence after rereading that you can recall everything at a moment’s notice

questions.explain: Real learning shows up as recall under test, application in new contexts and accurate self-judgment. Fluency, ease of following and confidence born of rereading are the feelings the authors say masquerade as mastery.

questions.q: What two liabilities do the authors say hobble even the most diligent students?
questions.a: First, a failure to know the areas where their learning is weak, that is, where they need to do more work to bring up their knowledge. Second, a preference for study methods that create a false sense of mastery, such as rereading notes and texts to fluency. Both come from poor metacognition: they do not know what they do not know.

questions.q: Dev watches a video that explains a statistics concept so clearly that he decides he does not need to review it. What warning from Illusions of Knowing applies?
options: The ease of following a clear explanation gives a false feeling of already knowing it
Clear instruction is enough, so skipping review is a reasonable choice
Video works only for visual learners, so he should find a text instead
He should watch the video several more times to burn the concept into memory
questions.explain: The authors say that when material is a paragon of clarity, the ease of following it feels like knowledge, and students then find under test that they cannot recall or apply it. Repeated watching would only add fluency, not mastery.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say most students quiz themselves regularly, which is why their estimates of their own mastery are usually accurate.
questions.explain: The authors say most students do not quiz themselves, and that students who do not tend to overestimate how well they have mastered the material. Self-quizzing is the corrective they recommend, not the norm.

questions.q: The section on knowledge opens with Albert Einstein's declaration that ____ is more important than knowledge, a sentiment the authors say college students share.
questions.explain: Einstein declared creativity more important than knowledge, and the authors note the slogan on college t-shirts before arguing that the dichotomy between creativity and knowledge is false.

questions.q: Why do the authors call the opposition between creativity and knowledge a false dichotomy?
questions.a: Because without knowledge you have no foundation for the higher-level skills of analysis, synthesis and creative problem solving; as Sternberg and his colleagues put it, you cannot apply what you know if you do not know anything to apply. You would not want a neurosurgeon or an airline captain who valued creativity over knowledge. The right question is not which matters more but how to do better at building both knowledge and creativity.

questions.q: Match each person or image in the knowledge section to the idea the authors attach to it.
pairs: Creativity is more important than knowledge
You cannot apply what you know if you know nothing to apply
Stocking a construction site with the supplies to build a house
A gradual accretion of knowledge, conceptual understanding, judgment, and skill
questions.explain: Einstein supplies the slogan the authors push back on, Sternberg supplies the rebuttal that knowledge is necessary, and the construction-site image shows that facts are the supplies while mastery also needs the understanding to build with them.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, has the sentiment that creativity matters more than knowledge gained currency?
options: Because research has shown that memorizing facts crowds out creative thinking
Because cognitive psychologists have endorsed creativity over knowledge in their studies
Because college students already possess more knowledge than their courses require
Because it is a reaction to standardized testing, which is feared to favor memorization over higher-level skills
questions.explain: The authors tie the slogan to a backlash against standardized testing and the fear that it emphasizes memorization at the expense of high-level skills. They do not claim research or psychologists support the slogan; they argue knowledge is necessary.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors name as the sources from which mastery in a field grows?
options: Variety in the practice of new skills
Striving
Reflection and mental rehearsal
Rereading the material until it feels fluent
Rapid-fire repetition of a single skill until it is down pat
questions.explain: Mastery, the authors say, is the fruit of varied practice, striving, reflection and mental rehearsal. Rereading to fluency and single-minded massed repetition are the strategies the chapter has been arguing against.

questions.q: Using the authors' house-building image, sort each item into ready knowledge (the supplies on the site) or conceptual understanding (knowing how to build with them).
groups: Conceptual understanding of how to use it

items.t: Knowing the countless different fittings and materials
Grasping the load-bearing properties of a header or roof truss system
Knowing how energy transfer keeps the house warm but the roof deck cold
Having memorized the tolerances of a Cessna 401
Predicting whether a plane on one engine can still level out for landing
Memorizing the whole skeletal system in the first year of medical school

questions.explain: Facts and tolerances held in memory are the stocked supplies; judging how a truss bears load, how heat moves through a roof, or how a crippled plane will behave is the conceptual understanding needed to use them. The authors say mastery requires both.

questions.q: A chef has memorized hundreds of recipes but cannot adjust a dish when an ingredient runs out. Which point from the knowledge section does this illustrate?
options: Creativity matters more than knowledge, so the recipes were wasted effort
Knowledge alone is sufficient for mastery once enough of it is accumulated
Ready knowledge is necessary but not sufficient without conceptual understanding of how to use it
Massed practice of recipes produces durable skill in the kitchen
questions.explain: The authors say mastery needs both ready knowledge and the conceptual understanding of how to use it; the chef has the supplies but not the building know-how. The recipes are not wasted, since knowledge is the necessary foundation.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the first-year medical student who hopes to become a neurosurgeon must memorize the whole nervous, skeletal and muscular systems, and that her success depends on diligence together with study strategies suited to the sheer volume of material.
questions.explain: The would-be neurosurgeon must memorize entire body systems or she will not become a neurosurgeon, and the authors say success depends on diligence but also on finding strategies that let her learn so much in limited hours.

questions.q: When Matt Brown decided whether to kill his failing right engine, what did he need to know from memory, and what does the example show about knowledge?
questions.a: He was problem solving, but he needed to know from memory the procedures for flying with a dead engine and the tolerances of his plane in order to predict whether he would fall out of the air or be unable to straighten up for landing. The example shows that creative problem solving rests on ready knowledge: mastery requires both possessing the knowledge and the conceptual understanding of how to use it.

questions.q: What shift in thinking about testing do the authors propose in Testing: Dipstick versus Learning Tool?
options: Replace standardized tests with essays that reward creativity
Treat testing as retrieval practice rather than as a dipstick
Test students less often so that testing causes them less stress
Save testing for the end of a course, once learning is complete
questions.explain: The authors ask readers to stop seeing testing only as a dipstick for measuring learning and to see it as retrieval practice, which opens the possibility of using testing as a tool for learning. They are not proposing fewer or later tests.

questions.q: Which of these are charges against testing that the authors say fill online forums and news articles?
options: Emphasis on testing favors memorization at the expense of context or creative ability
Testing creates extra stress for students
Testing gives a false measure of ability
Testing takes too much class time away from lectures
Testing makes students overconfident about what they know
questions.explain: The complaints the authors list are that testing favors memorization over a larger grasp, adds stress, and gives a false measure of ability. Lost lecture time is not among them, and overconfidence is what the authors say rereading causes, not testing.

questions.q: What are the two profound benefits of retrieving learning from memory, according to the testing section?
questions.a: One, retrieval tells you what you know and do not know, and therefore where to focus further study to shore up weak areas. Two, recalling what you have learned causes the brain to reconsolidate the memory, which strengthens its connections to what you already know and makes it easier to recall in the future. In effect, the authors say, retrieval interrupts forgetting.

questions.q: One of the most striking research findings is that active retrieval strengthens memory, and that the more ____ the retrieval, the stronger the benefit.
questions.explain: The authors say that the more effortful the retrieval, the stronger the benefit, which is why they contrast a flight simulator with a PowerPoint lecture and a quiz with rereading.

questions.q: Put the stages of the eighth grade science study in Columbia, Illinois in order.
items: Researchers divided the course material into a part to be quizzed and a part to be reviewed
Over the semester one part got low-stakes quizzes with feedback three times while the other was reviewed three times
A test on all the material was given a month later
Students averaged A- on the quizzed material and C+ on the reviewed material
questions.explain: The researchers first set up the two conditions, then quizzed one set of material three times with feedback while the other was studied in review, then tested everything a month later, and the quizzed material came out roughly a grade and a half ahead.

questions.q: Match each detail of the Columbia, Illinois classroom study to its value.
pairs: An eighth grade science class at a middle school
Treatment of one part of the material
Low-stakes quizzing with feedback at three points in the semester
Never quizzed, but studied three times in review
Average on the quizzed material a month later
Average on the reviewed material a month later
questions.explain: Low-stakes quizzing with feedback at three points lifted the eighth graders to an A- average a month later, while material reviewed three times but never quizzed averaged C+.

questions.q: True or false: Even after ten years piloting the same business jet, Matt Brown's employer reinforces his mastery every six months with a battery of tests and flight simulations.
questions.explain: The authors report that Matt is tested and put through flight simulations every six months, requiring him to retrieve the information and maneuvers essential to controlling his plane, even after a decade on the same aircraft.

questions.q: Why does Matt Brown say the recurring tests and simulations are necessary?
options: Regulators require pilots to pass a written exam every six months
The jet's systems are redesigned often, so the procedures keep changing
The simulator is the only place a pilot can learn new maneuvers
Emergencies are rare, so without practice there is no way to keep the responses fresh
questions.explain: Matt points out that you hardly ever have an emergency, so unless you practice what to do there is no way to keep it fresh. The authors use this, with the classroom study, to show retrieval practice keeps knowledge accessible.

questions.q: The authors write, think flight simulator versus PowerPoint lecture, think quiz versus rereading. What contrast are they drawing and why does it matter?
questions.a: Each pair sets effortful, active retrieval against passive exposure. The simulator and the quiz force you to pull knowledge out of memory, which strengthens the memory, reconsolidates it and shows you where you are weak; the lecture and rereading merely re-expose you and build fluency without durable learning. The authors say active retrieval strengthens memory and that the more effortful the retrieval, the stronger the benefit.

questions.q: Ms. Ortiz replaces her Friday review session with a short, ungraded quiz followed by the answers. Based on the Columbia, Illinois study, what does the book predict?
options: Students will remember the reviewed material better because review covers more ground
Students will remember the quizzed material better on a test a month later than material that was only reviewed
Results will be the same, since a quiz and a review are both exposure to the material
The quiz will help only the strongest students and leave the others behind
questions.explain: In the eighth grade study, low-stakes quizzing with feedback produced an A- average a month later versus C+ for material reviewed three times. A quiz is retrieval practice, not just another exposure, so the authors would expect it to beat review.

questions.q: Summarize the main points of the chapter's Takeaway.
questions.a: We are mostly going about learning the wrong way and passing poor advice to those behind us, because much of what we think we know about learning is taken on faith and intuition and fails under empirical research. Persistent illusions of knowing keep us laboring at unproductive strategies, so one of the best habits is regular self-quizzing to recalibrate what we do and do not know. Simple strategies anyone can use include retrieval practice such as low-stakes quizzing and self-testing, spacing, interleaving related topics, trying to solve problems before being taught, and distilling the rules that differentiate problem types; the book revisits these repeatedly and gathers them into tips in Chapter 8.

questions.q: Kiley Hunkler, the West Point graduate and Rhodes Scholar, uses the phrase shooting an ____ to describe how she takes practice tests to refocus her studying.
questions.explain: Shooting an azimuth is a term from overland navigation: you climb to a height, sight an object in the direction you are heading, and adjust your compass to stay on course. Hunkler uses practice tests the same way, to check and correct her studying.

questions.q: Match each term or person from the Takeaway to the role it plays there.
pairs: West Point graduate and Rhodes Scholar who takes practice tests to refocus her studying
Sighting a landmark and adjusting your compass heading while navigating overland
Habit that recalibrates your understanding of what you do and do not know
Potent persuaders that keep us laboring at unproductive strategies
questions.explain: The Takeaway uses Hunkler and her navigation metaphor to illustrate self-quizzing as a way of recalibrating, which is the remedy for the illusions of knowing that the chapter has shown lead learners astray.

questions.q: Which of these are among the simple, practical strategies the Takeaway lists for learning better and remembering longer?
options: Low-stakes quizzing and self-testing
Spacing out practice
Interleaving the practice of different but related topics or skills
Rereading the text until it feels fluent
Highlighting the critical passages in the textbook
Concentrating on one subject at a time until it is fully mastered
questions.explain: The Takeaway lists forms of retrieval practice such as quizzing and self-testing, spacing, interleaving, trying problems before being taught, and distilling underlying rules. Rereading, highlighting and single-minded focus on one subject are the habits the chapter argues against.

questions.q: Sort each study habit into shooting an azimuth (recalibrating what you know) or laboring under an illusion of knowing.
groups: Laboring under an illusion of knowing

items.t: Closing the book and writing down everything you can remember
Taking a practice exam a week before the real one
Rereading highlighted notes until they feel familiar
Deciding you know a topic because the lecture was easy to follow
Having a friend quiz you with flashcards
Counting the hours spent poring over the text as proof of mastery

questions.explain: Self-testing in any form, like writing from memory, practice exams or flashcards, checks your heading the way Hunkler’s practice tests do. Familiarity, ease of following and hours logged are the signals the chapter says create false confidence.

questions.q: Put the steps of shooting an azimuth in overland navigation, as the authors describe it, in order.
items: Climb to a height
Sight an object on the horizon in the direction you are traveling
Adjust your compass heading to make sure you are still gaining on your objective
Beat on through the forest below toward that objective
