questions.explain: The authors describe climbing to a height, sighting an object on the horizon in your direction of travel, and adjusting your compass heading so you keep gaining on the objective as you push through the forest. Hunkler uses practice tests to refocus her studying in the same way.

questions.q: Why do the authors say they will circle through the book's main topics several times rather than covering each once?
questions.a: Because learning is an iterative process: you have to revisit what you learned earlier, continually update it and connect it with new knowledge. The book therefore returns to retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving and the other strategies repeatedly, and then pulls everything together in Chapter 8 with specific tips and examples for putting the tools to work.

questions.q: The Takeaway says that a great deal of what we think we know about how to learn is taken on ____ and based on intuition, but does not hold up under empirical research.
questions.explain: The authors say much of our thinking about learning is taken on faith and intuition, which is why the chapter contrasts theory, lore and intuition with empirical evidence.

questions.q: Which of these does the Takeaway claim about illusions of knowing?
options: They persist even in people who took part in empirical studies and saw the evidence firsthand
They lead us to labor at unproductive strategies
Regular self-quizzing helps recalibrate what we do and do not know
They disappear as soon as a student is told that they exist
They affect only low-ability students
questions.explain: The Takeaway calls illusions potent persuaders that keep us at unproductive strategies, notes that Chapter 3 shows them surviving even in study participants who saw the evidence, and offers self-quizzing as the recalibrating habit. Nothing suggests they vanish on being named or spare strong students.

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 1, Learning Is Misunderstood, in the order they appear.
items: Claims We Make in This Book
Empirical Evidence versus Theory, Lore, and Intuition
People Misunderstand Learning
Illusions of Knowing
Knowledge: Not Sufficient, but Necessary
Testing: Dipstick versus Learning Tool
questions.explain: The chapter states its claims, explains its reliance on empirical evidence, then works through the misunderstanding of learning, the early evidence and the illusions of knowing, before turning to knowledge, testing and the Takeaway.

questions.q: Put in book order the later chapters that Chapter 1 explicitly points ahead to, with what it says each will cover.
items: To Learn, Retrieve: the power of active retrieval
Mix Up Your Practice: illusions of knowing persist even in people who saw the evidence firsthand
Make It Stick: Kiley Hunkler, and specific tips for putting the tools to work
questions.explain: The testing section hands off to Chapter 2 on retrieval, the Takeaway cites Chapter 3 for illusions surviving firsthand evidence, and it closes by promising that Chapter 8 pulls everything together with tips and examples.

questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 1 to the job it does in the chapter's argument.
pairs: Tulving and the rereading studies show that repetition alone does not build memory
Explains why learners keep favoring rereading despite its ineffectiveness
Answers the objection that creativity matters more than facts
Reframes testing as retrieval practice and sets up Chapter 2
Sums up the chapter and maps the strategies the rest of the book develops
questions.explain: The chapter moves from evidence against repetition, to the metacognitive reason the evidence is ignored, to defending knowledge as a foundation, to testing as the remedy, and finally to a summary that previews the book.

questions.q: Sort each topic into those Chapter 1 develops in its own sub-sections and those it only previews for later chapters.

items.t: Tulving’s noun-list experiment
The rereading studies at Washington University
The eighth grade science quizzing study in Columbia, Illinois
Spacing out practice and interleaving topics in depth
Trying to solve a problem before being taught the solution
Specific tips and examples for putting the tools to work

questions.explain: Chapter 1 works through the Tulving, rereading and Columbia classroom studies itself. Spacing, interleaving, solving before instruction and the practical tips are named in the Takeaway as topics the following chapters describe in depth.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 1 end with the sections on testing and the Takeaway rather than stopping after the evidence against rereading?
questions.a: The chapter moves from diagnosis to remedy. Having shown that repetition and rereading fail and that illusions of knowing hide the failure, it needs to offer the alternative, so the testing section reframes tests as retrieval practice and hands off to Chapter 2, To Learn, Retrieve. The Takeaway then lists the strategies the book will develop, explains that learning is iterative so the topics will be revisited, and points to Chapter 8 where everything is pulled together.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 2, To Learn, Retrieve, follow directly on Chapter 1, Learning Is Misunderstood?
options: Chapter 1 ended by contrasting testing as a dipstick with testing as a learning tool, and Chapter 2 lays out the evidence for the learning-tool view
Chapter 1 described spaced and interleaved practice, and Chapter 2 turns to the single remaining strategy of retrieval
Chapter 1 showed that learning styles are a myth, so Chapter 2 proposes retrieval as the universal replacement
Chapter 1 introduced the growth mindset, and Chapter 2 shows how retrieval builds it
questions.explain: Chapter 1 closes with a section called Testing: Dipstick versus Learning Tool and argues that knowledge is necessary but not sufficient; Chapter 2 takes up that thread and gives the full case for retrieval as a learning tool. Spacing and interleaving belong to Chapter 3, learning styles to Chapter 6 and growth mindset to Chapter 7.

questions.q: In the opening story of Chapter 2, what had actually happened to the Wisconsin deer hunter found unconscious in a cornfield?
options: He had stumbled and cracked his skull on something, as the men who found him supposed
He had been hit in the back of the head by a nearly spent 12-gauge slug fired from some distance away
He had been struck by a falling branch while climbing into a deer stand
He had suffered a stroke that made him fall and bleed from the scalp
questions.explain: Ebersold saw brain protruding from the wound and recognized a gunshot wound; he reasoned that a shotgun slug had arced over a long distance and lodged about an inch into the brain, having largely spent its force. The men who brought the hunter in had assumed he fell.

questions.q: Mike Ebersold, whose story opens Chapter 2, is by profession a ____.
questions.explain: Ebersold is a neurosurgeon trained over four years of college, four of medical school and seven of neurosurgery training, with a long career at the Mayo Clinic before returning to the Wisconsin clinic.

questions.q: Why do the authors say the hunter was lucky even before Ebersold operated on him?
options: The slug had missed the brain entirely and lodged in the scalp instead
A passing hunter had applied pressure that stopped all of the bleeding
The bullet had missed the venous sinus beneath the wound altogether
The bullet and bone chips plugged the torn vein, so he did not bleed out
questions.explain: The bullet entered above a large venous sinus that drains the brain cavity, and the bullet and bone acted as plugs; the authors say that if the wound had not corked itself he would not have lived more than two or three minutes.

questions.q: Put the stages of Ebersold's treatment of the shot hunter in the order they happened.
items: He recognizes the wound as a gunshot, not a fall
He goes through his checklist, sets up blood and briefs the operating room
He works around the edges of the wound to free things up before touching the bullet
He removes the bullet and the torn vein lets loose a torrent of blood
He stitches two small pieces of muscle to the ends of the torn vein
The bleeding stops and the hunter leaves the hospital a week later
questions.explain: The story moves from diagnosis in the emergency room, through deliberate preparation, to the moment the vein bursts and the reflexive muscle-plug repair. The patient left minus some peripheral vision but otherwise unscathed.

questions.q: Describe how Ebersold's mental mode changed once he removed the bullet and the vein began to bleed.
questions.a: Before and during the early part of the operation he was in a deliberate mode, thinking through the options, reviewing the steps and preparing for what could go wrong. When the vein let loose and he lost two or so units of blood within five minutes, he shifted into what he called reflex, mechanical action: he knew he had very little time and simply had to get a suture around the structure in the particular way previous experience had taught him. The authors use this shift to show how repeated recall makes knowledge reflexive.

questions.q: Explain the technique Ebersold used to close the torn sinus vein and why an ordinary stitch would not have worked.
questions.a: The vein is a flat structure, so a stitch tightened around it tears the tissue and the ligature leaks. Ebersold cut two small pieces of muscle from where the patient's skin had been opened, brought them to the site and stitched the ends of the torn vein to them, which closed the vein without deflecting its natural shape or tearing it. It is a solution he taught himself out of necessity and says you will not find written anywhere.

questions.q: Match each detail of the Ebersold story to its description.
pairs: A soft-tissue channel that drains the brain cavity
About the size of an adult’s small finger, torn over about an inch and a half
Cut from where the patient’s skin had been opened in surgery
Left the hospital a week later minus some peripheral vision
The risk of closing the sinus
Some people get increased brain pressure because blood does not drain properly
questions.explain: These details show what Ebersold had to know and anticipate: the anatomy beneath the wound, the vein's size and shape, the improvised repair, and the chance that a patient would not tolerate having the sinus closed off.

questions.q: True or false: Ebersold learned the muscle-plug method for closing the sinus vein from a standard surgical textbook.
questions.explain: He describes it as a technique he developed out of necessity in past surgeries and taught himself, one he says you will not find written anywhere.

questions.q: To what did Ebersold compare the protocol of reviewing steps and preparing the operating room before surgery?
options: A pilot running through a preflight checklist
A quarterback dodging a tackle
A cop getting ready to pull over a car
A race car driver in a tight situation
questions.explain: Ebersold says going through the checklist is like a cop preparing to pull over a car, because you know what the book says and have gone through all the steps. The quarterback and the race car driver are his images for acting out of reflex, the opposite mode.

questions.q: Ebersold said that once the vein was bleeding heavily he left the mode of thinking through the options, and the work became ____, mechanical.
questions.explain: With two units of blood lost in five minutes, he says you transfer out of the thinking-through mode and it becomes reflex, mechanical, relying on what previous experience has taught.

questions.q: Which of these were part of Ebersold's preparation before he opened the hunter's wound?
options: Setting up blood in case a transfusion was needed
Telling the operating room staff ahead of time what he might encounter
Planning to free up the edges of the wound before pulling the bullet out
Asking the hunter to describe exactly how he had been shot
Deciding to leave the bullet in place to avoid any bleeding
questions.explain: Expecting the vein to be torn, he set up blood, briefed the operating room and planned to work around the edges first. The hunter had no idea how he was hurt, and the bullet had to come out because brain was coming out of the wound.

questions.q: Sort these moments from Ebersold's surgery into the two modes he describes.

items.t: Reviewing steps A, B, C and D before the operation
Setting up blood for a possible transfusion
Working around the edges to free things up before removing the bullet
Getting a suture around the vein as blood pours out
Cutting and stitching the muscle plugs in about sixty seconds
Telling the operating room ahead of time what to expect

questions.explain: Everything before the bullet came out was done with time to think through the options; once the vein let loose, with two units of blood lost in five minutes, there was no time to think and the repair had to be reflexive.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: In the section Reflection Is a Form of Practice, what kind of learning do the authors say the Ebersold story illustrates?
options: Learning that comes from reflection on personal experience
Learning that comes from rereading textbooks until they feel familiar
Learning that comes from immediate feedback from a supervisor
Learning that comes from matching instruction to one's learning style
questions.explain: The authors say there is an essential kind of learning, in neurosurgery and arguably in all of life, that comes from reflecting on personal experience, as Ebersold did when he went home and thought about how a suturing had gone.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: Which of these cognitive activities do the authors say reflection can involve?
options: Retrieving knowledge and earlier training from memory
Connecting that knowledge to new experiences
Visualizing and mentally rehearsing what you might do differently next time
Rereading the original lecture notes until they feel fluent
Getting immediate correction from an expert observer
questions.explain: The authors list retrieval, connection to new experience and mental rehearsal as the activities that make reflection a form of practice. Rereading and immediate correction are not part of their description of reflection.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: How did Ebersold describe using reflection after a surgery had gone less well than he wanted?
questions.a: He would go home that night and think about what happened and what he could do differently, for example to improve a suturing: a bigger or smaller bite with the needle, closer stitches, or modifying it one way or another. The next day, or later, he would try the change and see if it worked better. He says this both revisits what he learned from lectures and from watching others and adds something of his own that he missed during the teaching process.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: Ebersold warned that unless you keep recalling a maneuver, it will not become a ____.
questions.explain: He says that in a tight situation you have to act out of reflex before you have had time to think, and that recalling and practicing the maneuver over and over is what makes it reflexive.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: True or false: Ebersold's technique for repairing the sinus vein became dependable because he practiced it in his mind and in the operating room until it was reflexive.
questions.explain: The authors say reflection led him to try the new technique, which he practiced mentally and in surgery until it became a reflexive maneuver he could rely on when a patient was losing two hundred cubic centimeters of blood a minute.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: Which of these does Ebersold compare the surgeon who must act out of reflex to?
options: A race car driver in a tight situation
A quarterback dodging a tackle
A cop getting ready to pull over a car
A chess grandmaster planning several moves ahead
A student rereading notes the night before an exam
questions.explain: Both the race car driver and the quarterback must act before they have time to think, which is Ebersold's point about a reflexive maneuver. The cop pulling over a car is his image for the deliberate protocol beforehand, not for reflex.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: Put in order the stages by which, in the Ebersold story, a surgical maneuver becomes a dependable reflex.
items: Learning the basics from lectures and from watching others operate
Reflecting at home on a difficulty that came up in surgery
Trying the modified technique the next day in the operating room
Recalling and practicing the maneuver over and over
Acting on it reflexively in a tight situation with no time to think
questions.explain: The authors trace the path from initial instruction through reflection and trial to repeated recall, ending in the reflexive action Ebersold relied on when the vein burst.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: A pianist who, after each recital, mentally replays the passages that went wrong, imagines alternative fingerings, and tries them at the next day's practice is doing what the authors would call which of the following?
options: Massed practice, because all of the review happens in one sitting
Reflection, combining retrieval, new experience and mental rehearsal
Rereading, because the pianist goes back over familiar material
Dipstick testing, because the recital measured what the pianist knew
questions.explain: This is exactly Ebersold's routine of going home, thinking about what happened and trying a change the next day, which the authors describe as retrieving earlier training, connecting it to a new experience and mentally rehearsing what to do differently.

questions.section: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
questions.q: Why, according to Ebersold, is it not enough to know the steps A, B, C and D for a given situation, and what must one do instead?
questions.a: Knowing the steps lets you think them through when there is time, but in a tight situation there is no time to think and the correct action has to come as a reflex. So he says you memorize the list of things to worry about and drill on them, recalling the maneuver over and over and practicing it over and over. Unless you keep recalling it, he says, it will not become a reflex.

questions.q: In the section The Testing Effect, what does the image of a child stringing cranberries without tying a knot stand for?
options: Cramming, which crowds too many facts onto one string
Interleaving, in which different kinds of items are strung together
Feedback, which shows the child where the string broke
Learning without retrieval, which slips away as the cranberries slide off the thread
questions.explain: The authors say retrieval ties the knot for memory and repeated retrieval snugs it up; without the knot there is no string, no necklace and no tapestry, just as without retrieval what we learn slips away.

questions.q: Since 1885, psychologists have plotted ____ showing how fast we lose what we have just heard or read.
questions.explain: Forgetting curves illustrate that we lose something like 70 percent of new material in very short order, after which forgetting slows.

questions.q: According to the forgetting curves the authors cite, roughly how much of what we have just heard or read do we lose in very short order?
options: About 30 percent
About 50 percent
About 70 percent
About 90 percent
questions.explain: The authors say we lose something like 70 percent in very short order, after which forgetting slows and the remaining 30 percent or so falls away more gradually.

questions.q: True or false: According to the forgetting curves, after the initial rapid loss forgetting keeps up the same fast pace until almost nothing is left.
questions.explain: After the early loss of about 70 percent, forgetting begins to slow, and the last 30 percent or so falls away more slowly.

questions.q: The power of retrieval as a learning tool is known among psychologists as the ____.
questions.explain: The testing effect, also called the retrieval-practice effect, is the finding that practicing retrieval makes learning stick far better than reexposure to the original material does.

questions.q: Match each name or date to its place in the authors' account of the testing effect.
pairs: Wrote in his essay on memory that repeated recall strengthens the memory
A psychologist who, like Francis Bacon, wrote about retrieval strengthening memory
The year from which psychologists have been plotting forgetting curves
The year the New York Times reported a study on testing and retention
questions.explain: The authors stress that the idea has a long pedigree, from Aristotle through Bacon and James, before modern empirical research and the 2010 newspaper report that drew hostile comments.

questions.q: What did the study reported by the New York Times in 2010 find?
options: Students who reread a passage three times retained about 50 percent more than students who read it once
Students who were tested felt more anxious and retained about 50 percent less than untested students
Students who were tested after reading a passage retained about 50 percent more of it a week later than students who were not tested
Students who discussed a passage in groups retained about 50 percent more than students who studied alone
questions.explain: The students who took a recall test after reading retained an astonishing 50 percent more a week later than untested students. The authors note that online commenters nonetheless dismissed the finding as mere memorization.

questions.q: How did many online commenters respond to the 2010 report on testing, and how do the authors answer them?
questions.a: Commenters said the author confused learning with recalling information, that learning under the stress of a test does not help retention, and that memorization does not matter because education should be about high-order skills. The authors reply that if memorization were irrelevant to complex problem solving, you should not tell your neurosurgeon, and that pitting basic knowledge against creative thinking is a false choice: the stronger your knowledge, the more nuanced your creativity can be.

questions.q: Why do the authors say that retrieval, to be most effective, must be repeated in spaced-out sessions?
questions.a: Spacing the sessions means that recall requires some cognitive effort instead of becoming a mindless recitation. Repeated, effortful recall appears to help memory consolidate into a cohesive representation in the brain and to strengthen and multiply the neural routes by which the knowledge can later be retrieved.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors say repeated retrieval appears to do?
options: Help memory consolidate into a cohesive representation in the brain
Strengthen and multiply the neural routes by which knowledge can later be retrieved
Embed knowledge and skills so deeply that they become reflexive
Remove the need for any initial exposure to the material
Make the forgetting curve disappear after a single test
questions.explain: The authors describe consolidation, multiplied neural routes and knowledge that becomes reflexive as the fruits of repeated retrieval. Retrieval cannot replace first learning the material, and a test interrupts forgetting rather than abolishing it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that teachers and students in traditional educational settings commonly use testing as a learning tool.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: despite the research, testing as a learning tool is rarely used and remains little understood in traditional educational settings.

questions.q: The authors understand the frustration people feel toward standardized ____ tests given for the sole purpose of measuring learning.
questions.explain: Dipstick tests measure learning without helping it; the authors say the frustration they cause steers people away from appreciating retrieval as one of the most potent learning tools available.

questions.q: Explain the authors' claim that pitting the learning of basic knowledge against the development of creative thinking is a false choice.
questions.a: Both need to be cultivated. The stronger one's knowledge of a subject, the more nuanced one's creativity can be in addressing a new problem. Knowledge amounts to little without ingenuity and imagination, but creativity without a sturdy foundation of knowledge, in the authors' words, “builds a shaky house”.

questions.q: Sort these statements by who makes them in the section The Testing Effect.

items.t: Practicing retrieval makes learning stick far better than reexposure to the material
Another author confuses learning with recalling information
Education should be about high-order skills, so forget memorization
Knowledge and creative thinking both need to be cultivated
Trying to learn in a stressful test environment does not help retention
The stronger the knowledge, the more nuanced the creativity

questions.explain: The commenters treated testing as stressful rote memorization irrelevant to higher skills; the authors answer that retrieval beats rereading and that knowledge is the foundation of nuanced creativity.

questions.q: Sort these study activities into retrieval practice or reexposure, as the authors use the terms.

items.t: Closing the book and writing down what you remember
Rereading the chapter a third time
Quizzing yourself with flashcards
Listening again to a recording of the lecture
Reciting the steps of a procedure to yourself
Reviewing your highlighted passages

questions.explain: Retrieval means calling knowledge up from memory, which the authors say makes learning stick far better than reexposure; rereading, relistening and reviewing highlights all simply present the material again.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' argument in the section The Testing Effect in the order they appear.
items: The cranberry image: retrieval ties the knot for memory
Forgetting curves plotted since 1885 show how fast we lose new material
The testing effect is named and traced from Aristotle to modern research
The 2010 New York Times report draws hostile online comments
Pitting knowledge against creativity is declared a false choice
questions.explain: The section moves from a picture of the problem, through its measurement and the name of the remedy, to the public resistance to testing and the authors' rebuttal.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors list as knowing from experience that repeated retrieval makes knowledge and skills reflexive?
options: A seasoned quarterback
A jet pilot
A teenaged texter
A chess grandmaster
A concert pianist
questions.explain: The authors say studies confirm what Mike Ebersold and every seasoned quarterback, jet pilot and teenaged texter know: that the brain can act before the mind has time to think.

questions.q: What do the authors identify as a central challenge to improving the way we learn?
options: Finding a way to make initial exposure to material more vivid
Finding a way to match teaching to each learner's style
Finding a way to reduce the stress that tests cause
Finding a way to interrupt the process of forgetting
questions.explain: The lesson the authors draw from the forgetting curves is that the central challenge is interrupting forgetting, which is what retrieval does by tying the knot for memory.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Put the steps of the 1917 study of children studying Who’s Who biographies in order.
items: Children in grades 3, 5, 6 and 8 study brief biographies from Who’s Who in America
Some children spend part of the study time looking up and silently reciting the material to themselves
At the end of the period all the children write down what they can remember
The recall test is repeated three to four hours later
questions.explain: Children who recited retained more than those who simply reread, with the best results from those who spent about 60 percent of their study time reciting.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: In the 1917 study, the best retention came from children who spent about ____ percent of their study time reciting to themselves.
questions.explain: All the reciting groups beat those who merely reread, and the strongest results came from spending about 60 percent of the time in recitation.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: True or false: In the 1917 study, every group that spent time reciting the biographies retained more than the children who only kept rereading.
questions.explain: The authors report that all the recitation groups showed better retention than those who merely continued to review the material.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: What did the 1939 study of over three thousand Iowa sixth graders show?
options: Students who read articles twice retained as much as students who were tested
The longer the first test was delayed, the more was forgotten, but once a student had taken a test, forgetting nearly stopped
Testing soon after study caused the most forgetting, so tests should be delayed as long as possible
Scores on later tests dropped sharply after every test, showing that repeated testing wears memory down
questions.explain: The students studied six-hundred-word articles and were tested at various times before a final test two months later; delaying the first test increased forgetting, and after a test the scores on later tests dropped very little.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Why did interest in testing as a learning tool fade around 1940, according to the authors?
questions.a: Around 1940 researchers turned to the study of forgetting, and testing as a form of retrieval practice fell out of favor. Testing also stopped being used as a research tool, because testing interrupts forgetting: you cannot use a test to measure forgetting without contaminating the subject you are trying to measure.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: What did the 1967 study using lists of thirty-six words show, and why did it matter?
options: Repeated studying taught far more than repeated testing, which confirmed the received wisdom about rereading
Testing contaminated the measurement of forgetting, which ended testing research for decades
Longer word lists were forgotten faster, which showed that forgetting curves depend on list length
Repeated testing after initial exposure taught as much as repeated studying, which challenged the received wisdom and revived testing research
questions.explain: Subjects learned as much from repeated testing as from repeated studying, a result that turned researchers' attention back to testing as a learning tool and stimulated a boomlet in testing research. Contamination of forgetting measures was the earlier reason research had faded.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: In the 1978 study, massed studying, better known as ____, produced higher scores on an immediate test but faster forgetting than retrieval practice.
questions.explain: Two days after an initial test the crammers had forgotten 50 percent of what they first recalled, while those who had spent the same period practicing retrieval had forgotten only 13 percent.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Put these milestones in the history of testing-effect research in chronological order.
items: Children reciting Who’s Who biographies retain more than children who reread
Over three thousand Iowa sixth graders show that forgetting nearly stops after a test
Interest turns to forgetting and testing research falls out of favor
A study with lists of thirty-six words shows testing teaches as much as studying
Crammers are found to forget 50 percent in two days against 13 percent for retrieval practice
questions.explain: The sequence runs 1917, 1939, around 1940, 1967 and 1978, after which researchers took their inquiries into classrooms.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: In the study in which students heard a story naming sixty concrete objects, match each group or measure to its result.
pairs: Tested once immediately, then tested a week later
Not tested at all until a week later
Tested three times immediately, then tested a week later
Recalled 53 percent, matching the one-test group’s immediate score
Gain from a single immediate test, measured a week later
questions.explain: The single test boosted a week's retention from 28 to 39 percent, and three tests held recall at 53 percent, the same level the one-test group had reached on its initial test.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: In the story study with sixty objects, what did the authors mean when they said one group had been immunized against forgetting?
options: The untested group recalled more a week later than either tested group
The group tested once immediately showed no decline at all over the week
The three-test group a week later matched the one-test group's first score
The three-test group forgot everything except the first few objects
questions.explain: The three-test group recalled 53 percent a week later, equal to the one-test group's immediate score, so its week of forgetting had effectively been prevented. The one-test group still dropped from 53 to 39 percent, and the untested group did worst at 28 percent.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Studying the pair foot-shoe from a clue like foot-s_ _e, and so having to produce the word, demonstrates what researchers call the ____.
questions.explain: The modest effort of generating the cued answer while studying strengthened memory of the target word compared with studying the pair intact.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Explain the generation effect and the reason researchers suggested for why delayed retrieval of a word pair worked better than immediate retrieval.
questions.a: In the generation effect, people who study a word pair from a clue such as foot-s_ _e, and so must generate the missing word, remember the target better than people who study the pair intact; the modest effort of producing the answer strengthens the memory. The same study found recall was better when the practice retrieval came after twenty intervening pairs rather than right away, and one argument was that the greater effort required by the delayed recall solidified the memory better.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Which of these conclusions do the authors draw from the laboratory research on the testing effect?
options: Multiple sessions of retrieval practice are generally better than one, especially if they are spaced out
Spaced retrieval practice, which allows some forgetting between tests, produces stronger long-term retention than massed practice
Cramming yields higher scores on an immediate test but faster forgetting than retrieval practice
Rereading produces as much long-term retention as testing when study time is equal
A single test permanently contaminates whatever a student learns afterward
questions.explain: Spacing, repetition and the fragility of crammed knowledge are the section's main lessons. The 1967 result was that testing matched studying, not that rereading matched testing in the long run, and contamination referred only to measuring forgetting in research.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Sort these laboratory findings according to which kind of study they describe.

items.t: Higher scores on an immediate test in the 1978 study
Forgot 50 percent of the initially recalled material within two days
Forgot only 13 percent of the initially recalled material within two days
Silently reciting the Who’s Who biographies during study time
Simply continuing to reread the biographies
Stronger long-term retention when sessions are spaced out

questions.explain: Cramming and rereading look good immediately but fade fast; recitation, testing and spaced retrieval hold knowledge over the longer term.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: A student learning vocabulary with flashcards can test each new card either immediately after reading it or after twenty other cards have gone by. Which schedule does the laboratory research in this section favor, and why?
options: Immediately, because the word is still fresh and the retrieval will succeed
After twenty other cards, because the greater effort of delayed recall solidifies the memory better
Immediately, because any delay lets the forgetting curve wipe the word out
After twenty other cards, because by then the word has been reexposed several times
questions.explain: In the word-pair study, recall was better when practice retrieval was delayed by twenty intervening pairs, and researchers argued that the extra effort of delayed recall strengthened the memory. Delay works because of effort, not because of extra exposure.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Describe the design of the 1978 study and what it showed about cramming compared with retrieval practice.
questions.a: Subjects either spent a period in massed studying, that is cramming, or spent the same period practicing retrieval, and all took an initial test followed by a second test two days later. Cramming produced higher scores on the immediate test, but the crammers had forgotten 50 percent of what they first recalled by the second test, while those who had practiced retrieval had forgotten only 13 percent. The authors use it to show that cramming buys a short-term gain at the price of faster forgetting.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Match each landmark study to its key finding.
pairs: 1917 study of children and Who’s Who biographies
Reciting during study beat rereading, best at about 60 percent of the time
Once a student had taken a test, forgetting nearly stopped
1967 study with lists of thirty-six words
Repeated testing taught as much as repeated studying
Crammers forgot 50 percent in two days, retrievers only 13 percent
questions.explain: These four studies form the pedigree the authors cite: early evidence for recitation and for testing's power to halt forgetting, then the 1967 revival and the 1978 demonstration that crammed knowledge fades fast.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
questions.q: Match each laboratory study to the material its subjects learned.
pairs: Brief biographies from Who’s Who in America
A story naming sixty concrete objects
questions.explain: The materials ranged from word lists and word pairs to short texts and a story, before researchers moved on to the kinds of material students must learn in school.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 2, To Learn, Retrieve, in the order they appear.
items: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
The Testing Effect
Studying the Testing Effect in the Lab
Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
Exploring Nuances
The Takeaway
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the Ebersold story and reflection to the general principle, then to laboratory evidence, classroom evidence, finer points and a summary.

questions.q: True or false: The title To Learn, Retrieve signals the chapter's central claim that retrieving knowledge from memory is itself an act of learning, not merely a way of measuring it.
questions.explain: The chapter argues that the act of retrieval makes knowledge easier to call up later, the testing effect, in contrast to the common view of tests as dipsticks that only measure learning.

questions.q: The laboratory section of Chapter 2 ends by noting that spaced retrieval practice beats massed practice. Which later chapter takes up that thread?
options: Chapter 3, Mix Up Your Practice, with its sections on spaced and interleaved practice
Chapter 5, Avoid Illusions of Knowing, with its section on mental models
Chapter 6, Get Beyond Learning Styles, with its section on dynamic testing
Chapter 7, Increase Your Abilities, with its section on memory cues
questions.explain: Spacing is introduced at the end of the lab section as a nuance of retrieval practice and becomes the main subject of Chapter 3, which opens with The Myth of Massed Practice and Spaced Practice.

questions.q: Why do the authors open Chapter 2 with the story of neurosurgeon Mike Ebersold rather than with the research on the testing effect?
questions.a: The story shows retrieval at work in a life-or-death setting: Ebersold's repair became a reflex only because he reflected on it and recalled and practiced it over and over. From this concrete case the authors draw the general principle, give it its scientific name, the testing effect, and then present the evidence. The story also arms their rebuttal to critics who dismiss memorization: if it is irrelevant to complex problem solving, they say, don't tell your neurosurgeon.

questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 2, To Learn, Retrieve, signal about the chapter's place in the book?
options: That the chapter is mainly about how neurosurgeons are trained for emergencies
That the chapter reviews the long history of testing in American schools
That the chapter argues against the use of tests anywhere in education
That retrieval is the first concrete strategy, developing Chapter 1's testing claim
questions.explain: Chapter 1 ends with the section Testing: Dipstick versus Learning Tool; Chapter 2 makes retrieval practice the strategy itself, moving from Ebersold's reflection through the testing effect, the lab, the classroom and the nuances. Ebersold's surgery is an opening illustration, not the subject.

questions.q: Why does the section on studying the testing effect ‘in the wild’ come immediately after the section on studying it in the lab in Chapter 2?
options: The lab section ends with researchers wanting to try real school materials
The classroom studies came first, and lab studies later confirmed them
The authors wanted to present the weakest evidence before the strongest
The lab studies showed only a small effect, so a classroom test was needed
questions.explain: The lab section closes with researchers looking for opportunities to take their inquiries out of the lab and into the classroom, using the materials students must learn; the Columbia and Sobel stories deliver that. The lab evidence came first historically and was already strong.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: In 2005, why did the authors propose a study to Roger Chamberlain, the principal of Columbia Middle School in Illinois?
options: Retrieval practice had been demonstrated many times in the laboratory but rarely in a regular classroom
The school's test scores had been falling and the principal had asked for help
The authors wanted to measure how much children forget when no tests are given
The school had new clickers and smart boards that needed a research use
questions.explain: The positive effects of retrieval practice were well established in controlled laboratory settings, so the authors wanted to see how the testing effect would work in a real classroom. The clickers and smart boards were enticements the study brought with it, not the reason for it.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: What was Principal Chamberlain's main reservation about joining the testing-effect study?
options: He doubted quizzes could be fitted into the existing textbooks
He expected parents to object strongly to any extra testing
He was not interested if it was only about memorization
He feared no-stakes quizzes would make students stop studying
questions.explain: Chamberlain wanted to raise students to higher forms of learning and was not interested in mere memorization; he also worried about disrupting his energetic teachers' curricula and methods. The textbooks were not the issue, since the study kept the same ones.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Which of these were terms or features of the Columbia Middle School study as the school and the researchers agreed it?
options: The study would fit within existing curricula, lesson plans, test formats and teaching methods
The same textbooks would continue to be used
The only change in class would be occasional short quizzes
Teachers would rewrite their lesson plans around the quizzed material
Quiz scores would count toward students' grades
The study would last a single semester
questions.explain: The school's terms were that the study be minimally intrusive, so curricula, textbooks and teaching methods stayed as they were and only short quizzes were added. The quizzes were for no stakes, and the study ran for three semesters.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Participation in the Columbia study brought teachers enticements in the form of smart boards and ____, the automated response systems students used to answer quiz questions.
questions.explain: Clickers are handheld, cellphone-like remotes that let every student answer A, B, C or D. Money for such technology is famously tight, so they were a real inducement.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Patrice Bain, the Columbia teacher who was eager to try the quizzing study, taught sixth grade ____.
questions.explain: Bain's sixth grade social studies classes, covering ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, India and China, were where the study was launched in 2006.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Match each person in the Columbia Middle School story with his or her role.
pairs: Principal who agreed to host the study
Sixth grade social studies teacher in the study
Research assistant who designed and ran the quizzes
Eighth grade history teacher outside the study who adopted retrieval practice
English teacher who used reading aloud and discussion as retrieval
questions.explain: Chamberlain agreed to the study despite his concerns, Bain volunteered her classes, and Agarwal ran the clicker quizzes. Wehrenberg and Spivey show retrieval practice spreading through the school in forms that owe nothing to the research design.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Put the events of one unit in Patrice Bain's quizzed social studies classes in the order they happened.
items: Quiz at the start of class on assigned reading not yet discussed
The teacher covers the material in the day's lesson
Quiz at the end of class on the lesson
Review quiz twenty-four hours before the unit exam
The unit exam, a normal pencil-and-paper test
questions.explain: A quiz on the assigned reading opened class before discussion, a second quiz followed the lesson, and a review quiz came twenty-four hours before the unit exam. This schedule gave each quizzed fact three retrievals before the exam.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Why did the teacher leave the classroom during each quiz in the Columbia study?
options: So that students would feel less anxious about being watched
So that she would remain unaware of which material was being tested
Because the research assistant graded the quizzes on the spot
Because the quizzes were given on the school's smart boards
questions.explain: If the teacher did not know which facts were quizzed, she could not emphasize them in her teaching, so differences on the exam could be credited to the quizzes. The authors note that under normal circumstances teachers would stay and use the results to guide further discussion.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: In the Columbia study, why were some nonquizzed facts shown to students as plain review statements, such as a statement about the two tributaries of the Nile?
options: To give students extra help on the hardest material in each unit
To keep each quiz session to only a few minutes
To let the teacher see how well students were tracking the lesson
To rule out the objection that mere reexposure, rather than retrieval, explained any gains
questions.explain: Without this control, a critic could argue that simply seeing the material again in the quiz sessions caused the better exam scores. Reviewing statements with no retrieval required produced no gain, which showed that retrieval was doing the work.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Match each number from the Columbia Middle School study with what it describes.
pairs: Share of the material that the quizzes covered
Times each quizzed fact was tested before the unit exam
How long before each unit exam the review quiz was given
How long the sixth grade study ran
How much later the eighth grade science effect still held at year's end
questions.explain: Roughly one-third of the material was quizzed three times, with the review quiz a day before the exam. The sixth grade study ran three semesters, and the eighth grade science effect was still visible eight months on at the end-of-year exams.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: The Columbia quizzes were for ‘no ____’, meaning that the scores were not counted toward a grade.
questions.explain: The quizzes carried no stakes, which is part of why students found them enjoyable rather than onerous and why 64 percent said they reduced anxiety over the unit exams.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Describe how the material in the Columbia Middle School study was divided into three parts and what the exams showed for each part.
questions.a: About one-third of the material was quizzed three times, another third was presented three times as statements of fact for extra study with no retrieval, and the rest was neither quizzed nor reviewed beyond the normal lesson. On the exams, students scored a full grade level higher on the quizzed material than on the material not quizzed. The material reviewed as statements but not quizzed scored no better than the material never reviewed, showing that mere rereading does not much help.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Put these milestones of the Columbia, Illinois research in chronological order.
items: The authors propose the classroom study to Principal Chamberlain
Quizzing begins in sixth grade social studies classes
The research is extended to eighth grade science classes
Students' views on the quizzing are surveyed after the studies end
questions.explain: The proposal came in 2005, the project launched in 2006 in sixth grade social studies, the science extension followed in 2007, and students' views were surveyed after the research concluded.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: In the Columbia sixth grade study, students scored a full ____ higher on material that had been quizzed than on material that had not.
questions.explain: The gain was a full grade level on the quizzed material, while the material merely reviewed as statements of fact did no better than material that was never reviewed.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: In the 2007 extension to eighth grade science at Columbia Middle School, how did students score on quizzed versus nonquizzed material at the end of three semesters?
options: 68 percent on quizzed material versus 54 percent on nonquizzed
89 percent on quizzed material versus 64 percent on nonquizzed
92 percent (A−) on quizzed material versus 79 percent (C+) on nonquizzed
53 percent on quizzed material versus 39 percent on nonquizzed
questions.explain: The quizzed science material averaged 92 percent, an A−, against 79 percent, a C+, for the material that was not quizzed. The 68 versus 54 figures come from a laboratory experiment with college students described in Exploring Nuances.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: True or false: In the eighth grade science study at Columbia, the advantage for quizzed material had disappeared by the end-of-year exams eight months later.
questions.explain: The testing effect persisted eight months later at the end-of-year exams, confirming the long-term benefits seen in the lab. The authors add that the effect would doubtless have been greater had retrieval practice continued monthly.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Sort these topics by the Columbia class in which they were part of the quizzing research.

items.t: Ancient Egypt
Mesopotamia
India
China
Genetics
Evolution
Anatomy

questions.explain: The sixth grade social studies study worked through textbook chapters on ancient civilizations; the 2007 extension to eighth grade science covered genetics, evolution and anatomy with the same regimen.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: The authors say the eighth graders' testing effect at the end-of-year exams would doubtless have been greater under one condition. What was it, and why does that follow from the chapter's argument?
questions.a: The effect would have been larger if retrieval practice had continued in the intervening months, with a quiz once a month, say. The chapter argues that retrieval must be repeated in spaced sessions to keep interrupting forgetting, and that multiple spaced tests protect against forgetting better than a few early ones do.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Jon Wehrenberg, an eighth grade history teacher at Columbia who was not part of the research, has his students write down ten facts about slavery they did not know before reading a passage. What point do the authors make with this example?
options: That history requires more memorization than science or social studies
That retrieval practice can be knitted into a classroom in many forms, well beyond clicker quizzes
That teachers outside a study usually resist adopting its methods
That writing is a more effective form of retrieval than multiple choice
questions.explain: Wehrenberg adopted retrieval practice on his own, in forms including quizzing, flashcards, online games and this writing exercise. The authors' point is that the lesson spread beyond the study and that retrieval does not require any one format or gadget.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: A reading tutor with no technology has a struggling student read a paragraph aloud, has him try again where he stumbles, and then asks the group what the characters were thinking. In the chapter's terms, what is the tutor doing?
options: Massed practice followed by immediate feedback
Reexposure through rereading, which the book says does little
Dipstick testing to measure comprehension for a grade
Retrieval and elaboration, with no technology required
questions.explain: This is Michelle Spivey's English classroom at Columbia: reading aloud and retrying is retrieval, and explaining the passage's meaning is elaboration. The authors stress that you do not need electronic gadgetry to practice retrieval.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: When Columbia students were surveyed after the research, ____ percent said the quizzing reduced their anxiety over unit exams.
questions.explain: Sixty-four percent reported less anxiety and 89 percent felt the quizzing increased their learning; the quizzes were not onerous events.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: True or false: In the survey of Columbia students after the research, 89 percent felt that the quizzing increased their learning.
questions.explain: Eighty-nine percent felt it increased learning, and 64 percent said it reduced their anxiety over unit exams. Students were even disappointed on days when the clickers were not used.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Which of these describe how Columbia Middle School students responded to the quizzes, according to the chapter?
options: Most said the quizzing reduced their anxiety over unit exams
A large majority felt the quizzing increased their learning
They were disappointed on days when the clickers were not used
They found the quizzes onerous and asked that they be dropped
Many dropped the class rather than take the quizzes
They asked for the quiz scores to count toward their grades
questions.explain: Sixty-four percent reported less anxiety, 89 percent felt they learned more, and the kids liked how the clicker activity broke up the lecture. Dropping a course over quizzes happened in Andrew Sobel's college class with graded pop quizzes, not at Columbia.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: When Principal Chamberlain was asked what the Columbia study results indicated, what did he say?
questions.a: He replied simply, “Retrieval practice has a significant impact on kids’ learning.” The results, he said, show that it is valuable and that teachers are well advised to incorporate it into their instructional technique. Many Columbia teachers took the lesson to heart and kept quizzing long after the research ended.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Put the steps of a Columbia clicker quiz in the order they happened.
items: The teacher steps out of the classroom
Pooja Agarwal projects a slide and reads it to the students
Students click A, B, C or D on their handheld remotes
Once all have answered, the correct answer is revealed
questions.explain: Each slide held either a multiple choice question or a statement of fact. Revealing the right answer once everyone had clicked provided feedback and corrected errors, and the whole quiz took only a few minutes of class time.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Put Andrew Sobel's attempts to fix attendance and learning in his international political economics course in the order he tried them.
items: Withholding his PowerPoint slides from students
Replacing the midterm and final with nine unannounced pop quizzes
Reinstating lectures with a midterm and a final
Adding a third major test during the semester
Announcing nine scheduled quizzes with no midterm or final
questions.explain: Withholding slides did not stop students leaving; the graded pop quizzes drove a third of them to drop the course, so he went back to a midterm and final. After hearing about the benefits of testing he added a third test, and finally moved to nine announced quizzes.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Why did Andrew Sobel's first quiz experiment, nine graded pop quizzes in place of a midterm and final, end in failure?
options: Students hated the unannounced graded quizzes, and many dropped the course
The quizzes took so much lecture time that he could not cover the syllabus
Attendance fell further because students no longer feared a final exam
The quizzes were far too easy, and nearly everyone earned an A-plus
questions.explain: Students who did badly on a quiz dropped the course, Sobel was hammered in his teaching reviews, and grades split into A-plusses and Cs. The pushback left him little choice but to go back to the old format.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Sobel said his pop quizzes produced a ____ between students who showed up and did the work and those who did not, leaving him handing out both A-plusses and more Cs than ever.
questions.explain: The pop quizzes split the class in two: those who attended and worked earned A-plusses he had never given before, while the rest earned more Cs than he had ever given.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: True or false: When Sobel switched to nine announced quizzes with no midterm or final, enrollment in his course plummeted as he had feared.
questions.explain: Despite his fears, enrollments actually increased by a handful, attendance improved on quiz days, and the course has since grown to 185 students and counting.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Why did Sobel's nine announced quizzes succeed where his pop quizzes had failed, according to his own account?
questions.a: The announced quizzes were all on the syllabus, so there were no surprises: if students missed one it was their own fault, not Sobel springing something on them, and they were comfortable with that. Students showed up on quiz days, the quizzes were cumulative like the course, and by midsemester the quality of answers was much better than he used to see on midterms. The pop quizzes, by contrast, had felt punitive and drove students to drop the course rather than take a bad grade.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Which of these did Andrew Sobel report after five years of teaching with nine announced quizzes?
options: The quality of class discussions went way up
By semester's end students wrote essays comparable to his upper division classes
Course enrollment grew to 185 and counting
Attendance became perfect even on days without a quiz
He eventually reinstated the final exam to check retention
The quizzes were made ungraded to reduce anxiety
questions.explain: Sobel saw better discussions, better written work and growing enrollment. Students still skipped some non-quiz days, particularly in spring, and he kept the quizzes graded and dropped the midterm and final entirely.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Match each number from Andrew Sobel's story with what it describes.
pairs: Students in his lecture course when the story begins
Share of the class absent on a given day by midsemester
Share of the class absent early in the semester
Number of quizzes in both his pop-quiz and his announced-quiz formats
Course enrollment after five years of announced quizzes
questions.explain: His lecture course of 160 to 170 mostly freshmen and sophomores lost 25 to 35 percent of students on a given day by midsemester, against about 10 percent early on. Both his failed and his successful formats used nine quizzes, and enrollment later reached 185.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: A lecturer notices that attendance collapses by midsemester once she posts her slides online, and students cram for a single final. Following Andrew Sobel's experience, what does the chapter suggest?
options: Stop posting slides and add a second high-stakes exam to raise the cost of skipping
Replace the final with surprise quizzes so students never know when to skip
Schedule frequent, announced, cumulative quizzes in place of the big exams
Keep the final but offer extra credit for attendance
questions.explain: Sobel found that withholding slides and adding a third major test helped little, and that surprise quizzes drove students away. Announced, cumulative quizzes improved attendance on quiz days, class discussion and written work.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: What did Andrew Sobel come to recognize about his own teaching after adopting nine quizzes?
questions.a: He realized that as good a teacher as he might think he is, “my teaching is only a component of their learning,” and that how he structures the course has a lot to do with it, maybe even more. He regretted not having done it years earlier, since he would have taught his students that much more, and he notes that anybody can design this structure.

questions.section: Studying the Testing Effect “In the Wild”
questions.q: Sort these results from Andrew Sobel's course by which quiz format produced them.

items.t: A third or more of the students dropped the course
He got hammered in his teaching reviews
Grades split into A-plusses and more Cs than ever
Enrollment increased by a handful
Students reliably showed up on quiz days
Answers by midsemester were better than on his old midterms

questions.explain: The unannounced graded quizzes made students bail out and bifurcated the grades, while the announced quizzes were accepted as fair, brought students to class on quiz days and raised the quality of their work.

questions.q: Why do the authors call Andrew Sobel's success with quizzes anecdotal, and what influence do they single out as probably mixed in with the testing effect?
options: He never measured his students' grades; his own enthusiasm for the course
It was one uncontrolled class; cumulative quizzing compounding over the term
The students who stayed were unusually able; their self-selection
It came from one semester only; a change of textbook that year
questions.explain: Sobel's story is not a controlled experiment and likely reflects several beneficial influences, especially the cumulative, compounding effects of quizzing carried across the whole semester. The authors then turn to experiments designed to tease the effects apart.

questions.q: Match each set of figures from the laboratory experiments described in Exploring Nuances with what it compares.
pairs: Recall two days later for college students who were tested versus those who restudied
Recall one week later for the same tested versus restudied students
Share of initially recalled material a study-only group forgot in one week
Share of initially recalled material a repeated-testing group forgot in one week
questions.explain: College students who took an immediate recall test beat those who restudied by 68 to 54 percent after two days and 56 to 42 percent after a week. In a separate experiment, a study-only group forgot 52 percent of what it first recalled, against 10 percent for a repeated-testing group.

questions.q: In the experiment where college students studied prose passages on scientific topics, what two conditions were compared after the initial study period?
options: Taking an immediate recall test versus restudying the material
Taking a multiple choice test versus taking an essay test
Receiving immediate feedback versus receiving no feedback
Studying the passage once versus studying it three times
questions.explain: Students who took the immediate recall test outperformed the restudy group two days later and again a week later. Feedback timing and test format are examined in separate experiments later in the section.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, giving feedback on wrong answers strengthens retention more than testing alone does.
questions.explain: Studies show feedback adds to the benefit of testing, and, counterintuitively, briefly delaying the feedback produces better long-term learning than giving it immediately.

questions.q: A tutor marks a student's practice test but decides to go over the wrong answers the next day rather than immediately. According to the chapter, what effect should this brief delay have?
options: The errors will become permanent because they were not corrected at once
It will make no difference, since feedback timing does not matter as long as feedback is given
It will help only for motor skills, not for written material
It should produce better long-term learning than immediate feedback would
questions.explain: The finding is counterintuitive but holds for written tests as for motor tasks like layups and golf shots: briefly delayed feedback produces better long-term learning than immediate feedback. It may work because it gives the learner practice that is spaced out in time.

questions.q: A pianist who always practiced with her teacher correcting every note instantly falls apart when performing alone. The chapter would compare that instant correction to the ____ on a bicycle, which the learner comes to depend on.
questions.explain: Immediate feedback is like training wheels: the learner quickly comes to depend on the continued presence of the correction, so its absence in a real setting disrupts performance.

questions.q: Explain the two theories the chapter offers for why immediate feedback can hurt the learning of motor skills.
questions.a: One theory holds that immediate feedback becomes part of the task itself, so that later, in a real-world setting where it is absent, its absence is a gap in the established pattern that disrupts performance. The other holds that frequent interruptions for feedback make the learning sessions too variable, preventing a stabilized pattern of performance from forming. Either way, trial and error with delayed feedback is more awkward but more effective.

questions.q: A golf coach corrects a pupil's swing after every single shot; another lets her pupil hit several balls and judge the results before offering corrections. Which approach does the chapter's account of feedback predict will serve the pupil better on the course, and why?
options: The immediate correction, because errors are fixed before being practiced
The immediate correction, because constant attention keeps her motivated
The delayed feedback, because the skill will not depend on the coach
Neither, because the chapter says feedback does not matter for motor skills
questions.explain: Trial and error with delayed feedback is a more awkward but more effective way of acquiring a motor skill. Immediate correction acts like training wheels: the learner comes to depend on it, and its absence on the course disrupts performance.

questions.q: Put the stages of the classroom feedback experiment in order for the students who did not have the passage during the test.
items: Students study a prose passage on a science topic
They take a test without the study material at hand
Afterward they are given the passage and look over their responses
On a later test they retain the material better than the open-book group
questions.explain: The other group answered with the passage in front of them, like an open-book exam, which amounted to continuous feedback. They did best on the immediate test but retained less on the later one.

questions.q: Describe the comparison between the open-book style group and the delayed-feedback group in the science-passage experiment, and what each outcome showed.
questions.a: One group was shown the passage while answering the questions, which gave them continuous feedback during the test, much like an open-book exam. The other took the test without the material and only afterward received the passage to look over their answers. The open-book group naturally did best on the immediate test, but the group that got corrective feedback after finishing retained the learning better on a later test, which the authors link to spacing practice out in time.

questions.q: The chapter suggests delayed feedback on written tests may help because it gives the student practice that is ____ out in time, a topic the next chapter develops.
questions.explain: Delayed feedback amounts to spaced practice, and spacing improves retention, as Chapter 3 goes on to discuss.

questions.q: Sort these test formats as the chapter classifies them.

items.t: Essay test
Short-answer test
Flashcard practice
Multiple choice test
True/false test

questions.explain: Tests that make the learner supply the answer appear more effective than recognition tests, though even the multiple choice clicker quizzes at Columbia yielded strong benefits. Flashcards count as supplying the answer because the learner must produce it before turning the card.

questions.q: True or false: A teacher who can only give multiple choice clicker quizzes should expect, according to the chapter, no meaningful learning benefit from them.
questions.explain: Supply-the-answer tests appear more effective, but the authors stress that even multiple choice tests like those at Columbia Middle School can yield strong benefits; any kind of retrieval practice generally helps.

questions.q: What general implication do the authors draw about cognitive effort in retrieval, and what does the analysis of many studies show about the number of tests in a class?
questions.a: Where more cognitive effort is required for retrieval, greater retention results, which is why supplying an answer tends to beat recognizing one. An analysis of the many retrieval-practice studies shows that even a single test in a class can produce a large improvement in final exam scores, and the gains keep increasing as the number of tests increases. Whatever theory of memory proves correct, the testing effect itself is real.

questions.q: The authors sum up the empirical finding this way: the testing effect is real, meaning that the act of retrieving a memory ____ the memory, making it easier to retrieve again later.
questions.explain: Retrieval is not a neutral readout; it changes the memory so that it can be called up more easily next time, whatever the eventual theory of how repeated retrieval strengthens memory.

questions.q: In the survey the chapter cites, what share of college students said they use self-testing as a study strategy?
options: 64 percent
11 percent
89 percent
28 percent
questions.explain: Only 11 percent reported using the strategy, and another survey found students largely unaware of its effectiveness. The 64 and 89 percent figures are Columbia students' views about quizzing.

questions.q: A student says she quizzes herself only to find out which chapters she should reread. According to the chapter, how typical is this, and what is she missing?
options: It is typical: most self-testers test to find gaps to restudy, and they miss that retrieval itself creates greater retention
It is unusual: most self-testers test to reduce anxiety, and she misses that retrieval saves study time
It is typical, and she is missing nothing, since finding gaps is the whole benefit of testing
It is unusual: most self-testers test to memorize facts, and she misses that testing works only for concepts
questions.explain: Most students who self-test say they do it to discover what they do not know so they can study that material more. That is a valid use, but few realize that the act of retrieval itself creates greater retention.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say research indicates about testing compared with rereading?
options: It can facilitate better transfer of knowledge to new contexts and problems
It improves the ability to retain and retrieve related material that was not tested
It can make information more accessible when needed in various contexts
It confines learning to the exact facts that were tested
It makes corrective feedback unnecessary
It works only for rote learning of lists
questions.explain: The authors raise the worry that testing is merely a shortcut to rote learning and answer that testing improves transfer and retention of related untested material, though more research is needed. Feedback still adds to testing's benefit.

questions.q: True or false: In all the studies of testing that reported students' attitudes, students who were tested frequently rated their classes more favorably at the end of the semester than those tested less often.
questions.explain: Although students generally dislike the idea of tests, especially high-stakes ones, every study that reported attitudes found frequently tested students rating their classes more favorably. They reached the end of the semester on top of the material and did not need to cram.

questions.q: Students generally dislike tests, yet frequently tested students rate their classes more favorably. How does the chapter reconcile these two facts?
questions.a: The dislike is understandable for high-stakes tests like midterms and finals, where the score carries significant consequences. Frequent low-stakes testing is different: students who are tested often reach the end of the semester on top of the material and do not need to cram, and in every study that reported attitudes they rated their classes more favorably than students tested less frequently.

questions.q: Maya has taken weekly quizzes all term; Sam has only reread the textbook. Which of these make up the double advantage the chapter says Maya has over Sam?
options: A more accurate sense of what she knows and does not know
The strengthening of learning that comes from retrieval practice
Higher scores on the quizzes themselves
Freedom from any need to restudy
Fluency with the text from repeated readings
questions.explain: After a test, students spend more time restudying what they missed and learn more from it, while rereaders show overconfidence in their mastery. Fluency with the text is what the authors warn against mistaking for mastery.

questions.q: Students whose study strategies emphasize rereading but not self-testing show ____ in their mastery of the material.
questions.explain: Rereading breeds fluency with the text, which feels like knowing; without testing, such students are overconfident about how much they have mastered.

questions.q: A professor adds short low-stakes quizzes to her online course. Which of these effects does the chapter give her reason to expect?
options: Better attendance
More studying before class because students know they will be quizzed
A chance to identify gaps in students' understanding and adapt her instruction
No further need to give feedback on wrong answers
No benefit at all, because the effects hold only in face-to-face classrooms
An end to any need for unit exams
questions.explain: The chapter lists better attendance, more studying before class, more attentiveness when tested at the end of class, better calibration of what students know, lower test anxiety and the chance for instructors to find and fill gaps. The benefits accrue whether instruction is online or in the classroom, and feedback still matters.

questions.q: A student who panics before midterms asks why her friend's class with weekly quizzes feels so much less stressful. Using the chapter, explain how frequent low-stakes testing reduces test anxiety.
questions.a: Frequent low-stakes testing diversifies the consequences over a much larger sample of tests, so no single test is a make-or-break event. Students also arrive at exams already on top of the material and with a better sense of where they need to bone up, which is why 64 percent of Columbia students said quizzing lowered their anxiety over unit exams.

questions.q: A student rereads her lecture notes until every line feels familiar and decides she has mastered the topic. According to the chapter, what is she doing, and what would correct it?
options: Practicing spaced retrieval; nothing needs correcting
Elaborating on the material; a final reread would confirm mastery
Generating answers; she should now switch to recognition tests
Mistaking fluency with the text for mastery; low-stakes testing is the antidote
questions.explain: Repeated reading breeds fluency with the text that feels like knowing, and rereaders show overconfidence. Low-stakes testing calibrates what she actually knows and strengthens it through retrieval.

questions.q: Dev takes a practice test a week before his exam. Put in order what the chapter says will follow.
items: Dev takes the practice test on the material
The test reveals which material he missed
He spends more time restudying the missed material
He learns more from that restudying than untested classmates do
