questions.explain: Taking a test shows a student what was missed, and tested students then spend more time restudying that material and learn more from it than peers who restudy without having been tested.

questions.q: Match each question raised in Exploring Nuances with the chapter's answer.
pairs: Briefly delayed feedback beats immediate feedback for long-term learning
Tests that make the learner supply the answer beat recognition tests
Only 11 percent of college students report doing so
Testing improves transfer to new contexts and problems
Frequently tested students rate their classes more favorably
questions.explain: The section runs through a series of questions about feedback, formats, student habits, transfer and attitudes, answering each from the research and finding that retrieval practice holds up on every count.

questions.q: True or false: When Exploring Nuances notes that spacing practice improves retention, it points ahead to Chapter 4, Embrace Difficulties.
questions.explain: The chapter says the point is discussed in the next chapter, which is Chapter 3, Mix Up Your Practice, with its section on Spaced Practice. Chapter 4 takes up desirable difficulties more broadly.

questions.q: Which of these claims appear in the Takeaway of Chapter 2?
options: Effortful retrieval makes for stronger learning and retention
After an initial test, delaying further retrieval practice is more potent than immediate practice
Including even one test in a class yields a large improvement in final exam scores
Cramming gives an advantage over retrieval practice that lasts
Self-testing is appealing because it takes less effort than rereading
Testing must be initiated by the instructor to work
questions.explain: The Takeaway says cramming's advantage quickly fades, that self-testing is unappealing precisely because it takes more effort than rereading, and that students can practice retrieval anywhere with flashcards, without an instructor.

questions.q: The Takeaway warns that we are easily seduced into believing that learning is better when it is ____, but the research shows the opposite.
questions.explain: When the mind has to work, learning sticks better; the greater the effort to retrieve, provided you succeed, the more the learning is strengthened.

questions.q: The Takeaway says the greater the effort to retrieve learning, the more that learning is strengthened. What condition does it attach to this claim?
options: That the material was first learned by rereading
That the retrieval attempt succeeds
That the retrieval happens within a day of first learning
That the learner receives immediate feedback
questions.explain: Effort strengthens learning provided that you succeed in retrieving it. Delayed rather than immediate practice is favored, and feedback is best briefly delayed, so neither of those is the condition.

questions.q: True or false: The Takeaway says cramming can produce better scores on an immediate exam, but the advantage quickly fades because forgetting is much greater after rereading than after retrieval practice.
questions.explain: Cramming wins the immediate test and loses the long run; the benefits of retrieval practice are long-term.

questions.q: Priya crams by rereading the night before each exam; Tom quizzes himself on the material over the weeks. Sort these outcomes by the approach the Takeaway associates them with.

items.t: Better scores on an immediate exam
Much greater forgetting afterward
Feels easier while studying
Long-term benefits to retention
Knowledge that can be applied to a wider variety of problems
Takes more effort, which strengthens learning

questions.explain: Cramming produces better immediate scores but much greater forgetting, and it feels easier. Retrieval practice takes more effort, which is exactly why it yields durable, flexible knowledge.

questions.q: A law student quizzes herself with homemade flashcards every evening instead of waiting for her professor's exams. Which point from the Takeaway does this illustrate?
options: Recognition tests are as effective as supplying the answer
Flashcards work only for young children learning multiplication tables
Testing need not be initiated by the instructor; students can practice retrieval anywhere
Self-testing is best reserved for the night before an exam
questions.explain: The Takeaway says the way second graders learn multiplication tables works just as well for learners of any age quizzing themselves on anatomy, mathematics or law. No classroom quizzes are necessary.

questions.q: A student says flashcards feel like far more work than rereading her notes. Why does the Takeaway say self-testing feels unappealing, and how does it answer her?
questions.a: Self-testing takes more effort than rereading, so it feels less attractive. But the greater the effort at retrieval, the more will be retained, and students who take practice tests also get a better grasp of their progress than those who simply reread the material.

questions.q: Match each practice named in the Takeaway with the benefit the chapter attributes to it.
pairs: Gives students a better grasp of their progress than rereading does
Lets an instructor spot gaps and misconceptions and adapt instruction
Keeps students from retaining material they misunderstood
Students come to embrace it and rate their classes more favorably
questions.explain: Practice tests calibrate the learner, classroom tests inform the instructor, corrective feedback prevents misunderstandings from sticking, and low-stakes quizzing wins students over.

questions.q: Sort these benefits from the Takeaway by who gains them most directly.

items.t: Memories that are more durable
A better grasp of one's own progress
Knowledge retrievable in more varied settings
Spotting gaps in understanding
Adapting instruction to correct misconceptions

questions.explain: Retrieval practice gives learners durable, flexible knowledge and an accurate view of their progress, while testing lets instructors see gaps and misconceptions and adjust their teaching.

questions.q: Put the steps of Principal Chamberlain's final reasoning about practice quizzing in the order he gives them.
items: Students build a base of knowledge and retention
They stop wasting time going back to figure out what a word or concept meant
They become more efficient at evaluating, synthesizing and applying concepts in different settings
They are able to go to a higher level
questions.explain: Chamberlain's answer to his own worry about rote learning is that a base of knowledge and retention makes higher-order work more efficient: “It allows them to go to a higher level.”

questions.q: Principal Chamberlain had worried that practice quizzing might be a glorified path to rote learning. How did he answer that worry after the Columbia study?
questions.a: He said he had gained a comfort level with the idea that for kids to evaluate, synthesize and apply a concept in different settings, they get there much more efficiently when they have the base of knowledge and the retention, so they are not wasting time trying to figure out what a word or concept meant. In his words, “It allows them to go to a higher level.”

questions.q: After a first quiz on Monday, a student wonders whether to re-quiz herself that evening or later in the week. The Takeaway says that after an initial test, ____ subsequent retrieval practice is more potent for reinforcing retention than practicing immediately, because it requires more effort.
questions.explain: Delayed retrieval demands more effort, and effortful retrieval, provided it succeeds, strengthens learning more; the next chapter develops this as spaced practice.

questions.q: How does Chapter 2 connect backward to Chapter 1 and forward to Chapter 3?
questions.a: Chapter 1 ends by distinguishing testing as a dipstick for measuring learning from testing as a learning tool; Chapter 2 takes up that second idea and builds the case for retrieval practice with lab studies, the Columbia and Sobel classroom stories, and the nuances of feedback and format. Within Exploring Nuances the authors say delayed feedback may help because it spaces practice out in time, as discussed in the next chapter, which leads into Chapter 3, Mix Up Your Practice, and its sections on spaced, interleaved and varied practice.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Make It Stick in the order they appear, starting with Chapter 2.
items: To Learn, Retrieve
Mix Up Your Practice
Embrace Difficulties
Avoid Illusions of Knowing
questions.explain: Chapter 2 opens the strategies with retrieval practice; Chapter 3 adds spacing, interleaving and variation; Chapter 4 explains why such difficulties help; Chapter 5 turns to the illusions that mislead our judgment of learning.

questions.q: Which of these later parts of the book, according to the table of contents and this chapter's own signposts, return to ideas from Chapter 2?
options: Chapter 3, Spaced Practice, which develops the spacing that Exploring Nuances defers to the next chapter
Chapter 8's tip for students, Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
Chapter 8's tip for teachers on the Columbia, Illinois, Public School District
Chapter 7, Is IQ Mutable?
Chapter 6, Rule versus Example Learning
questions.explain: The spacing point is explicitly deferred to the next chapter, and Chapter 8 lists both retrieval practice and the Columbia school district among its tips. IQ and rule-versus-example learning belong to later arguments about abilities and learning styles.

questions.q: Sort these section headings by the chapter they belong to.

items.t: Reflection Is a Form of Practice
The Testing Effect
Exploring Nuances
The Myth of Massed Practice
Spaced Practice
Interleaved Practice

questions.explain: Chapter 2 builds the case for retrieval practice, while Chapter 3 turns to how practice should be scheduled and mixed: against massing, for spacing and interleaving.

questions.q: In the beanbag study with eight-year-olds, which group did best by far when everyone was finally tested on tossing into a three-foot bucket?
options: Children who had practiced only on the three-foot bucket for all twelve weeks
Children who had practiced only on the two-foot bucket for all twelve weeks
Children who had practiced on two-foot and four-foot buckets but never on the three-foot bucket
Children who had practiced on all three distances in equal amounts
questions.explain: The surprise of the study is that the children who never practiced the three-foot toss beat those who had practiced it all along. Mixed distances built more flexible skill than repetition of the tested toss.

questions.q: In the beanbag study, after twelve weeks of practice every child was tested on tossing into a bucket ____ feet away.
questions.explain: Half the children had practiced at that distance only, and the other half had practiced at two and four feet. The test distance was the same for everyone.

questions.q: True or false: In the beanbag study, the children who practiced only on the three-foot bucket did best on the final three-foot test.
questions.explain: The reverse happened: the children who had practiced on two-foot and four-foot buckets did best by far, even though they never practiced the three-foot toss.

questions.q: Researchers call focused, repetitive practice of one thing at a time until we have it nailed ____ practice.
questions.explain: Faith in massed practice is widespread among teachers, athletes, corporate trainers and students, but the authors say it is misplaced.

questions.q: According to the authors, why does so much of our faith in massed practice persist?
options: When we do it we can see it making a difference, because the gains come quickly
Studies have shown that it produces the longest retention of any method
It takes less effort than other kinds of practice, so people keep it up
Teachers are trained to use it, so students never see another method
questions.explain: The authors say our faith rests largely on the visible, rapid improvement. What we do not see is the rapid forgetting that follows.

questions.q: Why can massed practice give learners a misleading picture of how well they are learning?
questions.a: Massed practice produces rapid gains that are easy to see, so it feels productive and affirming. The rapid forgetting that follows is not evident at the time. Learning is about being able to use the knowledge or skill later, so how quickly you pick something up is only part of the story.

questions.q: Which of these does the author give as examples of massed practice?
options: Summer language boot camps
Colleges that offer concentration in a single subject for fast learning
Continuing education seminars condensed into a single weekend
A course that rolls earlier material forward into each new quiz
Practicing flashcards in a shuffled order
questions.explain: The authors list boot camps, single-subject concentrations and condensed weekend seminars, plus cramming. Rolling material forward and shuffling are the opposite of massing.

questions.q: Sort each effect by the kind of practice the authors link it to.

items.t: Rapid gains that are easy to see
Rapid forgetting that goes unnoticed
Feels productive and affirming
Longer retention
Greater versatility
Feels slower and takes more effort

questions.explain: Massed practice gives visible quick gains with hidden fast forgetting. The other forms give better mastery, retention and versatility at the price of more felt effort.

questions.q: A student crams all night, does well on the next day's midterm, but remembers little by the final. Which idea from the chapter explains this?
options: Interleaving too many topics prevented the material from being learned
Varied practice transferred the learning to the wrong exam
Spaced practice left too much time for forgetting between sessions
Massed practice yields rapid gains that are quickly followed by rapid forgetting
questions.explain: Cramming is the authors' example of massed practice. It may get you through the next test, but most of the material is long forgotten by the time of the final.

questions.q: The authors say spaced, interleaved and varied practice come at a price. What is the price, and what do learners tend to conclude because of it?
questions.a: These kinds of practice require more effort, and learning feels slower, with none of the rapid improvements and affirmations that massed practice gives. You feel the effort but not the benefits it produces. Even when participants did better after spaced learning, they believed they had learned better on the material where practice was massed.

questions.q: Why does spacing out your practice feel less productive than massing it?
options: The material is presented in a confusing order, which slows recall
Some forgetting has set in, so you must work harder to recall the concepts
You are practicing fewer skills overall, so progress seems smaller
Short-term memory is not engaged, so nothing feels familiar
questions.explain: The extra effort of recalling after a little forgetting makes you feel you are not on top of it. What you do not sense is that this effort is making the learning stronger.

questions.q: Which of these describe how spaced, interleaved and varied practice feel to learners, according to the authors?
options: They require more effort
Learning seems slower
Learners may believe they did better on massed material, even after doing better on spaced material
They deliver rapid improvements and affirmations during practice
They feel easier because less is being practiced
questions.explain: The authors say the benefits are felt as extra effort and slower progress, and learners misjudge which method worked. The rapid affirmations belong to massed practice.

questions.q: Match each kind of practice to how the chapter describes it.
pairs: Focused, repetitive practice of one thing at a time
Practice broken into separate periods that are spaced out
Practicing two or more subjects or skills in a mixed order
Practicing under changing conditions, such as buckets at mixed distances
questions.explain: The chapter presents the last three as alternatives to massed practice, which most of us wrongly trust.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it is massed practice or one of the alternatives the chapter recommends.

items.t: A summer language boot camp
Cramming the night before a midterm
A weekend seminar that condenses all the training
Four lessons a week apart
Problem types worked in a mixed sequence
Tossing at buckets two and four feet away

questions.explain: Boot camps, cramming and condensed seminars are the authors' examples of massed practice. The others are the alternatives.

questions.q: Embedding new learning in long-term memory requires a process of ____, in which memory traces are strengthened, given meaning and connected to prior knowledge.
questions.explain: The authors say this process unfolds over hours and may take several days, which is why rapid-fire practice falls short.

questions.q: In the microsurgery study, sort each detail by the schedule it belongs to.
groups: All four lessons in one day

items.t: The normal in-service schedule
Scored lower on all measures a month later
16 percent damaged the rats' vessels beyond repair
A week's interval between the four lessons
Outperformed colleagues on time and hand movements
Better success at reattaching the aortas of live rats

questions.explain: The same four lessons were given to both groups of surgical residents. Only the spacing differed, and the spaced group won on every measure.

questions.q: Which of these does the author say consolidation does to memory traces?
options: Strengthens them
Gives them meaning
Connects them to prior knowledge
Converts them into short-term memory
Erases the weakest ones
questions.explain: Consolidation strengthens the brain's representations of new learning, gives them meaning and links them to what is already known. Rapid-fire practice, in contrast, leans on short-term memory.

questions.q: What role does the effort of retrieving something after a little forgetting play in spaced practice?
questions.a: The increased effort needed to retrieve the learning after a little forgetting retriggers consolidation. This further strengthens the memory, which is why spacing works better than rapid-fire practice.

questions.q: Match each term from the discussion of spaced practice to its meaning.
pairs: The brain's representations of the new learning
Strengthening traces, giving them meaning and linking them to prior knowledge
Practice that leans on short-term memory
questions.explain: The authors explain spacing through consolidation: it takes time, and massed practice does not allow that time.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order in which, by the authors' account, spacing strengthens memory.
items: Practice sessions are separated by time
A little forgetting sets in
Retrieving the learning takes more effort
Consolidation is retriggered
The memory is strengthened further
questions.explain: Time between sessions lets forgetting begin. The effort of retrieving then retriggers consolidation, which strengthens the memory.

questions.q: A guitarist wants to keep a new song for the long term. Which plan fits what the surgical residents study suggests?
options: One long session of equal total length, so that practice is not interrupted
Four short sessions spread over a week, each with some instruction and practice
Four sessions back to back in a single evening, with brief breaks
One long session followed by a long break and no further practice
questions.explain: The residents who spaced their lessons a week apart outperformed those who took them all in one day, because spacing allows consolidation.

questions.q: According to the authors, rapid-fire practice leans on ____ memory.
questions.explain: Durable learning needs time for mental rehearsal and consolidation, which rapid-fire practice does not give.

questions.q: In the geometric solids study, the students whose practice was interleaved averaged ____ percent correct on the final test a week later.
questions.explain: The clustered group averaged only 20 percent on that test.

questions.q: True or false: In the geometric solids study, the group that practiced in clusters by problem type scored higher than the interleaved group on the final test a week later.
questions.explain: The clustered group averaged only 20 percent on the final test, against 63 percent for the interleaved group.

questions.q: In the geometric solids study, mixing the problem types boosted final test performance by a remarkable ____ percent.
questions.explain: The mixing actually impeded performance during initial learning, yet gave this large later boost.

questions.q: Describe the geometric solids study and what it shows about performance during practice versus performance later.
questions.a: College students learned to find the volumes of four obscure solids, then practiced problems either clustered by type or in a mixed (interleaved) sequence. During practice the clustered group did better, 89 percent against 60 percent. On a test a week later the result reversed: the clustered group averaged 20 percent and the interleaved group 63 percent, so interleaving impeded initial learning but boosted later performance.

questions.q: In the authors' example of interleaved practice for a trainer teaching ten procedures, the trainees move through the procedures in what order?
items: Procedure 1, a few times
Procedure 4
Procedure 3
Procedure 7
questions.explain: The sequence jumps around instead of repeating procedure 1 many times until it is down cold. This switching is what makes it interleaved.

questions.q: Sort each item by the kind of practice it describes.

items.t: Four wedge problems, then four spheroid problems
Repeating procedure 1 many times before starting procedure 2
Averaged 89 percent correct during practice
Averaged 20 percent correct on the test a week later
Problem types worked in a mixed sequence
Procedure 1 a few times, then switching to procedure 4
Averaged 60 percent correct during practice
Averaged 63 percent correct on the test a week later

questions.explain: Clustering looks best during practice but loses badly a week later. Mixing looks worse during practice and wins on the later test.

questions.q: Why do students often find interleaved practice confusing?
options: The problems in the mixed sequence are harder than those in clusters
They are given too little practice on each skill to learn any of them
Interleaving works only for experts who already know the material
They are just starting to get a handle on the material when they are forced to switch
questions.explain: Students do not yet feel on top of the new material when practice switches. The authors say this is why interleaving is unpopular, despite its long-term advantage.

questions.q: Which of these are reasons the authors give for interleaving being unpopular and seldom used?
options: Teachers dislike it because it feels sluggish
Students find it confusing to switch before they feel on top of the material
The compensating long-term advantage is not apparent to teachers and students
Research shows it lowers mastery and retention
It requires costly equipment
questions.explain: The authors say interleaving feels slower and the later payoff is hidden. They add that the research shows unequivocally that mastery and retention are better with interleaving.

questions.q: A piano teacher has a student play scales, then a piece, then sight-reading, and rotates among them within each lesson without finishing any one before switching. Which idea does this illustrate?
options: Interleaved practice, where you switch before each practice is complete
Massed practice, where each skill is polished before the next
Blocked practice, where a drill is run over and over at stations
Varied practice, where one skill is practiced from different positions
questions.explain: Switching among skills before any one is complete is interleaving. It feels slower than polishing each in turn, but builds better mastery and retention.

questions.q: What would interleaved training look like for a trainer teaching a complicated process with ten procedures, and how does it compare with the typical approach?
questions.a: The typical approach drills procedure 1 many times until it is down cold, then procedure 2, and so on, which appears to produce fast learning. Interleaved training practices procedure 1 only a few times, then switches to another such as 4, then 3, then 7. It feels slower, but the research shows mastery and long-term retention are much better.

questions.q: What is the basic idea behind varied practice, such as tossing beanbags into buckets at mixed distances?
options: It lets you repeat one movement until it becomes automatic muscle memory
It reduces the effort of practice so that sessions can be longer
It improves your ability to transfer learning from one situation and apply it in another
It stops forgetting by running practice sessions closer together
questions.explain: Varied practice builds a broader understanding of how conditions relate to the movements needed. That is what supports transfer to a new situation.

questions.q: Varied practice helps you develop a more flexible movement ____, meaning different movements for different situations.
questions.explain: The authors describe this as a more flexible “movement vocabulary”, built by practicing under varied conditions.

questions.q: According to the neuroimaging studies the authors describe, where is learning from varied practice consolidated?
options: In the same area as massed practice, only more strongly
In an area used for learning simple and unchallenging motor skills
In an area that is idle during other kinds of practice
In an area associated with the more difficult process of learning higher-order motor skills
questions.explain: Different kinds of practice engage different parts of the brain. Massed practice is consolidated in an area used for cognitively simpler motor skills.

questions.q: True or false: The authors infer that learning gained through massed practice is encoded in a simpler or comparatively impoverished representation than learning gained through varied practice.
questions.explain: Varied practice is more challenging and is encoded in a more flexible representation that can be applied more broadly.

questions.q: Why does the author say that hockey coach Jamie Kompon's one-touch pass drills were like throwing beanbags into the three-foot bucket, and what did he change?
questions.a: He ran practice on one-touch passes from the same position on the rink, so the pass was always practiced under the same conditions, even if it was interleaved with other moves. Doing it always at the same place or in the same sequence is like tossing only into the three-foot bucket. Kompon came to see the difference and changed up his drills.

questions.q: In the anagram experiment, students rearranged the letters of tmoce to form the word ____.
questions.explain: The experiment adapted the beanbag test to verbal learning, showing that variable practice helps with cognitive skills too.

questions.q: True or false: In the anagram experiment, students who practiced multiple anagrams for the word did better on the one anagram the other group had practiced than the students who had practiced that anagram over and over.
questions.explain: This mirrors the beanbag result: varied practice beat repeating the very task that was tested.

questions.q: Put the stages of the beanbag study in order.
items: Children are split into a three-foot group and a two-and-four-foot group
The groups practice tossing in gym class for twelve weeks
All children are tested on the three-foot bucket
The group that never practiced three feet does best
questions.explain: The twist is in the last step: the group that never practiced the tested distance did best by far.

questions.q: Match each example from the discussion of varied practice to what it involved.
pairs: Eight-year-olds tossing into buckets at mixed distances
Rearranging letters to form words, adapting the beanbag test to verbal learning
Receiving the puck and immediately passing it to a teammate moving down the ice
Evidence that different kinds of practice engage different parts of the brain
questions.explain: Each example supports the claim that varied practice transfers better than repeating the same task.

questions.q: Which of these does the author say the benefits of varied practice will apply to?
options: Identifying tree species
Differentiating the principles of case law
Mastering a new computer program
Reciting one memorized poem word for word
questions.explain: The author lists these as cognitive learning where the benefits of varied practice will apply.

questions.q: True or false: The authors state that it is settled that the range of varied training must include the particular task that will be tested.
questions.explain: They say whether variable training must encompass the particular task, such as the three-foot toss, is subject for further study.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it is a motor-skill or a cognitive-skill example from the discussion of varied practice.

items.t: Tossing beanbags into buckets
The one-touch pass in hockey
Solving anagrams
Identifying tree species
Differentiating principles of case law

questions.explain: The beanbag study focused on motor skills, and the authors say the same principle applies to cognitive learning.

questions.q: A volleyball player wants to get better at serving from the baseline. Which plan reflects the idea of varied practice?
options: Serve from exactly the baseline spot every time, to build muscle memory
Serve from a range of spots and distances, not only from one fixed position
Serve fifty times from the same spot, then switch to another skill
Serve only when a coach is present to check each serve
questions.explain: Varied practice, like tossing at mixed distances, builds a more flexible movement vocabulary that transfers to the target situation.

questions.q: According to the authors, what significant advantage do interleaving and variation have over massed practice?
options: They help us read the context and pick the right solution
They remove the need for any further retrieval practice later
They make each individual problem type easier to learn at first
They make learning feel faster and more confident from the start
questions.explain: Mixed practice builds the sorting skill of working out what kind of problem you face. Massed practice never trains that skill.

questions.q: Why does the massing built into a math textbook leave students unprepared for a mixed final exam?
options: They have practiced too few problems of each type to remember them
The exam problems are always much harder than the homework problems
They have never practiced deciding which solution each problem needs
The textbook teaches the different solutions in the wrong order
questions.explain: Each chapter dedicates itself to one problem type, so on the exam students must ask which algorithm applies. Life too presents problems out of sequence.

questions.q: For learning to have practical value, we must be adept at discerning what kind of ____ we face, so we can select and apply an appropriate solution.
questions.explain: The authors say life presents problems and opportunities unpredictably, so this sorting skill is critical. They quote the question as “What kind of problem is this?”

questions.q: True or false: In the painting study, the researchers had predicted that interleaving would work best and the results confirmed it.
questions.explain: The researchers had predicted that massed practice, one artist at a time, would work best. They were wrong.

questions.q: In the painting study, which kind of learning proved more useful for matching works to painters later?
options: Learning the differences between the works of several painters through interleaving
Learning the commonalities among one painter's works through massed practice
Learning the painters' names before seeing any of their works
Learning each painter's biography alongside their paintings
questions.explain: The commonalities learned through massed practice were less useful than the between-painter differences learned through interleaving.

questions.q: Which of these were findings of the painting study?
options: Interleaving gave better scores on a later test matching works to painters
The interleaving group did better with new examples of work they had never viewed
Students still preferred massed practice even after taking the test
Massed practice gave better scores on matching works to painters
Students who preferred interleaving at the start learned best
questions.explain: Interleaving won on the test and on unseen works, yet the students clung to their belief in massed practice.

questions.q: What did students in the painting experiments believe about massed practice after the test, and what does the author conclude from this?
questions.a: They persisted in preferring massed practice, convinced it served them better, even after taking a test where they could have seen from their own performance that interleaving was better. The author concludes that the myths of massed practice are hard to exorcise, even when you experience the evidence yourself.

questions.q: The bird classification study addressed ____ different bird families, with a dozen species in each family.
questions.explain: Examples of the families were thrashers, swallows, wrens and finches.

questions.q: Why does the author say bird classification is a matter of learning concepts and making judgments, not simply memorizing features?
options: Birds in each family look identical, so the traits cannot be told apart
Only the typical species of each family can be identified from its traits
Families share many traits, but none occurs in every member to serve as a unique identifier
Each family is defined by one trait that experts must learn to spot
questions.explain: Rules can only rely on characteristic traits, those typical of a family, rather than defining traits that hold for every member. That means judgment is needed.

questions.q: Which of these does the author name among the traits considered when identifying a bird's family?
options: Size
Beak shape
Iris color
The distance of its annual migration
questions.explain: The author lists size, plumage, behavior, location, beak shape, iris color and so on. Migration distance is not named.

questions.q: Match each term from the bird classification discussion to its meaning.
pairs: Typical of a family but not found in every member
One that holds for every member
Recall and recognition, considered a lower level of learning
Understanding how basic elements interrelate within a larger structure
questions.explain: Classification relies on characteristic traits, so it requires conceptual knowledge rather than facts alone.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to factual knowledge or conceptual knowledge, as the author describes them.

items.t: Recall and recognition
Considered a lower level of learning
Understanding interrelationships of elements within a larger structure
Required for classification
Grasping family resemblances among species

questions.explain: The author says conceptual knowledge is needed for classification, and the bird studies show interleaved and varied practice helps build it.

questions.q: Sort each detail by the study it comes from.

items.t: Students learned to attribute paintings to artists
Researchers first predicted massed practice would work best
Tested on works never viewed during learning
Twenty families with a dozen species in each
Members of a family share many traits but not all
Interleaved and varied practice helped students learn the underlying concepts

questions.explain: Both studies showed that interleaved practice improves discrimination.

questions.q: A nursing student must learn to tell several similar-looking rashes apart. Which study plan fits the authors' findings on discrimination?
options: Study all the images of one rash before moving on to the next
Study images of all the rashes mixed together, naming each one
Study only the single most typical image of each kind of rash
Reread the definitions of all the rashes the night before the test
questions.explain: Interleaving trains the skill of working out what kind of case you face. The painting and bird studies show this beats massed practice for discrimination.

questions.q: Why is real life more like a mixed final exam than like a chapter-by-chapter textbook, and how does interleaving prepare us for that?
questions.a: Problems and opportunities come at us unpredictably, out of sequence, so we have to work out what kind of problem it is before choosing a solution. Massed practice, as in the textbook chapters, gives no practice at that sorting. Interleaved and varied practice trains discrimination between problems and the selection of the correct solution.

questions.q: What do the neuroimaging studies suggest about why varied practice produces more flexible learning than massed practice?
questions.a: Different kinds of practice engage different parts of the brain. Varied practice is more cognitively challenging and appears to be consolidated in an area for higher-order motor skills, while massed practice is consolidated in an area for simpler skills. The inference is that massed practice gives a simpler, poorer representation, and varied practice a more flexible one that applies more broadly.

questions.q: Match each study in the chapter to what it found.
pairs: Lessons a week apart beat all four lessons in one day
Mixed practice scored 63 percent on the later test against 20 percent for clusters
Interleaving gave better matching of works to painters, including unseen works
Interleaved and varied practice helped learners grasp underlying concepts
questions.explain: Across these studies, the less massed condition produced the better later performance.

questions.q: How does the opening of Chapter 3 connect to the previous chapter, To Learn, Retrieve?
questions.a: Chapter 2 argued that retrieval practice is more powerful than repeated review and rereading. The opening of Chapter 3 picks this up by pointing to sports, where testing is taken for granted as practice-practice-practice. It then asks how practice should be arranged, using the beanbag study as its first hint.

questions.q: What does the title Mix Up Your Practice signal about the chapter's argument?
options: Practice should be replaced entirely by retrieval testing alone
Different subjects should each be studied by different methods
Learners should practice mostly what they find easiest to do
Practice should be spaced, interleaved and varied, not massed
questions.explain: The chapter argues that massed practice is a myth. Spacing, interleaving and variation produce better mastery, longer retention and more versatility.

questions.q: Put the first five sections of Chapter 3 in the order in which they appear.
items: The Myth of Massed Practice
Spaced Practice
Interleaved Practice
Varied Practice
Developing Discrimination Skills
questions.explain: The chapter first removes the belief in massed practice, then presents its alternatives, and then shows how interleaving and variation build discrimination.

questions.q: Put these book chapters in the order in which they appear.
items: Learning Is Misunderstood
To Learn, Retrieve
Mix Up Your Practice
Embrace Difficulties
questions.explain: Retrieval practice comes in Chapter 2, how to arrange practice in Chapter 3, and the role of difficulty and effort in Chapter 4.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 3 says that the theories about how spaced practice strengthens memory are explored in the next chapter.
questions.explain: After explaining consolidation, the authors write that they explore some of the theories about this process in the next chapter, Embrace Difficulties.

questions.q: Why might the authors open the chapter's main discussion with the myth of massed practice before presenting spaced, interleaved and varied practice?
questions.a: Because most people believe in focused repetition, and the alternatives feel slower and harder. The authors must first show that this faith is misplaced, since the rapid gains are visible while the rapid forgetting is not. Only then can spacing, interleaving and variation be seen as better despite how they feel.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: According to Douglas Larsen, the skills needed to classify birds are most similar to the skills needed for which task?
options: A doctor diagnosing what is wrong with a patient
A surgeon reattaching tiny blood vessels
A coach planning a weekly practice schedule
A teacher writing a final exam
questions.explain: Larsen says every patient visit is a test in which the doctor must discriminate between symptoms and their interrelationships, much as a birder tells species and families apart. Variety helps because it shows more nuances to compare against.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: In Larsen's findings, why do medical students who examined patients and those who learned from written tests score equally well on written final exams?
options: Examining patients teaches facts that written exams never ask about
A written test supplies considerable structure and asks for specific information
A written test forces students to build their own mental model
Students who examined patients also had more spaced retrieval practice
questions.explain: On a written test the student is given structure and asked for particular information, whereas with a real patient the student must come up with the mental model and the steps alone. That is why the kind of practice shows up in the clinic test but not the written one.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: A nursing program wants its students to perform well in a real clinic examination. Following Larsen's conclusions about practice, which learning plan fits best?
options: Reread the clinic manual carefully shortly before the exam
Take many extra written tests about typical patient cases
Rehearse whole patient encounters with simulated patients
Attend more lectures on patient care during the final term
questions.explain: Larsen found the most effective retrieval practice is the kind that reflects what you will be doing with the knowledge later, and that reading about patients is not enough. Written tests are retrieval, but they do not mirror a clinic visit.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: What risk does Larsen see in placing too much emphasis on variety in medical training?
options: It may make students overconfident about diagnosing rare diseases
It may weaken the students' habit of reflecting on their experience
It may leave students unable to pass their written final exams
It may slight repeated practice on how a disease usually presents
questions.explain: Larsen wants students to see a wide range of patients but also to see core cases again and again until they do them well. He says the answer is a balance, not variety against repetition.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Why does Larsen think daily reflection matters in the real-world practice of medicine?
options: He thinks it is a form of spaced retrieval, as vital as quizzing
He believes it can replace hands-on clinical experience entirely
He believes it lets doctors skip repeated practice on common diseases
He believes it makes conference lectures effective on their own
questions.explain: Larsen is experimenting with having students write regular summaries of what they did, how it worked, and what to do differently. He speculates that daily reflection is spaced retrieval practice, probably as important in practice as testing is in training.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: In Larsen's description of diagnosing a patient, what is implicit memory?
options: Conscious review of a mental library of diseases
Automatic retrieval of past experience used to interpret a new case
Memorized lists of symptoms for each disease
Notes a doctor writes after each patient visit
questions.explain: The chapter separates the conscious search through a mental library from the unconscious polling of past experiences that happens at the same time. The second is implicit memory.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: What minimum change does Larsen propose for conferences where physicians only sit and listen to talks?
options: Replace all of the talks with full simulation sessions
Hand out the slides so doctors can reread them at home
A quiz at the end, followed by spaced retrieval practice
Compress the whole conference into a single long day
questions.explain: Larsen's complaint is that attendees have no repeated exposure and are not tested, so forgetting goes unchecked. At a minimum he wants a quiz and then spaced retrieval practice to interrupt the forgetting.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: True or false: Larsen found that medical students who had learned only by reading about patients did just as well as clinic-trained students on a test of seeing patients in a clinic.
questions.explain: Equal performance appeared only on written final exams. On the clinic competency test, students whose learning involved seeing patients did better, because simply reading about patients is not enough.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: True or false: Larsen says medical training should balance variety of patients with repeated practice, rather than treating them as rivals.
questions.explain: He says it is not a matter of choosing one over the other, and that the school must stay balanced. In his words: “It’s not either/or, variety versus repetition.”

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Larsen defines implicit memory as your ____ retrieval of past experience in interpreting a new one.
questions.explain: Implicit memory works automatically in the background while the doctor consciously searches a mental library.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: At the medical school, ____ patients are actors who follow scripts and exhibit symptoms the students must diagnose.
questions.explain: These actors let students practice a whole patient encounter in a setting set up like a regular clinic.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Larsen asks students to write daily or weekly summaries in order to build the habit of ____.
questions.explain: The summaries cover what they did, how it worked, and what to do differently, which structures reflection as part of training.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: The sports adage Larsen's point echoes says that if you practice like you ____, you will play like you practice.
questions.explain: The adage supports his finding that practice should reflect what you will be doing with the knowledge later.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Larsen warns that students fall into the trap of ____ when they think they have already seen enough patients with a problem.
questions.explain: The feeling of having seen it already tempts students to stop the repeated retrieval practice that long-term retention needs.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Which of these are teaching methods the medical school uses, according to the chapter?
options: Lectures and labs
High-tech mannequins in simulation centers
Standardized patients who are actors
Leitner boxes of flashcards
Beanbag tossing drills
questions.explain: The chapter lists classroom lectures and labs, mannequins in three simulation centers, and standardized patients. The Leitner box and the beanbag study appear elsewhere in the chapter.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Which of these does Larsen say about the typical lecture conferences that medical residents attend?
options: Attendees have no repeated exposure to the topic
Whether they later see a related patient is a matter of happenstance
Attendees are not tested on the material
Attendees receive weekly quiz questions by email
A spaced follow-up session is built in
questions.explain: Larsen describes conferences where residents just listen and walk out, with no repeats and no testing. The weekly emailed questions are what he wishes for, not what exists.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Put in order the three things Larsen has students put in a reflective summary, as the chapter lists them.
items: What they did
How it worked
What they might do differently next time
questions.explain: The summaries move from the experience itself, to its result, to a plan to improve, which adds elaboration to the retrieval.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Put in order the three critical aspects of medical training Larsen discusses, as he presents them.
items: Practice that mirrors the real task of seeing patients
Balancing variety with repeated retrieval of the basics
Practical experience that gives natural spacing, interleaving and variety
questions.explain: Larsen states the first, then the second with the word second, then a third critical aspect, practical experience.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Match each element of the medical school's training with what it is.
pairs: Actors who follow scripts and exhibit symptoms to be diagnosed
Patients with heartbeat and pupils run by a controller in a back room
Automatic retrieval of past experience when interpreting a new case
Written reflection on what was done, how it worked and what to change
questions.explain: Each pairs a tool or concept from Larsen's account with its role in training doctors.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Match each learning situation in Larsen's account with its result.
pairs: Learning by seeing patients in a clinic
Better performance on a clinic competency test
Learning by reading or taking written tests
Equal performance on written final exams
Risk of underemphasizing repeated practice on the basics
Conferences with no quiz or repeat
questions.explain: These pair the conditions Larsen examines with what he concludes about them.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Sort these into what Larsen values in medical training and what he criticizes.

items.t: Practicing with simulated patients
Seeing standardized patients again and again until the basics are solid
A weekly email of ten quiz questions
Daily reflection summaries
Lectures with no repeated exposure afterward
Relying on chance that a later patient matches a conference topic

questions.explain: Larsen praises hands-on practice, repetition of the basics, regular quizzing and reflection. He calls conferences ineffective because they give no repetition and no testing.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Why did Larsen find that clinic-trained and book-trained medical students scored the same on written exams but not in a clinic test?
questions.a: On a written test the student is given considerable structure and asked for specific information, so the two groups do equally well. When examining a patient you must come up with the right mental model and steps on your own, and practicing those steps on real or simulated patients improves performance. The most effective retrieval practice reflects what you will be doing with the knowledge later.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: Explain Larsen's point that variety and repetition are not rivals in medical training.
questions.a: Seeing many kinds of patients builds breadth, but too much variety underemphasizes repeated retrieval of the typical way a disease presents. Larsen has students see certain standardized patients again and again until they do it well. He warns of the trap of familiarity, since repeated retrieval is crucial to long-term retention.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: What does Larsen criticize about the typical conference for medical residents, and what would he change?
questions.a: He says residents listen and leave with no repeated exposure and no testing, so with so much forgetting it is a poor use of resources. At a minimum he would end with a quiz and follow it with spaced retrieval practice, such as ten questions emailed each week. He wants quizzing to be a standard part of the culture and curriculum.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: How is Larsen trying to build reflection into medical training, and why does he think it matters?
questions.a: He is experimenting with requiring students to write daily or weekly summaries of what they did, how it worked, and what they might do differently. He speculates that daily reflection works as spaced retrieval practice. Reflection also helps people learn from experience, since many experiences teach us nothing.

questions.section: Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
questions.q: A driving school teaches new drivers only by having them read the manual and take written tests. Using Larsen's ideas, how would you improve the program?
questions.a: Add hands-on practice, such as simulators and real driving, because the most effective retrieval practice reflects what you will do with the knowledge later. Reading and written tests give structure that the road does not. Also mix varied situations with repeated practice of the basics, and add reflection after each drive.

questions.q: How did Vince Dooley's Georgia team treat its special plays?
options: Drilled them every day to keep them sharp
Practiced them only in the Saturday morning meeting
Practiced them in the same order each week to build habit
Practiced them only on Thursdays, a week apart, in a varied sequence
questions.explain: Dooley's narrative treats the special plays as exemplars of spaced learning: only Thursdays, so there is a week between sessions, and the plays are run in a varied sequence.

questions.q: Why does Dooley say you need to change up practice rather than only repeat the fundamentals?
options: Too much repetition is boring
Fundamentals are forgotten after one week
Special plays cannot be learned any other way
Repetition makes players too tired
questions.explain: Dooley holds two beliefs: keep practicing the fundamentals forever so they stay sharp, and change it up because too much repetition is boring.

questions.q: According to Dooley, why is mental rehearsal of the playbook useful?
options: It replaces the need to keep practicing the fundamentals forever
It adds practice, including adjustments, without physical strain
It is useful only in the final quarterback meeting before games
It lets players skip the classroom study of the week's opponent
questions.explain: Dooley says not everything in practice can be physically strenuous, so players rehearse in their heads and can adjust mentally. That is added to what they get in the classroom and on the field.

questions.q: What does the chapter say the seasoned quarterback's Saturday mental run-through has in common with a neurosurgeon's preparation?
options: Both repeat the same steps until they are bored
Both avoid any physical practice beforehand
Both are rehearsing what is about to unfold in action
Both depend only on written tests
questions.explain: The chapter closes the Dooley section by saying the quarterback running through plays and adjustments is doing the same thing as the neurosurgeon rehearsing for the operating room.

questions.q: True or false: Coach Dooley believes players should stop practicing the fundamentals once they are mastered.
questions.explain: He says you have to keep practicing the fundamentals from time to time, forever, so you keep them sharp, otherwise you are cooked.

questions.q: True or false: In Dooley's weekly schedule, the team slows play down again as game time approaches and rehearses without physical contact.
questions.explain: After full-speed real-time play by midweek, Dooley says close to game time you slow it down for a rehearsal without contact, practicing adjustments to what the opponent might do.

questions.q: Dooley says players must keep practicing the ____, such as blocking and tackling, from time to time forever.
questions.explain: He lists blocking, tackling, catching and carrying the ball as the fundamental skills that must stay in top form.

questions.q: Dooley's special plays are practiced only on ____, so there is always a week between sessions.
questions.explain: This weekly gap is why the special plays stand as exemplars of spaced learning.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say are present in Coach Dooley's practice regime?
options: Spacing
Interleaving
Reflection
Cramming
Massed repetition of one drill
questions.explain: The chapter says that for Dooley's team it is all there: retrieval, spacing, interleaving, variation, reflection and elaboration. Cramming and massed repetition are what the chapter argues against.

questions.q: Which of these are part of the weekly cycle Dooley describes between one Saturday game and the next?
options: Studying the opposition's game in the classroom
Breaking strategies down to the movements of individual positions
Repeating moves until they run like clockwork
Practicing only the special plays all week
Dropping the fundamentals midweek
questions.explain: Dooley's cycle runs from classroom study through field work to repetition. He also keeps the fundamentals going and practices special plays only on Thursdays.

questions.q: Put in order the stages of the weekly cycle Coach Dooley describes for learning to play the next opponent.
items: Study the opposition's type of game in the classroom
Discuss offensive and defensive strategies
Take the discussion onto the playing field
Break the strategies down to individual positions and try them out
Knit the parts into a whole
Repeat the moves until they run like clockwork
questions.explain: Dooley moves from classroom study to discussion, to the field, to individual positions, to the whole, and finally to repetition.

questions.q: Put in order the elements of a typical practice day in Dooley's schedule.
items: Fundamentals of each player's position
Small groups working on maneuvers involving several positions
Parts brought together and run as a team
Midweek: plays run in real time at full speed
Near game time: slowed down, rehearsal without contact
questions.explain: A day starts with fundamentals, then small groups, then the team. Across the week the speed rises to full midweek and is then slowed again.

questions.q: Match each feature of Dooley's practice with the principle it illustrates.
pairs: Special plays practiced only on Thursdays
Plays run in a varied sequence
Daily and weekly schedule mixing individual and team work
questions.explain: The chapter calls the Thursday plays exemplars of spaced learning, notes the varied sequence, and says the schedule interleaves individual and team practice.

questions.q: Match each of Dooley's statements with its stated purpose.
pairs: Not all practice can be physically strenuous
Review the game plan and run through it mentally
questions.explain: Each pairs one of Dooley's practices with the reason he gives.

questions.q: Sort these into Dooley's fundamental skills and his special plays.

items.t: Blocking
Tackling
Carrying the ball
Practiced only on Thursdays
Run in a varied sequence
Often make the difference between winning and losing

questions.explain: Dooley says fundamentals must be kept sharp from time to time, while special plays are spaced a week apart and varied.

questions.q: How does Dooley's weekly schedule show spacing, interleaving and variation?
questions.a: The special plays are practiced only on Thursdays, so there is a week between sessions, and they are run in a varied sequence. The daily and weekly schedule interleaves individual and team practice, starting with the fundamentals of each position and building up to the whole team. Dooley also varies the speed, running plays at full speed midweek and slowing them down near game time.

questions.q: Dooley says a player gets on top of the playbook by rehearsing in his mind. Explain how this works and why it matters.
questions.a: The player takes the playbook home, goes over the plays in his mind, and may walk through a step or two. Because practice cannot all be physically strenuous, this simulates the play and lets him mentally adjust if the opponent reacts differently. It adds rehearsal to what he gets in the classroom and on the field.

questions.q: What two beliefs about practice does Dooley hold, and how do they fit with the chapter's principles?
questions.a: He believes you must keep practicing the fundamentals from time to time, forever, or you are cooked. He also believes you need to change it up in practice because too much repetition is boring. Together these show spaced repeated practice of the basics combined with variation.

questions.q: What do scientists call the heightened performance seen during the acquisition phase of a skill?
options: Underlying habit strength
Consolidation strength
Blocked strength
Momentary strength
questions.explain: Scientists distinguish momentary strength from underlying habit strength. Spacing, interleaving and variation build habit strength but slow visible acquisition.

questions.q: According to the Takeaway, how long should the interval between practice sessions be?
options: Long enough for a little forgetting, not so long it becomes relearning
As short as possible so that the material always stays fresh in mind
Long enough that nearly all of the material has been forgotten
Exactly one week between sessions for every kind of skill or subject
questions.explain: The simple answer is enough so that practice does not become mindless repetition. A little forgetting prompts effort, but too much turns retrieval into relearning.

questions.q: In the Leitner box system, what happens when you miss a question?
options: You move it to a rarely practiced box until next week
You move it up a box so you will practice it more often
You remove it from the set until you review it again
You leave it where it is and repeat it once
questions.explain: The better your mastery, the less frequent the practice, so errors move a card up toward more frequent practice. Mastered material never disappears completely.

questions.q: How does the Takeaway describe the difference between interleaving and finishing one topic before the next?
options: You practice each topic until mastered and then review it
You practice only the topics you answered wrongly
In interleaving you switch before practice on a topic is complete
You alternate days of study with days of rest
questions.explain: The text says you do not move from a complete practice set of one topic to another. The hockey student frustrated by switching skills is an example.

questions.q: Why does the Takeaway say practicing with at least a day between sessions is good?
options: A full day guarantees nothing is forgotten
Consolidation only happens during classroom lessons
Mental fatigue ends only after twenty-four hours
Sleep seems to play a large role in memory consolidation
questions.explain: The time between sessions lets memories consolidate, and sleep appears to be a large part of that.

questions.q: A basketball player shoots free throws from the same spot with the same drill order every day. Which change best applies the Takeaway's advice?
options: Shoot from changing spots and vary the sequence of drills
Add more repetitions from the same spot until it is automatic
Practice only the free throws on days with no other drills
Stop practicing free throws once they feel easy
questions.explain: The Takeaway warns that always practicing the same skill in the same way, from the same place, starves learning of variety. It also says to avoid the familiarity trap.

questions.q: True or false: The Takeaway says the more forgetting between practice sessions the better, even if retrieval then means relearning the material.
questions.explain: A little forgetting helps because it leads to more effort, but you do not want so much that retrieval is essentially relearning.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Takeaway, blocked practice is easily mistaken for varied practice.
questions.explain: In blocked practice a drill is run over and over, or the player moves through stations in the same sequence, which looks like variety but is not.

questions.q: Scientists call the heightened performance during the acquisition phase of a skill ____ strength.
questions.explain: It contrasts with underlying habit strength, which spacing, interleaving and variation build.

questions.q: The German scientist Sebastian ____ developed a system for spaced practice of flashcards using boxes.
questions.explain: The Leitner box is a series of four file-card boxes in which better mastery means less frequent practice.

questions.q: The Takeaway says cramming has been likened to ____ eating.
questions.explain: A lot goes in, but most of it comes right back out in short order.

questions.q: Which of these does the Takeaway say about the Leitner box?
options: It is a series of four file-card boxes
Cards you often miss are practiced most frequently
The better your mastery, the less frequent the practice
Mastered cards are eventually removed for good
A missed card moves down a box
questions.explain: Poorly known material is practiced often and well-known material less often, but retained material never disappears completely. A missed card moves up a box, not down.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of spaced retrieval practice named in the Takeaway?
options: Working through many flashcards between repetitions of one card
Andy Sobel's quizzes rolled forward over the semester
Practicing with at least a day between sessions
Cramming the night before a midterm
Practicing one skill in one block until polished
questions.explain: Flashcard decks, Sobel's quizzes and day-long gaps all space retrieval. Cramming and single-skill blocks are massed practice.

questions.q: Which of these does the Takeaway say about reflection?
options: It is a form of retrieval practice
It is enhanced with elaboration
It is a habit that may separate those who learn from experience
It replaces the need for spaced practice
It is mainly useful for motor skills
questions.explain: Reflection asks what happened and what you did, then adds what you would do differently. It is not described as a replacement for spacing.

questions.q: Put in order the Leitner box levels from the most frequently practiced to the least.
items: Box one: material you often get wrong
Box two: cards you are pretty good at
Box three: cards practiced less often than box two
questions.explain: Box one is practiced most, box two perhaps half as often, and box three less often still.

questions.q: Match each term from the Takeaway with its meaning.
pairs: Heightened performance during the acquisition phase
What spacing, interleaving and variation build
A drill run over and over, or stations in the same sequence
The feeling you know something and no longer need to practice it
The ability to assess changing conditions and adjust responses
questions.explain: These are the key terms the Takeaway uses to summarize the chapter.

questions.q: Match each person with how the chapter describes them.
pairs: Pediatric neurologist who researches medical education
Georgia football coach whose weekly practice shows the principles
German scientist behind a four-box flashcard system
Teacher who gives nine quizzes over twenty-six meetings
questions.explain: Each figure appears in the chapter as an example of the principles at work.

questions.q: Sort these into momentary strength and underlying habit strength.

items.t: Heightened performance during the acquisition phase
The visible improvement during practice-practice-practice
What spacing, interleaving and variation build
Strength built by techniques that slow visible acquisition

questions.explain: Massed practice shows quick visible gains, while the techniques that build lasting strength feel slower.

questions.q: Sort these practice examples into blocked practice and varied or interleaved practice.

items.t: Always practicing flashcards in the same order
Practicing the same skill from the same place on the ice
Running one drill over and over, station to station
Shuffling the flashcards
Switching from skating to stick handling before either is polished
Changing the spot from which a pass is practiced

questions.explain: The Takeaway says to shuffle flashcards and vary the setting, since fixed order and place starve learning of variety.

questions.q: Sort these into practice that is more often given and less often given in the Leitner system.

items.t: Material you often make mistakes in
A card you just missed
Cards you are pretty good at
Cards in the third box

questions.explain: Frequent errors earn frequent practice, and better mastery earns less.

questions.q: Sort these into spaced practice and massed practice.

items.t: Working through many cards between repeats of one card
Sobel's quizzes that roll earlier material forward
Practicing with at least a day in between
Cramming for an exam
Single-minded, dogged repetition

questions.explain: Spacing leaves time between sessions; cramming and dogged repetition do not.

questions.q: Sort these into disciplined self-quizzing and falling into the familiarity trap.

items.t: Making yourself recall all of it and checking what you missed
Treating an instructor-generated quiz as something you simply have to do
Feeling you know it so you stop practicing
Taking mental shortcuts around recall

questions.explain: The familiarity trap is the feeling of knowing, which can lead to shortcuts. Larsen says discipline is needed.

questions.q: Explain the difference between momentary strength and underlying habit strength, and why it matters for how we judge practice.
questions.a: Scientists call the heightened performance during the acquisition phase of a skill momentary strength and distinguish it from underlying habit strength. Spacing, interleaving and variation build habit strength but slow visible acquisition, so they do not give the improvement that motivates us. That is why we keep believing in massed practice.

questions.q: According to the Takeaway, how should you choose the interval between practice sessions?
questions.a: The interval should be enough that practice does not become mindless repetition, at a minimum enough that a little forgetting has set in. A little forgetting leads to more effort, but too much makes retrieval essentially relearning. At least a day between sessions is good, since sleep plays a large role in consolidation.

questions.q: Describe how the Leitner box works and the idea behind it.
questions.a: It is a series of four file-card boxes. The first holds material you often get wrong and is practiced most often, the second holds cards you know fairly well and is practiced less often, and so on. A missed card moves up a box, and the idea is that better mastery means less frequent practice, but important material never disappears completely.

questions.q: How does the Takeaway describe reflection and how it connects to learning from experience?
questions.a: Reflection is a form of retrieval practice (What happened? What did I do? How did it work out?) enhanced with elaboration (What would I do differently next time?). Spacing, interleaving and variability are natural features of life, and every patient visit or traffic stop is a test. Those who learn from experience may have cultivated the habit of reflection.

questions.q: How does the final section of Chapter 3, The Takeaway, relate to the rest of the chapter?
options: It introduces a new strategy that was not covered anywhere earlier
It gives a quick rundown of massed practice and its alternatives
It reports the full results of the beanbag study for the first time
It argues that spacing matters much less than retrieval practice does
questions.explain: The Takeaway pulls together spacing, interleaving, variation and reflection and the myth of massed practice into a summary.

questions.q: The medical students section refers back to Mike Ebersold from Chapter 2. What idea links them?
options: Simulation is a way to rehearse surgery
Quizzing at the end of lectures improves memory
Reflection is a practice that helps us learn from experience
Cramming before surgery fails
questions.explain: The chapter says one form of practice that helps us learn from experience, as Ebersold recounted in Chapter 2, is reflection, and Larsen builds it into training.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 3, the section on medical students comes before the section on bird and painting studies.
questions.explain: The bird and painting studies come under Developing Discrimination Skills, which Larsen then links to the medical section that follows.

questions.q: Put these Chapter 3 sections in the order they appear.
items: Varied Practice
Developing Discrimination Skills
Improving Complex Mastery for Medical Students
These Principles Are Broadly Applicable
The Takeaway
questions.explain: The chapter moves from varied practice to discrimination, then to the medical school, the football coach, and finally the summary.

questions.q: The chapter that follows Mix Up Your Practice is titled Embrace ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 4 follows, titled Embrace Difficulties.

questions.q: Why does the medical students section come right after the studies on birds and painters?
questions.a: Larsen says the skills needed for bird classification are similar to those a doctor needs to diagnose a patient, so the section carries the discrimination idea into a high-stakes field. It then adds practice that mirrors real tasks, balance between variety and repetition, and reflection.

questions.q: Who coined the term desirable difficulties for short-term impediments that make learning stronger and more enduring?
options: The psychologists Elizabeth and Robert Bjork
The psychologist B. F. Skinner
The psychologists Carol Dweck and Anders Ericsson
The Marine Corps jump-school instructors
questions.explain: The chapter credits the term to Elizabeth and Robert Bjork. Skinner appears later as an advocate of errorless learning, and Dweck and Ericsson as researchers on ability and expertise.

questions.q: At the army's jump school at Fort Benning, what does the author say is the principal instructional medium?
options: Lectures backed by detailed written notes
Testing, since the test is in the doing
Repeated reading of the parachuting manual
Watching demonstrations until the skill is memorized
questions.explain: Trainees may not carry a notebook; they listen, watch, rehearse and execute, so the learning is tested through performance. The author puts it as “the test is in the doing”.

questions.q: In the twelve-foot harness stage of jump school, why does the instructor, not the trainee, pull the release for the last two or three feet?
options: So the trainee can practice one direction of fall until it is perfect
So the trainee no longer needs any corrective feedback
So the trainee executes the fall randomly, from all directions, as in a real jump
So the trainee gets a rest between spaced attempts
questions.explain: The instructor's release makes the landing direction unpredictable, which simulates what is to come. That unpredictability is part of the escalating difficulty, not a way to simplify the drill.

questions.q: What does the author draw from Mia's calm response when she landed on another jumper's inflated parachute?
options: Thorough training removes all fear of the jump door
Feeling confident in your knowledge is as good as demonstrating mastery
Instinctive fear can be beaten by willpower alone
Confidence built on repeated performance, tested under realistic conditions, can be trusted
questions.explain: The author says confidence resting on repeated performance, demonstrated through testing that simulates real conditions, is something you can lean into. Feeling confident of knowledge is a different thing from demonstrating mastery, and the fear at the door can still return.

questions.q: Two students feel ready for a driving test. One has only reread the manual and feels confident. The other has repeatedly passed practice tests under conditions like the real exam. Which student's confidence does the author's reasoning support trusting more?
options: The second, because confidence based on repeated, realistic testing is reliable
The first, because familiarity with the material is the best guide
Neither, because confidence never says anything about skill
Both equally, because feeling ready is what matters
questions.explain: The author contrasts feeling confident of your knowledge with demonstrating mastery. Testing that simulates real-world conditions is a reality check on your own judgment, so only the second student's confidence has been checked.

questions.q: True or false: Trainees at jump school are encouraged to carry a notebook and write detailed notes during instruction.
questions.explain: Jump school does not allow notebooks. Trainees listen, watch, rehearse and execute, and testing through doing is the main way they learn.

questions.q: Short-term impediments that make for stronger learning have come to be called ____ difficulties.
questions.explain: The term desirable difficulties was coined by Elizabeth and Robert Bjork for effortful conditions such as spacing and interleaving that slow learning but make it more lasting.

questions.q: In military parlance, the technique of hitting the ground and rolling to spread the impact over the body is the parachute landing ____, or PLF.
questions.explain: The PLF is a technique of hitting the ground and rolling so the impact is distributed along the feet, calf, thigh, hip and back.

questions.q: Which of these are true of the jump school training described in the chapter?
options: Trainees are not allowed to carry a notebook and write notes
Difficulty is raised in stages, and each must be mastered to move on
Practice ends up spaced and interleaved, by default and by necessity
Trainees make their first real jump in week 1 so they learn by doing
Instruction relies mainly on lectures followed by a written exam
questions.explain: Notes are forbidden, levels of difficulty escalate, and waiting turns at many stations makes practice spaced and interleaved. Real jumps come only in week 3, and testing is done by doing rather than by written exam.

questions.q: Which of these are true of Mia's third jump?
options: She was first in line at the port jump door
She fell onto another jumper's inflated parachute
She swam out of the other parachute and steered away
Her main parachute failed and she pulled her reserve
She hesitated at the door and was taken off the line
