questions.explain: Mia was first at the port door and landed on top of the other door's first jumper, then swam out of that chute. Her own parachute had opened, and she did not hesitate off the line.

questions.q: Put these jump school training stages in the order a trainee meets them, from first to last.
items: Gravel pit, where the PLF is explained, demonstrated and practiced
Two-foot platform, jumping off on command
Zip line a dozen feet up, gripping an overhead T-bar
Twelve-foot platform with a harness and a mockup jump door
Thirty-four-foot tower with full jump choreography
Five real jumps from a military transport
questions.explain: Difficulty is notched up through the training: from the gravel pit to platforms, zip line, harness, tower, and finally real jumps in week 3.

questions.q: In the parachute landing fall, in what order does the impact spread along the body, starting at the feet?
items: Balls of the feet
Side of the calf
Side of the thigh
Side of the hip
Side of the back
questions.explain: The landing technique rolls the impact up the body from the balls of the feet through calf, thigh and hip to the back.

questions.q: Put these moments from Mia's third jump in the order they happened.
items: She hands her static line to the Sergeant Airborne
She gets the one-minute warning
She gets the thirty-second warning
The jumper at the other door goes, then she jumps
Around the count of four thousand she finds a green parachute wrapped around her
questions.explain: She cleared her static line, got the one-minute and thirty-second warnings, jumped after the other door's first jumper, and landed on his canopy while counting.

questions.q: In the two-foot platform drill, what is the order of actions?
items: Stand on a platform two feet off the ground
On the command Ready, rock up on the balls of the feet with arms skyward
On the command land, jump off the wall
Execute the PLF on landing
questions.explain: The drill is a command-driven rehearsal: ready position, rock up, jump on command, then execute the roll.

questions.q: Match each jump school stage to what it involves.
pairs: The PLF is explained and demonstrated, then practiced with corrective feedback
The instructor releases you the last feet, so falls come from random directions
Practice of all jump elements, a mass exit and equipment malfunctions
Five real exits from a military transport earn jump wings
questions.explain: Each stage adds difficulty and realism, leading from demonstration to simulation to real jumps.

questions.q: Match each number from the opening story to what it refers to.
pairs: The altitude of Mia's third jump
The real jumps needed to earn jump wings
The height of the practice tower
The minimum pull-ups under the Marines' 2014 rules
questions.explain: These are the figures the author gives in the jump school and Marine Corps account.

questions.q: According to the author, why is testing valuable beyond being a powerful learning strategy, and when can you lean on your confidence?
questions.a: Testing is also a reality check on the accuracy of your own judgment of what you know how to do. Feeling confident of your knowledge is different from demonstrating mastery. When confidence is based on repeated performance, shown through testing that simulates real-world conditions, you can lean into it, as Mia did when she swam out of the other jumper's parachute.

questions.q: Define desirable difficulties as the author uses the term, name some examples, and state the trade-off involved.
questions.a: Desirable difficulties are short-term impediments that elicit more effort and slow learning down, such as spacing, interleaving and mixing up practice. They are an inconvenience, but they more than compensate by making the learning stronger, more precise and more enduring. The term was coined by the psychologists Elizabeth and Robert Bjork.

questions.q: Explain why the author calls army jump school a model of learning through desirable difficulty.
questions.a: Trainees cannot take notes; they listen, watch, rehearse and execute, so testing in the doing is the main instruction. Difficulty is notched up in escalating stages, from the gravel pit to platforms, zip line and tower, each to be mastered before progressing, with random falls and simulated malfunctions. Practice is spaced and interleaved by default as trainees wait their turn at different stations.

questions.q: True or false: On her third jump, Mia's own parachute failed to open, so she had to pull her reserve chute.
questions.explain: Her chute opened and she felt the lift; she had landed on top of another jumper's parachute and swam out of it, so no reserve was needed.

questions.q: In the chapter's account of how learning occurs, what is the order of the stages?
items: Encoding
Consolidation
Retrieval
questions.explain: Perceptions are first encoded, then the traces are consolidated into stable long-term memory, and retrieval later brings the knowledge back and updates it.

questions.q: The process of converting sensory perceptions into meaningful representations in the brain is called ____.
questions.explain: Encoding is the author's name for turning perceptions, such as watching the PLF demonstration, into mental representations.

questions.q: The new representations that encoding forms within the brain are called memory ____.
questions.explain: The author calls the new representations memory traces.

questions.q: In the author's picture of memory, what is short-term memory likened to?
options: A filing cabinet that sorts knowledge by topic
Notes jotted or sketched on a scratchpad
An archive that is reorganized during sleep
A stack of cheat sheets kept for later years
questions.explain: Short-term memory is compared to scratchpad notes, much of which is ephemera that is soon forgotten. The reorganizing of material happens in consolidation instead.

questions.q: Why does the author say that experiences we want to keep for the future must be made stronger and more durable?
options: Because the brain cannot form memory traces without repetition
Because long-term memory has very little capacity
Because short-term memory holds mostly ephemera that are soon forgotten
Because encoding only happens during sleep
questions.explain: Short-term memory is cluttered with passing details that fade. Learning we want for the future, like Mia's landing moves, needs more work to last.

questions.q: Which of these are given as examples of everyday ephemera in short-term memory?
options: How to jigger the broken latch on a gym locker
Remembering to stop for an oil change after a workout
The moves that let Mia hit the ground without breaking an ankle
How to pull the reserve chute cord
questions.explain: The locker latch and the oil-change reminder are fleeting details. The landing moves and reserve chute procedure are the kind of learning that must be made durable.

questions.q: Sort each item into the group the author's discussion of short-term memory would put it in.
groups: Fine to let fade from short-term memory
Must be made durable for the future

items.t: How to jigger a broken locker latch for today
A reminder to stop for an oil change after the workout
The moves that let a jumper hit the ground without breaking an ankle
What to do with the reserve chute rip cord before a jump

questions.explain: Passing details are fine to forget. Skills with real consequences, such as landing correctly, need strengthening beyond short-term memory.

questions.q: Using Mia in the gravel pit, explain what encoding is and why encoded material still needs more work to last.
questions.a: While Mia watches the PLF explained and demonstrated, her brain converts her perceptions into chemical and electrical changes that form a mental representation, called encoding, and the new representations are memory traces. Short-term memory is like scratchpad notes that are soon forgotten. Learning we want for the future, such as the moves that keep her from breaking an ankle, must be made stronger and more durable.

questions.q: The process of strengthening mental representations for long-term memory is called ____.
questions.explain: Consolidation is the brain reorganizing and stabilizing memory traces for long-term memory.

questions.q: New learning is ____, meaning its meaning is not fully formed and it is easily altered.
questions.explain: Newly encoded learning is labile, which is why consolidation is needed to stabilize it.

questions.q: Retrieving a memory after a lapse of time can strengthen the traces and make them modifiable again, a process called ____.
questions.explain: Reconsolidation is how retrieval practice modifies and strengthens learning, letting it connect to more recent learning.

questions.q: True or false: Consolidation is quick, finishing within moments of the learning.
questions.explain: Consolidation may occur over several hours or longer, and the transition to long-term storage takes place over a period of time.

questions.q: True or false: The authors note that sleep seems to help memory consolidation.
questions.explain: They say sleep seems to help consolidation, though consolidation occurs over a period of time in any case.

questions.q: What happens to memory traces during consolidation?
options: The brain converts them back into raw sensory perceptions
They are copied into long-term storage without change
The brain deletes those that lack emotional weight
The brain reorganizes and stabilizes them
questions.explain: Consolidation reorganizes and stabilizes the traces, giving them meaning and connecting them to prior knowledge, rather than simply copying them.

questions.q: How can retrieving a memory after a lapse of time help learning?
options: It strengthens the traces and lets them link to newer learning
It freezes the traces so that they can never change again later
It replaces the old memory with an unrelated new one entirely
It helps only when the retrieval is easy and almost instant
questions.explain: The author says retrieval after some time both strengthens the traces and makes them modifiable again, which is reconsolidation. Easy rapid retrieval gives little benefit.

questions.q: Why does rapid-fire repetition of a skill, such as conjugating foreign verbs, do little to strengthen the underlying learning?
options: It forces so much forgetting that the skill fades
It leans on short-term memory and takes very little mental effort
It mixes too many different skills together
It keeps the traces labile so they never stabilize
questions.explain: Rapid-fire practice shows gratifying quick improvement but uses short-term memory with little effort, so it does little to strengthen the underlying representation.

questions.q: A student drills the same twenty Spanish verbs back to back and quickly gets every one right. Based on the chapter, what should she conclude?
options: She has consolidated the verbs into long-term memory
She should drill even faster to strengthen the traces
Her quick gain shows performance in the moment, not durable learning
Her fast progress shows spacing would be a waste of time
questions.explain: Quick gains from rapid-fire practice rest on short-term memory. Letting some forgetting happen, as spacing does, makes retrieval harder but learning deeper.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say the brain is believed to do during consolidation?
options: Replay or rehearse the learning
Fill in blank spots and give the learning meaning
Connect the learning to past experience and stored knowledge
Permanently delete older memories that compete with it
Move the traces back into short-term memory
questions.explain: Scientists believe the brain replays the learning, gives it meaning, fills gaps and links it to what is already stored. Nothing in the account says it deletes or returns traces to short-term memory.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter link to consolidating or reconsolidating learning?
options: Sleep
Retrieval after a lapse of some time
Rapid-fire repetition of a skill within moments
Keeping new learning unrelated to prior knowledge
questions.explain: Sleep seems to help consolidation, and retrieval after a lapse supports reconsolidation. Rapid-fire practice leans on short-term memory, and connection to prior knowledge is central to consolidation.

questions.q: In the author's essay analogy for consolidation, what is the order of events?
items: Write a rangy, imprecise first draft
Revise a couple of times, sharpening and cutting extra points
Put the piece aside to ferment
Return to find the main points clearer
Connect the points to examples and rearrange the argument
questions.explain: As with an essay left to ferment, learning that starts disorganized becomes clearer and more tightly organized over time.

questions.q: Put these steps of reconsolidation in order.
items: Some time passes after the learning
You make an effortful attempt to retrieve it from long-term memory
The traces are strengthened and made modifiable again
The memory connects to more recent learning
questions.explain: Retrieval after a lapse strengthens the traces while making them modifiable, so they can connect to newer learning.

questions.q: Sort each practice approach by how it feels and what it does for learning.

items.t: Practicing the PLF over and over in rapid-fire fashion
Conjugating the same foreign verbs again and again right away
Spacing the practice
Interleaving the practice
Letting the memory recede a little before retrieving it

questions.explain: Rapid-fire repetition gives quick gratifying gains but leans on short-term memory. Spacing and interleaving make retrieval harder and performance weaker at first, but learning deeper.

questions.q: Sort each description under consolidation or reconsolidation.

items.t: Sleep seems to help it
The brain replays the learning and links it to prior knowledge
It reorganizes and stabilizes memory traces
It is triggered by retrieval after a lapse of time
It makes traces modifiable again so they connect to recent learning
A ragged effort to recall the PLF on day 2 helps it

questions.explain: Consolidation is the initial strengthening and organizing of traces. Reconsolidation follows effortful retrieval, when traces are pliable again.

questions.q: Match each term from the chapter's account of how learning occurs to its meaning.
pairs: Converting sensory perceptions into meaningful representations in the brain
The new representations the brain forms
Reorganizing and stabilizing traces for long-term memory
Retrieval after a lapse that strengthens traces and makes them modifiable again
questions.explain: These are the key terms of the how-learning-occurs account.

questions.q: Match each type of practice to its effect.
pairs: Quick gains that lean on short-term memory
Harder retrieval but deeper, more retrievable learning
Strengthened traces that can be modified again
questions.explain: The author contrasts easy short-term repetition with effortful retrieval after a gap.

questions.q: Using the day-2 jump school example, explain how a ragged effort to recall a skill leads to reconsolidation.
questions.a: On day 2 you are put on the spot to do the PLF and struggle to recall the posture, throwing out an arm and forgetting to tuck the elbows. The effort to reconstruct what you learned is ragged, but retrieval after a lapse makes the traces modifiable again. In making the effort, critical elements of the maneuver come clearer and are reconsolidated for stronger memory.

questions.q: Why is performance in the moment not a reliable sign of durable learning? Contrast rapid-fire practice with spaced or interleaved practice.
questions.a: Rapid-fire practice, whether of the PLF or foreign verbs, leans on short-term memory and takes little effort, so improvement is quick but the underlying representation is not strengthened. When you let the memory recede a little through spacing or interleaving, retrieval is harder, performance is less accomplished and you feel let down. But the learning is deeper and easier to retrieve in the future.

questions.q: How does the author use the experience of composing an essay to explain consolidation?
questions.a: The first draft is rangy and imprecise, and you discover what you want to say by writing it. After revisions and time to ferment, your point is clearer, you see main points, connect them to examples and rearrange them. Learning likewise starts out disorganized, and consolidation organizes and solidifies it.

questions.q: Explain the role of prior knowledge in consolidation, using Mia as the example.
questions.a: Prior knowledge is a prerequisite for making sense of new learning, and forming connections to it is an important task of consolidation. Mia's considerable athletic skills, physical self-awareness and prior experience are a large body of knowledge to which the elements of a successful PLF would find many connections.

questions.q: Which of these does the author say durable, robust learning requires?
options: Anchoring new material securely in long-term memory
Associating the material with a diverse set of retrieval cues
Keeping the material in short-term memory by rapid rehearsal
Avoiding competition with any older memories
questions.explain: The two requirements are anchoring material in long-term memory and linking it to many cues so it can be recalled later. Short-term rehearsal does not make learning durable.

questions.q: Which aspect of learning does the author say often goes overlooked?
options: Anchoring new material securely in memory
Making the first exposure to material enjoyable
Keeping short-term memory uncluttered
Having effective retrieval cues
questions.explain: The author says that having effective retrieval cues is an aspect of learning that often goes overlooked; being able to retrieve knowledge is as important as storing it.

questions.q: In the knot story, what turns buying a fishing boat into a learning opportunity?
options: Needing an anchor knot makes the learner retrieve and relearn the bowline
The boat gives massed practice of all the knots at once, every day
The Eagle Scout comes back the next spring to repeat the whole lesson
The anchor line removes any need to look at the cheat sheet again
questions.explain: The need to attach the anchor makes the learner recall that there was a loop knot, find the cheat sheet and relearn it. The author calls this practicing retrieval.

questions.q: True or false: Knowledge, skills and experiences that are vivid and significant, and those that are periodically practiced, tend to stay with us.
questions.explain: The author says vividness, significance and periodic practice keep knowledge with us, as when a jumper listens closely to reserve-chute instructions.

questions.q: True or false: The author counts mental rehearsal in your bunk the night before a jump as a form of spaced practice.
questions.explain: The mental rehearsal conducted in the bunk before the jump is described as a form of spaced practice that helps.

questions.q: Practicing the bowline during TV commercials over weeks is an example of ____ practice.
questions.explain: Practicing the knot repeatedly over time, with gaps in between, is spaced practice.

questions.q: The knot with a loop in the end of a line, which the learner relearns for the anchor, is the ____.
questions.explain: The learner relearns the bowline from the cheat sheet, silently reciting the rabbit-and-tree memory device.

questions.q: Put the events of the knot story in order.
items: Take an hour's knot lesson from an Eagle Scout in the park
Fail to practice and soon forget the knots
Buy a boat and need to attach an anchor line
Recall a loop knot exists and relearn it from the cheat sheet
Practice the bowline during TV commercials
Find uses for the knot in many little jobs
questions.explain: The story runs from the forgotten lesson, to retrieval prompted by a real need, to spaced practice and everyday use.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether the author's account says it tends to stay with us or fade.

items.t: A skill that is periodically practiced
Knowledge that is vivid and holds significance
Knots learned in one park lesson and never practiced
Material taken in once and never applied afterward

questions.explain: Vivid, significant and periodically practiced knowledge stays; material that is not practiced and applied is soon forgotten.

questions.q: Explain the two things durable learning requires, and why the author says retrieval cues are often overlooked.
questions.a: First, as we move new material from short-term to long-term memory we must anchor it there securely. Second, we must associate it with a diverse set of cues that make us adept at recalling it later. Cues are often overlooked because people focus on committing knowledge to memory, but being able to retrieve it when needed is just as important.

questions.q: Use the Eagle Scout knot story to explain how learning that seemed lost can be rebuilt.
questions.a: After the park lesson the learner never practices and the knots are forgotten. The next spring, needing an anchor line on a boat, the learner recalls there was a loop knot, finds the cheat sheet and relearns the bowline, which is retrieval. Practicing it during commercials and in many small jobs is spaced practice, so the knowledge stays with the learner.

questions.q: Match each element of the knot story to its role.
pairs: Teaches eight or ten knots in an hour's lesson
Used to relearn the bowline when the anchor line is needed
Lets you practice the bowline during commercials
The need that prompts retrieval of the loop knot
questions.explain: Each element marks a stage in the story, from the initial lesson, through forgetting, to retrieval and spaced practice.

questions.q: According to the author, how do the capacity of memory and the capacity of retrieval compare?
options: Both storage and retrieval are severely limited, so we forget most things
Storage is nearly unlimited if linked to what we know; retrieval is limited
Retrieval is nearly unlimited, but storage in memory is severely limited
Both storage and retrieval become nearly unlimited when learning is spaced
questions.explain: New learning depends on prior learning, so the more we know the more connections we can make. Our retrieval capacity, though, is severely limited, so most of what we know is not accessible at any moment.

questions.q: Why does the author call the limit on retrieval helpful?
options: It makes sure that weak or unimportant memories are erased for good
It keeps new learning from ever competing with older learning
If every memory were always at hand, finding the right one would be hard
It lets retrieval cues be kept in memory without any practice at all
questions.explain: With a sheer volume of material always at hand, sorting out the knowledge needed at the moment would be difficult.

questions.q: When well-entrenched knowledge such as fluent French is easily relearned after disuse, what had actually been lost?
options: The knowledge itself
The memory traces, which must be encoded again
The meaning of the knowledge
The cues that enable you to find and retrieve it
questions.explain: The author says it is not the knowledge that has been forgotten, but the cues that enable you to find and retrieve it.

questions.q: A person who has moved many times cannot recall an address from twenty years ago, yet picks it out easily on a multiple choice test. What does the author conclude?
options: The memory is still stored, but the cues to retrieve it have weakened
The memory was lost and has just been re-encoded by the test question
The test question supplied knowledge the person never actually had
Multiple choice tests tend to create false memories of past addresses
questions.explain: Through disuse or reassignment of cues you forget in the sense of being unable to call something up easily, but it remains in the uncleaned closet of the mind.

questions.q: After years on one operating system, a worker switches to a very different one and keeps reaching for the old commands. What does the chapter say she must do?
options: Practice the old system more so that its cues grow stronger
Forget much of the old system so she can learn the new one
Wait for sleep to erase the old knowledge before switching
Avoid the new system until the old one is fully consolidated
questions.explain: Changing from a PC to a Mac takes enormous forgetting to learn the new architecture and use it fluently. The chapter treats some forgetting as essential for new learning.

questions.q: According to the author, why is army jump school training a disadvantage for smoke jumping?
options: Smokejumpers always jump from much higher altitudes than paratroopers
Army training avoids any hands-on practice with the jump equipment
They must unlearn procedures practiced to the point of reflex
Paratroopers are never taught to count before their chute opens
questions.explain: Smokejumpers use different aircraft, equipment and protocols, so cues to reflexive army procedures must be forgotten to acquire the new set.

questions.q: True or false: The author says retrieval capacity is virtually limitless while the amount we can remember is severely limited.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: there is virtually no limit on how much learning we can remember, but retrieval capacity is severely limited.

questions.q: True or false: As we learn new things, most of what we learned well in life is lost from long-term memory.
questions.explain: The author calls it a critical point that we do not lose most of what we learned; through disuse or reassigned cues we merely cannot call it up easily.

questions.q: To learn Italian in middle age, you may have to forget cues linked to your high school ____.
questions.explain: When you hope to produce the Italian essere, the French etre pops up, so old cues have to be set aside.

questions.q: The paradox is that some ____ is often essential for new learning.
questions.explain: The author's paradox is that “some forgetting is often essential for new learning,” because old cues compete with new ones.

questions.q: When entrenched knowledge seems forgotten after disuse, it is not the knowledge that is lost but the ____ that enable you to find it.
questions.explain: Cues are lost or displaced, not the knowledge, which is why entrenched knowledge is easily relearned.

questions.q: In Proust's Remembrance of Things Past, the narrator's lost adolescence comes rushing back when he tastes a cake dipped in ____ tea.
questions.explain: The taste of the cake dipped in lime blossom tea unlocks old memories, showing that context can unleash them, as when “the right key works to open an old lock”.

questions.q: Which of these make knowledge more deeply entrenched and so more durable?
options: Firmly and thoroughly comprehending the concept
Practical importance or keen emotional weight in your life
Connection with other knowledge held in memory
Having learned it in a single long session
Keeping it separate from other knowledge
questions.explain: The author lists thorough comprehension, importance or emotional weight, and connections to other knowledge. Isolation weakens entrenchment.

questions.q: Which of these determine how readily you can recall knowledge from your internal archives?
options: Context
Recent use
The number and vividness of cues linked to it
How many hours you slept last night
Whether it was learned in school
questions.explain: Ease of recall depends on context, recent use, and the number and vividness of cues linked to the knowledge.

questions.q: Which of these does the author give as cases where old cues must be set aside to learn something new?
options: Learning Italian after school French
Driving on the left in England
Moving from a PC to a Mac
Tying the bowline for an anchor line
Writing an essay through several drafts
questions.explain: The author's examples of displaced cues are French versus Italian, right versus left driving, and changing computing platforms.

questions.q: Put these steps of the author's reasoning about memory and retrieval in order.
items: There is virtually no limit to what we can remember if we relate it to what we know
The more we learn, the more connections we create for further learning
Our capacity for retrieval is severely limited
That limit is helpful because we are not swamped by everything stored
questions.explain: The section moves from the near-unlimited capacity of memory to the limit on retrieval and why that limit is useful.

questions.q: Put the Jack and Joan story in order.
items: Jack takes up with Joan, and the couple is sometimes called Jack and Jill
The cue Jack and begins reliably calling up Joan
Joan throws him over and he takes up with Jenny
The speaker catches themselves saying Jack and Joan for Jenny
questions.explain: The story shows an old cue pulling up the old rhyme, then being repurposed, then competing again when the partner changes.

questions.q: Sort each cue by whether it is an old cue to set aside or a new cue to build.

items.t: French etre for to be
Italian essere for to be
Driving on the right side of the road
Driving on the left in England
Jack and Jill
Jack and Jenny

questions.explain: In each example the old cue competes with the new one, so the old cue must be suppressed or reassigned.

questions.q: Match each situation to what must be set aside to learn the new thing.
pairs: Cues to high school French words
Cues to drive on the right side of the road
Moving from a PC to a Mac
Habits tied to the old system's architecture
Smoke jumping after army jump school
Jump procedures practiced to the point of reflex
questions.explain: Each case shows the paradox that some forgetting is essential for new learning.

questions.q: Match each anecdote in the chapter to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Eagle Scout knot lesson, then a boat
Retrieval prompted by need after a lapse
Army jump training before smoke jumping
Unlearning reflex procedures to make way for new ones
Jack and Jill, then Joan, then Jenny
Reassigning cues without losing the old names
Proust's cake dipped in lime blossom tea
A taste setting off long-lost memories
questions.explain: The author uses each story to illustrate a point about consolidation, cues or retrieval.

questions.q: Why does the author say some forgetting is essential for new learning? Give examples.
questions.a: As you go through life you often need to forget cues tied to older, competing memories so you can associate them with new ones. Learning Italian may mean setting aside the cues to high school French, and traveling in England means suppressing the cue to drive on the right so you can build one for the left. Changing from a PC to a Mac likewise takes enormous forgetting.

questions.q: What is actually forgotten when well-entrenched knowledge seems lost after disuse? Use the old address and Proust examples.
questions.a: It is not the knowledge itself but the cues that enable you to find it, through disuse or reassignment of cues. A person may not recall an address from twenty years ago but can pick it out of a multiple choice list, because it remains in long-term memory. Context, like the taste of the cake in Proust, can unleash memories that seemed lost.

questions.q: Distinguish between how much we can remember and how much we can retrieve, and say what makes knowledge durable.
questions.a: There is virtually no limit to what we can remember as long as we relate it to what we know, so more learning gives more connections, but retrieval capacity is severely limited, which spares us from sifting through everything. Knowledge is more durable if deeply entrenched: firmly comprehended, of practical importance or emotional weight, and connected to other knowledge. Recall depends on context, recent use and the number and vividness of cues.

questions.q: Why is jump school training a disadvantage for smoke jumping, and what general point does the author draw?
questions.a: Smokejumpers use different aircraft, equipment and protocols, so a trained paratrooper must unlearn procedures practiced to the point of reflex and replace them. Even when two bodies of learning look alike to the uninitiated, you may have to forget the cues to one complex body of learning to acquire another.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes memory capacity or retrieval capacity.

items.t: Virtually no limit as long as learning relates to what we know
Grows richer because new learning depends on prior learning
Severely limited at any given moment
Most of what we have learned is not accessible at once

questions.explain: The author contrasts a nearly boundless ability to remember with a severely limited ability to retrieve at any moment.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 4 explain how learning occurs, through encoding, consolidation and retrieval, before turning to difficulties?
options: To argue that learning mostly happens during sleep
To show that desirable difficulties apply only to military training
To replace the earlier chapters' advice on testing
To help the reader understand how difficulty can be desirable
questions.explain: The section opens by saying it describes how learning occurs to help you understand how difficulty can be desirable.

questions.q: The chapter's opening names spacing, interleaving and mixing up practice as desirable difficulties. Which earlier chapter of the book covers these practices?
options: Chapter 3: Mix Up Your Practice
Chapter 1: Learning Is Misunderstood
Chapter 2: To Learn, Retrieve
Chapter 5: Avoid Illusions of Knowing
questions.explain: Spacing, interleaving and mixed practice are the subject of Chapter 3, so Chapter 4 builds on them. Chapter 5 comes after Chapter 4.

questions.q: Which chapter follows Chapter 4, Embrace Difficulties?
options: Chapter 3: Mix Up Your Practice
Chapter 5: Avoid Illusions of Knowing
Chapter 6: Get Beyond Learning Styles
Chapter 8: Make It Stick
questions.explain: The table of contents places Avoid Illusions of Knowing directly after this chapter.

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 4 in the order they appear.
items: How Learning Occurs
Extending Learning: Updating Retrieval Cues
Easier Isn’t Better
How Effort Helps
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the mechanics of learning and retrieval cues to the ease-versus-benefit paradox and then how effort helps.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 4 explains encoding, consolidation and retrieval before it describes the Cal Poly batting experiment.
questions.explain: How Learning Occurs and Extending Learning come before Easier Isn’t Better, where the batting experiment appears.

questions.q: What does the chapter title Embrace Difficulties signal, and how does the opening jump school story set it up?
questions.a: The title signals that effortful conditions which slow learning, such as spacing and interleaving, are worth welcoming because they make learning stronger and more enduring. The opening presents army jump school, with escalating difficulty and testing through doing, as a model of these desirable difficulties before the chapter explains how learning occurs.

questions.q: What relationship do psychologists find between how easy a retrieval practice is and how much it entrenches learning?
questions.explain: The authors call this an inverse relationship: the more effort retrieval takes, the more the practice entrenches the learning. Easy practice mostly reuses what is already readily available.
options: The easier the retrieval, the less the practice strengthens retention of the knowledge or skill
The easier the retrieval, the more the practice strengthens retention of the knowledge or skill
Ease of retrieval has no effect, because only the number of repetitions decides retention
Easy retrieval helps skills but hurts factual knowledge, while hard retrieval does the reverse

questions.q: In the Cal Poly batting experiment, how did the massed-practice group take their forty-five extra pitches?
questions.explain: The massed group got fifteen fastballs, then fifteen curveballs, then fifteen changeups. The other group had the types randomly interspersed.
options: In forty-five pitches whose types were randomly mixed across the whole block
In three sets of fifteen, each set made up of a single pitch type
In nine sets of five, rotating through fastballs, curveballs and changeups in turn
In forty-five fastballs, since that is the pitch batters most need to master

questions.q: After six weeks of extra batting practice, how did the Cal Poly players who practiced randomly interspersed pitches compare with those who practiced one pitch type at a time?
questions.explain: The random-practice group ended up hitting markedly better, which was the opposite of what the players expected. The difficulty slowed their apparent progress but made the learning last.
options: They hit about the same, but they felt more confident about their progress
They hit worse, because their practice had never felt like real improvement
They hit markedly better, even though their practice had felt slower and harder
They hit better only against the pitch types they had practiced most often

questions.q: According to the authors, why did the growing ease of massed curveball practice lead to little durable learning for the Cal Poly batters?
questions.explain: Hitting a curveball you know is coming is a different skill from hitting one that may come at any time. Massed practice trains the former by leaning on short-term memory.
options: The batters stopped paying attention once they saw the same curveball repeatedly
Curveballs are too hard to learn without first mastering the fastball
Practicing only one pitch type exhausted the batters physically before the session ended
The practice built performance gains on short-term memory rather than requiring them to retrieve the skills anew

questions.q: True or false: In the Cal Poly batting study, the players who practiced one pitch type at a time felt they were improving during practice, yet ended up hitting worse than the players who practiced mixed pitches.
questions.explain: Massed practice felt gratifying because each pitch type became easier to anticipate, but the interleaved group hit markedly better in the end.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that the less you have forgotten about a topic, the more effective relearning will be in shaping your permanent knowledge.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: the more you have forgotten, the more effort relearning demands and the more effective it is at shaping permanent knowledge.

questions.q: Which of these describe the Cal Poly players who practiced with randomly interspersed pitches?
questions.explain: The random group found practice arduous but ended with better hitting. They were already skilled hitters, and fifteen-of-one-type blocks belong to the massed group.
options: They practiced fifteen pitches of one type before switching
They hit markedly better when assessed at the end
They struggled to connect during practice and learning felt slower
Each pitch had to be met without knowing its type in advance
They were beginners with little hitting experience

questions.q: Psychologists have found an ____ relationship between how easy retrieval practice is and how much it entrenches learning.
questions.explain: More effort in retrieval means more entrenchment, and less effort means less.

questions.q: The Cal Poly group who threw fifteen of one pitch type per set were doing a form of ____ practice.
questions.explain: Massed practice of one pitch type felt easy but built gains on short-term memory.

questions.q: The paradox that the more effort is required to retrieve something, the better you learn it is at the heart of the concept of ____ difficulties.
questions.explain: The authors call such short-term impediments that strengthen learning desirable difficulties.

questions.q: Put the main steps of the Cal Poly batting experiment in order.
items: Skilled players agreed to extra batting practice twice a week
The team was split into a massed-practice group and a randomly mixed group
Practice continued for six weeks
The players' hitting was assessed
The random-practice group was found to hit markedly better
questions.explain: The two groups practiced differently throughout, and the difference only showed at the final assessment.

questions.q: Put the chain of perceptions and responses a batter must carry out, as the author describes it, in order.
items: Determine the type of pitch
Anticipate how the ball will move
Aim and time the swing to meet the ball
questions.explain: All of this must become automatic because the ball reaches the catcher's mitt in less than half a second.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order they lead from massed practice to little durable learning for the Cal Poly batters.
items: A batter sees one pitch type fifteen times in a row
Perceptions and responses for that pitch become easier to recall
Performance during practice improves
Little durable learning results
questions.explain: The growing ease is built on short-term memory, so the gains do not last.

questions.q: Match each Cal Poly practice group and stage to what happened.
pairs: They got gratifyingly better at anticipating and connecting
They hit worse than the other group
They were still struggling somewhat to connect
questions.explain: Easy-feeling massed practice produced only short-term gains; hard random practice paid off later.

questions.q: Sort each description by the Cal Poly practice group it fits.

items.t: Fifteen pitches of one type per set
Felt gratifying as anticipation improved
Built gains on short-term memory
Batter had no idea which pitch to expect
Felt more arduous and slower
Produced markedly better hitting after six weeks

questions.explain: The group that felt productive built less durable learning than the group that struggled.

questions.q: Explain the inverse relationship between ease of retrieval and benefit, using the Cal Poly batters.
questions.a: The easier it is to retrieve knowledge or a skill, the less the practice entrenches it. Batters who practiced fifteen pitches of one type found it easy and improved quickly, but they built gains on short-term memory. Batters whose pitch types were mixed struggled, yet after six weeks they hit markedly better.

questions.q: Why is hitting a curveball you know is coming a different skill from hitting one you do not expect?
questions.a: With known pitches, a batter only has to repeat the perceptions and responses just used, which short-term memory handles. Not knowing the pitch means retrieving the right perceptions and responses from scratch, which is the skill a game demands. Players often practice the first although they need the second.

questions.q: What two familiar lessons do the authors draw from the Cal Poly study?
questions.a: First, difficulties that require more effort and slow apparent gains, like spacing, interleaving and mixing up practice, feel less productive but make learning stronger, more precise and more enduring. Second, our judgments about which strategies work best are often mistaken, colored by illusions of mastery.

questions.q: In the book's account of effortful recall, what does spaced practice require you to do compared with mindlessly repeating a skill?
questions.explain: Effortful recall reconstructs the learning from long-term memory, which makes it pliable again and sets reconsolidation in motion. Mindless repetition just loops information through short-term memory.
options: Reload or reconstruct the components of the skill from long-term memory
Hold the components in short-term memory for longer than usual
Simplify the skill into smaller parts that can be recalled without effort
Look up the correct answer first so that the recall cannot go wrong

questions.q: The authors say the more effort recall or execution takes, the more it benefits learning, with what condition?
questions.explain: The text says effort helps in proportion to its difficulty, provided that the effort succeeds. Failed recall without any success does not deliver the same benefit.
options: The learner has to be rested before attempting it
The effort has to succeed in the end
The material must have been seen only once before
Someone else has to supply a hint partway through

questions.q: True or false: Because massed practice gives a warm sensation of mastery, the authors treat the fluency it produces as a lasting sign of learning.
questions.explain: They say the fluency gained through massed practice is transitory and the sense of mastery illusory, much as with rereading.

questions.q: Which of these does reconsolidation help do, according to the authors?
questions.explain: Reconsolidation also weakens competing routes and happens because effortful recall makes the learning pliable again, so the other options reverse what the authors say.
options: Reinforce meaning
Fix the learning so that it can never be modified
Bolster the cues and routes for recalling the learning later
Strengthen routes to competing memories
Strengthen connections to prior knowledge

questions.q: Effortful recall reconstructs the skill from ____ memory, rather than mindlessly repeating it from short-term memory.
questions.explain: This reloading makes the learning pliable and sets off reconsolidation.

questions.q: The fluency gained through massed practice is transitory, and our sense of mastery from it is ____.
questions.explain: The authors compare it to rereading as a study strategy.

questions.q: Put these steps of effortful recall and reconsolidation in order.
items: The skill is reloaded from long-term memory
The learning is made pliable again
Its most salient aspects become clearer
Reconsolidation reinforces meaning and strengthens connections and cues
questions.explain: The effort of reconstruction is what triggers reconsolidation and deeper learning.

questions.q: Sort each feature by whether it goes with rapid-fire repetition or effortful reconstruction.

items.t: Gives a warm sensation of mastery
Yields fluency that is transitory
Little mental effort is needed
Triggers reconsolidation
Makes learning pliable and clearer
Strengthens cues and routes for later retrieval

questions.explain: Only effortful reconstruction strengthens the underlying representation.

questions.q: How does spaced practice strengthen learning through reconsolidation?
questions.a: Spaced practice lets some forgetting occur, so recall takes effort and the learner has to reconstruct the skill from long-term memory. This makes the learning pliable again, clarifies its salient aspects and reinforces meaning, connections to prior knowledge and retrieval routes, while weakening competing routes.

questions.q: A driver who once struggled with every step of parallel parking now does the whole maneuver smoothly without conscious thought. Which idea from the book best describes what has formed?
questions.explain: The authors use driving, including parallel parking and the stick shift, as an example of effortful practice becoming ingrained mental models. Such models can then be adapted to varied circumstances.
options: A retrieval cue: a prompt that happens to bring one memory to mind
A massed-practice gain: fluency that depends on short-term memory
A mental model: a set of perceptions and motor skills fused into a meaningful whole
An undesirable difficulty: a hurdle that cannot be overcome with effort

questions.q: True or false: The authors say expert performance is built through thousands of hours of practice in varying conditions, which builds a vast library of mental models.
questions.explain: Experts accumulate many mental models, which lets them discern a situation and instantly choose the correct response.

questions.q: Which of these does the author give as examples of mental models?
questions.explain: Mental models are deeply entrenched skills or knowledge structures that can be adapted to varied circumstances. A cheat sheet or short-term list is neither.
options: A cheat sheet kept in a pocket
The perceptions and maneuvers of parallel parking
A memorized sequence of chess moves
Seeing and unloading on a curveball
A list of facts held for a few seconds in short-term memory

questions.q: Deeply entrenched, efficient skills or knowledge structures that, like habits, can be applied in varied circumstances are called mental ____.
questions.explain: Examples include the maneuvers of driving and seeing and unloading on a curveball.

questions.q: Put the stages by which expertise is built, as the author describes it, in order.
items: Effortful practice fuses ideas or skills into a meaningful whole
Thousands of hours of practice in varying conditions follow
A vast library of mental models accumulates
The expert instantly selects the correct response to a situation
questions.explain: The library of models is what lets an expert discern a given situation and respond instantly.

questions.q: What is a mental model in this chapter, and how does one form?
questions.a: A mental model is a deeply entrenched, efficient skill or knowledge structure that, like a habit, can be adapted to varied circumstances, such as the perceptions and maneuvers of driving. It forms when effortful practice fuses interrelated ideas or motor skills into a meaningful whole, and experts build a vast library of them over thousands of hours.

questions.q: How do retrieval practice at different times and contexts and interleaving broaden mastery?
questions.a: They link new associations to the material, building interconnected networks of knowledge and multiplying the cues for retrieving it. Mixing up the contexts and the other skills the material is tied to makes mental models more versatile, so the learning applies to a broader range of situations.

questions.q: In the study of bird types, what did learners believe about studying many examples of one species before moving to the next, and what did the results show?
questions.explain: The learners' preference was a mistaken judgment: interleaving felt clunky yet produced better discrimination without hindering the learning of commonalities within a type.
options: They believed it was worse, but it gave superior discrimination between types
They believed it was better, and it did give superior discrimination between types
They believed it made no difference, and interleaving also made no difference
They believed it was better, but the interleaved strategy gave superior discrimination between types

questions.q: Why does interleaved practice with different geometric solids help learners, according to the authors?
questions.explain: Choosing among related but dissimilar solids heightens sensitivity to what makes each type distinctive, which is thought to produce richer and more nuanced encoding.
options: It forces them to notice similarities and differences in order to pick the right volume formula
It lets them memorize each volume formula separately without any confusion
It removes the need to understand why each formula works
It lowers the effort of choosing a formula because the solids are always shown in a fixed order

questions.q: Which of these were results of interleaved study in the bird and painting studies?
questions.explain: Interleaving felt clunky and learners favored the blocked approach, yet it improved discrimination without costing the learning of within-type commonalities.
options: Learning commonalities within a type was clearly hindered
Learning commonalities within a type was not hindered
Learners correctly predicted that it would work better
Better discrimination between types
Difficulty retrieving past examples, which further solidified the learning of each type

questions.q: Noticing particulars, such as that a turtle comes up for air but a fish does not, is the skill of ____.
questions.explain: It is paired with induction, which is surmising the general rule.

questions.q: Surmising a general rule, such as that fish can breathe in water, from varied examples is called ____.
questions.explain: Spaced and interleaved exposure to varied examples strengthens both induction and discrimination.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order the authors suggest interleaved practice leads to better understanding.
items: Related but dissimilar items are practiced in mixed order
The learner notices similarities and differences
More complex and nuanced representations are encoded
The learner understands why different types call for different solutions
questions.explain: The heightened sensitivity to similarities and differences is thought to be what produces the richer encoding.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it is discrimination or induction.

items.t: Noticing that a turtle comes up for air but a fish does not
Telling one painter's works from another's
Telling apart bird types
Surmising that fish can breathe in water
Identifying what is common within a species
Inferring a general rule from varied examples

questions.explain: Discrimination is about particulars that differ; induction is about the general rule.

questions.q: Why is interleaved study better than blocked study for learning concepts such as bird types, even though it feels clunky?
questions.a: Interleaving strengthens discrimination between types without hindering learning of the commonalities within a type. The difficulty of retrieving past examples further solidifies which are representative of a type, and it heightens sensitivity to similarities and differences, which encodes more nuanced representations.

questions.q: In the grade school study, students practiced tossing beanbags into two-foot and four-foot baskets. How did they do when later tested on a three-foot basket, compared with students who had practiced only on a three-foot basket?
questions.explain: The authors cite this as an example of varied practice building transfer. Practicing at different distances gave a broader set of mental processes than repeating a single distance.
options: They were less adept, because they had never practiced at that exact distance
They were more adept at hitting the three-foot basket
They did equally well, since distance does not affect the skill
They were more adept only when allowed to practice again at three feet first

questions.q: The ability to apply what you have learned in new settings is what scientists call ____ of learning.
questions.explain: Practice that mimics real challenges improves it.

questions.q: Match each example from the chapter to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Beanbag tossing at two and four feet
Varied practice improving transfer to a new distance
Anchor line on a fishing boat
Struggling with a problem before being shown the solution
Overcoming difficulty building a broader vocabulary of mental processes
questions.explain: The chapter reuses these examples to show different benefits of difficulty.

questions.q: How do spacing, interleaving and variation improve transfer of learning?
questions.a: Overcoming their retrieval difficulties uses the same mental processes needed to apply learning in everyday settings, so they mimic practical experience. This follows the advice to practice like you play, and it builds a broader vocabulary of mental processes than massed, nonvaried practice.

questions.q: You must attach an anchor line to your new fishing boat and have never learned a knot. Which does the author's idea predict?
questions.explain: Struggling with a problem before being shown the solution makes the later solution better learned and more durably remembered. The boat scenario supplies that struggle.
options: You will remember it equally well either way, since the knot itself is the same
You will remember it better from the park lesson, because instruction avoids wasted effort
You will learn and remember the bowline better by struggling on the boat first than by being shown it in a park lesson
You will remember it better only if you avoid all errors on the first attempt

questions.q: Why is the anchor-line scenario on a boat more likely to teach you the bowline than a park lesson?
questions.a: Struggling to solve a problem before being shown the solution makes the later solution better learned and more durably remembered. On the boat you have a real need and have already tried and failed, so the answer lands on prepared ground, unlike a lesson with no prior struggle.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: What do the authors report about recall of content when text is slightly out of focus or set in a font that is a little hard to decipher?
questions.explain: The slight difficulty disrupts fluency and makes the reader work harder to construct meaning, which increases comprehension and learning.
options: People recall the content worse, because fluent reading is essential
People recall it equally well but read it faster
People recall it better only if the type is not blurred at all
People recall the content better

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: When a lecture outline proceeds in a different order from the textbook passage, why does recall of the content improve?
questions.explain: The mismatch introduces a difficulty that makes learners work to reconcile the discrepancy. The added effort increases comprehension and learning, provided the difficulty can be overcome.
options: The effort of discerning main ideas and reconciling the mismatch strengthens learning
Hearing the same facts in a new order makes them seem more novel and interesting
The mismatch gives students extra time to take notes during the lecture
Students learn to ignore the textbook, so they concentrate on the lecture alone

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: A person from Vermont is asked the capital of Texas, thinks through Dallas, Houston and others, and is then told it is Austin. Why does the author say that guessing first helps?
questions.explain: Retrieving related knowledge while searching strengthens the route to a gap before the answer arrives, creating fertile ground for encoding. In the author's words, “It’s better to solve a problem than to memorize a solution.”
options: Wrong guesses are stored and later recalled in place of the right answer
Casting about for answers strengthens the route to the gap, so the answer connects to related material when supplied
The wrong guesses show the person which answers a teacher is likely to prefer
Frustration alone is what produces strong memory, whatever the person does about it

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: On tests, what does the author say about supplying an answer compared with choosing from multiple choice options?
questions.explain: Generation is stronger when the learner has to produce rather than recognize an answer. The authors add that even filling in a blank on familiar material strengthens memory.
options: Choosing from options provides stronger benefits because there is less chance of error
Both give identical benefits, since only the material being tested matters
Supplying an answer often provides stronger learning benefits, and a short essay stronger still
Supplying an answer helps only when the material is new to the student

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: In the study of more than eight hundred psychology students, what happened in follow-up tests about two months later?
questions.explain: Students scored about half a letter grade better on concepts written about in their own words. The follow-up showed the effect had dropped but remained robust.
options: The benefit had vanished completely, matching the copied concepts
The benefit had grown larger as the writing was consolidated
The benefit had stayed exactly as large as on the semester exams
The benefit of writing in their own words had dropped but remained robust

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: True or false: The authors report that omitting letters from words in a text slows reading but improves retention.
questions.explain: Supplying missing letters disrupts fluency and forces the reader to construct meaning, which raises learning even though reading is slower.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: True or false: In the write-to-learn study, students scored better on concepts they had copied verbatim from slides than on concepts they had restated in their own words.
questions.explain: The reverse was found: concepts written about in their own words scored about half a letter grade better, showing exposure alone was not what helped.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: True or false: Having to supply an answer in a test, rather than select from multiple choice options, often gives stronger learning benefits.
questions.explain: Producing an answer is a form of generation, and the authors say it often brings stronger benefits than selecting an option.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Which of these changes to normal presentation are described as adding a helpful difficulty?
questions.explain: Each of the first three disrupts fluency and makes the learner work harder to construct meaning. Following the textbook exactly or copying verbatim adds no such difficulty.
options: A lecture outline that follows the textbook flow exactly
Letters omitted from words that the reader must supply
A lecture outline ordered differently from the textbook
Slightly out-of-focus text
Copying key ideas verbatim from a slide

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Which of these are cognitive activities that reflection can involve?
questions.explain: Reflection draws on retrieval (recalling recent learning), elaboration (connecting it to what you know) and generation (such as rephrasing in your own words).
options: Elaboration
Passive rereading
Massed repetition
Generation
Retrieval

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Which of these are examples of generation?
questions.explain: Generation is trying to produce an answer rather than being presented with it. Reading or copying a given answer is passive.
options: Reading the answer that has been supplied
Trying to solve a problem before being shown the solution
Filling in a blank on material you already know
Writing a short essay instead of choosing from options
Copying a solution from a slide

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: The act of trying to answer a question or solve a problem rather than being presented with the information is known as ____.
questions.explain: The authors note that even filling in a blank on familiar material strengthens memory.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Taking a few minutes to review what has been learned and ask yourself questions about it is known as ____.
questions.explain: It can involve retrieval, elaboration and generation.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Blurred type, a mismatched lecture outline and omitted letters all introduce a difficulty that works as a disruption of ____.
questions.explain: That disruption makes the learner work harder to construct an interpretation.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Put the explanation for why generation helps, as the author gives it, in order.
items: You cast about for a solution, retrieving related knowledge
You strengthen the route to a gap in your learning
The answer is supplied to fill the gap
Connections form to related material fresh in your mind
questions.explain: The attempt prepares the ground so that the answer is deeply processed when it arrives.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Put the steps of the write-to-learn study of psychology students in order.
items: The instructor presents a key concept in a lecture
Students write their own summary of it or copy a slide verbatim
Exams during the semester test understanding of the concepts
Follow-up tests about two months later measure retention
questions.explain: Own-word writing beat copying on both, though the benefit dropped by the follow-up.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Match each learning term from the How Effort Helps and Other Learning Strategies sections to its meaning.
pairs: Noticing the particulars that distinguish one example or type from another
Surmising the general rule from varied examples
The ability to apply what you have learned in new settings
Trying to answer a question or solve a problem rather than being presented with the answer
Taking a few minutes to review what was learned and ask yourself questions
questions.explain: These are the chapter's working terms for how difficulty builds stronger learning.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Match each change to normal study with its reported effect.
pairs: Lecture outline out of textbook order
Effort to reconcile the discrepancy improves recall
Reading is slowed and retention improves
Filling in a blank on familiar material
Memory of the material and later recall are strengthened
questions.explain: Each introduces a difficulty that makes the learner work harder to construct meaning.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Match each cognitive activity in reflection to its description in the chapter.
pairs: Recalling recently learned knowledge to mind
Connecting new knowledge to what you already know
Rephrasing key ideas in your own words or mentally rehearsing a next attempt
questions.explain: The authors say reflection can draw on all three.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Sort each strategy by whether it disrupts fluency or is a form of generation.

items.t: Text in a slightly hard-to-read font
Lecture outline in a different order from the textbook
Text that is a little out of focus
Filling in a blank
Writing a short essay
Trying a problem before being shown the solution
Guessing a capital before being told it

questions.explain: Both kinds of difficulty make the learner work harder to build understanding.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Sort each reflection question by when it is asked.
groups: After practicing new knowledge or skills

items.t: What are the key ideas?
What are some examples?
How do these relate to what I already know?
What went well?
What could have gone better?
What strategies might I use next time to get better results?

questions.explain: The first set reviews content; the second reviews performance.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Sort each item by the group in the write-to-learn study it describes.

items.t: Restated concepts in their own words
Generated examples of the concepts
Scored about half a letter grade better
Copied key ideas verbatim
Copied examples verbatim
Scored lower on questions about those concepts

questions.explain: Writing in their own words, not mere exposure, produced the benefit.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Why can making text harder to read improve learning, and what limit do the authors give?
questions.a: Blurred type, a mismatched outline or missing letters disrupt fluency and make the learner work harder to construct an interpretation, which increases comprehension and learning. The limit is that learning does not improve if the difficulty completely obscures the meaning or cannot be overcome.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Why does attempting an answer before being given it help, even when the attempt is wrong?
questions.a: Searching for a solution retrieves related knowledge and strengthens the route to the gap in your learning, and you become acutely aware of the hole. When the answer arrives it connects to material fresh in your mind and is processed more deeply than if you simply read it.

questions.section: Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties
questions.q: Describe the write-to-learn study of psychology students and what it showed.
questions.a: After key concepts in lectures, students wrote summaries in their own words with examples, or copied key ideas verbatim from slides. They scored about half a letter grade better on the concepts they had written about, so exposure alone was not the cause. Two months later the benefit had dropped but remained robust.

questions.q: Which earlier chapter's ideas does the baseball example in Easier Isn’t Better revisit, calling them familiar lessons?
questions.explain: The batting study shows again that spacing, interleaving and mixing up practice feel less productive but make learning stronger. That ties it to the preceding chapter and its themes.
options: Chapter 3, Mix Up Your Practice, on spacing, interleaving and varied practice
Chapter 1, Learning Is Misunderstood, on the dipstick view of testing
Chapter 2, To Learn, Retrieve, on the testing effect in the wild
Chapter 5, Avoid Illusions of Knowing, on two systems of knowing

questions.q: The Priming the Mind for Learning subsection says that struggling with a problem before being shown the solution improves learning. Which later section of the chapter returns to this idea?
questions.explain: The failure section says strategies likely to cause errors, such as trying a problem before being shown how, still produce stronger learning than passive ones, provided there is corrective feedback.
options: Undesirable Difficulties, which says every unaided attempt helps
Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning, given corrective feedback
The Takeaway, which says errors should be avoided so none are learned
Encoding, which says new learning is first held in short-term memory

questions.q: In the Improving Versatility subsection, how does the author support the claim that difficulty in practice improves transfer?
questions.explain: The subsection leans on cases already described, recalling the batting study, the beanbag baskets, jump school and the jet simulator, to show that practicing like you play builds transfer.
options: By introducing a new experiment on transfer that appears nowhere else in the chapter
By arguing that transfer requires abandoning spacing and interleaving
By recalling earlier examples: the Cal Poly batters, the beanbag students and the jump school simulations
By contrasting the results of the French sixth graders with those of the baseball players

questions.q: True or false: In the chapter, Reconsolidating Memory is the final subsection under How Effort Helps.
questions.explain: It is the first of six subsections; Priming the Mind for Learning is the last one before Other Learning Strategies That Incorporate Desirable Difficulties.

questions.q: Which of these are subsections of How Effort Helps?
questions.explain: How Effort Helps contains six subsections; Encoding and Retrieval belong instead to the earlier section How Learning Occurs.
options: Broadening Mastery
Encoding
Creating Mental Models
Retrieval
Priming the Mind for Learning

questions.q: Put the subsections of How Effort Helps in the order they appear in the chapter.
items: Reconsolidating Memory
Creating Mental Models
Broadening Mastery
Fostering Conceptual Learning
Improving Versatility
Priming the Mind for Learning
questions.explain: The subsections run from what effortful recall does to memory, through mental models and wider mastery, to concept learning, transfer, and finally struggling before being shown the answer.

questions.q: Match each subsection of How Effort Helps to its main idea.
pairs: Effortful recall makes learning pliable again and reinforces it
Effortful practice fuses skills or ideas into adaptable wholes
Varied, interleaved retrieval builds networks of knowledge and multiplies cues
Practice that mimics real challenges improves transfer
Struggling with a problem first makes the later solution stick
questions.explain: Each subsection names one way effort pays off.

questions.q: Why does the chapter put Easier Isn’t Better before the How Effort Helps subsections?
questions.a: Easier Isn’t Better first states the paradox that harder retrieval entrenches learning more, using the Cal Poly batting study. How Effort Helps then explains what that effort does: reconsolidation, mental models, broader mastery, concept learning, transfer and priming.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: What did B. F. Skinner believe about errors when he advocated errorless learning methods?
questions.explain: Skinner held that learners' errors are counterproductive and stem from poor instruction, so his methods made errors nearly impossible. The authors reject this view.
options: Errors are counterproductive and stem from faulty instruction
Errors are essential and should be provoked in every lesson
Errors reveal a learner's native ability and should be recorded
Errors are harmless if learners wait before correcting them

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Why do the authors consider errorless-learning techniques ineffective?
questions.explain: The small bites were quizzed immediately, while still fresh in short-term memory, and the authors say retrieval from short-term memory is an ineffective learning strategy. The problem was too little delay and effort, not too much material.
options: Learners are given too much new material in one large block
Short-term retrieval does little for lasting learning
Learners cannot give any answers at all without teacher help
Learners are tested only after a long delay, so they forget

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: According to the authors, what must accompany a learner's wrong attempt for the error not to be learned?
questions.explain: When learners commit errors and are given corrective feedback, the errors are not learned. Even attempts likely to produce errors beat passive study, provided feedback follows.
options: A long delay before trying again
A reward for making the attempt
Corrective feedback
A warning about the likely mistake

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: In the authors' account, why can students with a high fear of errors do worse on a test?
questions.explain: Worrying about how they are doing uses up part of the limited working memory capacity. The authors do not say these students have smaller working memories to begin with.
options: Fear leads students to study less in the days before a test
Fear makes students skip the harder questions on the test
Their working memory is smaller than that of calmer classmates
Working memory goes to monitoring their performance

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: In the French sixth-grader study, what were half the children taught after they failed the anagrams?
questions.explain: That ten-minute lesson led the children to use working memory better on the later test than the group who only described how they had tried the anagrams.
options: That difficulty is part of learning and errors are natural
That anagrams are easy once a few simple tricks are known
That the anagrams were too hard for anyone and did not matter
That fast solvers are usually the students with higher IQs

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: In the French study, what did the group taught that errors are natural show on the later working-memory test?
questions.explain: The children taught that errors are part of learning did not spend their working memory agonizing over difficulty. That left more capacity for the test.
options: Slightly worse use of working memory than the other group
Significantly better working-memory use than the others
About the same use of working memory as the other group
Better memory only for the anagrams they had already seen

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: According to Carol Dweck's work as the authors describe it, why do people who think ability is fixed from birth avoid challenges?
questions.explain: For those who see ability as wired in the genes, failure looks like a verdict on ability. People who understand that effort and learning change the brain persist instead.
options: Challenges cost more time than their abilities allow
Challenges are usually set by people they distrust
Failing would seem to show lesser native ability
Success would raise expectations they cannot meet

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: What does Anders Ericsson's research on expert performance imply about failure?
questions.explain: Ericsson found that expertise takes thousands of hours of dedicated practice aimed at surpassing one's current level, so failure becomes part of the path to mastery.
options: Failure is a sign that a person lacks the talent for expertise
Failure can be avoided by choosing easier practice tasks
Failure matters only in the first weeks of practice
Failure is essential when striving beyond one's ability

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: What message did Paris's Festival of Errors aim to give French schoolchildren?
questions.explain: The organizers argued that a focus on showing results had bred intellectual timorousness, and they wanted children to see errors as effort.
options: Mistakes are constructive and a sign of effort, not failure
Mistakes should be hidden until a teacher has corrected them
Mistakes are rare among children who prepare well enough
Mistakes matter only when a competition is being scored

questions.q: What does Bonnie Blodgett mean by blundering?
questions.explain: She says the risk of knowing what you are getting into is that it becomes an overwhelming obstacle to getting started. Blundering lets her begin and learn by trial and error.
options: Copying a trusted expert's method step by step at first
Starting before working out the proper way to do it
Planning every stage of a garden before planting anything
Avoiding any writing about her mistakes until they are fixed

questions.q: Which two learning processes does Bonnie engage in by writing about her gardening experiments?
questions.explain: Writing means recalling the details of what she found out, and explaining it to readers connects the outcome to what she already knows.
options: Spacing her reading of plant books and testing herself on them
Copying expert advice and memorizing it for later quizzes
Retrieving what she found and explaining it to readers
Relearning Latin names and then dropping common names

questions.q: Why did Bonnie come to value Latin plant names even though she began by resisting them?
