questions.explain: Names like tardiva (late) hint at a plant's nature, and one Latin name picks out a single plant whereas common names are regional. Her earlier Latin classes also helped cues reawaken.
options: They were required by the farmers who consulted her
They made her garden writing look more scholarly
They replaced the need to record gardening experiments
They aided memory and gave precision

questions.q: What caveat do the authors add about blundering as a learning strategy?
questions.explain: The authors close the example by noting that in settings like jumping out of airplanes, blundering is not the optimal way to learn.
options: It is risky where a mistake could be fatal
It works only for adults who already have years of training
It works only for art and design, not for practical skills
It slows learning unless an expert supervises each attempt

questions.q: By the Bjorks' definition, when does a desirable difficulty turn into an undesirable one?
questions.explain: Difficulties are desirable because they trigger encoding and retrieval processes, but only if the learner can respond to them. Otherwise they are undesirable.
options: The learner has practiced the material more than three times
The learner lacks the background to respond successfully
The learner finds the difficulty unpleasant or frustrating
The learner is tested rather than taught the answer

questions.q: Why is a textbook written in Lithuanian not a desirable difficulty for someone who does not know the language?
questions.explain: To be desirable, a difficulty must be something learners can overcome through increased effort. The authors use this example to show an impassable impediment.
options: It is too easy to need any effort from the reader
It removes the need to retrieve earlier knowledge
No increase in effort can overcome it
It interrupts spacing between study sessions

questions.q: Why might heckling by role-playing protestors help a politician but not an aspiring YouTube blogger?
questions.explain: The authors say difficulties that do not strengthen the skills you will need in real-world application are not desirable. Heckling suits a campaign speech, not stage presence for a blogger.
options: Hecklers disrupt spacing, which only helps politicians
Politicians have more background knowledge about speeches
Bloggers learn best from errorless practice sessions
It matches challenges the politician will really face

questions.q: Does the book offer an overarching rule for which difficulties make learning stronger?
questions.explain: The authors say they cannot yet be definitive about undesirable difficulties for lack of research. They point to well-documented desirable difficulties, such as testing and spacing, as a ready toolkit.
options: No; research may someday yield one, but a toolkit exists now
Yes; any difficulty that slows the learner's progress is useful
Yes; any difficulty that the learner enjoys will be useful
No; it says no such rule could ever be found by research

questions.q: According to The Takeaway, what does consolidation do to memory traces after initial encoding?
questions.explain: Encoding holds information in short-term working memory, and consolidation turns it into a cohesive representation in long-term memory. It is more than a plain copy.
options: Copies them unchanged from working memory into long-term storage
Reorganizes and stabilizes them, linking to prior knowledge
Erases them gradually so that only the strongest cues remain
Holds them in short-term memory until a later retrieval attempt

questions.q: What does The Takeaway say follows from long-term memory's virtually limitless capacity?
questions.explain: Because capacity is vast, the key is locating and recalling what you know, and prior knowledge supplies connections for new learning.
options: Storage is the main limit on what you can learn in a lifetime
Repeated use of information becomes less important over time
More knowledge means more connections for new knowledge
Only the first few retrievals strengthen a memory at all

questions.q: Why does rapid-fire practice produce little long-term benefit, according to The Takeaway?
questions.explain: Practice that is easy does little for learning, whereas recalling after some time, when your grasp has become a little rusty, requires effort to reconstruct.
options: It spaces the recall attempts too far apart
It prevents the learner from seeing any feedback
It forces the learner to guess too many answers
It takes little mental effort to recall

questions.q: Why does the section on undesirable difficulties come near the end of Chapter 4?
questions.explain: After presenting many desirable difficulties, the authors qualify the title: a difficulty must be one the learner can overcome and that builds needed skills.
options: It repeats the chapter's opening story of jump school
It qualifies the call to embrace difficulties
It introduces spacing and interleaving as new techniques
It argues that desirable difficulties lack research support

questions.q: How do the chapter's closing sections on failure and generative learning connect to the chapter's title, Embrace Difficulties?
questions.explain: The failure section argues that errors followed by corrective feedback are not learned and aid learning, and Bonnie's gardening is an example of learning by struggle.
options: They show that errors should be avoided until mastery is reached
They show that difficulty matters only for experts
They show that struggle and error with feedback aid learning
They show that difficulty is useful only in testing

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: True or false: Skinner's errorless learning gave learners new material in small bites and quizzed them immediately, so errors were very unlikely.
questions.explain: That was the design: material was fresh in short-term memory and easy to give back. The authors say this does not build lasting learning.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: True or false: When learners make errors and then receive corrective feedback, the authors say the errors themselves are learned.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: when errors are followed by corrective feedback, the errors are not learned. The belief that they are is described as a misguided impulse.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: True or false: Students with a high fear of making errors may do worse on a test partly because anxiety uses up working memory.
questions.explain: Monitoring their own performance takes up working memory, leaving less to solve the test problems.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: True or false: In the French study, the sixth graders were given anagram problems that most of them could solve easily.
questions.explain: The anagrams were very difficult, and none of the children could solve them. That failure set up the later comparison of the two groups.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: True or false: Dweck's work shows that people who believe ability is fixed tend to avoid challenges at which they may fail.
questions.explain: For them, failure would suggest lesser native ability. Those who see effort as changing the brain take on challenges and persist.

questions.q: True or false: Bonnie Blodgett learned ornamental gardening by following the instructions of trained experts.
questions.explain: She had no training and did not take direction from experts. She learned by doing, which the authors call generative learning.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say research has already given a definitive list of which kinds of difficulties are undesirable.
questions.explain: They say they have an intuitive sense of undesirable difficulties but cannot yet be definitive for lack of research. Desirable difficulties like testing and spacing are well documented.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter's title, Embrace Difficulties, is later qualified by the point that a difficulty has to be one the learner can overcome.
questions.explain: The undesirable-difficulties section makes that qualification, noting that the Bjorks call difficulties undesirable when learners lack the background to respond.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: B. F. Skinner advocated ____ learning methods in the belief that errors are counterproductive.
questions.explain: Skinner's errorless learning kept learners from making errors. The authors call it a myth that this builds lasting learning.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Errors made while learning do not become learned if the learner receives corrective ____.
questions.explain: Corrective feedback is the condition under which even error-prone attempts strengthen learning.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: The amount of information you can hold in mind while working through a problem, especially amid distraction, is called ____ memory.
questions.explain: Working memory is limited, and fear of failure can use up part of it.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Carol Dweck found that people who believe their intellectual ability is ____ from birth tend to avoid challenges.
questions.explain: Those who think ability is fixed see failure as a sign of lesser native ability.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Anders Ericsson found that expertise requires thousands of hours of ____ practice aimed at surpassing one's current level.
questions.explain: Dedicated practice that strives beyond current ability makes failure an essential experience.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Paris held a 'Festival of ____' to teach children that mistakes are part of learning.
questions.explain: The festival was inspired by the French sixth-grader study and presents mistakes as a sign of effort.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Thomas Edison is said to have remarked that he had found ____ ways that don't work.
questions.explain: Edison's remark shows failure as useful information that supports perseverance.

questions.q: Bonnie Blodgett's garden writing appears under the name 'The ____ Gardener.'
questions.explain: The name tells her voices of doubt to take a hike and gives readers permission to make mistakes.

questions.q: The process of trying to solve a problem without having been taught how is called ____ learning.
questions.explain: The learner generates the answer rather than recalling it. The authors call it old-fashioned trial and error.

questions.q: In Bonnie's example, the species name tardiva comes after the genus ____.
questions.explain: Tardiva means late, so the plant is a late bloomer. This showed her how Latin names help you remember.

questions.q: The phrase 'desirable ____' was coined by Elizabeth and Robert Bjork.
questions.explain: The Bjorks argue such difficulties trigger encoding and retrieval processes that support learning.

questions.q: The Takeaway says learning is at least a ____-step process, from encoding through consolidation to retrieval.
questions.explain: Initial encoding in working memory, consolidation into long-term memory, and retrieval that updates learning and applies it.

questions.q: The author says generation is another name for old-fashioned trial and ____.
questions.explain: Generative learning means working out the answer yourself instead of being shown it.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say a fear of failure can do to learning?
questions.explain: Fear of failure can poison learning by discouraging risk taking and by hurting performance under pressure. The chapter does not claim it makes errors permanent or shrinks memory.
options: Create aversions to experimentation and risk taking
Reduce performance under pressure, as in a test
Make learners permanently remember their errors
Shrink long-term memory capacity

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Which of these were taught in the ten-minute lesson to half the French sixth graders?

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: What was errorless learning, and why do the authors reject it?
questions.a: Skinner advocated errorless learning in the 1950s and 1960s, believing errors came from faulty instruction. Learners were fed small bites and quizzed at once from short-term memory, so they almost never erred. The authors say retrieval from short-term memory is ineffective and that errors with corrective feedback are part of striving for mastery.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Explain why letting learners attempt a problem before being shown the solution can help even when the attempt is wrong.
questions.a: Attempting a problem, even unsuccessfully, produces stronger learning and retention of the correct answer than passive study, provided corrective feedback follows. The learner is aware of a gap, and the answer then meets prepared ground. The errors are not learned when feedback corrects them.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: How can fear of failure reduce a student's score on a test, according to the chapter?
questions.a: A student with a high fear of errors spends part of limited working memory on monitoring performance, asking how he or she is doing. That leaves less working memory to solve the test problems, so the anxiety lowers the score. The authors call test anxiety an undesirable difficulty.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: Describe the French sixth-grader study and what it found.
questions.a: Sixth graders in France were given very hard anagrams that none could solve. Half then got a ten-minute lesson that difficulty is part of learning, errors are natural and practice helps, while the others were asked how they tried the anagrams. The taught group used working memory significantly better on a later difficult test.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: How do the work of Dweck and Ericsson support the view that failure is part of learning?
questions.a: Dweck found that people who believe ability is fixed avoid challenges, while those who see that effort changes the brain persist and view failure as a turn in the road. Ericsson found expertise requires thousands of hours of dedicated practice striving beyond current ability, so failure is essential.

questions.section: Failure and the Myth of Errorless Learning
questions.q: What does the chapter say is desirable about failure, and what is not?
questions.a: Failure itself is not desirable. What is desirable is the dauntless effort despite the risks and the discovery of what works and what does not, which sometimes only failure reveals. The authors use Edison, Jobs, FailCon and the Festival of Errors to show failure as useful information.

questions.q: Why is Bonnie Blodgett an example of generative learning?
questions.a: Bonnie, a self-taught gardener, started projects before knowing the proper way, learning by trial and error. This struggle led her to complex mastery and to knowledge of how things interrelate, without formal training. Generation is old-fashioned trial and error, and her success shows how struggling with a problem makes for strong learning.

questions.q: How does Bonnie Blodgett's writing add to her learning beyond the gardening itself?
questions.a: In writing about her experiences, she retrieves the details and the story of what she discovered. She then elaborates by explaining the experience to her readers and connecting it to what she already knows. Retrieval and elaboration are two potent learning processes.

questions.q: Describe how Bonnie came to embrace Latin plant names despite her early resistance.
questions.a: She began with no interest in plant names, but while working in her garden she found that Latin names give shortcuts to understanding plants and help her remember them. Her school Latin cues began to reawaken, and the names let her be specific, since common names are regional. So she used them more and more.

questions.q: What caveat do the authors add to blundering as a strategy for learning, and why does it matter?
questions.a: They note that in some settings, such as learning to jump out of airplanes and walk away alive, blundering is not the optimal learning strategy. This shows that trial and error suits cases where mistakes are survivable and that desirable difficulty has limits.

questions.q: How do the Bjorks define desirable difficulties, and when do they become undesirable?
questions.a: The Bjorks say difficulties are desirable because they trigger encoding and retrieval processes that support learning, comprehension and remembering. If the learner does not have the background knowledge or skills to respond successfully, they become undesirable difficulties.

questions.q: Why is a mismatched lecture outline or a Lithuanian textbook not a desirable difficulty for some learners?
questions.a: A desirable difficulty must be something learners can overcome through increased effort. A learner lacking the reading skills or language fluency cannot reconcile the discrepancy in the outline, and a Lithuanian textbook is impassable for someone who does not know the language. Such impediments are undesirable.

questions.q: Using the TV anchor, politician and Rotary Club examples, explain a second test for whether a difficulty is desirable.
questions.a: A difficulty should strengthen the skills you will need and the challenges you will meet in real-world application. A whisper in the ear or heckling can train a TV anchor or politician, but neither helps a Rotary Club president or YouTube blogger improve stage presence.

questions.q: According to The Takeaway, why does easy retrieval practice do little, and what makes retrieval more effective?
questions.a: Easy practice, such as rapid-fire recall from short-term memory, takes little effort and brings little long-term benefit. When you recall after time has passed and your grasp is a little rusty, you must reconstruct it. That effort strengthens the memory and makes it pliable, leading to reconsolidation.

questions.q: How do the chapter's last four sections build on the earlier discussion of desirable difficulties, and what do they add?
questions.a: Earlier sections explain how difficulties like retrieval, interleaving and generation help learning. The failure section adds the importance of embracing errors with feedback, the gardening example illustrates trial and error, and the undesirable-difficulties section sets limits. The Takeaway then summarizes the process of encoding, consolidation and retrieval.

questions.q: A student quizzes herself, finds she cannot explain a concept, and changes how she studies. Which skill from the chapter is she using?
options: The curse of knowledge, assuming a topic is simple for others
Metacognition, watching her own thinking and adjusting it
Motivated reasoning, favoring conclusions she finds congenial
Fluency illusion, mistaking ease of reading for mastery
questions.explain: Metacognition is monitoring your own thinking and performance and adjusting as you go. The other options are hazards the chapter warns about, not the skill of self-observation.

questions.q: In the Minneapolis delivery-robbery story, what flaw in the robbers' system does the author point out?
options: They always chose restaurants whose drivers were known to carry guns
They always waited until the police had left each neighborhood
They always paid for part of each order to avoid suspicion
They always used the same two cell phones and the same two addresses
questions.explain: The robbers kept at their scheme without considering the wisdom of repeating the same phones and addresses, which let an undercover cop set a trap. The other options are not part of the story.

questions.q: According to the opening, what makes poor judgment especially hard to correct?
options: People rarely know when their judgment is poor
Few people ever receive any instruction in how to reason
Poor judgment shows up only after years of experience
It is caused by a single bias that cannot be learned away
questions.explain: The authors say one problem with poor judgment is that we usually do not know when we have it. They add that the sheer number of ways judgment can go astray is a second problem.

questions.q: According to the opening, why does incompetence tend to persist?
options: People avoid tasks, so they never get any feedback at all
People get so much negative feedback that they stop trying
They overrate their skill and see little reason to change
People forget what they learned between practice sessions
questions.explain: When we are incompetent we tend to overestimate our competence, so we see little reason to improve. Nothing in the opening says the cause is too much criticism or forgetting.

questions.q: Why do the authors mention the Darwin Awards and the attorney who fell through an office window?
options: Reckless people are a small group whose errors differ from ours
Dramatic risks teach judgment better than ordinary practice does
We feel smarter than most, yet all of us are prone to misjudge
Professionals such as attorneys judge worse than other workers
questions.explain: The awards feed our delusion that we are smarter than average, but the authors say we are all hardwired to make errors in judgment. Good judgment is a skill we must acquire.

questions.q: Define metacognition, and explain why accurate self-observation matters and why poor judgment is hard to fix.
questions.a: Metacognition is monitoring your own thinking and performance, keeping an eye on yourself and adjusting as you go. Being an accurate self-observer helps you stay out of blind alleys, make good decisions and reflect on how to do better. Poor judgment is hard to fix because we usually do not know when we have it, and because there are so many ways judgment can be led astray.

questions.q: What happened to the Minneapolis stickup artists, and what point about judgment do the authors build on that story together with the Darwin Awards?
questions.a: The robbers kept phoning in orders from the same two cell phones to the same two addresses, and an undercover cop posing as the delivery man shot the first gunman through the food bag. With the Darwin Awards, the authors say we like to think we are smarter than average but are all hardwired to make errors in judgment. Good judgment is a skill we must acquire by becoming astute observers of our own thinking and performance.

questions.q: According to the chapter's opening, why do we start at a disadvantage in judging ourselves, and what must we do to become more competent?
questions.a: First, when we are incompetent we overestimate our competence and see little reason to change. Second, we are readily misled by illusions, cognitive biases and the stories we construct about the world and ourselves. To improve we must learn to recognize competence in others, judge more accurately what we know, adopt learning strategies that get results, and find objective ways to track our progress.

questions.q: Monitoring your own thinking is what psychologists call ____.
questions.explain: Metacognition (meta is Greek for about) is thinking about your own thinking, and accurate self-observers stay out of blind alleys.

questions.q: The Minneapolis stickup artists phoned from the same two cell phones and took delivery at the same two ____.
questions.explain: They failed to consider the wisdom of repeating the same phones and delivery addresses, which let a cop pose as the delivery man.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter's opening say we must do to become more competent?
options: Learn to recognize competence when we see it in others
Adopt learning strategies that get results
Find objective ways to track our progress
Trust our own sense of progress above outside measures
Ignore feedback that conflicts with our self-image
Stop monitoring performance to avoid biased judgments
questions.explain: The opening lists recognizing competence in others, judging ourselves accurately, adopting effective strategies and finding objective ways to track progress. Relying on subjective feeling is the problem it describes.

questions.q: True or false: One problem the authors name with poor judgment is that we usually do not know when we have it.
questions.explain: They say poor judgment is hard to catch from the inside, and that the many ways it can go astray add to the problem.

questions.q: True or false: In the Minneapolis story, the undercover cop put his .45 automatic in the food bag because it was the more reliable weapon in a bag.
questions.explain: He used the .38 with a covered hammer, since the automatic would jam if fired inside the bag.

questions.q: Put the main moves of the Minneapolis undercover operation in the order they happened.
items: Robbers phone in a large order to a restaurant
Garman picks up the food posing as the delivery man
Garman parks with his brights on the front door
Two more men flip hoods over their heads and approach
Garman fires four rounds through the bag
questions.explain: The story runs from the phoned-in order, through the decoy delivery, to the ambush and the shooting through the bag.

questions.q: Match each element of the opening with what it is.
pairs: Self-inflicted fatalities from spectacularly poor judgment
Repeated the same phones and addresses
Undercover cop who posed as the delivery man
questions.explain: Each item is a concept or example from the chapter's opening.

questions.q: Sort each item by its role in the opening.
groups: Reason we start at a disadvantage

items.t: Incompetence leads us to overestimate our competence
We are misled by illusions, biases and the stories we tell
Recognizing competence in others
Finding objective ways to track progress
Adopting learning strategies that get results

questions.explain: The opening names two reasons for our disadvantage and then lists what we must do to improve.

questions.q: Which description fits what Kahneman calls System 1?
options: Unconscious, intuitive, immediate sizing-up of a situation
Slower conscious analysis that considers choices and self-control
Deliberate rehearsal of moves until they become second nature
Skeptical analysis that checks impulses and plans ahead
questions.explain: System 1 is the automatic system: unconscious, intuitive and immediate. The other options describe System 2, which analyzes, plans and trains System 1.

questions.q: A violinist slowly talks through the fingering of a hard passage, planning each shift, so that it will later come automatically. According to the two-systems idea, what is she using now?
options: System 1, because the passage is already automatic for her
System 1, because planning is a form of intuition
Neither system, because practice is a habit and not thinking
System 2, used to train System 1 for later reflex use
questions.explain: System 2 is the slower, conscious process, and we use it to train System 1 to respond to demanding situations. This is like the running back walking through his playbook.

questions.q: In the example of the infant who calls a passing stranger Dada, what role does the blushing mother play?
options: A System 1 reflex warning the infant of danger
A surrogate System 2 helping the infant refine her System 1
A source of leading questions that distort the infant's memory
A teacher suffering from the curse of knowledge
questions.explain: The infant's outburst is System 1 at work. The mother's correction acts as a stand-in System 2 that helps the child refine her automatic responses.

questions.q: What makes System 1 so powerful, according to the authors?
options: It is the only system able to plan ahead and identify choices
It cannot err once a person has practiced for thousands of hours
It checks impulses and keeps us in charge of our actions
It draws on accumulated years of experience and deep emotions
questions.explain: System 1 draws on accumulated experience and deep emotions, giving survival reflexes and the deftness earned through deliberate practice. Checking impulses and planning ahead belong to System 2, and System 1 can still be misled by illusion.

questions.q: According to the flight book, what should the Flight 006 crew have done when engine number 4 lost power at altitude?
options: Climb above 41,000 feet and let the autopilot restart the engine
Take manual control and descend below 30,000 feet to restart it
Shut down the remaining engines and prepare an emergency landing
Hold altitude with the autopilot and wait for the engine to recover
questions.explain: The prescribed procedure was to take manual control and descend below 30,000 feet. Instead the crew held altitude on autopilot, which is what they actually did.

questions.q: Why did the Flight 006 captain feel he was flying level while the plane was rolling to the right?
options: The attitude gauges had already failed and showed him a false horizon
The first officer reported that the wings were level at that moment
The plane's trajectory made his inner ear report level flight
Thick clouds had numbed his senses and hidden every cue of motion
questions.explain: His System 1 clue, the vestibular reflex of the inner ear, gave the sensation of level flight because of the plane's trajectory. His System 2 clues would have been the horizon and the instruments.

questions.q: In the aviation term spatial disorientation, which two elements combine to make it deadly?
options: No visible horizon plus sensations so convincing that gauges seem wrong
Engine failure at altitude plus an autopilot that corrects the roll
Fatigue on a long flight plus a hasty reading of the airspeed gauge
Thick clouds plus radio instructions that conflict with the flight book
questions.explain: The authors define it as losing sight of the horizon combined with sensory perception that does not match reality but is so convincing that pilots decide their instruments have failed.

questions.q: What lesson do the authors take from the Flight 006 incident?
options: Cultivate a disciplined System 2 that keeps checking instruments
Rely on System 1 once training has made its responses reliable
Switch off the autopilot whenever an engine loses power in flight
Trust your senses when they conflict strongly with the gauges
questions.explain: The report shows how quickly training and professionalism can be hijacked by System 1 illusion, so we need a disciplined System 2 that keeps one eye on the instruments.

questions.q: Contrast System 1 and System 2 as Kahneman describes them, and explain how System 2 can help System 1.
questions.a: System 1 is automatic, unconscious, intuitive and immediate, sizing up a situation in the blink of an eye, like the running back dodging tackles. System 2 is the slower, controlled process of conscious analysis that considers choices, makes decisions and exerts self-control. We also use System 2 to train System 1 to respond to situations that demand reflexive action, as when the running back walks through his playbook or the cop practices taking a gun from a shooter.

questions.q: Using the two systems, explain what went wrong on China Airlines Flight 006 and what the authors conclude from it.
questions.a: After engine 4 lost power, the captain stayed at altitude on autopilot and fixed on the engine restart and the airspeed indicator instead of monitoring all his instruments, a lapse of System 2. He then trusted his sense of flying level over his gauges and decided the gauges had failed when they showed an unlikely dive, so System 1 illusion won out. The authors conclude that we need to cultivate a disciplined System 2 that keeps one eye on the instruments.

questions.q: Why is System 1 both powerful and risky, and what must we learn to do about it?
questions.a: It is powerful because it draws on years of accumulated experience and deep emotions, giving us survival reflexes and the deftness earned through thousands of hours of deliberate practice. It is risky because when its conclusions arise from misperception or illusion they can steer us into trouble, and it can be very hard to overrule. We must learn when to trust our intuition and when to question it, using System 2 to check impulses and think through implications.

questions.q: What Kahneman calls the ____ system is unconscious, intuitive and immediate.
questions.explain: System 1, the automatic system, sizes up a situation in the blink of an eye using our senses and memories.

questions.q: System 2 is the ____ system, our slower process of conscious analysis and reasoning.
questions.explain: System 2 considers choices, makes decisions and exerts self-control, and it also trains System 1.

questions.q: Malcolm Gladwell's book on the interplay between instant judgment and thoughtful analysis is titled ____.
questions.explain: The authors cite Gladwell's Blink as the book on how instant sizing-up plays against our capacity for skepticism and analysis.

questions.q: Pilots lose sight of the horizon and trust convincing sensations over gauges in what is called spatial ____.
questions.explain: Spatial disorientation is the aeronautical term for losing sight of the horizon while relying on sensory perception that does not jibe with reality.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of System 2 at work in the chapter?
options: The running back walking through his playbook
The cop practicing taking a gun from a shooter
The neurosurgeon rehearsing his repair of the torn sinus
The running back dodging tacklers in his dash
The infant calling a passing stranger Dada
questions.explain: Rehearsing and practicing deliberately are System 2 activities used to train System 1. Dodging tacklers and the infant's cry are System 1 responses.

questions.q: Which of these contributed to the Flight 006 emergency?
options: Holding at 41,000 feet on autopilot instead of descending
Preoccupation with the restart and the airspeed indicator
Deciding that the gauges had failed when they showed a dive
Following the flight book step by step
The first officer overriding the captain's orders
questions.explain: The crew ignored the prescribed descent, the captain fixed on a single indicator, and they distrusted a gauge reading that seemed too unlikely. They did not follow the flight book.

questions.q: True or false: System 1 is the slower process of conscious analysis and reasoning.
questions.explain: That describes System 2. System 1 is automatic, unconscious, intuitive and immediate.

questions.q: True or false: On Flight 006, the captain trusted his senses over his gauges once the situation spiraled out of control.
questions.explain: The crew decided the dive angle was so unlikely that the gauges had failed, an example of System 1 illusion overriding instruments.

questions.q: Put these events of China Airlines Flight 006 in the order they happened.
items: Engine 4 loses power at 41,000 feet
The crew holds altitude on autopilot to restart it
The plane rolls to the right as thrust becomes asymmetrical
The plane descends into high clouds that hide the horizon
The plane turns upside down and dives
The crew breaks through the clouds at 11,000 feet
questions.explain: The sequence runs from the engine loss, to holding altitude, to the roll, to cloud cover, to the inverted dive, to recovery below the clouds.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning in the chapter.
pairs: Slower, controlled conscious analysis and self-control
Losing the horizon while convincing senses contradict the gauges
questions.explain: Systems 1 and 2 are Kahneman's two analytic systems, metacognition is self-monitoring, and spatial disorientation is the pilot's illusion.

questions.q: Match each Flight 006 detail with what it was.
pairs: Cruising altitude where engine 4 lost power
Altitude below which the flight book said to descend
Altitude at which the crew broke through the clouds
Bank beyond which the plane turned upside down
The outboard engine that lost power
questions.explain: These numbers mark the key points in the Flight 006 sequence.

questions.q: Match each example from the Two Systems section with what it illustrates.
pairs: Infant cries Dada at a stranger
Cop notes a bead of sweat
Captain feels he is flying level
questions.explain: These examples show System 1 and System 2 at work, and System 1 being misled.

questions.q: Sort each example into the system it shows.

items.t: A running back dodging tackles
An infant crying Dada at a stranger
A cop reacting to a bead of sweat
A survival reflex in danger
Walking through the moves in a playbook
Rehearsing a surgical repair
Planning ahead and checking impulses

questions.explain: System 1 is automatic and immediate; System 2 is deliberate, planned and used to train System 1.

questions.q: What does David Dunning mean by motivated reasoning, as quoted in the chapter?
options: Underestimating how long another person needs to learn a skill we have mastered
Assuming that other people share our own beliefs and interpretations
Skill at convincing ourselves of pleasing conclusions, not unwelcome ones
Viewing events after the fact as more predictable than they were
questions.explain: Dunning describes the sheer genius people have at convincing themselves of congenial conclusions while denying inconvenient ones. The other options are the curse of knowledge, the false consensus effect and hindsight bias.

questions.q: In the study where people overheard a phone conversation while doing reading and anagram tasks, what was found?
options: Hearing both sides was more distracting, since it carried more content
Hearing one side was more distracting than hearing both sides
Both versions distracted equally, but half-conversations were recalled worse
Neither version distracted, since participants ignored the calls successfully
questions.explain: Overhearing half a conversation proved more distracting than overhearing both halves, and its content was better recalled later by the unintentional eavesdroppers.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, was overhearing half a conversation so distracting?
options: One-sided talk is usually louder and more emotional than ordinary talk
Listeners lost track of the reading task and never returned to it
Hearing one voice triggers System 2 to start planning a reply
Listeners tried to infer the missing half to complete the narrative
questions.explain: The authors suggest listeners felt strongly compelled to infer the missing half so as to make a complete narrative, showing our drive to resolve ambiguity.

questions.q: Witnesses watch the same video of a car hitting a fence. One group is asked how fast it was going when it “crumpled” into the fence, another when it “touched” the fence. Based on the book's findings on suggestion, what is likely?
options: Both groups give about the same estimate, since they saw the same video
The “crumpled” group tends to give the higher speed estimate
The group asked about “touched” tends to give the higher speed estimate
Estimates differ only if the witnesses were hypnotized beforehand
questions.explain: In the book's study, the verb smashed produced higher speed estimates than contacted for the same collision. This shows memory can be shaped by the way a question is asked.

questions.q: Why are people interviewed after hypnosis barred from testifying in court in almost all states?
options: Guesses made under hypnosis later get recalled as real
Hypnosis blocks recall of events that did actually take place
Hypnotized people are legally treated as unable to give consent
Hypnotic interviews are usually done too long after the event
questions.explain: The hypnotic interview encourages producing everything that comes to mind, so people generate much erroneous information that they later remember as actual experience.

questions.q: In the case of Donald Thomson, why did the victim's description of her attacker match him?
options: Police showed her his photograph before she described the attacker
She remembered him from an earlier meeting and recognized him at once
A hypnotic interview led her to produce guesses that she later believed
Under extreme stress, she gave the face she had just seen on television
questions.explain: Thomson had been on live television at the time, and the woman had been watching. Her quick but mistaken System 1 reaction, probably due to her extreme emotional state, supplied the wrong description.

questions.q: A veteran carpenter tells a first-day apprentice that a tricky joint takes only an hour to learn, though it usually takes days. Which illusion does this best show?
options: Hindsight bias, seeing events as more predictable after they occur
False consensus, assuming others share one's beliefs
The curse of knowledge, underestimating others' learning time
Imagination inflation, believing a vividly imagined event happened
questions.explain: The curse of knowledge is the tendency to underestimate how long it takes another person to learn what we have already mastered, as with the calculus instructor.

questions.q: After a surprising election result, a neighbor says it was obvious all along, though he made no such prediction beforehand. Which bias is this?
options: The curse of knowledge, underestimating how hard others find a task
Memory conformity, absorbing a friend's wrong detail into memory
Hindsight bias, viewing events as more predictable after the fact
Flashbulb memory, keeping a vivid image of where one heard the news
questions.explain: Hindsight bias, the knew-it-all-along effect, is viewing events after the fact as more predictable than they were before they occurred, like the market pundits.

questions.q: A student rereads a beautifully clear textbook chapter three times and feels certain she has mastered it. Which idea from the book explains her confidence?
options: Rereading strengthens memory routes, so her confidence is justified
Her flashbulb memory of the chapter has made it feel indelible
Her false consensus leads her to assume classmates know less
Fluency with the text is being mistaken for mastery of its content
questions.explain: Fluency illusions arise when we mistake fluency with a text, gained from rereading, for accessible knowledge, so students overestimate how well they will do on a test.

questions.q: In the long-running survey of memories of the September 11 attacks, which memories changed most over the years?
options: The most emotional personal details, which were also held most confidently
The broad outlines of the attacks that the media had thoroughly reported
The least emotional details, which respondents held with little confidence
The details respondents had reported to others within the first week
questions.explain: The most emotional personal memories were those respondents were most confident about and, paradoxically, those that changed most. The broad outlines were well remembered.

questions.q: Explain what the one-sided phone conversation study shows about our need for narrative.
questions.a: Participants doing reading and anagram tasks were more distracted by overhearing one side of a phone conversation than both sides, and they recalled the content of the partial conversation better. The authors suggest they felt compelled to infer the missing half to make a complete narrative. This shows how strongly we are drawn to resolve ambiguity and give events a rational explanation, which also applies to the story we build about our own lives.

questions.q: Explain what it means to say that memory is a reconstruction, using the Helen Keller example.
questions.a: We cannot remember every aspect of an event, so we keep the elements with the greatest emotional significance and fill the gaps with details of our own that fit our narrative but may be wrong. We also remember things that were implied but not stated. People who read a paragraph about a troubled girl named Helen Keller later wrongly recalled the phrase deaf, dumb, and blind as being in the text, while a group that read about Carol Harris rarely did.

questions.q: A friend keeps asking you to picture in detail a time you got lost at a fair as a child, though it never happened. Using the book's idea of imagination inflation, what might happen to your memory?
questions.a: Vividly imagining an event can lead you, later, to believe it actually happened. Adults who were asked whether they ever broke a window with their hand were more likely to say on a later inventory that they believed it happened. Imagined events can seat themselves in the mind as firmly as memories of real events, so you might eventually come to remember getting lost at the fair.

questions.q: Explain why guessing, as in a hypnotic interview, can corrupt a witness's memory.
questions.a: Witnesses struggling to recall are sometimes told to let their minds roam and say whatever comes to mind, even a guess. Guessing makes people produce their own misinformation, which, if left uncorrected, they may later retrieve as memories. Under hypnosis people produce much erroneous information and later remember those events as actual experiences, even when it is known they did not occur, which is why such testimony is barred in almost all states.

questions.q: Define the curse of knowledge and hindsight bias, and say how they are related.
questions.a: The curse of knowledge is our tendency to underestimate how long it will take another person to learn something or perform a task that we have already mastered, as with the calculus instructor who can no longer see things as a beginner does. Hindsight bias, the knew-it-all-along effect, is viewing events after the fact as more predictable than they were before they occurred, like pundits explaining the day's market moves. The authors call the curse of knowledge close kin to hindsight bias.

questions.q: How can familiarity and fluency create a false feeling of knowing? Give an example of each.
questions.a: Something we have heard before carries a warmth of familiarity that can be mistaken for memory, so repeated claims, even a big lie, can come to be accepted as true. Fluency illusions arise when we mistake ease with a text for mastery of its content. For example, a lucid presentation can make a difficult idea seem simple, and rereading can make a student overestimate how well she will do on a test.

questions.q: Describe memory conformity and the false consensus effect, and say how they differ.
questions.a: Memory conformity, or the social contagion of memory, is the tendency for our memories to align with those of people around us, so one person's wrong detail can infect another's memory, although a partner's accurate details can also improve ours. The false consensus effect, the obverse, is assuming that others share our beliefs and failing to see how idiosyncratic our own understanding is. In the first, others shape our memory; in the second, we wrongly project our views onto them.

questions.q: Why is confidence in a memory not a reliable sign of its accuracy? Use the findings on flashbulb memories.
questions.a: Flashbulb memories of national tragedies feel vivid and indelible, and the broad outlines are well remembered, but our memory of personal circumstances, such as where we were, may not be accurate. In a survey of fifteen hundred Americans a week, a year, three years and ten years after 9/11, the most emotional personal details were those held with the most confidence and, paradoxically, those that changed most. So a vivid, confident memory can still be wrong.

questions.q: Explain the paradox that the changeable nature of memory both skews our perceptions and is essential to learning.
questions.a: Each time we recall a memory we strengthen the routes to it, and this ability to strengthen, expand and modify memory is how we deepen learning and broaden connections. The more associations we link to a memory, such as an image, a place or a story, the more cues we have to retrieve it, rather like a Google search. But because memory is a shape-shifter, even cherished memories may not match what happened, so we should stay open to the fallibility of our certainties.

questions.q: Dunning's term for the genius people have at convincing themselves of congenial conclusions is ____ reasoning.
questions.explain: Motivated reasoning is the penchant for believing conclusions we like and denying the truth of inconvenient ones.

questions.q: When asked to imagine an event vividly, people may later come to believe it occurred, a tendency called imagination ____.
questions.explain: Imagination inflation shows that vividly imagined hypothetical events can seat themselves in the mind as firmly as memories of real ones.

questions.q: Our tendency to underestimate how long it takes another person to learn what we have mastered is the curse of ____.
questions.explain: The curse of knowledge afflicts teachers who can no longer place themselves in the shoes of a beginner.

questions.q: In hindsight bias, we view events after the fact as more ____ than they were before they occurred.
questions.explain: Hindsight bias is also called the knew-it-all-along effect, as when pundits explain the market's moves after the fact.

questions.q: Mistaking ease with a text for mastery of its content is called a ____ illusion.
questions.explain: Fluency illusions explain why students who reread a text overestimate how well they will do on a test.

questions.q: Memory conformity is also called the social ____ of memory.
questions.explain: One person's error can infect another person's memory when a group reminisces, so memory aligns with the people around us.

questions.q: Humans tend to assume that others share their beliefs, a process called the false ____ effect.
questions.explain: The false consensus effect is the obverse of social influence: we fail to see that our understanding is idiosyncratic.

questions.q: Vivid, seemingly indelible memories of national tragedies are called ____ memories.
questions.explain: Flashbulb memories, named for the vivid images we retain, are confident but their personal details can change.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter list among the ways System 1 and System 2 judgments can be led astray?
options: Perceptual illusions
Faulty narrative
Distortions of memory
Retrieval practice spread over time
Delaying feedback until after a test
questions.explain: The chapter lists perceptual illusions, faulty narrative, memory distortions, failing to see that a new problem needs a new solution, and cognitive biases. Spaced retrieval is a learning strategy, not a hazard.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter give as ways memory can be distorted?
options: The wording of a question that suggests an answer
Vividly imagining an event that never occurred
Interference from other events, such as photos viewed earlier
Recalling the material several times with spacing
Receiving corrective feedback after a test
questions.explain: Suggestion, imagination inflation and interference from other events are all described as distortions. Spaced recall and corrective feedback are not.

questions.q: Which of these were part of the car-collision study of suggestion?
options: Viewers watched a video of a car running a stop sign
Those asked about cars that “contacted” gave about thirty-two miles per hour
Those asked about cars that “smashed” gave about forty-one miles per hour
The witnesses were hypnotized before judging speed
Witnesses read a police report before judging speed
questions.explain: The study used a video and compared the verbs contacted and smashed, with average estimates of thirty-two and forty-one miles per hour. Hypnosis and police reports were not part of it.

questions.q: Which of these statements about memory conformity does the chapter support?
options: A wrong detail added by someone in a group can enter your own memory
One person's error can infect another person's memory
A partner's accurate details can sometimes improve your memory
It occurs only for memories of childhood events
It affects only people who feel unsure of their memories
questions.explain: The chapter says that memories align with those of people around us, so errors can spread, though accurate details from others can also update a hazy memory.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say about why changeable memory is valuable?
options: Recalling a memory strengthens the routes to it
More associations to a memory give more cues for retrieval
Modifying memory helps deepen learning and broaden connections
Memories are stored unchanged like objective records
Vivid memories are always accurate
questions.explain: The authors call memory's changeability essential to learning because each recall strengthens and modifies it, and associations add retrieval cues. It also makes memory fallible.

questions.q: Which of these are true of flashbulb memories according to the chapter?
options: The broad outlines of the events are well remembered
Memory of personal circumstances may not be accurate
The most emotional details were held with most confidence yet changed most
Confidence is a reliable sign that a memory is accurate
They stay exactly as first formed for ten years
questions.explain: The 9/11 survey found that confident emotional personal details changed most over time, so confidence does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.q: True or false: Readers of a paragraph about Helen Keller were more likely than readers of a paragraph about Carol Harris to wrongly recall the phrase deaf, dumb, and blind as being in the text.
questions.explain: People remember things that were implied but not stated, and the Helen Keller paragraph implied this phrase.

questions.q: True or false: People interviewed after hypnosis are allowed to testify in almost all states because hypnosis reliably improves accuracy.
questions.explain: They are barred in almost all states because hypnosis leads people to produce erroneous information they later recall as real.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say humans give greater credence to an objective record of a past event than to their subjective remembering of it.
questions.explain: Humans do not give greater credence to an objective record, and it is nearly impossible to avoid basing judgments on subjective experience.

questions.q: True or false: A student who rereads a clear explanation and feels she knew it all along may be experiencing a fluency illusion.
questions.explain: A lucid presentation can make a difficult idea seem simple, and the fluency gained from rereading is easily mistaken for mastery.

questions.q: True or false: Social influences on memory are always harmful to the accuracy of what we remember.
questions.explain: If someone recalls details of a joint memory on which you are hazy, your later memory can become more accurate.

questions.q: Put the survey points of the study of memories of September 11 in time order.
items: One week after the attacks
One year later
Three years later
Ten years later
questions.explain: Respondents were surveyed a week after the attacks and again at one, three and ten years.

questions.q: Put these memory distortions in the order the chapter presents them.
items: Imagination inflation
Suggestion through the wording of a question
Interference from other events
The curse of knowledge
Memory conformity
questions.explain: The chapter moves from imagination inflation to suggestion, interference, the curse of knowledge, and later to social influence on memory.

questions.q: Put the steps of imagination inflation in order.
items: A person is asked whether an event happened
The person vividly imagines the event
Later the person is more likely to believe it occurred
questions.explain: Asking the question leads people to imagine the event, and having imagined it makes them more likely to think it occurred.

questions.q: Put the steps of the one-sided phone conversation effect in order.
items: A person overhears only half of a phone conversation
The person tries to infer the missing half to form a narrative
The person is more distracted and recalls its content better
questions.explain: Compelled to complete the narrative, listeners were distracted more than by a full conversation.

questions.q: Put the steps by which guessing corrupts memory in order.
items: A witness is told to let the mind roam and produce guesses
The guesses become the witness's own misinformation
Later the witness recalls the guesses as actual experience
questions.explain: Guessing produces misinformation that, left uncorrected, may later be retrieved as memory.

questions.q: Match each person with what the chapter ties to them.
pairs: Wrote a New York Times series on illusion
Judgments are nearly impossible to separate from subjective experience
questions.explain: Each person is tied to a specific idea or work cited in the chapter.

questions.q: Match each illusion with its definition.
pairs: Believing a vividly imagined event actually happened
Underestimating how long others need to learn what we know
Mistaking ease with a text for mastery of it
Seeing events as more predictable after the fact
questions.explain: These are five illusions or biases defined in the chapter.

questions.q: Match each study with its finding.
pairs: Helen Keller and Carol Harris paragraphs
Implied phrase wrongly recalled as in the text
Video of a collision with the word smashed
Higher speed estimates than with contacted
Question about breaking a window with a hand
Later belief that the event happened
More distracting than hearing both sides
Survey of fifteen hundred Americans on 9/11
Most emotional details changed most over the years
questions.explain: Each study illustrates a different distortion of memory or judgment.

questions.q: Match each everyday scenario with the illusion it shows.
pairs: A witness who saw mugshots picks one of those faces from a lineup
Friends reminiscing and you absorb a friend's wrong detail
A pundit explains the day's market moves after they happen
A teacher forgets how hard the topic is for beginners
A repeated slogan starts to feel true
questions.explain: Each scenario is an application of an illusion the chapter describes.

questions.q: Match each memory idea with its meaning.
pairs: We fill gaps with details that fit our narrative
The wording of a question shapes what we recall
Other events muddle what we remember
Vivid memory of where we were during a tragedy
Our memory aligns with those around us
questions.explain: These match terms to their definitions as used in the chapter.

questions.q: Match each number with what it counts in the chapter.
pairs: Average estimate when the cars contacted each other
Average estimate when the cars smashed into each other
Speed limit in the speeding example
questions.explain: These are figures from the suggestion study and the 9/11 memory survey.

questions.q: Match each example from the chapter with the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Neighbors disagreeing on a bond issue
One-sided cell phone talk in public
questions.explain: Each example is used in the chapter to illustrate a distinct illusion.

questions.q: Sort each memory item by how the chapter treats it.

items.t: The broad outlines of the attacks
Facts thoroughly reported by the media
Where you were when you got the news
How you learned of the attacks
What you did afterward

questions.explain: The broad outlines of flashbulb events are well remembered, but personal circumstances may not be accurate.

questions.q: Sort each item as a hazard to judgment or a safeguard against it.

items.t: Motivated reasoning
Imagination inflation
Fluency with a reread text
Confidence in a vivid memory
Using System 2 to scan all instruments
Staying open to the fallibility of your certainties

questions.explain: The chapter treats these as hazards, and treats disciplined System 2 checking and openness to being wrong as safeguards.

questions.q: Sort each scenario by the effect it shows.

items.t: After a reunion chat you recall the wrong color a friend mentioned
A friend's accurate details fix a hazy part of your memory
You assume all coworkers see the bond issue as you do
You are surprised that a friend disagrees on something you thought obvious

questions.explain: Memory conformity is others shaping our memory; false consensus is assuming that others share our views.

questions.q: Sort each scenario by the bias it shows.

items.t: A mechanic underestimates how long an apprentice needs
A chess master expects a beginner to grasp an opening fast
A fan says a team's loss was obvious after the game
A commentator explains the market fall as predictable that same day

questions.explain: The curse of knowledge misjudges what is hard for others; hindsight bias misjudges how predictable the past was.

questions.q: Sort each point about memory by its effect.

items.t: Each recall strengthens the routes to the memory
More associations create more retrieval cues
Modifying memory broadens connections
Filling gaps with details that fit our narrative
Remembering things that were implied but not stated
Keeping what is emotionally significant

questions.explain: The changeable nature of memory both deepens learning and skews perceptions.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 5 present Kahneman's two systems before its catalogue of illusions and memory distortions?
options: The illusions are all caused by the pilot errors in Flight 006
System 1 is prone to illusion and needs System 2 to check it
The two systems are the tools offered at the end for calibrating judgment
Memory distortions affect System 2 alone and never System 1
questions.explain: The section on the two systems establishes that System 1 is deeply influential but susceptible to illusion and that System 2 must manage it, which frames the hazards that follow.

questions.q: What does the chapter's title, Avoid Illusions of Knowing, signal about the argument that follows?
options: Feeling that we know is unreliable, so objective gauges are needed
Knowing is mostly illusory, so learners should stop trusting any facts
Illusions affect only pilots, so ordinary learners can ignore them
Testing oneself creates illusions, so learners should avoid it
questions.explain: The chapter warns that our subjective sense of knowing misleads us and ends by recommending objective reference points, like cockpit instruments, for calibrating judgment.

questions.q: How do the five sections of Chapter 5 build from a problem toward a response?
questions.a: The opening poses the problem: we must judge our own thinking but are poor at it. Two Systems of Knowing introduces System 1 and System 2 with the pilot example, and Illusions and Memory Distortions catalogues how judgment goes astray. Mental Models and Unskilled and Unaware of It extend the problem to misapplied solutions and incompetence that hides itself, and the closing section, Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment, answers with objective gauges.

questions.q: What role does the Flight 006 story play in the chapter's argument, and how does the later material echo it?
questions.a: It gives a vivid case of System 1 illusion overriding trained professionals, and its lesson is to keep a disciplined System 2 watching the instruments. The chapter later reuses the cockpit image: after cataloguing the hazards it says we need objective gauges outside ourselves, like instruments, so that our judgment squares with the real world.

questions.q: Chapter 5 follows Embrace Difficulties and precedes the chapter titled Get Beyond ____ Styles.
questions.explain: Chapter 6, Get Beyond Learning Styles, comes next after the chapter on illusions of knowing.

questions.q: Which of these are sections of Chapter 5?
options: Mental Models
Unskilled and Unaware of It
Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
Interleaved Practice
Varied Practice
questions.explain: Mental Models, Unskilled and Unaware of It and Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment are Chapter 5 sections. Interleaved and Varied Practice are sections of Chapter 3.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter first catalogues illusions and memory distortions and only afterward introduces Kahneman's two systems.
questions.explain: The chapter begins with Two Systems of Knowing and then moves to Illusions and Memory Distortions.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 5 in the order they appear.
items: Two Systems of Knowing
Illusions and Memory Distortions
Mental Models
Unskilled and Unaware of It
Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the two systems, through hazards and misapplied models and incompetence, to tools for calibrating judgment.

questions.q: Match each chapter number with its title.
questions.explain: These are consecutive chapter titles from the book's table of contents.

questions.q: In Make It Stick, what are mental models?
options: Bundled problem-solving steps that run with little conscious thought
Conscious checklists that must be reread step by step before every task
Vivid memories of single events that become part of a personal narrative
Pictures of facts held in mind mainly so they can be repeated on a test
questions.explain: The authors liken mental models to smart-phone apps in the brain: steps that get bundled together as mastery grows, such as a cop's routine traffic-stop choreography. They are not checklists, because the steps have been compressed into one unit.

questions.q: According to physicist Eric Mazur, why does knowing something better make it harder to teach?
options: Experts lose patience with students who keep asking about the basics
The steps inside expert models fade into the background of memory
Experts forget much of the material itself once they stop using it daily
Experts depend on System 1 intuition and cannot put reasoning into words
questions.explain: As expertise grows, the models grow more complex and their small steps are no longer visible to the expert, which is the curse of knowledge. The problem is not forgetting the subject but losing sight of how it looked to a beginner.

questions.q: When an experienced physicist sorts physics problems, what does she tend to group them by?
options: The apparatus in the problem, such as a pulley or an inclined plane
How difficult each problem looked when she first met it
The underlying principle, such as Newton's laws
How many calculation steps each problem needs to solve
questions.explain: The expert has built a library of principles and sorts problems by which one applies. Novices instead group problems by surface features like the apparatus being manipulated.

questions.q: In the brain-tumor case that neurosurgeon Mike Ebersold was called in to help with, why did the usual slow-and-careful model of tumor removal fail?
options: The resident lacked the instruments needed to work carefully around the growth
A clean margin cannot be achieved when a tumor sits inside the brain tissue
Working slowly would have damaged the surrounding nerves more than cutting fast would
Bleeding behind the growth pressed on the brain, so the tumor had to come out fast
questions.explain: The usual model calls for taking your time, but with bleeding behind a brain tumor the situation needed the opposite: quick removal so the blood could drain. The lesson is knowing when to switch gears.

questions.q: A veteran mechanic sees symptoms that look just like ones he has fixed many times, applies his usual repair, and makes the car worse because the real fault was different. Which idea from the book does this show?
options: A new problem looked familiar, so he pulled out a stored solution that did not fit
He assumed other mechanics share his diagnosis, which is the false consensus effect
He confused fluent reading of the repair manual with real mastery of the repair
He imagined a past repair so vividly that he believed it had really happened
questions.explain: The book warns that mental models can trip us when a problem that appears familiar is actually different, so the solution we reach for fails or makes things worse. Noticing when a model is not working is a skill to cultivate.

questions.q: True or false: In the tune-tapping experiment, the listeners guessed the tune correctly about half the time, as the tappers had predicted.
questions.explain: The tappers, who had the tune in mind, predicted 50 percent success, but listeners guessed right only 2.5 percent of the time, no better than chance.

questions.q: True or false: Mazur says the person who best knows what a student is struggling with in grasping new concepts is another student rather than the professor.
questions.explain: A professor's own bundled mental models hide the steps a beginner must work through, whereas a fellow student is still close to those steps.

questions.q: In the tune-tapping experiment, each tune came from a fixed set of ____ tunes, so the statistical chance of guessing it was 4 percent.
questions.explain: One in twenty-five is 4 percent, yet tappers thought listeners would succeed half the time.

questions.q: A professor who assumes students will readily follow what seems fundamental to her is making a ____ error, a misjudgment of the match between what she knows and what her students know.
questions.explain: The authors call this a metacognitive error because it is a failure in judging the state of knowledge in her own and her students' minds.

questions.q: Match each person to the mental model the book gives as an example of their work.
pairs: The choreography of a routine traffic stop
The steps and ingredients for a sixteen-ounce decaf frappuccino
Newton's laws of motion and conservation of momentum
questions.explain: Each is a bundle of steps that a practiced person runs with little conscious thought.

questions.q: Which of these are true of the experienced physicist who goes to teach an intro physics class, as the book describes her?
options: She has bundled underlying steps into one unified mental model
She tends to sort problems by their underlying principles
She may forget that her students have not yet mastered those steps
She groups problems by surface features such as pulleys and inclined planes
questions.explain: Surface-feature grouping is what novices do. The expert's bundled principles are exactly what make it hard to see the students' difficulty.

questions.q: Sort each description by whether it fits the experienced physicist or the novice student in the book's account.

items.t: Sorts problems by Newton's laws or conservation of momentum
Groups all the pulley problems together
Groups all the inclined-plane problems together
Treats several steps as one bundled mental model
Takes the apparatus in a problem to be what matters
Recognizes which underlying principle a problem calls for

questions.explain: The expert organizes by principle; the novice organizes by the surface features of the apparatus.

questions.q: Using the physics professor and the tune-tapping experiment, explain why experts misjudge what beginners find easy.
questions.a: As people gain expertise, the steps of a complex skill are bundled into mental models and fade from memory, which is the curse of knowledge. The physicist therefore forgets that students lack the steps she has bundled, a metacognitive error. In the tapping experiment, tappers who had the tune in mind expected listeners to guess right 50 percent of the time, but listeners managed only 2.5 percent.

questions.q: What does the neurosurgery example teach about mental models, and what ability does the author say we must cultivate?
questions.a: Mental models are useful libraries of solutions, but they can fail when a situation looks familiar and is actually different. Ebersold's usual slow, careful tumor removal would have killed a patient with bleeding behind a brain tumor, which needed fast cutting. We must cultivate the ability to discern when our models are not working and reach for a different solution.

questions.q: What does the Dunning-Kruger effect claim about incompetent people?
options: They underrate their competence, so they avoid tasks they could do well
They overrate themselves, being unable to tell it from incompetence
They know they perform poorly but lack the motivation to do anything
They rate themselves accurately but misjudge how competent others are
questions.explain: Because they lack the skills to tell competence from incompetence, they sense no gap between their performance and what is desirable. The effect is that they feel little reason to change.

questions.q: In Dunning and Kruger's second experiment, what happened when bottom-quartile students were shown the other students' more competent answers?
options: They lowered their estimates to match the level of the better students
They became accurate about the questions missed but not about those they got right
They did not become more accurate and tended to raise their inflated estimates
They left their estimates exactly as they were, since nothing had changed
questions.explain: Seeing better answers did not help the weakest students recognize their mistakes. They actually raised their already inflated self-estimates.

questions.q: In Dunning and Kruger's third experiment, what happened to bottom-quartile students who got ten minutes of training in logic?
options: They scored much higher on a retest but still believed they had performed far better than they had
They became more accurate about other students' scores but not about their own
They changed nothing about their estimates, just like the half given an unrelated task
They became much more accurate in estimating how many questions they got right and how they ranked
questions.explain: Teaching them how to test the accuracy of a syllogism improved their metacognition, so their self-judgments were far closer to reality. The untrained half held to the mistaken belief that they had done well.

questions.q: A student keeps a stack of vocabulary flashcards and removes each card from the stack the first time she answers it correctly. What does the book say about this habit?
options: It is typical, but she drops cards far sooner than she should
It is efficient, because one correct answer shows that a word has been learned
It is sensible, as long as she shuffles the dropped cards back in after a week
It is harmless, provided she also rereads the whole stack before the test
questions.explain: The book reports that most students drop a card after getting it right once or twice, far sooner than they should. Even students who know retrieval is a good strategy often fail to persist long enough.

questions.q: Why do the authors say most students will learn academics better under an instructor than through self-directed learning?
options: Students who choose their own study methods generally learn nothing at all
An instructor knows where improvement is needed and structures the practice
Lectures from an instructor are more effective for retention than retrieval practice
Students become more motivated to practice when someone else sets the deadlines
questions.explain: Students tend to overestimate their learning, especially those using the weakest strategies. The football player does not leave practice to intuition; his coach guides it.

questions.q: True or false: Dunning and Kruger found that incompetent people cannot be helped to judge their own performance more accurately.
questions.explain: They showed that incompetent people can be taught to raise their competence by learning the skills to judge their own performance, which improves their metacognition.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, students who use the least effective study strategies tend to overestimate their learning the most.
questions.explain: This is the paradox the authors describe: misplaced confidence leaves these students with no inclination to change their habits.

questions.q: In Dunning and Kruger's first experiment, students who scored at the ____ percentile on average believed their logical reasoning ability fell at the sixty-eighth percentile.
questions.explain: The least competent students were the most out of touch with how they had actually performed.

questions.q: In the third experiment, half the students received ten minutes of training in how to test the accuracy of a ____.
questions.explain: The training in logic was brief but led to much better self-estimates among the weakest performers.

questions.q: One theory for why incompetent people do not learn through experience that they are unskilled is that people seldom receive negative ____ from others, because people do not like to deliver bad news.
questions.explain: Everyday life seldom tells us bluntly when we are not good at something, unlike the public picking of softball teams.

questions.q: Match each of Dunning and Kruger's logic-test experiments to its finding.
pairs: The least competent students rated their ability far above their actual standing
Weak students shown better answers raised their already inflated estimates
Weak students given brief logic training judged their performance much more accurately
questions.explain: Together the experiments show overestimation, resistance to peers' evidence, and the benefit of learning to judge performance.

questions.q: Match each theory about why incompetent people do not learn they are unskilled to its explanation.
pairs: Other people dislike delivering bad news about our abilities
Success needs everything to go right, but failure can be pinned on many outside causes
Weak performers are less able to spot competence, so comparisons with others suffer
questions.explain: The authors offer these as several theories, each of which helps explain why experience does not correct inflated self-views.

questions.q: Which of these are reasons Dunning and Kruger offer for why incompetent people fail to learn through experience that they are unskilled?
options: People seldom get negative feedback because others do not like to deliver bad news
Failure can be blamed on many external causes, while success needs everything to go right
Some people are poor at reading how others perform, so they cannot spot competence
Incompetent people receive so much negative feedback that they stop paying attention to it
questions.explain: The claim of excessive negative feedback reverses the first reason: the point is that negative feedback is rare.

questions.q: Put the steps of Dunning and Kruger's third experiment in the order they happened.
items: Students took a ten-problem test of logical reasoning
Students rated their logical skills and test performance
Half received ten minutes of logic training and half did an unrelated task
All students estimated again how well they had performed
questions.explain: The re-estimate after training or the unrelated task showed that only the trained bottom-quartile students became accurate.

questions.q: Sort each description by which bottom-quartile group in the third experiment it fits.

items.t: Became much more accurate in estimating questions answered correctly
Held to the mistaken conviction of having performed well
Learned how to test the accuracy of a syllogism
Judged their performance compared to other students much more accurately
Kept their grossly inflated view of their performance
Spent the ten minutes on something unrelated to logic
