questions.explain: Both groups overestimated at first, but only the trained group corrected its estimates.

questions.q: Describe the Dunning-Kruger effect and explain why it leaves incompetent people stuck.
questions.a: Dunning and Kruger showed that incompetent people overestimate their own competence, because the same lack of skill prevents them from telling competence from incompetence. Failing to sense a mismatch between their performance and what is desirable, they see no need to improve. Their first paper was titled “Unskilled and Unaware of It.”

questions.q: What do the second and third Dunning-Kruger experiments, taken together, show about whether weak performers can learn to judge themselves?
questions.a: In the second experiment, bottom-quartile students who saw better answers from peers did not become more accurate and even raised their inflated estimates. In the third, ten minutes of training in logic made bottom-quartile students much more accurate about their score and their standing, while untrained peers held to their mistaken view. So exposure alone does not fix poor judgment, but learning the relevant skills does.

questions.q: Why do the authors urge caution about student-directed learning, and what role do they give an instructor?
questions.a: Students are easily misled by their own judgments: the ones using the least effective strategies overestimate their learning the most and so do not change, and even those who know retrieval works drop flashcards after one or two correct answers. The football player does not rely on intuition, but his practice is guided by a coach. Likewise most students will learn better under an instructor who knows where improvement is needed and structures the practice.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which habit does the author call most important for checking what you really know versus what you only think you know?
options: Rereading your texts until the material feels fluent
Massing your study into one long session before the test
Making frequent use of testing and retrieval practice
Asking a confident friend to judge how well you know it
questions.explain: Testing is the first and most important of the objective gauges the chapter offers, since it shows what you can actually bring to mind.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which cue does the author say is a good indicator that you have learned something?
options: How easily you can retrieve it on a quiz soon after meeting it in a lecture
How familiar a passage feels each time you come back to it
How lucid and simple a difficult text seemed to you while reading
How easily you can retrieve a fact or phrase after a delay
questions.explain: Familiarity, fluency and quick recall right after exposure can all mislead. Ease of retrieval after a delay is the exception the author names as a good indicator.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: In Eric Mazur's peer instruction, whom does Mazur try to pair up when students discuss a conceptual question?
options: Students who first gave different answers
Students who initially gave the same answer to the question
The strongest students in the class with the weakest ones
Students who did not complete the reading before class
questions.explain: Pairing students with different answers lets them see another point of view and try to convince one another of who is right.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Why does the author call how ably you can explain a text an excellent cue for judging your comprehension?
options: Explaining is quick, so you can check many texts in a single sitting at your desk
You must recall the main points, reword them, and say why they matter
Explaining lets you glance back at the key passages as you talk it through
Explaining earns immediate praise from a listener for what you appear to know
questions.explain: Explaining draws on retrieval and on understanding of how the points relate to the larger subject, so it is a stronger check than a feeling of familiarity.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: In the police firearms training, one officer took a gun from an assailant on a call and handed it right back. What did this reveal about the take-the-gun-then-hand-it-back drill?
options: Role-playing with a fellow officer cannot teach the speed that the move needs
The officers had practiced the move too little to perform it under real stress
Repetition built the hand-back into the move, breaking the practice-as-you-play rule
Video-based scenarios should replace role-playing in training for such moves in future
questions.explain: The authors say the regime violated the cardinal rule: “practice like you play, because you will play like you practice.” It shows simulation is not perfect.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: A teacher wants to know whether her class has actually learned this week's material rather than only seeming to. What does the book recommend she do?
options: Ask at the end of class whether anyone has questions
Watch whether students look engaged during the lecture
Assign extra reading and check that students finish it
Give frequent low-stakes quizzes in class
questions.explain: Frequent low-stakes quizzes help the instructor verify that students are learning as well as they appear to be and show where extra attention is needed.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: What is the main reason a manufacturer's product representative stands in the operating room when a surgeon implants a device such as a pacemaker?
options: The rep adds complementary expertise so the device is used correctly
The rep teaches the surgeon basic surgical technique during the operation itself
The rep gives the patient a second opinion about whether to have surgery at all
The rep records the surgeon's errors in order to report them to the hospital board
questions.explain: The book presents this as a team built from complementary areas of expertise: the rep has seen many surgeries with the device, and everyone benefits.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: True or false: Psychologist David Dunning argues that the path to self-insight leads through other people.
questions.explain: Dunning's point is that feedback from the world and from watching others shows us better ways to do things and that we are not as good as we thought.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: True or false: The author says each firearms simulation has a single right answer that officers should learn to apply every time.
questions.explain: The author says there is not so much a right or wrong answer as a complex set of factors, and the exercise is about clear thinking and appropriate reflexes rather than technique alone.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Andy Sobel uses ____ quizzing in his political economics course, which helps knit concepts from one stage of the course into later material.
questions.explain: Cumulative quizzing is especially powerful for consolidating learning, according to the author.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Ease of retrieval after a ____ is a good indicator of learning, unlike ease of retrieval shortly after meeting the material.
questions.explain: Quick recall right after a lecture can reflect momentary gains, but recall after a delay shows that the learning has held.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: In many fields, the practice of ____ review serves as an external gauge by providing feedback on one's performance.
questions.explain: Colleagues pick apart a case or a piece of work, as in the medical practice group conferences the author mentions.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Catherine Johnson recalls the mantra drilled into police officers: action beats ____ every time.
questions.explain: Her slow reaction to the man with the gun on the porch let him act first in the simulation.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: The cardinal rule of training is to practice like you play, because you will play like you ____.
questions.explain: The hand-back of the gun showed what can go wrong when drills are repeated in a way that does not match real conditions.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Match each person to the idea or practice the chapter ties to them.
pairs: Cumulative quizzing in a political economics course
Peer instruction with quick conceptual tests during lectures
Firearms simulations in Minneapolis police training
The path to self-insight leads through other people
questions.explain: Each is used in the chapter's section on objective tools for calibrating judgment.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Match each tool for calibrating judgment to what it provides.
pairs: Evidence for the instructor that students are learning as well as they appear to be
An external gauge on one's own performance from colleagues
Calibration from working alongside a more experienced partner
A way to assess mastery under changeable real-world demands
questions.explain: Each supplies an outside reference point in place of subjective experience.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Match each novice to the experienced partner the book pairs with them.
questions.explain: These pairings are examples of the apprentice model, which calibrates judgment by working alongside someone more experienced.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Match each stage of Mazur's peer instruction to what happens.
pairs: The material to be covered is assigned for reading
Quick tests present a conceptual question to grapple with for a minute or two
Small groups try to reach a consensus on the correct answer
Students who first gave different answers are matched to convince each other
questions.explain: The process engages students with concepts and also acts as a gauge for the instructor.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Match each firearms-training episode to the lesson drawn from it.
pairs: Trunk pops up in the traffic-stop video
Johnson now presses down hard on the trunk at every real stop
Man with a gun on the porch walks away
Her slow reaction let him act first: action beats reaction
Officer hands the gun back in the field
Drills must match real play: practice like you play
questions.explain: In each case a simulation or training habit changed how the officers acted in the field.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Match each party in the operating room to what it gains from the product representative.
pairs: Assurance of an appropriate and successful surgery
Product and troubleshooting expertise at her fingertips
Assurance that its products are used correctly
questions.explain: The author says every part of the team benefits from this complementary expertise.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which of these does the author list as ways to self-test your mastery?
options: Answering flashcards
Explaining key concepts in your own words
Peer instruction
Rereading the chapter until it feels familiar
Highlighting the key passages
questions.explain: Rereading and highlighting rely on familiarity, which the chapter warns can create an illusion of knowing.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which of these does the author say are unreliable cues for judging whether you have learned something?
options: A feeling of familiarity with the material
Fluency with a text you have read
Easy recall of a fact on a quiz soon after a lecture
Easy recall of a fact after a delay
How well you can explain the text in your own words
questions.explain: Delayed retrieval and explaining the text are the cues the author endorses.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which of these does Eric Mazur's peer instruction involve?
options: Assigning the class material to be read beforehand
Interspersing the lecture with quick conceptual tests
Small groups trying to reach consensus on an answer
Having students answer in silence without any discussion
questions.explain: Discussion is central: students explain, receive feedback and compare their understanding with others.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which of these does the author say the firearms simulation debriefs are about?
options: Clear thinking and appropriate reflexes
Visual and verbal clues to watch for
Memorizing the single correct technique
Being clear about the appropriate use of deadly force
Guaranteeing the officer wins every scenario
questions.explain: The author says the exercise is not all about technique, and that scenarios can play out in deadly or peaceful ways.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which of these does the author advise about practicing material you have already answered correctly?
options: Do not drop it from your testing once you have gotten it right a couple of times
Space your testing out over time
Vary your practice
Rely on the gains you see right after massed practice
questions.explain: Momentary gains from massed practice are exactly what the author says not to put stock in.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Put the steps of Mazur's peer instruction cycle in order.
items: Students read the assigned material before class
The lecture pauses for a conceptual question
Students grapple with the question for a minute or two
Small groups try to reach a consensus answer
questions.explain: Reading comes before class, and each quick test then moves from individual thought to group consensus.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Put the stages of a firearms-training simulation in order.
items: The officer enters a room of props with a video-linked gun
The video scenario plays and the officer decides and acts
The scenario reaches its conclusion
The officer debriefs with her trainer and gets feedback
questions.explain: The debrief at the end is where the feedback comes, and it is about thinking as well as technique.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Put the events of Catherine Johnson's traffic-stop simulation in order.
items: She walks toward the screen as the video shows her approaching the car
The trunk pops up and a man with a shotgun rises
The man shoots her in the simulation
She now presses hard on the trunk at every real traffic stop
questions.explain: The lesson from one training scenario still shapes her habits in the field.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Put the stages of the gun hand-back episode in order.
items: Officers practice taking the gun, handing it back, and taking it again
An officer takes a gun from an assailant on a call in the field
The officer hands the gun right back from habit
The officer manages to reseize the gun and keep it
questions.explain: The drill had trained the hand-back into the move.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Sort each cue by whether the book treats it as an unreliable cue for learning or a better cue.

items.t: A feeling that a passage is familiar
Ease of retrieval on a quiz right after the lecture
Fluency gained by rereading a text
Ease of retrieval after a delay
How ably you can explain the text in your own words
A mental model that integrates ideas and lets you draw inferences

questions.explain: The better cues require retrieval, understanding or inference, while the others reflect momentary familiarity.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Sort each practice by whether it is feedback from other people or self-testing on your own.

items.t: A hospital case conference where colleagues pick apart a bad outcome
A product representative watching a surgery in the operating room
A captain working alongside a first officer
Answering a stack of flashcards
Explaining key concepts in your own words
Quizzing yourself again on material you got right earlier

questions.explain: Both kinds give an objective gauge outside subjective experience, but only the first brings in other minds.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Sort each practice by whether it builds accurate judgment or misleads and backfires.

items.t: Cumulative quizzing across stages of a course
Debriefing with a trainer after a simulation
Practicing a drill in a way that does not match real play
Trusting gains seen right after massed practice
Dropping a flashcard after one or two correct answers
Simulating real-world demands and changeable conditions

questions.explain: Practice that matches real conditions and tests memory over time calibrates judgment.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Why does the author put testing and retrieval practice first among the tools for calibrating judgment, and how should a learner use it?
questions.a: Testing shows what you really know versus what you think you know. A learner can use flashcards, explain key concepts in her own words, or use peer instruction, and should not drop material once she has gotten it right a couple of times. She should space her testing, vary her practice and keep the long view rather than trusting gains from massed practice.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Describe Mazur's peer instruction and explain why it helps both students and instructors calibrate learning.
questions.a: Material is assigned for reading beforehand, and the lecture is interspersed with quick conceptual questions that students grapple with for a minute or two, then try to settle in small groups. Mazur pairs students who first gave different answers so they must convince one another. Students see problems in their understanding, explain, get feedback and compare themselves with peers, while the instructor gets a gauge of where more or less work is needed.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Which cues can mislead you about whether you have learned something, and which cues does the author recommend instead?
questions.a: Familiarity, fluency, and ease of retrieval soon after a lecture or text are not reliable indicators of learning. Ease of retrieval after a delay is a good indicator. Better still is to build a mental model that integrates ideas and connects them to what you know, and to explain the text, since explaining requires recalling the key points, rewording them and relating them to the larger subject.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: According to David Dunning and the chapter, how do feedback and other people help us judge our own performance? Give two examples from the chapter.
questions.a: Dunning says the path to self-insight leads through other people: feedback shows whether the world rewards you as a competent person would be and reveals better ways of doing things. Examples include peer review, such as medical morbidity and mortality conferences where doctors pick apart bad outcomes, and Mike Ebersold's view that surgeons should practice in a group so others will call them to task. Instructors should give corrective feedback and learners should seek it.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: How do the apprentice model and the product representative in the operating room each help calibrate judgment?
questions.a: In the apprentice model a novice works alongside a more experienced partner, as first officers do with captains, rookies with seasoned cops and residents with experienced surgeons. A product representative, who has seen many surgeries with a device and has a hotline to company engineers, is an example of a team of people with complementary expertise. The rep tracks placement and lead depth, so the patient, the doctor and the company all benefit.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: How do realistic simulations such as the police firearms scenarios help calibrate an officer's judgment, and what limit does the author note?
questions.a: Simulations imitate the demands and changeable conditions of the real world, so trainers and learners can assess mastery and see where competence must be raised. After a scenario the officer debriefs with her trainer, and the lesson is about clear thinking and reflexes, not just technique. The limit is that simulation is not perfect: drilling a gun take-away by handing the gun back led an officer to do so in the field, breaking the rule to practice like you play.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: What does the author mean by saying that the mistakes you make in the field can be powerful feedback, and what must be true for them to help?
questions.a: Mistakes in real situations can show you what you do and do not know better than your own sense of it can. For the lesson to be useful you must survive the mistake and be receptive to it. The author gives examples such as officers learning from errors in the field and Catherine Johnson learning from her simulated deaths.

questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 5, Avoid Illusions of Knowing, signal about the chapter's main concern?
options: Mental models are illusions that expert learners should avoid forming in the first place
Learners misjudge what they know, so they need ways to check their judgment
Only unskilled people are fooled by illusions, so experts can safely skip the checks
Intuition should be set aside in favor of slow deliberate analysis in every decision
questions.explain: The chapter shows how perceptual illusions, biases and memory distortions mislead everyone, then offers objective gauges for keeping judgment squared with reality.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 5 end its remedies with testing and retrieval practice, which earlier chapters had already promoted?
options: Earlier chapters had shown testing to be unreliable, so it needs correction
Testing replaces any need for feedback from other people in judging yourself
Testing gives an objective gauge outside yourself, like a cockpit instrument
The chapter has dropped spaced and varied practice as proving ineffective
questions.explain: The chapter's answer to illusion is to replace subjective experience with objective reference points, and testing is the most important of them.

questions.section: Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment
questions.q: Put these calibration tools in the order the authors present them in Tools and Habits for Calibrating Your Judgment.
items: Frequent testing and retrieval practice
Peer instruction
Checking the cues used to judge learning
Seeking corrective feedback
Simulation training for real-world conditions
questions.explain: The section starts with testing as the most important tool, then describes Mazur's peer instruction, warns about the cues we use to judge learning, urges corrective feedback and peer review, and ends with simulation training such as police firearms scenarios.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 5 offers its tools and habits for calibrating judgment before it describes the ways judgment is led astray.
questions.explain: The chapter first shows how illusions, memory distortions, faulty mental models and the Dunning-Kruger effect mislead us, and only in its last section offers the tools and habits.

questions.q: The chapter that follows Chapter 5 asks the reader to get beyond learning ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 6 is titled Get Beyond Learning Styles.

questions.q: How do the sections of Chapter 5 build the argument, from Two Systems of Knowing to the Tools and Habits section?
questions.a: The chapter starts with Kahneman's Systems 1 and 2 and shows how System 1 intuition can be fooled, then catalogs illusions and memory distortions. Mental Models and Unskilled and Unaware of It show how even experts and incompetent people misjudge what they know. It ends with objective tools such as testing, feedback, apprenticeship and simulation to square judgment with reality.

questions.q: According to the premise of learning styles theory, what happens to people whose instruction does not match their style?
options: They are at a disadvantage for learning.
They learn equally well but enjoy the lesson much less.
They switch to a second style and soon catch up fully.
They gain extra benefit because the mismatch forces effort.
questions.explain: The theory holds that people given instruction unmatched to their style are disadvantaged. The authors question exactly this claim, not the existence of preferences.

questions.q: What position do the authors take on learning preferences at the start of Chapter 6?
options: Preferences are imaginary, so the whole idea is an illusion.
Preferences are real, but matching instruction to them is unproven.
Preferences are real and matching instruction clearly boosts learning.
Preferences matter for children but never for adult learners.
questions.explain: They acknowledge that everyone has learning preferences but are not persuaded that learning improves when instruction fits them. They then turn to other differences that do matter.

questions.q: What lesson did the young Bruce Hendry take from his trips to buy fireworks in South Dakota?
options: Rich people are far smarter than ordinary people are.
Breaking rules is never worth the punishment that follows.
Goods in high demand and short supply earn a premium.
A paper route pays better than any form of trading.
questions.explain: The authors say he learned about high demand and short supply. He judged that the punishment was worth it, and that rich people simply had knowledge he lacked.

questions.q: What do people do who practice what psychologists call rule learning?
options: They memorize each experience exactly as it happened.
They follow the rules that a teacher sets for the class.
They match study materials to their preferred style.
They pull general principles from new experiences.
questions.explain: Rule learners infer lessons they can apply later in similar situations, whereas others take experiences at face value.

questions.q: In the authors' account, what do successful learners do when they engage in structure building?
options: They pick key ideas and link them into a mental model.
They collect as many facts as possible so nothing is missed.
They build physical models of the subject they are studying.
They rewrite notes in the same order the textbook uses.
questions.explain: Structure builders separate the salient concepts from less important information and connect the key ideas. The authors compare this to separating wheat from chaff and understanding how the wheat becomes flour.

questions.q: How did the teenage Bruce Hendry learn the steps involved in building his lake house?
options: He studied building manuals before beginning each stage.
He figured them out himself or found someone to show him.
His father taught him every step across the four summers.
He hired a professional crew and watched them work.
questions.explain: He tackled each step one at a time, working it out or asking around, with only occasional help from his father. The wiring was an example of how this could go wrong.

questions.q: Why, in Sam Leppla's approach, can buying junior bonds of a distressed company carry little risk?
options: Junior bonds are always paid before senior bonds in bankruptcy.
Shareholders guarantee repayment of every bond after a collapse.
Fear can push prices far below the assets' worth.
Bankruptcy courts set junior bond prices at their face value.
questions.explain: Investors' fear, laziness and ignorance can push prices far below the worth of the underlying assets. If you can ascertain that worth and know the price, the risk is very small.

questions.q: Why did Barney Donahue judge the Erie Lackawanna the best railroad to invest in?
options: It had issued the fewest bonds over its 150 years of operation.
It owned more miles of track than any other eastern railroad.
It was the railroad the government wanted for Conrail.
It had the most modern equipment when it filed for bankruptcy.
questions.explain: Donahue chose the Erie because of its modern equipment at the time of filing. The Erie had in fact issued fifteen different bonds.

questions.q: By what stage in a child's schooling do neurologists and psychologists urge that dyslexia be diagnosed and addressed?
options: Before third grade, while the brain is still plastic.
Before first grade, before any reading instruction begins.
After fifth grade, once reading habits have settled in.
Before high school, while teachers can still adjust the course.
questions.explain: Early work before the third grade can take advantage of the brain's plasticity, which may allow the rerouting of neural circuits.

questions.q: What did Geiger and Lettvin's experiments find about people with dyslexia?
options: Better with small print in focus but worse at peripheral vision.
Poorer in the focus field but better at peripheral vision.
Poorer at both central and peripheral visual information.
No difference from non-dyslexic people on any visual task.
questions.explain: The authors suggest this superior peripheral ability may hint at a neurological basis for grasping the big picture.

questions.q: How many distinct learning styles theories did a 2004 report for Britain's Learning and Skills Research Centre compare?
options: About twelve
Exactly eight
More than seventy
Over three hundred
questions.explain: The report compared more than seventy theories, each with its own assessment instrument, and described an industry full of vested interests.

questions.q: According to Neil Fleming, how much of a person's learning style does VARK describe?
options: Its entire scope, covering every dimension of style.
About half, with the rest being temperament and mood.
Its core, with temperature and light as minor extras.
Only one aspect, among eighteen dimensions of style.
questions.explain: Fleming says VARK covers only one aspect; the full style has eighteen dimensions, including temperature, light, food intake, biorhythms and working alone or with others.

questions.q: After sorting students by learning style, what did Pashler and colleagues say a credible test must do next?
options: Randomly assign them to different teaching methods, then test all.
Let each student choose a method, then compare satisfaction ratings.
Teach every group in its own style, then give style-specific tests.
Survey teachers on which method each group seemed to enjoy most.
questions.explain: Students must be randomly assigned to classes teaching the same material by different methods, followed by the same test for everyone. The test must then show each type does best with its own style.

questions.q: What did the Pashler team find when they searched for studies that met their standard of evidence?
options: Dozens, and nearly all of them validated the theory.
Very few, and virtually none validated the theory.
Several, and they were evenly split on its validity.
None, because no one had ever studied learning styles.
questions.explain: They found very few suitably designed studies; virtually none supported the theory and several flatly contradicted it.

questions.q: A teacher is planning a geometry lesson. According to the Pashler review, what should guide the choice of teaching mode?
options: Each student's assessed style, taught in separate groups.
The mode students say they like best, used for everyone.
The nature of the subject, which here suits visuals.
An equal mix of every style, whatever the subject.
questions.explain: The review found it is more important that the mode match the content, such as visual instruction for geometry. When it does, all learners learn better regardless of preference.

questions.q: What did Pashler and colleagues conclude about restructuring instruction around learning styles?
options: It is justified because most studies support the theory.
It should end because every such theory has been disproved.
It is justified for adults but not for young children.
The evidence cannot justify the investment it would need.
questions.explain: They said the available evidence does not justify the time and money. The authors add that some theories may be valid but the research base cannot tell us which.

questions.q: What does Tony LaRussa's career illustrate about skill and success?
options: Playing skill is not required to excel in another role.
Great managers must first have been great players in that sport.
Short playing careers always lead to long coaching careers.
Managers win through natural talent rather than study of the game.
questions.explain: He had a short, undistinguished playing career yet became one of the greatest managers. Many top managers and coaches were exceptional students of their games.

questions.q: After a rental-property venture goes sour, a young investor asks what general lesson will apply to future deals. Which habit does this show?
options: Style matching, favoring one mode of taking in information.
Rule learning, inferring principles for use in similar cases.
Example learning, memorizing the one case to reuse later.
Taking events at face value and drawing no lessons from them.
questions.explain: Bruce drew a lesson from each venture, which improved his focus and judgment. People who habitually infer principles from experiences learn better than those who do not.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 6 begin with the story of Bruce Hendry before turning to learning styles research?
options: It proves that self-made people never use learning styles.
It shows that formal schooling is wasted on future investors.
His story frames the argument about differences that matter.
It supplies the experiment later used to test learning styles.
questions.explain: The authors introduce his story to help frame their argument. It illustrates differences such as taking charge, rule learning and structure building.

questions.q: What does the chapter title Get Beyond Learning Styles signal about the argument?
options: Style preferences matter once they are combined with testing.
Learning styles should simply be replaced by multiple intelligences.
Learning styles have been validated and now need extending.
Other learning differences matter more than style preferences do.
questions.explain: The authors say some differences matter and some, like a verbal or visual style, do not. The chapter moves from style claims to differences such as structure building.

questions.q: Which later section of Chapter 6 takes up rule learning, first named in Bruce's story, by contrasting it with example learning?
options: Rule versus Example Learning
Successful Intelligence
Active Learning from the Get-Go
Structure Building
questions.explain: The section titled Rule versus Example Learning develops the contrast. Structure Building covers the companion idea but not that contrast.

questions.q: Bruce Hendry exemplifies people who habitually extract underlying principles from experience, which psychologists call ____ learning.
questions.explain: Rule learning and structure building are the two behaviors the authors name in his story.

questions.q: At twelve, Bruce Hendry hitchhiked 255 miles to buy fireworks in ____, South Dakota.
questions.explain: The fireworks were illegal in Minnesota, so he bought them across the border and sold them to paperboys.

questions.q: From his fireworks trips at thirteen, Bruce learned a lesson about high demand and short ____.
questions.explain: This supply-and-demand idea later became a building block in his much more complex investing model.

questions.q: In a troubled company, the bonds that are paid first are called ____ bonds.
questions.explain: Residual assets after the senior bonds are paid go to the junior bonds.

questions.q: Hendry, Leppla and Donahue made their major railroad bet on the ____ Lackawanna.
questions.explain: Donahue picked it because it had the most modern equipment when it filed for bankruptcy.

questions.q: Dyslexia is estimated to affect about ____ percent of the population.
questions.explain: It is one of the most common causes of reading difficulties, though not the only one.

questions.q: Dyslexia disrupts the brain's capacity to link letters to the ____ they make, which is essential for word recognition.
questions.explain: This arises from anomalous neural development during pregnancy.

questions.q: The VARK approach to learning styles was advocated by Neil ____.
questions.explain: VARK sorts preferences into visual, auditory, reading and kinesthetic.

questions.q: The Honey and Mumford questionnaire sorts people as activist, reflector, theorist or ____.
questions.explain: It is popular in managerial settings and helps employees improve in the areas where they score low.

questions.q: The Pashler review found that instruction works best when its mode matches the nature of the ____ being taught.
questions.explain: Visual instruction suits geometry and verbal instruction suits poetry, and then all learners benefit.

questions.q: Richard Branson quit school at the age of ____ to start businesses.
questions.explain: He is one of the dyslexic high achievers in the Fortune article the authors discuss.

questions.q: Experiments found that people with dyslexia significantly outperform others at interpreting information from their ____ vision.
questions.explain: This suggests that a superior grasp of the big picture might have a neurological origin.

questions.q: The Dunn and Dunn inventory assesses ____ different aspects of an individual's learning style.
questions.explain: They are environmental, emotional, sociological, perceptual, physiological and psychological.

questions.q: True or false: The authors accept that everyone has learning preferences but doubt that learning improves when instruction is matched to them.
questions.explain: They separate the existence of preferences from the claim that matching preferences improves learning, and doubt only the second.

questions.q: True or false: Bruce Hendry bought fireworks in Aberdeen because they were illegal in South Dakota.
questions.explain: They were illegal in Minnesota, which is why he brought them home from South Dakota.

questions.q: True or false: After the Pashler team's review, the authors say some learning styles theories may still be valid, but we cannot know which.
questions.explain: The research base is too small to say. This is different from saying that every theory has been disproved.

questions.q: True or false: The Pashler review found that many well-designed studies validated learning styles theory.
questions.explain: They found very few suitable studies; virtually none supported the theory and several contradicted it.

questions.q: True or false: When the electrical inspector rejected Bruce's wiring, he paid a union electrician to redo it.
questions.explain: He later judged that what he had done was totally dangerous.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, people with dyslexia generally get over it as they grow older.
questions.explain: The authors say people do not get over dyslexia, though with help they can work with and around the problems it poses.

questions.q: True or false: Neurologists and psychologists stress diagnosing dyslexia early, before third grade, while the brain is still quite plastic.
questions.explain: Early diagnosis allows work with children while neural circuits may still be rerouted.

questions.q: True or false: Neil Fleming holds that the VARK model describes a person's entire learning style.
questions.explain: Fleming says VARK describes only one aspect of a style that has eighteen dimensions.

questions.q: True or false: Carol Dweck's work on how you see your abilities, which this chapter cites, is described in Chapter 7, the chapter after this one.
questions.explain: The chapter points ahead to Chapter 7 for Dweck's work on self-belief.

questions.q: Which of these are behaviors of successful learners that the Bruce Hendry story is used to illustrate?
options: Extracting underlying principles from new experiences
Singling out key concepts and linking them into a mental structure
Taking charge of your own education
Choosing material that matches a preferred style
Memorizing each experience exactly as it occurred
questions.explain: The authors cite taking charge, rule learning and structure building. They doubt that matching style helps, and they do not recommend rote memorizing of experience.

questions.q: Which of these did Bruce Hendry do while building his first house?
options: Borrowed a trailer to dig the basement
Learned to lay block from a friend whose father was in the cement business
Learned to frame the walls from a lumberyard salesman
Hired a contractor to frame the walls
Took a night course on plumbing and wiring
questions.explain: He dug, laid block and framed by finding people to show him. He did not hire a contractor or take courses.

questions.q: Which of these people are named as dyslexic high achievers in the Fortune article?
options: Richard Branson
Diane Swonk
Craig McCaw
Tony LaRussa
Bruce Hendry
questions.explain: Branson, Swonk, McCaw and Orfalea are in the article. LaRussa is a baseball manager used to show that playing skill is not a prerequisite for success.

questions.q: Which of these skills of necessity did many dyslexic high achievers say they learned early?
options: Grasping the big picture instead of the component parts
Thinking outside the box
Managing risk taking
Memorizing texts word by word
Avoiding strategic action
questions.explain: They learned to see the big picture, think outside the box, act strategically and manage risk. These skills gave them a leg up later in their careers.

questions.q: Which of these are among the four preferences that the VARK approach distinguishes?
options: Visual
Reading
Kinesthetic
Musical
Logical
questions.explain: VARK stands for visual, auditory, reading and kinesthetic, where kinesthetic means moving, touching and active exploration.

questions.q: Which of these attributes must a credible study of learning styles have, according to the Pashler team?
options: Students are grouped by their learning style
Students are randomly assigned to classes with different instructional methods
All students take the same test afterward
Each student chooses the method he or she prefers
Each style group takes a test made for its own style
questions.explain: The design needs style grouping, random assignment to methods and one common test. Letting students choose or giving separate tests would not isolate the effect.

questions.q: Which of these does the book say are wrong with the student's conclusion that a low-auditory kinesthetic learner has no point reading a book?
options: It is not supported by science
It instills a sense of diminished potential
It overstates how rare kinesthetic learners are
It ignores that books are mostly auditory
questions.explain: The authors say the conclusion is not supported by science and instills a corrosive, misguided sense of diminished potential.

questions.q: Which of these are listed among the eighteen dimensions that Fleming says make up a learning style?
options: Preferences in temperature
Preferences in light
Food intake
Handwriting speed
Typing skill
questions.explain: Fleming includes temperature, light, food intake, biorhythms and working with others versus alone.

questions.q: Which of these did Bruce Hendry and his partners do to value the Erie Lackawanna?
options: Traveled the entire length of its track
Counted the remaining equipment and checked its condition
Used Moody's transportation manuals to calculate values
Hired a consultant to appraise the engines
Bought senior bonds at face value
questions.explain: They inspected the track, counted and examined equipment and consulted Moody's manuals to do the arithmetic. They bought underpriced junior bonds.

questions.q: Put these early moneymaking steps of Bruce Hendry in the order he took them, from youngest age to oldest.
items: Sold pieces of a ball of string
Got a paper route
Added caddying
Hitchhiked to Aberdeen for fireworks
questions.explain: He sold string at eight, took a paper route at ten, added caddying at eleven and made the fireworks trip at twelve.

questions.q: Put these stages of Bruce Hendry's career in order.
items: Built a house on a lake lot
Traded it for a fourplex in Minneapolis
Sold microfilm for Kodak
Sold stocks at a brokerage
Invested in Erie Lackawanna bonds
Became chairman and CEO of the Erie
questions.explain: He built the house over four summers, traded it at nineteen, joined Kodak, then a brokerage. After meeting Leppla he bet on the Erie and eventually led it.

questions.q: Put the steps of a credible test of learning styles theory, as described by the Pashler team, in order.
items: Divide students by learning style
Randomly assign them to classrooms using different methods
Teach the same material in each classroom
Give every student the same test
questions.explain: Grouping comes first, then random assignment and teaching of the same material, and finally a common test that shows which instruction suited each type best.

questions.q: Put these steps in Bruce Hendry's Erie Lackawanna investment in the order they happened.
items: Donahue picks the Erie
The team travels the entire length of its track
They count equipment and check Moody's manuals
Bruce finds the document setting the payoff sequence
Bruce buys underpriced junior bonds
Bruce is appointed to chair the bondholders' committee
questions.explain: Choice of railroad came first, then inspection and calculation, then the discovery of the payoff sequence that let him judge each bond class and buy, and finally he took the committee chair.

questions.q: According to the bond precept Leppla taught, put these in the order they are paid when a troubled company's assets are divided.
items: Senior bonds
Junior bonds
Shareholders
questions.explain: Creditors have the first claim, not the shareholders who own the company. Within the bonds, senior ones are paid first and junior ones are paid from what remains.

questions.q: Put these links in the author's chain from poor reading to criminality in order.
items: Children who cannot read fall into a pattern of failure
They develop low self-esteem
Some turn to bullying or antisocial behavior to compensate
Left unaddressed, this escalates into criminality
questions.explain: The authors describe this as a series of bad turns that often begins with failure in school.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 6 in the order they appear.
items: Active Learning from the Get-Go
Successful Intelligence
Dynamic Testing
Structure Building
Rule versus Example Learning
The Takeaway
questions.explain: The chapter moves from Bruce's story and learning styles to intelligence, testing, structure building, rule learning and the takeaway.

questions.q: Match each learning styles model to the dimensions it uses.
pairs: Visual, auditory, reading and kinesthetic preferences
Six aspects, such as environmental and emotional
questions.explain: The authors list these to show how wildly the dimensions differ across theories, which raises doubts about their scientific underpinnings.

questions.q: Match each person in Bruce Hendry's story to his or her role.
pairs: Bruce's mother, who spanked him for crossing the street
Father who threatened a licking over the fireworks
Roamed the skyways advising on bond deals
questions.explain: Each plays a part in Bruce's winding stair, from early self-direction to the Erie Lackawanna.

questions.q: Match each high achiever to what the Fortune article says about him or her.
pairs: Quit school at sixteen and started Virgin businesses
One of the top economic forecasters in the US
Pioneer of the cellular phone industry
questions.explain: All had dyslexia and trouble with accepted methods of learning, and nearly all were backed by people who believed in them.

questions.q: Match each age or period in Bruce Hendry's life to what he did.
pairs: Crossed the street every day despite a spanking
Sold pieces of a ball of string
Bought a wooded lot on a lake
Traded his house for a fourplex
questions.explain: These episodes show his early habit of taking charge of his own education.

questions.q: Match each party or class of bond in a troubled company to its place in the payoff order.
pairs: Paid from residual assets after the senior ones
Suppliers and bondholders with the first claim
The owners, whose claim comes after creditors
questions.explain: When a company runs into trouble, there is a pecking order of claims on its assets.

questions.q: Match each business setback or step in Bruce's story to the lesson he drew.
pairs: Being a rainmaker pays better than managing
Real money comes from investing your own money
You have no control of the downside
The reward did not justify the headaches
questions.explain: Each setback became another step on his winding stair.

questions.q: Match each researcher in the chapter's learning styles discussion to what he did.
pairs: Developed a six-aspect learning style inventory
Studied peripheral vision in dyslexia at MIT
Reviewed the evidence on learning styles in 2008
questions.explain: The first two represent the theories under review, while the last two supply evidence about dyslexia and about learning styles.

questions.q: Match each of Bruce Hendry's investments to its outcome.
pairs: Awarded 2 percent ownership of the new company
About 20 percent on his investment from leases
questions.explain: These conquests show how he used knowledge of assets, liabilities and structure to find value.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the chapter.
pairs: Linking key concepts into a mental structure
We learn better when presentation matches our style
questions.explain: These terms recur in the argument about which differences matter and which do not.

questions.q: Sort each description by the behavior it describes.

items.t: Drawing a lesson from each venture for later use
Pulling underlying principles out of new experience
Separating the key concepts from irrelevant detail
Linking the key ideas into a mental framework

questions.explain: Rule learning is about inferring principles from experiences, while structure building is about picking out and linking the salient concepts.

questions.q: Sort each preference by the learning styles model that uses it.

items.t: Visual
Auditory
Reading
Kinesthetic
Activist
Reflector
Theorist
Pragmatist

questions.explain: VARK has four sensory modes, and Honey and Mumford's questionnaire has four types of learner.

questions.q: Sort each difference by whether the authors say it matters for learning.

items.t: Ability to abstract principles from new experiences
Ability to convert knowledge into mental structures
Level of language fluency and reading ability
Having a verbal learning style
Having a visual learning style

questions.explain: The authors say some differences count for a lot, while having a verbal or visual style actually does not.

questions.q: Sort each event in Bruce Hendry's life by when it happened.

items.t: Bought a ball of string and sold the pieces
Took a paper route
Bought a wooded lot
Hitchhiked for fireworks
Worked for Kodak
Joined a brokerage firm
Chaired the Erie bondholders' committee
Took control of Kaiser Steel

questions.explain: His early ventures began at eight and he bought the lot as a young teenager, while the Kodak job and later deals came after college.

questions.q: Sort each description by the kind of bond it fits.

items.t: Paid first among the bonds
Higher in the pecking order
Paid from the residual assets
Sold at steep discounts when investors doubt repayment

questions.explain: Junior bonds are far down the food chain, so they may be cheap, while senior bonds come first.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it was required evidence or a finding of the Pashler review.

items.t: Students divided by learning style
Random assignment to classrooms
Same test for all students
Very few suitable studies existed
Virtually none validated the theory
Several flatly contradicted the theory

questions.explain: The team first set the standard and then asked whether evidence of that kind existed. The answer was no.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is a difficulty or a strength associated with dyslexia in the chapter.

items.t: Trouble linking letters to sounds
Losing the thread of a text while decoding words
Poor interpretation of the visual focus field
Better interpretation of peripheral vision
Grasping the big picture
Managing risk taking

questions.explain: The authors describe real reading difficulties but report that some people with dyslexia develop compensating strengths.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it reflects learning styles theory or the authors' view.

items.t: People learn better when instruction fits their style
People with unmatched instruction are disadvantaged
Instruction should match the nature of the subject
Preferences exist but matching is unproven
Evidence does not justify restructuring around styles

questions.explain: The theory makes the matching claim, which the authors say lacks evidence.

questions.q: What is the premise of learning styles theory, and what do the authors say about it at the start of Chapter 6?
questions.a: The theory says people receive and process information differently, for example visually or through text or sound, and that those taught in a way that does not match their style are at a disadvantage. The authors accept that everyone has learning preferences but are not persuaded that learning improves when instruction fits them. They say that other differences do matter.

questions.q: What is the critical claim of learning styles theory, and why does having a preference not support it?
questions.a: The critical claim is that we learn better when the mode of presentation matches the style in which we are best able to learn. Most of us do have a decided preference for how we like to learn, but a preference is not evidence that matched instruction produces better learning. That is the question Pashler and colleagues set out to test.

questions.q: How did Bruce Hendry learn to build a house as a teenager, and what does this show about taking charge of your own education?
questions.a: He tackled each step one at a time, figuring it out for himself or finding someone to show him, such as a friend's cement-business father for block laying and a lumberyard salesman for framing. He had no formal course; he went after the knowledge he needed. This fits the authors' point that taking charge of your own education is a learning difference that matters.

questions.q: How do rule learning and structure building show up in the way Bruce Hendry invested?
questions.a: He drew lessons from each scheme, which sharpened his focus and judgment, and this is rule learning. He knit what he learned into mental models of investing that let him pluck the telling details from masses of irrelevant information, which is structure building. The authors say people who do this as a habit are more successful learners.

questions.q: What was Sam Leppla's investment precept about distressed companies, and why did it lower risk?
questions.a: When a company is in trouble, creditors such as suppliers and bondholders have the first claim on assets, and senior bonds are paid before junior bonds. Investors' fear and ignorance can push junior bond prices far below the worth of the underlying assets. If you ascertain the real worth and know the price, you can invest with very little risk.

questions.q: What did Bruce Hendry and his partners do to gain knowledge that other Erie Lackawanna bondholders lacked?
questions.a: They traveled the length of the track, counted the equipment and checked its condition, and used Moody's manuals to estimate values. Bruce also found a document setting the sequence in which the bonds would be paid off. Armed with the asset values and bond structure, they knew what each class of bonds was worth, while others were in the dark.

questions.q: Why does dyslexia make learning hard, and what strengths do some people with dyslexia seem to develop?
questions.a: Dyslexia stems from anomalous neural development that disrupts the brain's ability to link letters to sounds, so poor readers lose the thread of a text while decoding words. Some high achievers with dyslexia learned early to grasp the big picture, think outside the box, act strategically and manage risk. Experiments also found that people with dyslexia are better at interpreting peripheral vision.

questions.q: What does the Fortune article's account of dyslexic achievers like Richard Branson suggest about self-narrative and learning?
questions.a: These achievers told stories of overcoming adversity; most had been mislabeled as low IQ, yet nearly all were supported by people who believed in them. The authors say the stories we create to understand ourselves shape our sense of ability, which affects how hard we try, our tolerance for risk and our persistence. Differences in skills also shape routes to success.

questions.q: Why does the book call the conclusion of the student who found he was a low auditory, kinesthetic learner wrongheaded?
questions.a: The student concluded there was no point in reading a book or listening for more than a few minutes. The authors say this is not supported by science and instills a corrosive, misguided sense of diminished potential. It also shows the danger of classifying, labeling and stereotyping people that the report's authors warned about.

questions.q: What kind of evidence did Pashler and colleagues say would be needed to justify basing instruction on learning styles?
questions.a: Students would be divided by learning style and randomly assigned to classrooms teaching the same material by different methods, and then all would take the same test. The test would have to show that each type does best with instruction in its own style compared with another style. Without this, the claim cannot be credited.

questions.q: What did the 2008 review by Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork find, and what did it say works for all learners?
questions.a: They found very few studies able to test learning styles theory; virtually none validated it and several flatly contradicted it. They found it matters more that the mode of instruction match the nature of the subject, such as visual for geometry and verbal for poetry. When it does, all learners learn better regardless of preference.

questions.q: Does the Pashler review mean every learning styles theory is wrong, and what did the authors recommend instead?
questions.a: No; some theories may be valid, but with so few rigorous studies we cannot know which. The evidence does not justify the huge investment in assessing students and restructuring instruction around styles. Until it exists, the authors say it makes more sense to emphasize techniques validated as benefiting learners regardless of style, like those in this book.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 6 open with Bruce Hendry's story, and how does it link to the rest of the chapter?
questions.a: The authors use his story to frame the argument that some learning differences matter more than others, such as taking charge, rule learning and structure building. Those ideas return in later sections such as Structure Building and Rule versus Example Learning, and Bruce's investing reappears when the authors revisit supply and demand and knowhow. The story shows what matters before the chapter examines the learning styles claim.

questions.q: What does the title Get Beyond Learning Styles signal, and where does the chapter take the reader?
questions.a: The title signals that learning styles are not the differences that matter, so the reader should move past them. The chapter acknowledges preferences but finds no evidence that matched instruction helps. It then turns to differences that do matter, such as intelligence, dynamic testing, structure building and rule learning, and ends with advice to take charge of your learning.

questions.q: In the chapter's account of the two kinds of intelligence psychologists generally accept, what is fluid intelligence?
options: The ability to reason, see relationships, and think abstractly while holding information in mind
One's accumulated knowledge of the world plus the procedures and mental models built from past experience
The ratio of a person's mental age to physical age, multiplied by one hundred, on a standard test
The ability to adapt to everyday life by working out what a particular setting requires and doing it
questions.explain: Fluid intelligence is the reasoning and working-on-a-problem ability. The accumulated knowledge and mental models describe crystallized intelligence, and the everyday-adaptation ability is Sternberg's practical intelligence.

questions.q: On a traditional IQ test, an eight-year-old solves problems that most ten-year-olds can solve. What IQ does the chapter's formula give this child?
questions.explain: IQ is mental age divided by physical age, times 100, so ten divided by eight times 100 gives 125. Reversing the ratio would wrongly give 80.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what do the learning styles model and Gardner's multiple intelligences model have in common?
options: Both have been shown by rigorous studies to improve test scores
Both lead people to see their learning abilities as limited
Both lack an underpinning of empirical validation
Both treat intelligence as fixed at birth and unchangeable
questions.explain: The authors say both theories lack empirical validation, and Gardner himself admits that finding one's mix of intelligences is more art than science. Only learning styles tend to make people feel their abilities are limited, since multiple intelligences stresses the variety of tools we have.

questions.q: In Sternberg's Kenyan study, why did the children best at identifying herbal medicines do worst on tests of formal school subjects?
options: They had lower underlying intelligence, which showed up in every area of learning they attempted
The herbal knowledge tests were harder than the school tests, so only the gifted children passed them
They had reading difficulties that blocked their progress in the formal academic subjects at school
Their families prized practical over academic knowledge, so school subjects got less emphasis
questions.explain: Sternberg explains the discrepancy by the values of the children's environments, not by their ability. There is no reason, the chapter says, that these children could not catch up with the right opportunities.

questions.q: Sternberg describes orphaned children in Brazil who run street businesses. What does their math performance illustrate?
options: Skill follows environment: they handle business math but not abstract paper-and-pencil math
Children from poor backgrounds have weaker reasoning skills than children who attend school regularly
High motivation alone is enough to make any child excel at abstract paper-and-pencil mathematics
Formal academic tests are the best way to find out how much mathematics a child truly understands
questions.explain: The children can do the math required to run successful businesses yet fail the same math in abstract form. Sternberg reads this through developing expertise: practical exigencies decide what and how they learn.

questions.q: What did the study of expert horse-track handicappers find about IQ?
options: Handicappers with higher IQs built more accurate betting models than those with average IQs
IQ was unrelated to handicapping ability, though the experts used complex mental models
Expert handicappers scored far above average on IQ tests because of their complex reasoning
Only handicappers with training in mathematics could manage a model of seven variables
questions.explain: The experts measured only average on standard IQ tests, and handicappers with equivalent IQs differed in skill. The study concluded that an IQ test does not measure the ability to do complex multivariate reasoning.

questions.q: Priya joins a new team, quickly works out what each situation requires, and does it without being told. Which of Sternberg's intelligences is she chiefly showing?
options: Analytical intelligence, the ability to complete problem-solving tasks like those found in tests
Creative intelligence, the ability to synthesize knowledge to handle new and unusual situations
Practical intelligence, the ability to adapt to everyday life, or street smarts
Crystallized intelligence, the stored knowledge built up from past learning and experience
questions.explain: Practical intelligence means understanding what needs to be done in a specific setting and then doing it. Analytical intelligence is the test-style problem solving, and creative intelligence is about new and unusual situations.

questions.q: True or false: Sternberg's three-part model of intelligence, like Gardner's eight-part model, lacks empirical support.
questions.explain: The chapter says that, unlike Gardner's theory, Sternberg's is supported by empirical research. Gardner himself admits that finding one's mix of intelligences is more art than science.

questions.q: True or false: In Sternberg's Kenyan study, the children who performed best on tests of herbal medicine knowledge did worst relative to their peers on tests of formal school subjects.
questions.explain: This is the discrepancy Sternberg set out to reconcile. He explained it by families valuing practical knowledge over academic knowledge, not by lower ability.

questions.q: True or false: The expert horse-track handicappers in the study scored far above average on standard IQ tests.
questions.explain: They measured only average on IQ tests. The study found that IQ is unrelated to handicapping ability.

questions.q: Howard Gardner hypothesizes that humans have as many as ____ different kinds of intelligence.
questions.explain: Gardner's list runs from logical-mathematical and spatial through interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic. Sternberg, in contrast, proposes three.

questions.q: The Intelligence ____ denotes the ratio of mental age to physical age, times 100.
questions.explain: IQ stands for Intelligence Quotient. An eight-year-old who solves ten-year-old problems has an IQ of 125.

questions.q: Sternberg's three kinds of intelligence are analytical, creative, and ____.
questions.explain: Practical intelligence is the ability to adapt to everyday life by working out what a setting requires and doing it.

questions.q: The authors call practical intelligence, our ability to adapt to everyday life, what we call ____ smarts.
questions.explain: Street smarts is the authors' lay term for practical intelligence. Standard IQ and aptitude tests can miss this competency.

questions.q: Which of these are among Gardner's eight intelligences?
options: Naturalistic intelligence
Musical intelligence
Analytical intelligence
Interpersonal intelligence
Practical intelligence
questions.explain: Naturalistic, musical, and interpersonal are on Gardner's list. Analytical and practical belong to Sternberg's three-part model.

questions.q: Which of these are among the three parts of Sternberg's theory of successful intelligence?
options: Analytical intelligence
Kinesthetic intelligence
Creative intelligence
Practical intelligence
Musical intelligence
questions.explain: Sternberg proposes analytical, creative, and practical intelligence. Kinesthetic and musical are two of Gardner's eight.

questions.q: Which of these groups did Sternberg describe as showing skill that standard academic or IQ-style tests missed?
options: Kenyan children who knew herbal medicines
Orphaned street-business children in Brazil
Expert handicappers at horse tracks
Dyslexic executives profiled in Fortune
Military pilots trained by learning styles
questions.explain: The Kenyan children, Brazilian street vendors, and expert handicappers are Sternberg's three stories. The dyslexic high achievers come from a Fortune article and the pilots are an example of learning styles use.

questions.q: Put these ideas in the order the chapter presents them in its discussion of intelligence.
items: Fluid and crystallized intelligence
Traditional IQ as a ratio of mental age to physical age
Gardner's eight intelligences
Sternberg's studies of Kenya, Brazil, and the horse track
questions.explain: The chapter defines the two kinds of intelligence, explains IQ, offers Gardner as a challenge, and then Sternberg's distillation with his supporting studies.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Ability to reason, see relationships, and think abstractly
Accumulated knowledge of the world and mental models from experience
Ability to complete problem-solving tasks like those found on tests
Ability to apply existing knowledge to new and unusual situations
Ability to adapt to everyday life, or street smarts
questions.explain: The first two are the two kinds psychologists accept. The last three are the parts of Sternberg's successful intelligence.

questions.q: Match each of Gardner's intelligences to its description.
pairs: Three-dimensional judgment and visualizing with the mind's eye
Physical dexterity and control of one's body
Ability to read other people and work with them effectively
Ability to understand oneself and judge one's own knowledge and abilities
Ability to discriminate and relate to one's natural surroundings
questions.explain: These are five of the eight intelligences Gardner proposes. The gardener, hunter, and chef illustrate the naturalistic kind.

questions.q: Match each group Sternberg described to what was found.
pairs: Best on indigenous knowledge but worst on formal school tests
Able to do business math but not the same math on paper
Complex mental models but only average scores on IQ tests
questions.explain: In each case the standard tests missed real competence that the environment had developed. Sternberg reads them through developing expertise.

questions.q: Sort each intelligence by whether it comes from Gardner's model or Sternberg's model.

items.t: Naturalistic
Musical
Interpersonal
Analytical
Creative
Practical

questions.explain: Gardner proposes as many as eight intelligences, while Sternberg distills the idea down to three.

questions.q: Sort each description by whether it describes fluid or crystallized intelligence.

items.t: Holding information in mind while working on a problem
Seeing relationships
Thinking abstractly
Accumulated knowledge of the world
Mental models developed from past experience
Procedures learned from past experience

questions.explain: Fluid intelligence is the reasoning ability itself. Crystallized intelligence is what has been accumulated from learning and experience.

questions.q: Explain the difference between fluid intelligence and crystallized intelligence, and why the chapter says both are needed.
questions.a: Fluid intelligence is the ability to reason, see relationships, think abstractly, and hold information in mind while working on a problem. Crystallized intelligence is one's accumulated knowledge of the world and the procedures or mental models built from past learning and experience. Together they enable us to learn, reason, and solve problems.

questions.q: How do the authors compare learning styles theory and Gardner's multiple intelligences, and what weakness do they share?
questions.a: Both have helped educators diversify the learning experiences they offer. Learning styles can have the perverse effect of making people see their abilities as limited, whereas multiple intelligences elevates the variety of tools in our native toolkit. Both lack empirical validation, and Gardner himself concedes that finding one's mix of intelligences is more an art than a science.

questions.q: Describe Sternberg's study of children in rural Kenya and explain the conclusions he draws about measuring intelligence.
questions.a: Children who knew the herbal medicines used daily in their communities, their uses and dosages, did best on that informal knowledge but worst on tests of formal school subjects. Sternberg suggests their families valued practical knowledge more than academic knowledge. So traditional measures fail to account for environment, and a test that captures what we know at one moment is a static measure that says nothing about potential.

questions.q: How do the Brazilian street-business children and the horse-track handicappers show that standard tests can miss important competencies?
questions.a: The Brazilian children can do the math needed to run profitable street businesses but cannot do the same math in abstract paper-and-pencil form, because their environment demands practical skills. The expert handicappers build mental models using as many as seven variables yet score only average on IQ tests, and IQ was unrelated to handicapping ability. Both fit Sternberg's view that learning is shaped by the setting, and that different situations draw on analytical, creative, and practical intelligence differently.

questions.q: How does dynamic testing differ from a standard test, according to Sternberg and Grigorenko?
options: It ranks people by their strengths so that each person can concentrate on the subjects they do best
It assigns a fixed score that predicts the highest level a learner will ever be able to reach
It replaces testing with instruction matched to each learner's preferred way of taking in material
It tracks progress from test to test and refocuses learning on weak areas, not a static snapshot
questions.explain: A standard test is a static snapshot of where you stand. Dynamic testing uses a weakness as a signal for what to work on and then re-tests to see the improvement.

questions.q: Marcus fails the parallel-parking part of a driving test, practises that skill for two weeks, and then retakes it, noting that he still drifts too far from the curb. Which idea from the chapter does this best illustrate?
options: Dynamic testing: a test reveals a weakness, practice remedies it, and a retest shows what remains
Learning styles, in which instruction must be matched to how Marcus prefers to take in information
Crystallized intelligence, in which Marcus relies on knowledge he already accumulated about driving
Rule learning, in which Marcus extracts one underlying principle that covers every kind of parking
questions.explain: Marcus is going through the three steps: a test shows where he comes up short, he practises, and he tests himself again paying attention to remaining weaknesses.

questions.q: What lessons did Bruce Hendry take from his setbacks in rental property and stock market investing, as the chapter tells it?
options: To avoid any future investing in which he could lose money, and to focus on salaried jobs instead
To be skeptical of sales pitches, figure out the right questions, and go dig out the answers
To trust experienced advisers completely, and to rely on his instincts about which opportunities to take
To concentrate on the investing methods he already did best, and to leave his weak areas alone
questions.explain: The chapter treats these lessons as essential elements of his education and calls this developing expertise. Setbacks show us where we need to do better.

questions.q: True or false: Dynamic testing treats a weakness revealed by a test as a sign of a fixed inability that the learner should work around.
questions.explain: Dynamic testing reads a weakness as a lack of skill or knowledge that can be remedied. It is aptitude tests and much of learning styles theory that push people toward their strengths.

questions.q: Sternberg's concept that with experience we are always moving from a lower state of competence to a higher one is called ____ expertise.
questions.explain: Because we are always developing, a test measuring only what we know at one moment says little about our potential.

questions.q: Sternberg views a test that measures only what we know at a given moment as a ____ measure of our potential.
questions.explain: Static means a snapshot. Dynamic testing replaces it with repeated testing that tracks improvement.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter give as advantages of dynamic testing over standard testing?
options: It focuses learner and teacher on areas that need to be brought up
Measuring progress from test to test gives a truer gauge of learning potential
It assigns each learner a fixed score showing how far they can go
It lets instruction be matched to each learner's preferred style
questions.explain: The two advantages are the focus on areas needing work and the progress measure. A fixed score is the static view that dynamic testing rejects.

questions.q: Put the three steps of dynamic testing in order.
items: A test shows where I come up short
I work to become more competent through reflection, practice, and spacing
I test myself again, noting where I still need more work
questions.explain: A test reveals a weakness, effective study techniques remedy it, and a retest shows what has improved and what still needs work. The cycle then repeats.

questions.q: Match each idea to its description in the discussion of testing and expertise.
pairs: Reports only where you stand on the learning continuum at one moment
Treats a weakness as a lack of skill that can be remedied
Continual movement from a lower state of competence to a higher one
Aptitude tests and learning styles theory
Tend to emphasize our strengths and encourage us to focus on them
questions.explain: Dynamic testing differs from these approaches by uncovering weaknesses and correcting them. It rests on the idea that expertise is always developing.

questions.q: Sort each feature by whether it belongs to a static test or to dynamic testing.

items.t: Reports where you stand at one moment
Cannot accurately rate your potential
Follow-up testing measures improvement
Learning is refocused on areas of low performance
A weakness is read as a lack of skill that can be remedied

questions.explain: A static test gives a snapshot and so cannot show potential. Dynamic testing is a cycle of testing, refocused learning, and retesting.

questions.q: Explain what dynamic testing is, its three steps, and how it differs from standard testing.
questions.a: Dynamic testing, proposed by Sternberg and Grigorenko, uses testing to assess ability dynamically: a test shows where I come up short, I work to improve using techniques such as reflection, practice, and spacing, and I test myself again, noting what works better and where I still need work. A standard test is a static report of where you stand at one moment. Dynamic testing treats a weakness as a remediable lack of skill and measures progress from one test to the next.
