questions.q: What limits do the authors acknowledge on how far dynamic testing can take a learner, and what do they still claim?
questions.a: They accept that the upper limits of performance in any cognitive or manual skill may be set by factors beyond our control, such as intelligence and natural limits of ability. Even so, most of us can learn to perform nearer our full potential in most areas by discovering our weaknesses and working to bring them up. Examples include toddlers learning to walk and a writer revising a story after feedback from a writers' group.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what do high structure-builders do better than low structure-builders when learning new material?
options: They memorize more of the individual details, which gives them a larger store of facts to draw on
They keep every concept they meet in mind so that no information is lost from their mental model
They single out the salient ideas and set aside competing information to form a workable model
They prefer to learn through one sensory channel, which lets them build structure more efficiently
questions.explain: High structure-builders learn better because they can separate the main ideas from the clutter. Low structure-builders hang on to too many concepts to condense into a workable model.

questions.q: In the Lego village analogy, what does each element such as the school, hospital, or fire station correspond to?
options: A single memorized fact in the textbook, which must be recalled exactly as it was written
A piece of extraneous information that does not fit and should be put aside while building
A learning style that determines the order in which the pieces should be sorted and laid out
A central idea in the textbook, which gains nuance as added pieces snap into place
questions.explain: The elements are like the central ideas, and together they form the larger structure of the village. Pieces that fit nothing are the extraneous information you set aside.

questions.q: What happens to low structure-builders when questions are embedded in a text to focus readers on the main ideas?
options: Their learning improves to a level commensurate with that of high structure-builders
Their learning gets worse, since the questions add extra concepts for them to remember
Their learning stays unchanged, because structure building is a fixed cognitive limitation
Their learning rises only if they have been diagnosed and given a matched learning style
questions.explain: The embedded questions promote a more coherent representation of the text than low-structure readers can build alone. The authors still call the underlying cause an open question.

questions.q: Dana studies a history chapter by trying to memorize every name and date with equal effort, and cannot say what the chapter's main points were. Which difference from the chapter does this describe?
options: Rule learning: extracting the principles that apply to a whole group of similar cases
Low structure-building: failing to separate central ideas from less important information
Dynamic testing: using a test to find weak areas and then re-testing after more practice
Fluid intelligence: holding information in mind while working through a problem step by step
questions.explain: Dana cannot winnow the main ideas from the clutter, which is the mark of a low structure-builder. The chapter's gossiping friend with the manure story is the same failing.

questions.q: True or false: Questions embedded in a text can raise the learning performance of low structure-builders to the level of high structure-builders.
questions.explain: The embedded questions help build a coherent representation of the text that low structure-builders cannot build alone. Why this works remains an open question.

questions.q: Psychologists call the act of extracting the salient ideas of new material and building a coherent mental framework from them ____ building.
questions.explain: These frameworks are sometimes called mental models or mental maps. High structure-builders learn new material better than low structure-builders.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say high structure-builders do?
options: Identify foundational concepts and their key building blocks
Sort new information by whether it adds to the larger structure
Put aside information that is extraneous
Hang on to as many concepts as they can
Memorize each example separately
questions.explain: High structure-builders find the foundations, sort what fits, and set aside what does not. Hanging on to too many concepts is the low structure-builder's difficulty.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Lego village analogy in order.
items: Dump out the pieces and sort them into a handful of piles
Lay out the streets and sidewalks that define the perimeter
Sort the remaining pieces into elements such as school and hospital
Add extra pieces as substructures such as porches and streetlights
questions.explain: The analogy moves from the big framework down to central elements and then to finer substructures. This mirrors how a learner builds a mental model from a textbook.

questions.q: Match each part of the Lego analogy to what it stands for.
pairs: Town pictured on the box cover
The coherent mental model you set out to build
Elements such as school and hospital
Central ideas that form the larger structure
Substructures that give an existing block more depth
Pieces from another set that do not fit
Extraneous information that is set aside
questions.explain: The analogy shows how high structure-builders sort material by whether it adds to the structure. Extra pieces may either deepen a block or be put aside.

questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it describes a high or a low structure-builder.

items.t: Sets aside irrelevant or competing information
Identifies foundational concepts and key building blocks
Sorts new information by whether it adds to the structure
Holds on to too many concepts to build a workable model
Struggles to stick with an overarching structure
Has difficulty knowing what to discard

questions.explain: High structure-builders can separate the wheat from the chaff. Low structure-builders cannot decide what fits and so end up overloaded.

questions.q: Use the Lego village analogy to explain structure building and the difference between high and low structure-builders.
questions.a: Structure building is extracting the salient ideas from new material and building a coherent mental model from them, like building the town pictured on the Lego box. Central ideas are like elements such as the school or hospital, and added pieces become substructures that give them depth. High structure-builders sort information by whether it fits the larger structure and put aside what is extraneous, while low structure-builders cannot separate main ideas from clutter.

questions.q: What does research on embedded questions suggest about low structure-builders, and how does the chapter connect this to reflection?
questions.a: When questions embedded in a text focus readers on the main ideas, low structure-builders improve to the level of high structure-builders, because the questions promote a more coherent representation than they could build alone. Why this works is still an open question. The authors link it to the earlier idea that reflecting on experience and making it into a story strengthens learning, since asking what went right, what went wrong, and what to do differently helps isolate key ideas and organize them into mental models.

questions.q: When an example learner meets an unfamiliar chemistry problem, what does the chapter say they tend to do?
options: Apply a rule they abstracted earlier to classify the problem and choose the right solution
Break the problem into parts and sort them into a mental structure of central ideas
Generalize from the nearest example they can remember, even if it is not very relevant
Wait until a teacher presents the problem in the style they prefer before trying to solve it
questions.explain: Example learners memorize examples rather than principles, so they lack the rules needed for new cases. Rule learners are the ones who apply abstracted principles.

questions.q: According to the chapter, how can example learners get better at extracting underlying rules?
options: By rereading each single example several times until they can recite it from memory
By avoiding comparisons and concentrating on the details of whichever example is nearest
By waiting for a rule to be stated by the teacher before looking at any of the examples
By comparing two different examples rather than studying one example at a time
questions.explain: The chapter says example learners improve when asked to compare examples, and are more likely to find a common solution to disparate problems if they first work out the similarities.

questions.q: In the castle-and-moat and tumor problems, what common solution do students reach once they look for similarities?
options: Split the large force into smaller ones sent by different routes to converge on the target
Send the whole force along the safest single route and accept the risk of the adverse outcome
Use a stronger force that is able to overcome the obstacle that stands between it and the target
Wait until the obstacle weakens so that a small force alone can be enough to destroy the target
questions.explain: A small force is insufficient and a full force cannot pass by one route without harm. Splitting the force and converging on the target avoids both problems, and students can then solve other convergence problems.

questions.q: Why can a five-year-old who has memorized the knock-knock joke format still be poor at other kinds of jokes?
options: He has not yet memorized enough examples of jokes to generalize from the nearest one
He has not yet learned the rule that a punch line of any kind needs a setup
He is a low structure-builder, who cannot recall the order of the lines in a joke
He lacks the language fluency and reading ability needed to follow most adult jokes
questions.explain: At five he has memorized one structure but not the underlying rule that makes jokes work. The three-year-old, by contrast, skips the setup entirely.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter reports that research has already established that high structure-builders also tend to be rule learners.
questions.explain: The authors say research is not yet available to answer whether the two tendencies are correlated. What is known is that both high structure-builders and rule learners transfer learning to unfamiliar situations better.

questions.q: Learners who memorize examples rather than the underlying principles are called ____ learners.
questions.explain: When they meet an unfamiliar case they generalize from the nearest example they remember. Rule learners abstract the principles instead.

questions.q: The authors say knowledge is not ____ until you understand the underlying principles and can fit them into a structure larger than the sum of its parts.
questions.explain: Knowhow is learning that enables you to go do, as Bruce Hendry's boxcar purchase shows.

questions.q: Which similarities between the castle problem and the tumor problem do students often notice when asked to look for them?
options: A large force must be directed at a target
The full force cannot go through a single route without an adverse outcome
Smaller forces can be delivered but a small force is insufficient
Both involve mines that must be avoided
Both involve radiation passing through healthy tissue
questions.explain: Those are the three shared features. Mines belong only to the castle problem and radiation only to the tumor problem.

questions.q: Put these stages of the castle and tumor research findings in order.
items: Students struggle with either problem on its own
Students are told to look for similarities between the problems
Students notice what the problems share
Students arrive at the strategy of dividing the force into smaller forces
questions.explain: Without the comparison students have trouble with either problem. After comparing, they find the common solution and can apply it to other convergence problems.

questions.q: Match each type of learner to what the chapter says it does.
pairs: Abstracts underlying principles and applies them to classify a new case
Memorizes examples and generalizes from the nearest one remembered
Sorts new information by whether it adds to an overarching structure
Struggles to stick with an overarching structure or know what to discard
questions.explain: Rule learning and structure building are described as akin to each other. The chapter says it is not yet known whether the two are correlated.

questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it describes a rule learner or an example learner.

items.t: Abstracts the underlying principles from what is studied
Applies rules to classify a new bird specimen
Selects a solution to a new chemistry problem by the rules
Memorizes the examples rather than the principles
Generalizes from the nearest example remembered
Gains from comparing two examples at once

questions.explain: Rule learners carry principles to new cases. Example learners rely on remembered cases but can improve by comparing examples.

questions.q: Contrast rule learners with example learners, and describe how example learners can improve.
questions.a: Rule learners abstract the underlying principles that differentiate the examples they study and apply them to classify or solve new cases. Example learners memorize the examples and, facing an unfamiliar case, generalize from the nearest one they can remember even if it is not relevant. They can improve at extracting rules by comparing two examples rather than studying one at a time.

questions.q: Describe the castle and tumor problems and what students gain when they are told to look for similarities between them.
questions.a: A general must get a large force over mined bridges to a castle, and a doctor must destroy a tumor with radiation without damaging healthy tissue. Students struggle with either problem unless told to look for similarities, which are a large force directed at a target, no safe single route for the full force, and small forces that are safe but insufficient. They then find the strategy of dividing the force and converging from different routes, and can solve a variety of other convergence problems.

questions.q: Using Bruce Hendry's boxcar purchase, explain what the authors mean by knowhow and how it differs from knowledge.
questions.a: Bruce used the same supply-and-demand building block he learned from the fireworks, but within a larger model that included credit risk, business cycles, and bankruptcy processes. He researched why boxcars were in surplus, what they were worth, their lifespan and scrap value, and the lease contracts. Knowledge becomes knowhow only when you understand the underlying principles and fit them into a structure larger than the sum of its parts, so that it enables you to go do.

questions.q: What does the author mean by knowhow, using the boxcar example?
options: Knowledge of a single principle, such as supply and demand, that can be applied unchanged to every case
A gift for spotting value that some people are born with and that others cannot learn however hard they try
Learning that enables you to go do, built from principles fitted into a structure larger than its parts
A large stock of memorized facts about an industry, such as the cost to build a boxcar and its scrap value
questions.explain: The chapter says “Knowhow is learning that enables you to go do.” Bruce's boxcar deal used supply and demand together with credit risk, business cycles, and bankruptcy processes, which is why it was more than the fireworks lesson.

questions.q: Why does the Takeaway tell learners not to assume they are doing something wrong if the learning feels hard?
options: Feeling that learning is hard is a sign that your preferred learning style is not being used here
Hard learning usually means the material is too advanced and should be put off until you are better prepared
The difficulty you feel is a reliable sign of how much you actually know about the subject matter
Difficulties you can overcome with extra effort repay you in depth and durability of learning
questions.explain: The authors point to desirable difficulties: extra effort that deepens and lengthens learning. Feelings alone are not a reliable guide, which is why they also urge quizzing and peer review.

questions.q: True or false: The Takeaway advises that if learning feels hard, you should conclude that you are doing something wrong and change your method.
questions.explain: It says the opposite: difficulties you can overcome with greater cognitive effort repay you in depth and durability of learning.

questions.q: In the winding stair model of Bruce Hendry's investing, each tread protects against losing money and each ____ lifts you up a notch.
questions.explain: Treads and risers must both be present for a deal to be attractive. Impending scarcity of boxcars is a riser.

questions.q: The Takeaway uses the old truism from sales school that you can't shoot a ____ from the lodge.
questions.explain: The point is that learning requires you to get out the door and go after what you want. Mastery is a quest.

questions.q: Which of these does the Takeaway recommend?
options: Use quizzing and peer review to check your judgment of what you know
Adopt active strategies such as retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving
If you are an example learner, study examples two or more at a time
Stay within your preferred learning style
Avoid study methods that feel difficult
questions.explain: The Takeaway recommends checking judgment, active strategies, and comparing examples. It tells learners to go wide beyond a pigeonhole style and not to read difficulty as a sign of error.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Takeaway's advice on being the one in charge in order.
items: Describe what you want to know, do, or accomplish
List the competencies required
Identify where you can find the knowledge or skill
Go get it
questions.explain: The chapter advises describing the goal, listing the competencies and sources, and then going after it. You cannot shoot a deer from the lodge.

questions.q: Match each Takeaway heading to its advice.
pairs: Do not roost in a pigeonhole of preferred style; tap all your intelligences
Embrace the notion of successful intelligence
Use active strategies and check your judgment with quizzing and peer review
Distill the underlying principles; build the structure
Abstract the rules and piece them into a structure to gain knowhow
questions.explain: These are the three bold run-in headings of the chapter's Takeaway. Each pairs a short heading with a paragraph of practical advice.

questions.q: Match each part of the winding stair model of Bruce Hendry's investing to what it stands for.
pairs: The investment opportunity that connects where we are to where we want to be
A tread that protects against dropping back and losing money
A riser that raises values and lifts the deal up a notch
questions.explain: Treads and risers must both be present for the deal to be attractive. A deal without them will not protect the downside or reliably deliver the upside.

questions.q: Sort each element of Bruce Hendry's boxcar deal by whether it is a tread or a riser in the winding stair model.
groups: Riser: lifts the deal up a notch

items.t: Scrap value of the boxcars
Guaranteed lease income while capital is tied up
Impending scarcity of boxcars
Like-new condition of the cars

questions.explain: Treads protect the downside and risers deliver the upside. Both must be present for the deal to be attractive.

questions.q: Sort each piece of advice by whether the Takeaway recommends it or warns against it.

items.t: Practicing dynamic testing to discover weaknesses
Studying examples two at a time if you are an example learner
Developing workarounds for holes in your aptitudes
Roosting in a pigeonhole of your preferred learning style
Relying on what feels best to judge what you know
Assuming you are doing something wrong because learning feels hard

questions.explain: The Takeaway pushes active, versatile learning and accurate self-checking. It cautions against comfort-based judgments and style pigeonholes.

questions.q: If you think you are a low structure-builder or an example learner, what does the Takeaway suggest you do while learning new material?
questions.a: Pause periodically and ask what the central ideas and rules are, then describe each idea and recall related points. Separate the big ideas from supporting concepts and nuances, imagine a scaffold or framework holding the central ideas together, and test yourself on the main ideas. An example learner should also study examples two at a time or more, asking how they are alike and different and whether they need different solutions or a common one.

questions.q: After setting aside learning styles, what does Chapter 6 turn to for the rest of the chapter?
options: Other learning differences that do matter, like intelligence, structure building, rule learning
A ranked review of the seventy-plus learning styles theories to find which assessments are best
Methods for matching instruction to each student's preferred sense so that every learner benefits
A catalogue of the cognitive tests that can fix each person's learning potential at an early age
questions.explain: The chapter says it acknowledges preferences but is not persuaded that matching instruction to them helps, and that other differences do matter. Successful Intelligence opens the move to those differences.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter introduces Sternberg's three-part theory of successful intelligence just before it proposes dynamic testing, which Sternberg and Grigorenko offer in tandem with that model.
questions.explain: Dynamic testing appears right after the successful intelligence section and is described as proposed in tandem with Sternberg's three-part model. It carries the idea of developing expertise into a practical learning strategy.

questions.q: The chapter says the work of Carol Dweck is described in Chapter ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 7, Increase Your Abilities, takes up Dweck's work. Chapter 6 only notes that how you see your abilities matters a lot.

questions.q: Which of these are sections of Chapter 6 that come after its discussion of successful intelligence?
options: Dynamic Testing
Structure Building
Growth Mindset
Rule versus Example Learning
Deliberate Practice
questions.explain: Dynamic Testing, Structure Building, and Rule versus Example Learning follow in that order, then The Takeaway. Growth Mindset and Deliberate Practice are sections of Chapter 7.

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 6, after its opening discussion of learning styles, in the order they appear.
items: Successful Intelligence
Dynamic Testing
Structure Building
Rule versus Example Learning
The Takeaway
questions.explain: The chapter moves from intelligence to testing to two cognitive differences, structure building and rule learning, and then closes with practical advice.

questions.q: Why does the chapter open with Bruce Hendry's story, and how does it come back to him in the sections on learning differences that matter?
questions.a: His story frames the argument that some learning differences matter more than others, such as taking charge of your own education, rule learning, and structure building. The chapter later returns to him to illustrate developing expertise through setbacks, the lesson of dynamic testing, and the boxcar deal as an example of knowhow. The winding stair in the chapter's opening quotation becomes the structure the Takeaway uses for his investment model.

questions.q: How does the Takeaway of Chapter 6 connect back to Chapter 5 and point ahead to Chapter 7?
questions.a: The Takeaway tells learners to use quizzing, peer review, and the other tools described in Chapter 5 to check that their judgment of what they know is accurate rather than relying on what feels best. Earlier in Chapter 6 the authors point to Chapter 7 for Carol Dweck's work on how you see yourself and your abilities, which matters for learning. The chapter's message that expertise is always developing leads naturally to Chapter 7's theme of increasing your abilities.

questions.q: In the marshmallow study led by Walter Mischel, what share of the more than six hundred nursery school children held out long enough to earn the second marshmallow?
options: About one-third of them
About half of them
About two-thirds of them
Nearly all of them
questions.explain: Only about one-third resisted for the full wait, so most children gave in. The follow-up studies then linked the ability to wait with later success.

questions.q: The word “mnemonic” comes from the Greek word for ____.
questions.explain: Mnemonic devices are mental tools for holding material in memory, cued for ready recall, and the term itself comes from the Greek word for memory.

questions.q: True or false: James Paterson first took up mnemonics because he wanted to become a memory champion.
questions.explain: He wanted a shortcut to memorize classwork quickly and free up time for friends. Entering the Cambridge competition came later, on a lark.

questions.q: Why did Nelson Dellis, the 2012 US Memory Champion, first turn to mind sports?
options: He wanted prize money to fund his mountain-climbing trips and expeditions
He hoped a trained memory would give him reserves against Alzheimer’s
He hoped mnemonics would shorten his time spent studying for university exams
He hoped to beat James Paterson at the World Memory Championships
questions.explain: Dellis watched his grandmother decline from Alzheimer’s, with memory going first, and wanted reserves in case the disease came for him. The study shortcut was James Paterson’s motive, not his.

questions.q: True or false: The author likens the infant brain to a fledgling nation that must build cities, roads and telegraph lines before it becomes capable.
questions.explain: Just as the young country needed infrastructure to become mighty, the brain starts with the raw material of genes and becomes capable through learning and neural pathways.

questions.q: What point does the story of Kit Carson’s mule journey carrying Fremont’s message make about the infant brain?
options: Like the young nation, it is fully equipped at birth and just needs time to grow up
Like the scout, it succeeds only by pushing itself past its limits on the way
Like the young nation, it starts with raw material and becomes capable by building
Like the continent, it already holds all the roads it will ever have
questions.explain: Carson’s journey showed how undeveloped the country was. The author says a brain likewise needs mental models and neural pathways built through learning.

questions.q: Name three kinds of evidence the author gives at the start of Chapter 7 that the brain and its abilities are not fixed from birth.
questions.a: Average IQs have risen over the past century; after strokes or accidents the brain reassigns duties so adjacent neurons take over from damaged areas; memory athletes have trained themselves to astonishing recall; and expert performance in fields like medicine, music, chess and sports comes from skills laid down through thousands of hours of practice. Any three of these answer the question.

questions.q: The author says the brain is remarkably ____, the neuroscience term for its ability to change, even into old age.
questions.explain: Plastic means mutable: the brain reorganizes itself with new tasks and keeps that ability for most people into old age.

questions.q: Which of these does the author cite as evidence that the brain and its abilities can change?
options: Average IQs have risen over the past century
Neighboring neurons taking over the work of areas damaged by a stroke
Memory athletes who train themselves to astonishing recall
Children’s brains forming no new circuits after their first birthday
Marshmallow-study results being fixed at birth by genes
questions.explain: The first three are offered as signs that the brain and its abilities are changeable. The other two contradict the author’s view.

questions.q: Match each person from the chapter’s opening to who they are or what they did.
pairs: Led the marshmallow study of delayed gratification in nursery school children
Welshman who won the beginner category at a Cambridge memory contest in 2006
Memory champion who founded Climb for Memory after his grandmother’s Alzheimer’s
Scout who carried Fremont’s report across the continent to President Polk
questions.explain: Each person is introduced in the opening story: Mischel with the marshmallow study, Paterson and Dellis as memory athletes, and Carson as the scout in the nation analogy.

questions.q: Put the steps of James Paterson’s path into memory competition in the order the author tells them.
items: A university instructor mentions mnemonics in a lecture
He buys a book and starts practicing memorizing
He wins the beginner category at a Cambridge contest
He competes at the World Memory Championships in London
questions.explain: He picked up mnemonics as a study shortcut and practiced, then entered the Cambridge contest in 2006 and won the beginner category before going on to London that same year.

questions.q: Put the stages of the marshmallow experiment in order, from setup to what researchers later learned.
items: A child is shown into a room with one marshmallow on a tray
The child is told to wait fifteen minutes to get a second one
The researcher leaves while observers watch through a mirror
Some children eat at once while others try to hold back
Follow-up studies track how the children fared later
questions.explain: The children faced the choice alone while observers watched, and only afterward did follow-up studies connect waiting with later success in school and careers.

questions.q: What did follow-up studies of the marshmallow children find, and what does the author conclude about what determines success?
questions.a: Children who had been better at delaying gratification grew up to be more successful in school and in their careers, as shown in follow-up studies up to 2011. The author concludes that, besides the gift of genes, success is shaped to a surprising degree by focus and self-discipline, which come from motivation and a sense of personal empowerment.

questions.q: A ____ is a connection between two neurons that lets them pass signals.
questions.explain: When an axon meets a dendrite, a synapse forms, and neural circuitry is made of these connections.

questions.q: Humans are born with about 100 billion nerve cells, which are called ____.
questions.explain: Neurons are the nerve cells that sprout axons and dendrites to connect with one another.

questions.q: Match each part of the nervous system to its description in the chapter.
pairs: Branch a neuron sprouts to reach out toward other neurons
Tiny nub on a neuron where an axon connects
Connection formed when an axon meets a dendrite, letting neurons pass signals
Waxy wrapping around some axons, like coating on a lamp cord
questions.explain: An axon reaches for a dendrite, and where they meet is a synapse. Myelin is the insulating wrap around some axons.

questions.q: Put the steps by which a synapse forms, as the author describes, in order.
items: A neuron sprouts microscopic branches called axons
The axons reach out in search of dendrites on other neurons
An axon meets a dendrite
A synapse is formed between the two neurons
questions.explain: Bruer describes the early wiring of the brain as “an exuberant burst of synapse formation.” Some axons must travel great distances to find their target dendrites.

questions.q: Put these points in the life of a child’s synapses in order.
items: A burst of synapse formation around birth
The number of synapses peaks at age one or two
A plateau lasts until about puberty
Pruning reduces the overabundance
The adult complement is reached around age sixteen
questions.explain: Synapses overshoot to about 50 percent above the adult number, hold steady, and are then pruned down to roughly 150 trillion connections by about sixteen.

questions.q: At their peak around age one or two, how does the number of synapses in a child’s brain compare with the adult number?
options: About the same number as adults have
About 50 percent below what adults have
About twice as many as adults have
About 50 percent above what adults have
questions.explain: Infants overproduce connections, reaching about half again the adult count before pruning begins around puberty.

questions.q: The brain reaches its adult complement of synapses at around age ____.
questions.explain: After the plateau and the period of synaptic pruning, the adult total of about 150 trillion connections is reached at about sixteen.

questions.q: Which of these are explanations the author mentions for how the infant brain decides which connections to prune?
options: Connections that go unused fade and die away
Genetics largely determines which synapses survive
Parents pick which connections survive through the toys they buy
The brain prunes the connections it uses most often
questions.explain: The author gives two theories: a use-it-or-lose-it view and a genetic view. The author also admits that scientists do not yet know how the brain decides.

questions.q: True or false: The author says scientists clearly understand why the infant brain produces an overabundance of connections.
questions.explain: The author says we do not know why the infant brain overproduces connections or how it later decides which ones to prune.

questions.q: According to neuroscientist Patricia Goldman-Rakic, when does most learning take place?
options: During the burst of synapse formation around the time of birth
Only in the first two years, before pruning begins
After synapse formation stabilizes and synapse numbers hold
During puberty, when pruning removes the weakest connections of all
questions.explain: She points out that from first grade through college, synapse numbers hardly change, and that is when adult-level skills in language, math and logic develop.

questions.q: What did the 2011 British review of the neuroscience evidence conclude about the brain’s structure?
options: Gross structure is shaped by experience, while fine network structure is fixed by genes
Both gross and fine network structure are fixed by genes before birth
Both gross and fine network structure are shaped almost entirely by experience
Gross structure is mostly genetic, while fine network structure is shaped by experience
questions.explain: Genes largely determine the brain’s overall architecture, but the fine structure of its networks can be substantially modified by experience.

questions.q: True or false: From first grade through college, there is little change in the number of synapses in a person’s brain.
questions.explain: Goldman-Rakic notes that synapse numbers change little after stabilization, yet most learning happens in this period.

questions.q: How does John Bruer illustrate the scale of the journey some axons make to find their target dendrites?
options: He likens it to crossing the United States to reach a waiting partner
He likens it to a river carrying messages from the mountains to the sea
He likens it to a telegraph line being built from coast to coast
He likens it to a marathon runner crossing a finish line
questions.explain: Bruer’s comparison echoes the author’s story of Kit Carson crossing the continent with a message for President Polk.

questions.q: Match each person to the contribution described in the Neuroplasticity discussion.
pairs: Reviewed the neuroscience of early circuit development and stabilization
Wrote about patients who overcame severe impairments through neuroplasticity
Pioneered devices that substitute one sensory system for another
Held that experience after infancy fine-tunes circuits and makes architecture unique
questions.explain: Each figure represents a different strand of the chapter’s discussion: early development, case studies, sensory-substitution devices and the role of experience.

questions.q: Paul Bach-y-Rita explained that the eyes only sense, while the ____ interprets and so does the seeing.
questions.explain: His device works only because the brain learns to interpret signals from the tongue as sight, and that is why the substituted sense gets better with practice.

questions.q: Which of these devices or methods does the author describe as using one sense or body area to stand in for another?
options: A strip of electrodes on the tongue, wired to head-mounted levels, for a patient with balance loss
A helmet camera sending pulses to the tongue of a man who had lost his sight
Stimulators on pilots’ chests that relay cockpit instrument readings
A drug that regrows damaged sensory organs
A cap that records neurons while a person sleeps
questions.explain: All three correct options send information through a different route to the brain. The other two are not described in the chapter.

questions.q: Sort each aspect of the brain by whether it is described as largely set by genes or shaped by experience and practice.

items.t: The gross structure of the brain
The starting robustness of neural connections
The fine structure of neural networks
The thickness of myelin along practiced pathways
The fine-tuning of circuits during the school years

questions.explain: The twin study and the British review point to genes for gross structure and early robustness, but experience fine-tunes networks and practice builds myelin.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it shows sensory substitution or growth through practice and learning.

items.t: Electrodes on the tongue to restore balance
A helmet camera sending signals to the tongue
Chest stimulators that help pilots sense altitude
Reading Braille through touch
Thicker myelin from piano practice
New hippocampal neurons during associative learning
A practiced routine recoded in the basal ganglia

questions.explain: The first group replaces a lost or failing sense with another route. The second group shows the brain physically changing through practice and learning.

questions.q: The UCLA study compared identical and fraternal twins. What did it suggest about the maturation of neural circuitry?
options: Circuitry matures fully by the end of childhood, in step with physical growth
Early robustness is largely genetic, but circuitry keeps changing into middle age
Circuitry is shaped by experience alone, as identical twins differ as much as fraternal ones
Circuitry stops changing at about sixteen, once the adult complement of synapses is reached
questions.explain: The speed of mental abilities depends on connection robustness, which is largely genetic at first. Circuitry does not mature as early as the body does, and goes on changing for decades.

questions.q: The word “connectome” was coined in the same spirit as “____,” the map of the human genetic code.
questions.explain: The Human Connectome Project aims to map the connections of the human brain, just as the genome project mapped the genetic code.

questions.q: In which direction does myelination generally proceed through the brain?
options: From the front toward the back, ending at the base of the skull
From the back toward the front, ending in the frontal lobes
From the deep center outward, finishing at the surface
From the left side to the right, finishing in the hippocampus
questions.explain: The frontal lobes, which handle executive functions such as reasoning and judgment, are reached last, and those skills develop through experience.

questions.q: Research suggests that increased practice builds greater ____, the waxy coating on axons, which improves signal strength and speed.
questions.explain: Thicker myelin along the pathways in use is linked to better performance, as seen in the finger-movement fibers of pianists.

questions.q: On this chapter’s account, which brain change would you expect in a pianist who greatly increases her practice?
options: More myelin on the fibers tied to finger movement and music
More synapses than an average adult, restoring the infant peak
A larger hippocampus that takes over from the basal ganglia
Thinner myelin that lets signals travel much faster
questions.explain: Increases in piano practice correlate with increased myelination of the relevant fibers, a change not seen in nonmusicians.

questions.q: Which of these statements about myelin does the author make?
options: It is a waxy sheath wrapped around some axons
Its thickness correlates with ability
Practice builds more of it along the related pathways
It makes up the gray matter of the brain
It is lost during pruning at puberty
questions.explain: Myelin coats axons in white matter, and practice thickens it where it is needed. Gray matter is the neural cell bodies.

questions.q: Match each brain region or tissue to its description in the chapter.
pairs: Deep region that directs actions that have become habit
Where learning and memory are consolidated, and new neurons can form
Home of executive functions, high-level reasoning and judgment
The wiring: axons and their myelin sheaths
Made up mostly of neural cell bodies
questions.explain: Each region has a different role: habits, memory consolidation, reasoning, and the two tissues that make up the brain’s cells and wiring.

questions.q: Put the steps by which a repeated motor skill becomes a habit, as the author describes, in order.
items: A person takes conscious action toward a goal
Extended training and repetition follow
The learning is recoded in the basal ganglia
The brain chunks the sequence into a single unit
The sequence becomes an automatic response to stimuli
questions.explain: Repeated practice moves the skill from conscious control to a deeper region, where chunking lets it run as one unit without a series of conscious decisions.

questions.q: Some researchers use the word “____,” a simple computer app, to describe how chunking consolidates a sequence of actions into one unit.
questions.explain: Like a macro, a chunked sequence runs as a single efficient unit rather than as separate conscious steps.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it is habit-driven and automatic or conscious and goal-directed.

items.t: A typist’s fingers moving without thought
A musician’s fingers outpacing conscious thought
An athlete reacting faster than he can think
Eye movements and other subconscious actions
Taking deliberate action toward a goal
Carefully planning how to reach a goal

questions.explain: Habitual actions are directed from the deeper basal ganglia, while consciously taking action toward a goal uses different circuits.

questions.q: What is chunking, and how does it help explain fast, skilled performance in sports, music and chess?
questions.a: As extended repetition recodes learning in the basal ganglia, the brain chunks motor and cognitive action sequences together so they run as a single unit, without a series of conscious decisions. This is why athletes can respond faster than they can think, a musician’s fingers can outpace conscious thought, and a chess player can foresee many possible moves.

questions.q: The generation of new neurons in the hippocampus is called ____.
questions.explain: Neurogenesis continues throughout life and is thought to play a central role in recovery from injury and in lifelong learning.

questions.q: Neurogenesis in the hippocampus begins to rise before a new learning task starts. What does the author say this suggests?
options: That new neurons are made only once learning is complete
That the learning task has no effect on neuron creation
That neurogenesis responds only to physical injury
That the brain is showing an intention to learn
questions.explain: The rise begins before learning, suggesting intention, and continues afterward, suggesting a role in consolidating memory.

questions.q: Which of these learning practices does the author say are consistent with neuroplasticity?
options: Retrieval practice
Spacing out practice
Constructing mental models
Avoiding effortful retrieval so as to prevent errors
Studying only in one’s preferred sensory style
questions.explain: Retrieval practice, spacing, rehearsal, rule learning and mental models all improve learning, which is evidence that neural pathways are strengthened by use.

questions.q: What does the author mean by calling the brain plastic, and what are two pieces of evidence from the Neuroplasticity section?
questions.a: Plastic means the brain is not hardwired but mutable, reorganizing itself with each new task. Evidence includes Bach-y-Rita’s devices, where the brain learns to read tongue signals as balance or sight; thicker myelin from practice, as in pianists; the habit recoding of skills in the basal ganglia; and new hippocampal neurons produced by learning.

questions.q: Describe the two theories about why the infant brain overproduces synapses and then prunes them, and what each implies about early stimulation.
questions.a: One theory says connections that are not used fade and die away, a use-it-or-lose-it idea that argues for stimulating as many connections as possible early on. The other says the burgeoning and winnowing is determined by genetics, so we have little or no influence over which synapses survive. The author notes that we do not yet know which is right.

questions.q: According to Goldman-Rakic and Chugani, when does most learning happen, and what does experience do during that time?
questions.a: Goldman-Rakic says most learning happens after synapse formation stabilizes, from first grade through college and beyond, when synapse numbers change little, and adult-level skills in language, math and logic develop. Chugani adds that it is likely during this period, more than infancy, that experience and environmental stimulation fine-tune circuits and make one’s neuronal architecture unique.

questions.q: What did the UCLA twin study and related research suggest about the speed of mental abilities and about when neural circuitry matures?
questions.a: The speed of mental abilities depends on the robustness of neural connections, which at the initial stages is largely determined by genes, as shown by comparing identical and fraternal twins. But circuitry does not mature as early as physical development: it keeps changing and growing through the forties, fifties and sixties, partly as myelin thickens.

questions.q: What is neurogenesis, and how does the author link it to learning and memory?
questions.a: Neurogenesis is the creation of new neurons in the hippocampus, which continues throughout life and is thought to help recovery from injury and lifelong learning. Associative learning, such as linking names and faces, increases it. The rise starts before the learning, suggesting an intention to learn, and continues afterward, suggesting a role in consolidating memory.

questions.q: The sustained rise in IQ scores since standardized sampling began in 1932 is called the ____ effect.
questions.explain: The effect is named after the political scientist who first brought it to wide attention.

questions.q: True or false: The author compares IQ to height: mostly inherited, yet raised across generations by better nutrition.
questions.explain: Both are products of genes and environment, so IQs have risen over decades just as height has with improved nutrition.

questions.q: Given the eighteen-point rise in average US IQ over sixty years, an IQ of 100 today corresponds to which score sixty years ago?
questions.explain: The mean is reset to 100 for each test-taking group, so today’s 100 equals about 118 on the scale of sixty years ago.

questions.q: What is the principal explanation the author gives for the Flynn effect?
options: Test makers made the standardized IQ tests easier with each decade
Genes for high intelligence spread rapidly through industrialized countries
Children now begin formal schooling about two years earlier than before
Changes in schools, television and nutrition raised verbal and math skills
questions.explain: These environmental changes affect the abilities measured by the subtests that make up IQ tests. The mean has risen, and several theories exist, with this one as the principal one.

questions.q: Which of these are given as reasons that average IQ has risen over recent decades?
options: Changes in schooling
Changes in culture, such as television
Improved nutrition
A faster evolution of genes for intelligence
Shorter IQ test sessions
questions.explain: The author names schools, culture and nutrition as changes affecting verbal and math abilities. Nothing is said about genes evolving or test length.

questions.q: Two equally bright children differ only slightly, in that one is a bit more curious. Which idea of Nisbett’s explains why the curious one may end up much smarter in a stimulating environment?
options: The Flynn effect raises both children’s IQs by the same amount
Socioeconomic status fixes both children’s IQs at the same level
Environmental multipliers amplify a small genetic difference
Synaptic pruning removes the connections of the less curious child
questions.explain: A slight inborn edge in curiosity is multiplied where curiosity is easily piqued and satisfied, as a tall kid’s basketball skill grows by playing.

questions.q: Explain Richard Nisbett’s idea of environmental multipliers using the basketball and curiosity examples.
questions.a: A small advantage can be amplified by the environment. A tall kid who goes out for basketball develops a proficiency a shorter kid with the same aptitudes won’t, and a curious kid who goes for learning gets smarter than an equally bright but incurious kid. A very small genetic difference in curiosity is multiplied in an environment where curiosity is easily piqued and satisfied.

questions.q: What is the Flynn effect, and why does the author present it as evidence that IQ is not purely inherited?
questions.a: It is the sustained rise in IQs in every industrialized part of the world since standardized sampling began in 1932, with the US average up eighteen points in sixty years. Like height, IQ is mostly inherited but influenced by environment, and the principal explanation is that schools, culture such as television, and nutrition have changed in ways that raise verbal and math abilities.

questions.q: Which statement matches the author’s report on children from impoverished families who were adopted into affluent families?
options: They scored higher only if their birth parents had been of high status
They scored higher than non-adopted peers regardless of birth parentage
They scored the same as non-adopted children from poor families
They scored higher only if they were adopted before turning one year old
questions.explain: This shows an environmental effect: affluent families offer more stimulation and nurturing, regardless of the birth parents’ socioeconomic status.

questions.q: How does socioeconomic status affect IQ according to the author, and what evidence is given?
questions.a: Children from affluent families test higher for IQ on average, because families with more resources and education generally provide more stimulation and nurturing. Children from impoverished families who are adopted into affluent families score higher than those who are not adopted, regardless of whether their birth parents were of high or low socioeconomic status.

questions.q: Which of these were requirements for a study to count in the 2013 review of raising intelligence in young children?
options: A randomized, experimental design
A general, nonclinical population
A widely accepted, standardized measure of intelligence
A one-shot treatment given just before the test
Participants who were all school-age children
questions.explain: The review also required sustained interventions, not one-shot treatments or manipulations during testing. It focused on children from the prenatal period through age five.

questions.q: The 2013 review of raising intelligence in young children drew on studies involving over ____ participants.
questions.explain: Strict inclusion criteria limited which studies counted, and the eligible ones still involved over 37,000 participants.

questions.q: Match each term from the IQ discussion to its meaning.
pairs: Sustained rise in IQ scores since standardized sampling began in 1932
Setting that magnifies a small genetic edge, such as curiosity
Treatment lasting over time, not a one-shot or test-time manipulation
Environmental enrichment and structured learning before preschool
questions.explain: These terms appear in the discussion of Nisbett’s ideas and of the 2013 review’s criteria and definitions.

questions.q: By how much did dietary supplements of fatty acids raise IQ in the 2013 review?
options: From 3.5 to 6.5 points
By less than one point
From 10 to 15 points
By 18 points
questions.explain: Fatty acid supplements given to pregnant women, breast-feeding women and infants raised IQ by roughly 3.5 to 6.5 points. The theory is that they supply building blocks for new synapses.

questions.q: True or false: The studies of iron and B complex vitamin supplements were considered definitive proof of IQ benefits.
questions.explain: They strongly suggested benefits, but the author says these need validation through further research before they can be considered definitive.

questions.q: In the 2013 review, why did center-based early education raise poor children’s IQ more than home-based programs?
options: At home, stimulation is less consistently sustained
Centers start earlier, within a narrow window of development
Home programs could only be given to affluent families
Centers added fatty acid supplements to the children’s diet
questions.explain: Early education raised poor children’s IQ by more than four points, and by more than seven if it was center-based, rather than home-based.

questions.q: True or false: The review found evidence that the younger children are when first enrolled in early education, the better the results.
questions.explain: No evidence supports that notion. The evidence suggests the earliest few years are not narrow windows that soon close.

questions.q: Which of these parent-focused approaches did the review link to IQ gains in young children?
options: Giving low-income mothers educational tools, books and puzzles, and training in helping children talk
Training mothers of three-year-olds to talk at length and ask open-ended questions
Reading to a child aged four or younger and encouraging the child to elaborate
Keeping children out of preschool until age five
Reading aloud only after the child turns five
questions.explain: Active participation by the child mattered in reading. After age four, reading to a child does not raise IQ but does speed language development.

questions.q: Sort each claim by whether the 2013 review supported it or found no evidence for it.
groups: No evidence, or not yet validated

items.t: Fatty acid supplements raise young children’s IQ
Center-based early education raises poor children’s IQ
Preschool with language training raises IQ by more than seven points
Earlier first enrollment always gives better results
Early education raises the IQ of children from better-off families
Iron and B vitamins are definitive IQ boosters

questions.explain: The review found gains for poor children from nutrition and education, but found no support for earlier-is-better or for gains among better-off children.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is a genetic contribution or an environmental contribution to IQ as the author describes.

items.t: A small inborn difference in curiosity
The mostly inherited part of IQ, like height
Better nutrition across generations
Changes in schools and television over decades
More stimulation in affluent families
Puzzle mazes in children’s meals harder than test mazes

questions.explain: IQ is a product of both, as height is. Genes provide a base, but nutrition, culture, schooling and family resources shift the average.

questions.q: What did the 2013 review find about nutrition and early education as ways to raise young children’s IQ?
questions.a: Fatty acid supplements raised IQ by about 3.5 to 6.5 points, while iron and B vitamins looked promising but need validation. Enrolling poor children in early education raised IQ by more than four points, and by more than seven if center-based. There was no evidence of gains for better-off children, or that starting younger gives better results.

questions.q: Match each number from the chapter to what it counts or marks.
pairs: Connections thought to make up the adult complement
Microelectrodes on the strip placed on a patient’s tongue
When we reach the adult complement of synapses
questions.explain: These figures come from the discussion of early brain development and Bach-y-Rita’s balance device.

questions.q: Match each intervention from the 2013 review to its reported result.
pairs: Raised IQ by roughly 3.5 to 6.5 points
Raised IQ by more than four points
Raised IQ by more than seven points
Strongly suggested benefits but need validation
Does not raise IQ but speeds language development
questions.explain: The review found clear IQ gains from fatty acids and early education for poor children, and weaker or different results for the others.

questions.q: After the chapter reviews neuroplasticity and whether IQ can be raised, what does it promise to describe?
options: A training program that reliably raises everyone’s IQ in weeks
A set of supplements that rebuild a person’s lost synapses entirely
Three strategies for getting more from the intelligence you have
A history of intelligence testing since the year 1932 onward
questions.explain: The chapter first asks about the brain’s ability to change and the chance of raising IQ, then turns to strategies that use the intelligence you already have.

questions.q: Put the first six sections of Chapter 7 in the order they appear.
items: Neuroplasticity
Is IQ Mutable?
Brain Training?
Growth Mindset
Deliberate Practice
Memory Cues
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the brain’s capacity to change, to raising IQ, to doubts about brain-training games, and then to three strategies, ending with the takeaway.

questions.q: What does the chapter title Increase Your Abilities signal, given that the chapter opens with sections on neuroplasticity and IQ?
options: That genes set abilities, so only study techniques can be improved a bit
That abilities, intelligence included, can be shaped by effort
That IQ can be raised mainly through online brain-training games
That abilities rise automatically with age, with no effort required
questions.explain: The author argues that effortful learning changes the brain, so abilities are, to a considerable degree, ours to shape.

questions.q: Why does the chapter take up neuroplasticity before it asks whether IQ is mutable?
options: IQ tests measure only the number of synapses a person has in the brain
The Flynn effect was first found through brain imaging studies
Neuroplasticity shows that IQ cannot be changed in adulthood
The brain’s ability to change underpins any hope of raising ability
questions.explain: The opening says the chapter will first review the brain’s ability to change itself, then people’s ability to influence those changes and to raise IQ.

questions.q: True or false: The Neuroplasticity section ends by framing intellectual development as a lifelong dialogue between inherited tendencies and life history, which the rest of the chapter explores.
questions.explain: The Barnets’ phrase, “a lifelong dialogue between inherited tendencies and our life history,” sets up the questions on IQ, mindset, practice and memory that follow.

questions.q: Match each Chapter 7 section to its focus.
pairs: How the brain changes itself throughout life
Whether and how intelligence can be raised
Whether online games can raise fluid intelligence
The belief that ability lies largely in your own hands
questions.explain: The section headings track the chapter’s argument from the brain’s changeability to IQ, to brain games, to strategies that multiply the intelligence you have.

questions.q: How does the chapter move from asking whether IQ can be raised to the strategies it recommends?
questions.a: It shows that IQ is shaped by genes and environment and can be raised somewhat, through nutrition and early education, and then examines brain-training games with doubt. Since raising IQ is unlikely for most adults, the author turns to strategies that act as cognitive multipliers for the intelligence you already have: a growth mindset, practicing like an expert, and constructing memory cues.

questions.q: In the Swiss study on brain training reported in 2008, which ability were researchers trying to improve?
options: Crystallized intelligence, the storehouse of knowledge built up through the years
Procedural memory, the facility for performing practiced motor sequences smoothly
Fluid intelligence, the facility for abstract reasoning and new problems
Sustained attention, the facility for ignoring distractions over long periods
questions.explain: The study aimed to raise fluid intelligence. Crystallized intelligence, the accumulated knowledge, is the other kind of intelligence and can already be raised through effective learning and memory strategies.

questions.q: Which is a criticism the authors raise about the Swiss working-memory study?
options: Only thirty-five participants took part, all from a similar, highly intelligent population
Only a handful of participants were retested, and none were tested on fluid intelligence at the start
Every participant trained for just one session, so the length of training could not be compared
Participants were drawn from a clinical population, so the findings cannot apply to healthy adults
questions.explain: The authors point to the small, similar sample, the single training task, the unknown durability and the lack of replication. The study did test fluid intelligence before and after training, and its participants trained for varying periods up to nineteen days.

questions.q: According to the authors, if brain-training products really do improve a person's efficacy and self-confidence, what is the more likely reason?
options: Stronger working memory, which then lifts every other intellectual skill the person uses
Faster signalling along axons, which then speeds up every kind of thinking the person does
New neurons in the hippocampus, which then improve all of the person's learning and recall
Better habits, such as learning to focus attention and to persist at practice
questions.explain: The authors say the ability to make practice a habit is generalizable, so any broad benefit is more likely the fruit of better habits. Strengthening one skill does not automatically strengthen others.

questions.q: A friend plays an online game that drills one type of memory puzzle and expects it to help her learn chemistry faster. Based on the authors' reasoning, what is the most likely outcome?
options: She will improve at the puzzle and also gain a smaller lift in every subject she studies afterward
She will improve at the puzzle itself, but the gain will not spread to mastering chemistry
She will improve at the puzzle, and her chemistry will benefit only if the game is played daily
She will see no improvement at the puzzle, because working memory cannot be changed by training
questions.explain: The authors write that the brain is not a muscle, so strengthening one skill does not automatically strengthen others. Benefits stay with the material or skill practiced.

questions.q: True or false: A 2013 attempt to replicate the exercises in the Swiss working-memory study found the same gains in fluid intelligence.
questions.explain: The 2013 attempt failed to find any improvement in fluid intelligence. Participants nonetheless believed their abilities had improved, which the authors call illusory.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, retrieval practice and building mental models improve ability in the material practiced, but the benefits do not extend to mastery of other material.
questions.explain: The brain is not a muscle, so strengthening one skill does not automatically strengthen others. Observed myelination in piano virtuosos is likewise specific to piano playing.

questions.q: Which of these are criticisms the authors make of the Swiss working-memory study?
options: It used only one training task
Its results have not been replicated
It did not test fluid intelligence before training
Its improvement was never measured after the training ended
It tested only thirty-five participants
questions.explain: The authors note the small sample, the single task and the lack of replication. The study did test fluid intelligence before and after training, though how long the gains last is unknown.

questions.q: Fluid intelligence is one of two kinds of intelligence that make up IQ; the other, the storehouse of knowledge accumulated through the years, is ____ intelligence.
questions.explain: Crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge, and the authors say it can be increased through effective learning and memory strategies. Fluid intelligence concerns abstract reasoning and new problems.

questions.q: A key determiner of fluid intelligence is the capacity of a person's ____ memory, the number of new ideas a person can hold in mind while working through a problem.
questions.explain: The Swiss study trained working memory because its capacity is a key determiner of fluid intelligence.

questions.q: The authors call the ability to ____ empirical results the bedrock of scientific theory, which is why the unreplicated Swiss study is treated cautiously.
questions.explain: The Swiss study sits at the top of a list of studies people most want to see replicated, and a 2013 attempt failed to reproduce its gains.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Swiss working-memory study in the order they happened.
items: Fluid intelligence tested at the outset
Working-memory exercises of rising difficulty for up to nineteen days
Fluid intelligence retested after training
Longest-trained participants showed the greatest improvement
questions.explain: Participants were tested, trained with an n-back task that grew harder, then retested. The longest training produced the largest gain, though the result was not later replicated.

questions.q: Match each term from the brain-training discussion with its meaning.
pairs: The facility for abstract reasoning and solving new kinds of problems
The storehouse of knowledge accumulated through the years
The number of new ideas a person can hold in mind while solving a problem
Repeating a study to see whether its results hold, the bedrock of scientific theory
questions.explain: Fluid and crystallized intelligence are the two kinds that make up IQ. Working memory capacity is a key determiner of fluid intelligence.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether the authors say it carries over to other areas or stays specific to what was practiced.

items.t: Habit of making practice routine
Learning to focus attention at practice
Persisting at practice
Piano virtuosos' myelination changes
Gains from retrieval practice on a given material
Expertise in a field such as chess

questions.explain: The brain is not a muscle, so strengthening one skill does not automatically strengthen others. The habit of practicing is the exception: it generalizes.

questions.q: Describe the Swiss study behind brain-training games and explain why the authors say its results should be treated cautiously.
questions.a: Participants did working-memory tasks of rising difficulty, matching combinations of numerals and squares of light n items back, for up to nineteen days. They improved on fluid intelligence tests afterward. The authors caution that only thirty-five similar, highly intelligent people took part, with one training task, unknown durability and no successful replication; a 2013 attempt found no gains.

questions.q: Why do the authors say the brain is not like a muscle, and what does that imply for brain-training games?
questions.a: Strengthening one skill does not automatically strengthen others. Retrieval practice and mental models improve ability in the material practiced but not in other material, and expert myelination is limited to the area of expertise. Any broad benefit from brain training is more likely due to better habits such as focusing attention and persisting at practice.

questions.q: In Dweck's workshop for low-performing seventh graders, what did one half of the group learn that the other half did not?
options: That intelligence unfolds naturally with age, so effort matters less than patience
That a good memory is the main reason some students outperform their classmates
That effortful learning builds new brain connections that make you smarter
That study techniques work best when they are matched to each student's style
questions.explain: Both groups were taught about the brain and study techniques, but one half was told how effort and new learning build new connections. That half later adopted a growth mindset and became higher achievers.

questions.q: According to Dweck, what separates people who become helpless after failing from people who try new strategies?
options: How they explain failure: as lack of ability, or as lack of effort or strategy
How much raw intelligence they have, since helpless people score lower on standard IQ tests
How often they have failed before, since a long run of failures wears down every learner
How much praise they get from teachers, since praise is what keeps most learners going
questions.explain: Dweck found that those who read failure as proof they are not intelligent become helpless, while those who read it as too little effort or an ineffective strategy dig deeper. The difference lies in interpretation, not in IQ.

questions.q: A father wants his daughter to keep choosing harder challenges after she solves a tough puzzle. Which comment fits Dweck's findings best?
options: You are clearly one of the smartest kids in your whole class
You are a natural at this kind of puzzle, just like your mother
You make hard puzzles look easy, which proves how bright you are
You must have worked really hard on that one
questions.explain: In Dweck's puzzle study, 90 percent of children praised for effort chose the harder puzzle next, while most children praised for being smart picked the easier one. Praising smarts conveys that looking smart is what counts.

questions.q: In Dweck's Tom and Bill study, why did few children praised for being smart solve Bill's puzzles in the second round?
options: Bill's puzzles in the second round were made harder than the ones Tom gave them
Failing Bill's puzzles earlier left them feeling defeated and helpless
They had not received enough practice on puzzles of that type before the second round
They stopped caring about the puzzles once the praise they wanted had been given
questions.explain: The second-round puzzles were solvable and were the same ones these children had solved when Tom gave them. Their earlier failure on Bill's puzzles, combined with a focus on seeming smart, left them helpless.

questions.q: True or false: In Dweck's puzzle study, most fifth graders who had been praised for being smart chose the harder puzzle for their next try.
questions.explain: A majority of those praised for smarts picked the easier puzzle, whereas 90 percent of those praised for effort picked the harder one.

questions.q: Which of these describe people who pursue learning goals, according to Dweck?
options: They pick ever-increasing challenges
They treat setbacks as useful information
They feel that ability is dynamic and malleable
They repeat the same stunt to look smart
They avoid practice so as not to seem untalented
questions.explain: People with learning goals work to acquire new knowledge or skills. Repeating a stunt to look smart and avoiding practice are signs of a focus on performance.

questions.q: Which of these does Paul Tough's argument, as the authors present it, say matter more for success than IQ?
options: Grit
Curiosity
Persistence
Early stimulation at home
Being praised for being smart
questions.explain: Tough argues that success depends less on IQ than on grit, curiosity and persistence. Being praised for being smart is one of the things that denies cosseted children the character-building experience of overcoming adversity.

questions.q: Dweck calls the belief that your intellectual ability was set at birth by natural talent a ____ mindset.
questions.explain: Students who held this conventional view did less well than those taught that effortful learning changes the brain, who adopted a growth mindset.

questions.q: In Dweck's terms, students who work mainly to validate their ability are pursuing ____ goals rather than learning goals.
questions.explain: Performance goals lead people to pick challenges they are sure they can meet so they look smart. Learning goals lead people to pick ever-increasing challenges.

questions.q: Put these events from Dweck's seventh-grade workshop study in order.
items: Low-performing seventh graders attend a workshop on the brain and study techniques
Half the group is told that effortful learning forms new brain connections
Students return to their classes with teachers unaware of who heard what
Students given the effort message adopt a growth mindset and become higher achievers
questions.explain: The workshop came first, with one half given the explanation of how effort changes the brain. The change in mindset and achievement showed up over the school year.

questions.q: Put the steps of Dweck's Tom and Bill puzzle study in order.
items: Children get solvable puzzles from Tom and unsolvable ones from Bill
Some children are praised for being smart and others for their effort
Children get more puzzles from both, and now all of them are solvable
Few of the smart-praised children solve the puzzles from Bill
questions.explain: The unsolvable puzzles from Bill came in the first round. In the second round, all puzzles were solvable, yet the smart-praised children mostly failed Bill's.

questions.q: Match each researcher or author with the idea the chapter credits to them.
pairs: The belief that your ability rests largely in your own hands
Success depends more on grit, curiosity and persistence than on IQ
Expert performance comes from thousands of hours of deliberate practice
Environmental multipliers amplify a small genetic predisposition
questions.explain: Each name is tied to the idea the chapter draws on. Nisbett's multipliers are turned around so that behaviors can multiply the intelligence you already have.

questions.q: Match each child or student response in Dweck's research with the group that showed it.
pairs: Attributes failure to insufficient effort or strategy
Mostly picks the easier next puzzle
Nine in ten pick the harder next puzzle
questions.explain: How failure is explained, and what kind of praise is given, shapes the response to challenge.

questions.q: Match each kind of goal or mindset with what it leads a person to do.
pairs: Pick challenges you are confident you can meet
Pick ever-increasing challenges and use setbacks as information
Treat ability as set at birth by natural talent
Treat intelligence as largely within your own control
questions.explain: Performance goals and a fixed mindset limit risk taking, while learning goals and a growth mindset invite challenge.

questions.q: Sort each behavior by the kind of goal behind it.

items.t: Doing the same stunt over and over to look smart
Avoiding practice because needing it shows weakness
Picking only challenges you are sure you can meet
Choosing ever-harder challenges
Treating a setback as information for sharpening focus
Working harder after a failure

questions.explain: Performance goals aim to validate ability, so people play safe. Learning goals aim to increase ability, so people stretch and treat failure as useful.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a fixed mindset and a growth mindset, and how each leads people to respond to failure.
questions.a: A fixed mindset is the belief that ability is set at birth by natural talent; a growth mindset is the belief that intelligence is largely within your own control. People who attribute failure to their own inability become helpless. Those who see it as insufficient effort or an ineffective strategy dig deeper and try different approaches.

questions.q: Contrast performance goals with learning goals, and explain why a focus on performance can trip up even star athletes.
questions.a: Performance goals aim to validate your ability, so you pick challenges you can meet and repeat the same stunt to look smart. Learning goals aim to increase ability, so you seek bigger challenges and treat setbacks as information. Athletes praised as naturals may avoid practice because needing it would show their gifts are not enough.

questions.q: Describe Dweck's puzzle experiments on praise and what they show about praising children for being smart.
questions.a: Fifth graders solved a puzzle and were praised for being smart or for working hard. Most smart-praised children chose an easier next puzzle, while 90 percent of effort-praised children chose the harder one. In the Tom and Bill version, the smart-praised children were left feeling defeated and helpless after failing Bill's puzzles, because praise for smarts takes success out of their control.

questions.q: How does Paul Tough's argument, as the authors present it, explain why children raised in cosseted settings can be held back?
questions.a: Tough argues that success depends less on IQ than on grit, curiosity and persistence, which are built by encountering and overcoming adversity. Children at the top who are praised for being smart and bailed out by helicopter parents are never allowed to fail on their own. They are denied those character-building experiences and do not learn to take risks.

questions.q: According to Anders Ericsson, why can some experts reconstruct a complex performance after hearing or seeing it once?
options: A sixth sense for patterns that works equally well in any field the expert tries
A genetic predisposition that shows up early and is simply amplified by practice
Years of skill in their field give them superior perception and memory there
An unusually high IQ that lets them store far more raw detail than other people
questions.explain: Ericsson attributes such feats not to a sixth sense but to domain-specific perception and memory built over years. This is why Mozart's score reconstruction does not need a special gift.

questions.q: Two pianists each practice an hour a day. Which one is doing what Ericsson calls deliberate practice?
options: The one who works just beyond her ability, with a teacher giving feedback
The one who replays her favorite pieces from start to finish, since repetition builds mastery
The one who plays only for enjoyment and stops whenever a passage becomes frustrating
The one who plays quickly through the full program, relying on natural talent to carry her
questions.explain: Deliberate practice is goal directed and consists of repeated striving to reach beyond your current level, usually with a coach who helps focus attention and gives feedback. Mere repetition or enjoyable playing is a different animal.
