questions.q: True or false: Ericsson's studies found that an expert's skill in one field gives a head start toward gaining expertise in another field.
questions.explain: The authors say expertise is particular to its field and confers no advantage toward expertise elsewhere. Most experts remain average performers in other realms of life.

questions.q: True or false: Among the experts Ericsson studied, the best performers had spent a larger share of their practice hours in solitary, deliberate practice.
questions.explain: Ten thousand hours or ten years was the average investment, and the best had spent the larger percentage of those hours in solitary deliberate practice. Quality of practice mattered as well as quantity.

questions.q: Which of these are features of deliberate practice as the authors describe it?
options: It is goal directed
It is often solitary
It involves repeated striving beyond your current level
It is usually enjoyable
It gives a head start toward expertise in other fields
questions.explain: Deliberate practice is goal directed, often solitary and a repeated reach beyond current ability. The authors say it usually is not enjoyable, and expertise is specific to its own field.

questions.q: Which of these does the author say a coach or trainer helps with in deliberate practice?
options: Identifying areas of performance that need improvement
Focusing attention on specific aspects
Providing feedback that keeps perception and judgment accurate
Making the practice more enjoyable
Transferring the skill to other domains
questions.explain: For most learners a coach identifies weak areas, directs attention and gives feedback. The book says deliberate practice usually is not enjoyable and that expertise does not transfer to other domains.

questions.q: Anders Ericsson says expert performance rises from thousands of hours of sustained ____ practice.
questions.explain: Deliberate practice is goal directed, often solitary and involves repeated striving beyond your current level. It is what the authors contrast with simply doing something repeatedly.

questions.q: The people Ericsson studied had invested an average of ten thousand hours, or ____ years, of practice to become expert in their fields.
questions.explain: The average was ten thousand hours or ten years of practice, and the best performers spent more of those hours in solitary, deliberate practice.

questions.q: Match each example in the Deliberate Practice section with the point the authors use it to make.
pairs: Apparent genius required years of hard work
Mozart reconstructing scores after one hearing
Expert memory comes from domain skill, not a sixth sense
Focal hand dystonia in guitarists and pianists
Repeated practice can rewire the brain
Experts hold many complex patterns that guide action in varied situations
questions.explain: Each example supports the claim that expert performance is built by practice and knowledge rather than a special gift.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether Ericsson's work treats it as a cause of expert performance or not.

items.t: Thousands of hours of practice
High-quality solitary deliberate practice
Motivation, time and discipline
Genetic predisposition
An IQ advantage
A sixth sense for performance

questions.explain: Expert performance is a product of the quantity and quality of practice, not genetic predisposition. Experts' feats rest on acquired skill, not a sixth sense.

questions.q: How does deliberate practice differ from simply doing something repeatedly, and what does Ericsson's research say about how experts are made?
questions.a: Deliberate practice is goal directed, often solitary and involves repeated striving beyond your current level, usually with a coach giving feedback. Ericsson found that experts averaged ten thousand hours or ten years of practice, with the best spending more of it in solitary deliberate practice. Expert performance reflects the quantity and quality of practice, not genetic predisposition.

questions.q: Why does the chapter move from Brain Training? to Growth Mindset?
options: Brain-training games were proven to work, so the authors next explain which attitude makes them pay off
The neuroscience of plasticity is finished, so the authors switch to studies of children from poor families
IQ studies were inconclusive, so the authors now offer growth mindset as a replacement for IQ tests
Raising IQ is unlikely, so the authors turn to multipliers for the intelligence you already have
questions.explain: The end of Brain Training? stands Nisbett's environmental multipliers on their head and names three cognitive multipliers: a growth mindset, practicing like an expert and constructing memory cues. Growth mindset is the first.

questions.q: Why does the section Brain Training? follow the section Is IQ Mutable? in this chapter?
options: After showing that brain training works, the authors ask what early interventions would help young children
After early-childhood IQ gains, the authors ask whether training can raise fluid intelligence
After showing that IQ cannot change, the authors ask whether anything else can improve the brain in later life
After defining fluid and crystallized intelligence, the authors ask which one the Flynn effect has changed
questions.explain: Is IQ Mutable? reviews what raises IQ in young children, and Brain Training? then tests the popular claim that games can raise cognitive ability. The answer there is that the evidence is thin and has not been replicated.

questions.q: In which order does the chapter present these four topics?
items: Brain training
Growth mindset
Deliberate practice
Memory cues
questions.explain: After asking whether brain training works, the chapter offers three cognitive multipliers in turn: a growth mindset, practicing like an expert and constructing memory cues.

questions.q: The authors end the Brain Training? section by asking about cognitive multipliers. What are the three they name, and why do they turn to them?
questions.a: Since it is unlikely that you will raise your IQ anytime soon, they look for strategies that amp up the performance of the intelligence you already have, like Nisbett's environmental multipliers. The three are embracing a growth mindset, practicing like an expert and constructing memory cues. The chapter then takes them in that order.

questions.q: In Make It Stick, what is a mnemonic device?
options: A mental tool for holding material in memory, cued for ready recall
A repeated drill that makes facts automatic through sheer volume of practice
A short test given after study to expose which facts are still missing
A reading method that speeds up study by skimming only the key words
questions.explain: The authors describe mnemonic devices as mental tools that hold material in memory so it is cued for ready recall. They are about cueing retrieval, not about drilling or testing.

questions.q: What does the method of loci involve?
options: Repeating a list aloud at growing intervals until it feels completely secure
Linking mental images to a series of physical locations that cue memories
Pairing each number with a rhyming concrete image to hang the items on
Turning the first letters of a list into a single memorable word
questions.explain: The method of loci, which goes back to the ancient Greeks, ties images to places, as in a memory palace. Rhyming number images belong to the peg method, and first-letter words are acronyms.

questions.q: Why do vivid mental images make verbal or abstract material easier to retrieve, according to the authors?
options: Images take longer to process, and the extra effort strengthens the trace
Images replace the need to understand the material before storing it
People remember pictures more easily than words, so images make good cues
Images spare the learner from ever having to retrieve the material again
questions.explain: The authors say humans remember pictures more easily than words, so tying vivid images to verbal material makes it easier to bring back. Images do not replace understanding or retrieval.

questions.q: Why did Mark Twain give up using a list of partial sentences to prompt himself through his speeches?
options: The sentences were too long to fit on one card he could carry on stage
Audiences noticed the notes and judged his talks less sincere as a result
He could not read his own handwriting under the lights of the stage
Snippets of text all look alike at a glance, so they did not cue him well
questions.explain: Twain found the system unsatisfactory because, in his words, “when you glance at snippets of text, they all look alike.” He switched to crude pencil sketches, which did the job.

questions.q: On Mark Twain's history road for the kings and queens of England, how was time shown?
options: One foot of roadway per year, with stakes at each reign's ends
One pace for each monarch, with a stake marking every castle they had built
One stake for each century, with a sketch hung on top of each stake
One foot of roadway per reign, however many years the reign lasted
questions.explain: Twain measured off 817 feet of road, a foot for each year, and drove a stake at the beginning and end of each reign, writing the name and dates on it. A long reign therefore took up a long stretch of road.

questions.q: What is the peg method?
options: A walk through a familiar building with an image placed in each room
A rhyme scheme pairing numbers with images to hang list items on
A list of partial sentences that prompts you through a speech
A song whose lyrics are linked to the steps of a task or a story
questions.explain: In the peg method each number is paired with a rhyming concrete image, such as bun for one and shoe for two, and list items are hung on those pegs. Walking through a building is the method of loci.

questions.q: According to Jack Weatherford, how may messages have been sent accurately across the Mongol Empire?
options: By written notes sealed and passed along relay stations of riders
By memory palaces built in each major city along the route
By traditional poems and songs serving as mnemonic devices
By coded drumbeats relayed between watchtowers on the steppe
questions.explain: Weatherford notes that the military were forbidden from sending written messages, and he thinks poems and songs, such as the Long Song, were a likely method. The Long Song can be sung in varying tones to signal movement through a place.

questions.q: In Marlys's psychology exam, what did the imagined characters in each café serve as?
options: A way to learn the essay's content for the first time in the exam
A guess at which essay question the examiners would set that day
Stand-ins for points she had not studied but could invent on the spot
Cues to the dozen key points of the essay she was writing
questions.explain: Marlys had already learned the material. The names and actions of the characters in her palace cued the twelve key points of each essay, so she did not freeze at the empty booklet.

questions.q: Before James Paterson takes students to build memory palaces, what has he already done?
options: Covered the material in class so that the students understand it
Tested the students on the essays to find which ones they had forgotten
Asked each student to memorize the full text of every essay in advance
Had the students practice card memorizing to build general memory power
questions.explain: The authors make the point that Paterson has thoroughly covered the material first. The palace is for organizing what has been understood, not for learning it.

questions.q: What did James Paterson discover after first using mnemonics as a study shortcut?
options: He recalled concepts well but could not hold on to names or dates
He had the facts at hand but not mastery of concepts and principles
He mastered the material but spent more hours than his classmates
He found the techniques worked well for numbers but failed for words
questions.explain: Paterson walked into exams with names, dates and facts at hand but lacked the concepts, relationships and underlying principles. The authors compare this to having mountaintops without the mountain range.

questions.q: Without mnemonic tools, about how many digits can most people hold in working memory?
options: About twelve
About twenty
About seven
About thirty-five
questions.explain: The authors say most people can hold about seven digits, which is why local telephone numbers were designed to be no longer. Paterson, using mnemonics, recites seventy-four spoken digits.

questions.q: How does James Paterson turn a three-digit number such as 615 into an image?
options: He rhymes the number with a concrete word, such as bun for one or shoe for two
He pictures the number written on a stake along a long road
He splits it into single digits and gives each digit a face of its own
Each numeral has a speech sound, and the sounds form a word like shuttle
questions.explain: For Paterson each numeral from 0 to 9 stands for a sound, so 615 becomes the sounds in shuttle and is pictured as a space shuttle. Rhyming pegs are a different, simpler scheme.

questions.q: Why does Michela feel free to skip a point she cannot recall during a psychology exam?
options: She is confident the content will come and fills the gap later
She knows the examiners give credit for the plan of key ideas alone
She keeps a hidden page of notes to consult once the plan is done
She expects a missing point to cost her very little in the final mark
questions.explain: Michela says skipping a point was unthinkable before mnemonics, but now she knows the content will come to mind momentarily. Her confidence is a stress buster and a time saver.

questions.q: According to the closing section, which single fact answers the nagging question of why bother with effort?
options: Genes set a ceiling, so effort helps only inside a fixed range of ability
Effortful learning changes the brain, building new connections and capability
Early education in the first few years permanently raises a child's IQ
Brain-training games strengthen every mental skill the way exercise does a muscle
questions.explain: The Takeaway says that our abilities are not fixed from birth but largely ours to shape, because effort itself extends our abilities. The other options are claims the chapter either rejects or qualifies.

questions.q: What happens to complex material that is retrieved again and again, according to the authors?
options: It fades unless the memory palace is rebuilt each time it is used again
It stays tied to its cues, which grow more elaborate with each new use
It becomes second nature, and the mnemonic cues are no longer needed
It moves to a conscious store where each step is decided in turn
questions.explain: With continued retrieval, concepts become mental models used as shorthand, and sequences are chunked until recall and use are as automatic as habit. The cues then drop away.

questions.q: Dana must give a talk with five points in a fixed order. She imagines her flat and, at the door, the sofa and the window, places a vivid image for each point, then plans to walk through the flat in her mind. Which technique is this?
options: The peg method, hanging each point on rhyming number images
A reverse acronym, spelling out a memorable sentence from the letters
Deliberate practice, with a coach who gives regular feedback on weak spots
A memory palace, built on the method of loci
questions.explain: Dana links images to familiar physical spaces, sequenced along a route so the order is kept, which is the method of loci and a memory palace. No rhyming numbers or first letters are involved.

questions.q: Raj has memorized the pegs one is bun, two is shoe and three is tree. Today he links buying a hat to bun, picking up dry cleaning to shoe and a birthday card to tree. Which technique is this?
options: The peg method
The method of loci
An acronym for the list
Training of memory span
questions.explain: Raj hangs items on fixed rhyming images. The pegs stay the same while the associations change with each new list, which is how the authors describe the peg method.

questions.q: Sam has not yet studied his history unit. The night before the exam he plans to build a memory palace to learn it from scratch. What would the authors say?
options: A palace works best on unfamiliar material because odd images force more learning
Palaces file away what is already learned, so he should learn the material first
He is right, because mnemonics are chiefly a tool for first-time learning
He should use it only for dates, since concepts cannot be linked to cues
questions.explain: The memory palace serves as a method to organize what has already been learned so that it is retrievable, not as a learning tool. Paterson's students understand the material before they build their palaces.

questions.q: How do the authors answer the criticism that mnemonics are useful only for rote memorization?
options: The criticism is correct, but rote memorization is still worth having today
Mnemonics are meant to replace understanding, so rote recall is the goal
Used properly, they organize large bodies of knowledge for retrieval
They help only people who are already experts in the field in question here
questions.explain: The authors call this a key point: after mastery, mnemonics let you file what you know in mental pockets and bring concepts and details back in depth when needed. They are not limited to rote facts.

questions.q: Why does Memory Cues appear where it does in Chapter 7, after the sections on mindset and deliberate practice?
options: It is the only strategy in the chapter that actually raises IQ itself
It replaces deliberate practice, which the chapter then sets aside
It introduces neuroplasticity, which the later sections go on to explain
It is the third of three strategies multiplying existing intelligence
questions.explain: After discussing IQ and brain training, the chapter names three multipliers: embracing a growth mindset, practicing like an expert and constructing memory cues. Memory cues is the last of the three.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 7 presents constructing memory cues as one of three strategies for getting more out of the intelligence a person already has.
questions.explain: After noting that raising IQ is unlikely, the chapter offers three multipliers: a growth mindset, practicing like an expert and memory cues.

questions.q: True or false: Humans remember pictures more easily than words, which is why tying vivid images to abstract material helps retrieval.
questions.explain: The authors give the example that an image of an elephant is easier to recall than the word. As they put it, “Images cue memories.”

questions.q: True or false: When Michela cannot recall one key idea during an exam, she stops planning and starts again with the first idea.
questions.explain: She moves on to the next point and fills in the blank later, confident that the content will come to mind.

questions.q: True or false: James Paterson learned a unique image for every number from 0 to 1,000 in only a few weeks.
questions.explain: The thousand images took him a year to master, fitted in between family, work and friends. The authors treat this as the kind of solitary striving that builds expertise.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' account, a memory palace is a way to organize what has already been learned, not a way to learn it in the first place.
questions.explain: The palace helps retrieve material that is already understood. That is why Paterson covers the content in class before the students build their palaces.

questions.q: True or false: Marlys knew which single essay question would be set, so she prepared for only that one.
questions.explain: She knew the main topic but not the question, so she had prepared for all thirty-five essays. Memory palaces made that large load manageable.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, Mongol military messengers were allowed to carry written messages across the empire.
questions.explain: The military were forbidden from sending written messages, so Weatherford thinks poems and songs were likely used as mnemonic devices.

questions.q: True or false: Without mnemonic tools, most people can hold about seven digits in working memory, which is why local telephone numbers were kept short.
questions.explain: The authors give seven as the typical limit and note that telephone numbers were designed with it in mind. Paterson can exceed it by far using mnemonics.

questions.q: Which of these are the three strategies Chapter 7 offers for getting more out of the intelligence you already have?
options: Embracing a growth mindset
Playing online brain-training games
Constructing memory cues
Enrolling young children in early education
Practicing like an expert
questions.explain: The chapter names growth mindset, practicing like an expert and constructing memory cues. Brain-training games and early education appear earlier, as discussions of raising abilities, not as these multipliers.

questions.q: Which of these does the book name as familiar structures that mnemonic devices can use to hold target information?
options: The floor plan of a home
A rhyme scheme for numbers
A well-known song
A list of partial sentences
A random shuffled deck
questions.explain: The authors say mnemonics share a deeply familiar structure, such as a number scheme, travel route, floor plan, song, poem or acronym. Twain found partial sentences unsatisfactory, and a shuffled deck is what Paterson memorizes, not a structure.

questions.q: Which of these were Mark Twain's reasons for giving William the Conqueror a whale as his icon?
options: Both names begin with the same letter
The whale is the biggest fish that swims
Both names have the same number of letters
William's reign was the longest on the road
questions.explain: Twain wrote that both names begin with W and that the whale is the biggest fish that swims, as William is the most conspicuous figure in English history. The names do not have equal length.

questions.q: Which of these did James Paterson's psychology students do in preparing to memorize their thirty-five essays?
options: Had the material covered in class first
Built memory palaces in cafés and on campus
Used the peg method for another group of topics
Shared one single palace for every essay
questions.explain: Paterson covered the material first, then groups of topics were assigned to café and campus palaces, the peg method, or imagery from songs and movies. The students did not share one palace.

questions.q: Which of these does Michela do in the exam hall once she learns the essay topics?
options: Spends ten minutes mentally walking the relevant palaces
Lists the key ideas for each essay
Skips a forgotten point and fills it in later
Writes out every sentence she remembers before planning
questions.explain: She takes ten minutes to walk through the palaces and list key ideas, and she skips any point she cannot recall for the moment. Her plan consists of key ideas, not whole sentences.

questions.q: Which of these does the book give as examples of mnemonic cues used by professionals?
options: A pilot's practiced hand-and-eye choreography for an emergency
A violinist's main melodic theme to cue a harmony change
A nanny drilling kings and queens by brute repetition
A speaker glancing at snippets of text
questions.explain: Matt Brown's choreographies and Karen Kim's melody are described as mnemonic cues. Brute repetition and glancing at text snippets are the things Twain found ineffective.

questions.q: Which of these claims does the closing section make?
options: Effortful learning changes the brain by building new connections
Abilities are not fixed at birth but largely ours to shape
The path to expert performance does not necessarily start from exceptional genes
Mnemonic devices make deliberate practice unnecessary
questions.explain: The Takeaway holds that effort builds capability, that expertise entails self-discipline, grit and persistence, and that mnemonics help only until deliberate practice and repeated use form deeper encoding. They do not make practice unnecessary.

questions.q: Which of these are true of James Paterson, according to the chapter?
options: He placed twelfth at his first World Memory Championships in 2006
He can memorize a shuffled deck in under two minutes
He holds the world record for spoken digits
He took a year to master his images for 0 to 1,000
questions.explain: Paterson placed twelfth in 2006, memorizes a deck in under two minutes and needed a year for his thousand images. The spoken-digit record of 364 belongs to Johannes Mallow.

questions.q: In Greek mythology, Mnemosyne, one of the nine Muses, was the goddess of ____.
questions.explain: The authors mention Mnemosyne when introducing mnemonic devices, which are tools for holding material in memory.

questions.q: “ROY G BIV,” a word built from the first letters of the rainbow colors, is an example of an ____.
questions.explain: An acronym is one of the simple mnemonic devices the authors name. A reverse acronym runs the other way, using a sentence to hold values such as Roman numerals.

questions.q: A memory palace is based on the method of ____, which goes back to the ancient Greeks.
questions.explain: The method of loci links mental images to a series of physical locations to cue memories.

questions.q: The peg method is a ____ scheme for remembering lists, pairing each number with a concrete image.
questions.explain: Each number from one to twenty is paired with a rhyming, concrete image, such as bun for one, which serves as a peg for hanging items.

questions.q: On Mark Twain's history road, each foot of roadway stood for one ____ of English history.
questions.explain: Twain measured off 817 feet of road, one foot for each of the years from the Conquest to the forty-sixth year of Victoria's reign.

questions.q: Mark Twain finally found a way to outline his speeches by using a series of crude pencil ____.
questions.explain: A haystack with a snake under it, for example, told him where to start his story. Pictures cued him better than text snippets.

questions.q: Without mnemonic tools, the maximum number of digits most people can hold in working memory is about ____.
questions.explain: The authors give seven as the typical limit, which is why local telephone numbers were designed to be no longer than that.

questions.q: James Paterson remembers long strings of digits by splitting them into groups of ____.
questions.explain: Every three-digit number is a distinct image for him, and the images are placed in a familiar space to be recalled in order.

questions.q: The authors say mnemonics help organize large bodies of knowledge so as to permit their ready ____.
questions.explain: Used after mastery, mnemonics act as mental pockets for what has been learned and cue it for retrieval when needed.

questions.q: The closing section states that effortful learning changes the ____, building new connections and capability.
questions.explain: This single fact is offered as the answer to the question of why bother, since effort extends the boundaries of our abilities.

questions.q: In the closing section, conscious mnemonic devices help cue learning until sustained, ____ and repeated use form deeper encoding and subconscious mastery.
questions.explain: Mnemonic cues serve as an aid on the way. Deliberate practice and repeated use eventually produce the subconscious mastery of expert performance.

questions.q: Chapter 7's three strategies for multiplying the intelligence you already have are a growth mindset, practicing like an expert and constructing memory ____.
questions.explain: Memory cues is the third of the three strategies, and it is the one the chapter develops through mnemonic devices.

questions.q: Put the steps of building and using a memory palace in order.
items: Imagine a space that is very familiar to you
Link each prominent feature to a vivid image of what you want to remember
Take an imaginary walk through the space to retrieve the memories
questions.explain: You start from a familiar space, tie images to its features, and later walk through it. If order matters, the cues are sequenced along the route.

questions.q: Put in order the places Marlys mentally visited for her three exam essays, from first to last.
items: Pret-a-Manger, for dieting
Krispy Kreme, for evolutionary explanations of aggression
Starbucks, for treatments of schizophrenia
questions.explain: She wrote the dieting essay first, then moved on to the Krispy Kreme shop and then to the Starbucks, working through each essay's twelve paragraphs.

questions.q: Put in order the steps Mark Twain took in making his history road for the kings and queens of England.
items: Staked the monarchs out along the carriage road
Measured 817 feet of road, one foot for each year
Drove a stake at the start and end of each reign
Sketched an icon for each monarch
Trotted the course calling out names, dates and reigns
questions.explain: Twain laid out the road to scale, marked each reign with a stake bearing the name and dates, added icons such as the whale, and then ran the course with the children.

questions.q: In the peg method, put these rhyming pegs in order from number one to number five.
items: Bun
Shoe
Tree
Store
Hive
questions.explain: The authors give one is bun, two is shoe, three is tree, four is store and five is hive. The images stay the same while the items hung on them change.

questions.q: Put in order how Michela prepares and then writes a psychology exam essay using a memory palace.
items: Reduce her material to key ideas, not whole sentences
Tie each key idea to a location in the palace
Populate each location with something crazy
In the exam, walk through the palace and list key ideas
Write the essay from the plan, filling in skipped points
questions.explain: She first prepares the palace, then in the exam spends ten minutes walking through it to sketch the plan before writing.

questions.q: Put in order the stages by which mnemonics are used for new material, according to the chapter.
items: Master the new material so that it is understood
Link the main ideas to vivid memory cues
Use the cues to retrieve concepts and details when needed
Through repeated retrieval, recall becomes automatic and cues fade
questions.explain: The authors place mnemonics after mastery, as a way to file and cue what is learned. With continued retrieval, complex material becomes second nature and the cues are no longer needed.

questions.q: Put in order the last three sections of Chapter 7, from first to last.
items: Deliberate Practice
Memory Cues
The Takeaway
questions.explain: After the sections on mindset and deliberate practice, the chapter turns to memory cues and closes with a short Takeaway.

questions.q: Match each mnemonic device or method with how the authors describe it.
pairs: An acronym for the colors of the rainbow
I Value Xylophones Like Cows Dig Milk
A reverse acronym for the ascending Roman numeral values
Associating mental images with a series of physical locations
Rhyming concrete images for the numbers 1 to 20, used to hang items on
questions.explain: These are the simple and complex mnemonic devices the section introduces, from acronyms to memory palaces and rhyming pegs.

questions.q: Match each person with their role in the Memory Cues story.
pairs: Memory athlete and psychology teacher at Bellerbys College
Student who used a memory palace in her A2 psychology exam
Former student who uses memory palaces for university exams
Historian who thinks Mongols used songs and poems as mnemonics
Second violinist of the Parker Quartet
questions.explain: Each person illustrates a different use of mnemonic cues, from exam essays to message sending to memorized quartet music.

questions.q: Match each of Marlys's imagined cues with the essay topic it stood for.
pairs: She-wolf with hungry pups at Krispy Kreme
Large aggressive potted plant in Pret-a-Manger
questions.explain: On exam day the three topics were aggression, schizophrenia treatments and dieting, each already tied to a vivid cue in a different café.

questions.q: Match each of Paterson's images with the number it stands for.
questions.explain: Paterson reads each three-digit number as speech sounds forming a word or name, such as 615 as shuttle, and pictures that image.

questions.q: Match each icon or sketch from Mark Twain's stories with what it cued.
pairs: Haystack with a snake under it
The start of his story about the Carson Valley in Nevada
Umbrella tilted against a stiff wind
The fierce winds that blew down from the Sierras
questions.explain: Twain's speech sketches and the children's monarch icons both turned things hard to recall into vivid, distinct images.

questions.q: Match each number from the chapter with what it describes.
pairs: Years of English history on Twain's history road
Spoken digits Paterson can recall without error
World record in spoken digits, held by Johannes Mallow
Essays Marlys had to be ready to write
questions.explain: These are figures the authors give: Twain's road, Paterson's spoken-digit span, the world record and the number of exam essays.

questions.q: Match each professional with the mnemonic cue or method the chapter describes.
pairs: Memorized choreographies of eye and hand for emergencies
The main melodic theme as a cue to change harmony
Methodically rehearsing what he is likely to find in surgery
Synchronizing the positions on the team for a new opponent
questions.explain: The authors treat movement patterns, melodies and rehearsed sequences as mnemonic cues that organize complex performance.

questions.q: In the peg method, match each peg with the image and errand the authors use.
pairs: A hairstyle, cuing a hat for the ski trip
Being well dressed, cuing the dry cleaning
A family tree, cuing a birthday card for a cousin
questions.explain: The rhyming pegs stay fixed, while the associations each evokes change every time you need to hold a new list in mind.

questions.q: Match each idea with how the closing section treats it.
pairs: Changes the brain, building new connections and capability
Sustains a person through life in the effort to shape abilities
Organize and cue learning for ready retrieval
Form the deeper encoding of expert performance
questions.explain: The Takeaway ties these ideas together: effort builds ability, and cues help only until practice and use produce lasting mastery.

questions.q: Sort each feature by the memory technique it belongs to.

items.t: Imagining a walk through your own home
Placing cues along the route to the corner store
Populating a café with vivid characters
Using rhyming images such as bun and shoe
Reusing the same images for every new list
Hanging errands on numbered pegs from 1 to 20

questions.explain: The method of loci uses places and routes, while the peg method uses a fixed set of rhyming number images with changing associations.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it describes Paterson's early use of mnemonics or the students' proper use.

items.t: Memorizing names and dates to skip full study
Having facts at hand but no grasp of the principles
Walking into exams without the concepts
Covering the material in class first
Filing learned ideas in mental pockets
Retrieving concepts in depth at the moment of need

questions.explain: Paterson learned that mnemonics are no shortcut: their value comes after mastery, as a way to file and cue what has been understood.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is Mark Twain's or James Paterson's.

items.t: Sketches of a haystack and an umbrella to cue a speech
Stakes along a road marking each English reign
A whale as the icon for William the Conqueror
An image for every number from 0 to 1,000
Memorizing the order of a shuffled deck of cards
Speech sounds standing for numerals 0 to 9

questions.explain: Twain used sketches and a scaled road to cue speeches and history, and Paterson uses a sound-based image system for numbers and cards.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is a familiar structure or the target information to be remembered.

items.t: The floor plan of your home
A rhyme scheme of numbers
A song you know well
The twelve key points of an essay
Tasks you want to get done today
The dates of English monarchs' reigns

questions.explain: The authors say mnemonics share a deeply familiar structure whose elements can be easily linked to the target information to be remembered.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is an early conscious aid or part of later subconscious mastery.

items.t: Walking mentally through a memory palace
Hanging a list on pegs of rhyming images
Using an acronym to cue facts
Concepts compressed into a shorthand mental model
Chunked sequences performed as automatically as a habit
Performance that no longer needs the cues

questions.explain: The closing section says conscious mnemonics help until deliberate practice and repeated use form deeper encoding and subconscious mastery.

questions.q: Sort each cue by whether it is a pattern of movement or sound, or a visual image.

items.t: A pilot's choreography of eye and hand
A violinist's main melodic theme
The Mongol Long Song sung in varying tones
Twain's pencil sketch of a haystack with a snake
Marlys's she-wolf at the Krispy Kreme window
Paterson's space shuttle for 615

questions.explain: Pilots, musicians and Mongol singers cue memory with movement and sound, while Twain, Marlys and Paterson rely on vivid pictures.

questions.q: Explain what a memory palace is and how you would use one to remember material in a certain order.
questions.a: A memory palace is a mnemonic device based on the method of loci, which links mental images to a series of physical locations. You imagine a very familiar space, such as your home, and tie a vivid image of each thing to remember to a prominent feature. If order matters, you sequence the cues along a route, and you retrieve them later by taking an imaginary walk through the space.

questions.q: Why does the book say vivid imagery makes mnemonic cues work?
questions.a: Humans remember pictures more easily than words, so linking vivid images to verbal or abstract material makes it easier to retrieve. The authors compare a strong image to a loaded stringer of fish: pull on it and the whole catch comes up. They add that when a friend names the place where a conversation happened, picturing the place brings the rest flooding back.

questions.q: Describe Mark Twain's history road and explain why it worked as a memory aid for his children.
questions.a: Twain staked out the English monarchs along a carriage road on his farm, a foot for each year, with a stake at the start and end of each reign bearing the name and dates. He and the children added icons, such as a whale for William the Conqueror, and ran the course calling out names and dates. It worked because the children could see and walk the whole of English history, unlike the nanny's brute repetition, and the places on the farm became named by reigns.

questions.q: What is the peg method, and what stays the same and what changes each time you use it?
questions.a: The peg method is a rhyme scheme for remembering lists in which each number from 1 to 20 is paired with a rhyming concrete image, such as bun for one and shoe for two. You hang the items you want to remember, such as errands, on these pegs. The rhyming images stay the same, while the associations they evoke change each time you need to hold a new list in mind.

questions.q: What do all effective mnemonic devices have in common, according to the authors?
questions.a: They share a structure of some kind that is deeply familiar and whose elements can easily be linked to the target information. Examples are a number scheme, travel route, floor plan, song, poem, aphorism or acronym. The authors say the versatility of mnemonic devices is almost endless.

questions.q: Describe how Marlys used a memory palace in her A2 psychology exam and why it helped her.
questions.a: Marlys had tied the key points of each essay to vivid characters in a particular café, and on exam day she mentally walked through the café for the topic set, such as dieting at Pret-a-Manger. The characters cued the twelve points of the essay in order. This let her tackle any of the thirty-five possible essays without freezing under the pressure of the empty exam booklet.

questions.q: A student has covered a biology unit in class and must write essays on questions that are unknown in advance. Using the chapter's ideas, how could she prepare with mnemonics, and what must she do first?
questions.a: She should first make sure she understands the material, since mnemonics file away what is already learned. She can then reduce each topic to key ideas, pick a familiar place as a memory palace, tie each key idea to a location and populate it with something vivid. In the exam she can walk through the palace to list key ideas, skipping any she cannot recall and returning to it later.

questions.q: How is Michela's way of preparing for exams like what Mark Twain did for his speeches, and what benefit does she gain?
questions.a: Michela turns her material into key ideas and ties each to a vivid, crazy image at a location in a palace, much as Twain turned the phases of a speech into crude sketches. In both cases a distinctive picture cues what comes next better than text would. Michela gains the confidence that she can pull up what she knows, which the authors call a huge stress buster and a time saver.

questions.q: Explain how James Paterson remembered the digit string 615392611333517 and why this takes both a system and practice.
questions.a: He remembers digits in groups of three, and each three-digit number is a distinct image built from speech sounds he has assigned to the numerals. So 615 is a space shuttle, and the images are placed in a familiar space, such as around a water cooler and bookshelves. It took him a year to master images for 0 to 1,000, the kind of solitary striving that Ericsson says characterizes expertise.

questions.q: Why can most people remember only about seven digits, and how do memory athletes like Paterson go beyond that?
questions.a: Without mnemonic tools, the most digits most people can hold in working memory is about seven, which is why local telephone numbers were designed to be no longer. Paterson uses mnemonic images and can memorize and recite seventy-four spoken digits without error. The world record in spoken digits, or memory span, is 364.

questions.q: How do the examples of the pilot Matt Brown and the violinist Karen Kim show mnemonic cues, and what happens to cues with continued retrieval?
questions.a: Brown rehearses distinct choreographies of eye and hand in a simulator, each of which is a mnemonic for a corrective maneuver. Kim uses the main melodic theme as a cue for when to change harmony. With continued retrieval, complex material becomes second nature, the cues are no longer needed, and recall becomes as automatic as habit.

questions.q: What single fact does the closing section of Chapter 7 offer in answer to the question of why we should bother making the effort?
questions.a: Effortful learning changes the brain, building new connections and capability, so our abilities are not fixed from birth but largely ours to shape. We make the effort because the effort itself extends the boundaries of our abilities. This is the principle that a growth mindset sustains.

questions.q: According to the Takeaway, how do conscious mnemonic devices relate to deliberate practice and expert performance?
questions.a: Whatever someone is striving to master, conscious mnemonic devices can help organize and cue the learning for ready retrieval. They do this until sustained deliberate practice and repeated use form deeper encoding and subconscious mastery. That deeper encoding is what characterizes expert performance, which requires self-discipline, grit and persistence.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 7 end with memory cues, and how does the Paterson story tie back to the chapter's earlier ideas?
questions.a: Memory cues is the third of the chapter's three multipliers, after growth mindset and practicing like an expert, for getting more out of the intelligence you already have. Paterson also opens the chapter as a memory athlete. His thousand images took a year of solitary striving, which fits Ericsson's deliberate practice, and his students show that mnemonics add value after mastery.

questions.q: Why do the authors of Make It Stick give specific, practical advice in Chapter 8 after holding back in the earlier chapters?
options: Reviewers found the research in the earlier chapters unconvincing without examples.
Their publisher required the book to end with a checklist for readers.
Early readers of the earlier chapters urged them to get specific with practical advice.
They realized the research findings applied only to classroom settings.
questions.explain: The authors say they had resisted being overtly prescriptive, preferring that readers reach their own conclusions, but early readers asked for concrete advice. Chapter 8 answers that request.

questions.q: True or false: In the chapters before Chapter 8, the authors laid out the big ideas from research and illustrated them with examples rather than being overtly prescriptive.
questions.explain: That is how the authors describe the earlier chapters, and it is why Chapter 8 turns to practical tips.

questions.q: Put the audiences that Chapter 8 addresses in the order the chapter takes them.
items: Students
Lifelong learners
Teachers
Trainers
questions.explain: The chapter opens with tips for students (high school, college and graduate school), then speaks to lifelong learners, then teachers, and finally trainers.

questions.q: What shift does Chapter 8, titled Make It Stick, mark compared with Chapters 1 through 7?
options: It moves from laying out research and examples to giving practical advice for applying them.
It moves from advice for students to a new theory that replaces the earlier findings.
It moves from classroom studies to experiments on lifelong learners alone.
It moves from practical advice to a review of the research methods used.
questions.explain: The earlier chapters presented the empirical ideas; this chapter responds to readers who wanted specific advice, organized by audience. It adds no new theory.

questions.q: Why does the book end with a chapter of tips organized by audience, and how are the tips made vivid?
questions.a: Early readers of the first seven chapters asked for specific, practical advice, so the authors turned to prescriptions for students, lifelong learners, teachers and trainers. Because the principles are the same but the settings and life stages differ, they also tell stories of people who have already found these strategies and use them to great effect.

questions.q: True or false: Setbacks during learning are signs that you lack the ability to master the material.
questions.explain: The authors say setbacks are signs of effort, not of failure. Setbacks come with striving, and striving builds expertise.

questions.q: According to the authors, what follows from the fact that effortful learning changes the brain by making new connections?
options: Your intellectual abilities are fixed early, so effort mainly reveals them.
Setbacks are a sign that you should switch to an easier subject.
Easy learning is the best way to build new connections in the brain.
Your intellectual abilities lie to a large degree within your own control.
questions.explain: Because effortful learning builds mental models and increases capability, the authors conclude that abilities are largely within your control. That is why they say the difficulties are worth tackling.

questions.q: Which of these are among the three keystone study strategies the authors recommend for students?
options: Practicing retrieving new learning from memory
Spacing out your retrieval practice
Highlighting key passages as you read
Interleaving the study of different problem types
Rereading the text until it feels fluent
questions.explain: The three keystone strategies are retrieval practice, spaced retrieval practice and interleaving. Highlighting and rereading are the habits that intuition favors instead.

questions.q: How should a student interpret setbacks, and why does the author say this matters?
questions.a: Setbacks are signs of effort, not of failure, because they come with striving and striving builds expertise. Effortful learning changes the brain by making new connections and building mental models, so your abilities lie largely within your own control, which makes the difficulties worth tackling.

questions.q: Match each strategy to what intuition tells most learners to do instead.
pairs: Underlining, highlighting and rereading the text and notes
Long stretches of single-minded, repetitive massed practice
Mastering one problem type fully before starting another
questions.explain: The authors pair each strategy with a compelling but mistaken intuition: rereading, massed practice and blocked practice all feel like learning.

questions.q: Sort each approach by how it feels versus how well it works, according to the authors.
groups: Feels productive but works less well

items.t: Rereading highlighted notes
Massed repetitive practice
Blocked practice of one problem type
Self-quizzing on the material
Spacing practice so you get rusty
Interleaving different problem types

questions.explain: Rereading, massed practice and blocked practice feel productive, but the authors say that feeling misleads. Self-quizzing, spacing and interleaving feel awkward, disruptive or difficult, yet they strengthen mastery.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: The authors say that retrieval practice means ____.
questions.explain: Retrieving knowledge and skill from memory by quizzing yourself should replace rereading as your primary study strategy.

questions.q: Later in Chapter 8, teachers are advised to have students read which profile from the student tips, and why?
options: Timothy Fellows's, because he overcame repeated early failure on his exams
Michael Young's, for its account of the strategies' difficulties and benefits
Michael Young's, because he lists the study habits every student should copy
Timothy Fellows's, because he explains the research on the testing effect
questions.explain: The Be Transparent advice for teachers points to Michael Young's profile because he vividly describes the difficulties and ultimate benefits of using these strategies.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Why does the familiarity gained from rereading a text mislead students, according to the authors?
options: It makes students stop reading before they reach the end of the chapter.
It creates illusions of knowing that do not reliably indicate mastery of the material.
It shows students which material the professor will put on the test.
It strengthens memory for peripheral details but not for central ideas.
questions.explain: Fluency with a text is a misleading indicator of what you have learned and creates a false impression that you will remember it.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: True or false: Making errors while you quiz yourself will not set you back, so long as you check your answers and correct your mistakes.
questions.explain: The authors stress checking answers so your judgments of what you know are accurate; errors that you then correct do no harm.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: The authors say that self-quizzing arrests ____, which is human nature.
questions.explain: Practice at recalling new learning secures it in memory and helps you recall it in the future.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: The familiarity gained from rereading a text creates illusions of ____.
questions.explain: These illusions are not reliable indicators of mastery, which is why the authors do not trust fluency.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: In the authors' advice on retrieval practice, what happens if you restudy something after failing to recall it?
options: You learn it no better than if you had simply restudied from the start.
You learn it worse, because the failed attempt strengthens the error.
You should skip it until the exam, since failure shows it cannot be learned.
You learn it better than if you had not tried to recall it first.
questions.explain: The authors say that restudying after a failed recall attempt produces better learning than not having tried. The effort of retrieval strengthens staying power.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Dana has read her chemistry chapter twice and has a test in a week. Which plan fits the authors' advice?
options: Close the book, quiz herself, check answers, and study weak spots.
Reread the chapter a third time until the terms feel fluent.
Highlight the chapter in more colors to mark important terms.
Wait until the night before and review everything in one sitting.
questions.explain: After one or two reviews, self-quizzing beats more rereading. Checking answers shows where mastery is weak so that study can focus there.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Which of these are questions the authors suggest you ask yourself, without looking in the text, when you pause while reading?
options: What are the key ideas?
Which terms or ideas are new to me?
How do the ideas relate to what I already know?
Which sections will the professor skip?
What exact phrases did the professor use?
questions.explain: The authors list key ideas, new terms and how they relate to prior knowledge. Quizzing helps you focus on central precepts rather than on a professor's turn of phrase.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Which of these are reasons the authors give for self-quizzing being better than rereading?
options: Quizzing gives a reliable measure of what you have mastered.
Quizzing arrests forgetting.
Quizzing feels more productive than rereading.
Quizzing takes less effort than rereading.
questions.explain: Self-quizzing is a reliable measure and arrests forgetting. It actually feels more awkward and frustrating than rereading, and its benefit comes from the effort.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: The authors describe each study strategy in the same pattern. Put the parts in order.
items: What does this mean?
How to use it as a study strategy
What your intuition tells you to do
Why it is better
How it feels
questions.explain: For retrieval, spaced and interleaved practice, the authors first define the strategy and say how to use it, then contrast it with intuition, give the reason it works, and describe how it feels.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Match each way of studying to how the authors say it feels.
pairs: Awkward and frustrating compared with rereading
Harder, because you have become a little rusty
More productive than it really is
questions.explain: Each effective strategy feels worse than the intuitive alternative. The authors say the feeling is misleading, since effort strengthens mastery.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Match each common belief about studying to the authors' correction.
pairs: Its gains come from short-term memory and fade quickly
Studies show that feeling is illusory
Errors in self-quizzing set you back
Not if you check answers and correct mistakes
questions.explain: These are the intuitions the authors address in the three keystone strategies, along with the evidence they offer against each.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Why does self-quizzing feel worse than rereading but work better?
questions.a: Self-quizzing feels awkward and frustrating, especially when new learning is hard to recall, whereas rereading feels productive because the text becomes familiar and fluent. But that fluency creates illusions of knowing, while every time you work hard to recall a memory you strengthen it. The harder the recall, the greater the benefit, and restudying after a failed attempt teaches you better.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Describe how a student should use retrieval practice as a study strategy during a course.
questions.a: Pause periodically while reading or reviewing notes and ask yourself, without looking, what the key ideas are, which terms are new and how they relate to what you know. Use chapter-end questions and write your own questions and answers. Quiz yourself weekly on current and earlier material, check your answers, and focus on weak areas, which also ends cramming.

questions.section: Practice Retrieving New Learning from Memory
questions.q: Put these steps of Michael Young's self-quizzing routine in the order he describes them.
items: Stop after reading a section
Ask what you just read was about
Think through how it happens
Go back and check whether you were right
questions.explain: Young describes stopping, asking what he just read, reasoning through it, and then checking whether he was off base or on the right track.

questions.q: Spaced practice means studying information more than once but leaving considerable ____ between practice sessions.
questions.explain: The schedule of self-quizzing is built so that time elapses between sessions.

questions.q: When practice is spaced, you have to reconstruct what you studied, in effect reloading it from ____ memory.
questions.explain: The effort of reconstructing makes ideas more salient and connects them to other knowledge.

questions.q: Long stretches of single-minded, repetitive practice of one thing are called ____ practice.
questions.explain: The authors say this practice-practice-practice regime feels essential, but its gains quickly fade.

questions.q: True or false: Massed practice feels more productive than spaced practice, and it is in fact more productive.
questions.explain: Massed practice feels more productive, but it is not. Spaced practice feels more difficult because you have become rusty, yet it strengthens mastery.

questions.q: Why do the gains from single-minded, repetitive practice fool us into trusting it?
options: They come from long-term memory, which makes them seem permanent.
They remain hidden until exam time, when they suddenly appear.
They come from short-term memory and quickly fade, but we do not notice the fading.
They come mainly from the effort of retrieving earlier material.
questions.explain: The authors give two reasons: performance visibly improves, and we fail to see how quickly the short-term gains fade.

questions.q: Sam meets forty new colleagues at a conference and wants to remember names and faces. According to the authors, when should he first review them?
options: After about a week, once first impressions have settled in.
The next morning, after a night's sleep has consolidated them.
Once a month, when they have had time to fade.
Within a few minutes, because such associations are forgotten quickly.
questions.explain: The authors say names and faces need review within a few minutes of first encounter, while new text material may wait a day or so.

questions.q: What should you do with flashcards you have answered correctly a couple of times?
options: Set them aside for good so your time goes to the missed ones.
Keep shuffling them in until mastered, then revisit them monthly.
Set them aside and look at them once, the night before the exam.
Drop them after two correct answers and rely on your notes.
questions.explain: The authors say to continue shuffling correct cards into the deck until well mastered, then keep them in a pile you revisit periodically, perhaps monthly.

questions.q: Which of these are reasons the authors give for why intuition favors massed practice?
options: We see our performance improving as we repeat it.
We fail to see how quickly the short-term gains fade.
Studies show massed practice gives the best exam results.
Teachers require students to space their study sessions.
questions.explain: Visible improvement reinforces the strategy and the fading goes unnoticed. The research points the other way, so the last two are wrong.

questions.q: Put the authors' advice for reviewing new material over a course in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Within a few minutes for names and faces
Within a day or so for new text material
After several days or a week
About once a month when sure of mastery
questions.explain: The authors sketch review that begins quickly for fast-fading material and stretches out as mastery grows, to monthly quizzing.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' flashcard advice in order.
items: Quiz yourself on the cards
Keep shuffling correct cards back into the deck
Set aside cards once they are well mastered
Revisit the set-aside pile about monthly
questions.explain: Correct cards stay in the deck until well mastered; only then are they set aside, in a pile that is revisited periodically.

questions.q: Match each kind of material to when the authors say it needs review.
pairs: Within a few minutes of first meeting them
Within a day or so of first reading it
Material you feel sure you have mastered
questions.explain: The timing depends on the material: fast-forgotten associations need quick review, and well-mastered material can wait longer.

questions.q: Sort each study habit as massed or spaced practice.

items.t: Going over the same chapter again and again the night before the exam
Burying yourself in the material as exams near
Quizzing a topic after a day, then a week, then a month
Shuffling mastered flashcards back into the deck
Reaching back to earlier-semester material while studying new topics
Repeating one skill over and over in one long stretch

questions.explain: Massed practice is repetition crammed into one stretch. Spaced practice leaves time for a little forgetting so you must reconstruct what you learned.

questions.q: Why do most students prefer massed practice, and why is that faith misplaced?
questions.a: As we repeat a thing, we see our performance improving, and we do not notice that those gains come from short-term memory and quickly fade, so students put off review and cram. Spaced practice lets a little forgetting happen, so you must reconstruct the learning from long-term memory. That effort makes the ideas more salient and connects them to other knowledge.

questions.q: What does it mean that spaced retrieval is like reloading from long-term memory, and why does it help?
questions.a: If you space sessions so that a little forgetting has happened, you have to work harder to reconstruct what you studied, in effect reloading it from long-term memory. This effort makes the important ideas more salient and memorable and connects them more securely to other knowledge and to more recent learning. It feels more difficult, but it strengthens both mastery and memory.

questions.q: Match each strategy to the chapter where the authors say it is explained more fully.
questions.explain: Chapter 8 gathers advice and points back to the earlier chapters that explain the reasons: Chapter 2 for retrieval, Chapter 3 for interleaving, Chapter 4 for spacing, Chapter 5 for illusions and Chapter 7 for mnemonics.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: Mastering all of one type of problem before moving on to another type is called ____ practice.
questions.explain: Many textbooks are built in study blocks, and the authors say blocked practice is not as effective as interleaved practice.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: In the baseball example, which player becomes the better hitter, and why?
options: The one who takes fifteen of each pitch in turn, since he gets deeper repetition.
The one who practices only fastballs until perfect, since he builds one skill well.
The one who asks for random pitches, since he learns to read each pitch as it comes.
Neither, since batting skill depends only on the total number of swings.
questions.explain: Blocked batting practice may look better in practice, but random pitches build the ability to decipher and respond to each pitch.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: According to the authors, what does mixing up problem types improve?
options: Your speed at solving the first type you practiced before moving on
Your sense of mastery while you are practicing
Your ability to discriminate between types and pick the right solution later
Your ability to remember solutions without ever seeing them again
questions.explain: Interleaving improves discrimination between types and helps identify the unifying characteristics within a type, which pays off on a later test or in real-world settings.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: Lena is studying Dutch painters for an art history exam. Which plan matches the authors' advice on interleaving?
options: Mix examples by different painters so she must tell their styles apart.
Master every work by one painter before starting the next painter.
Study one painter a week and revisit them only at the exam.
Reread her notes on each painter in alphabetical order.
questions.explain: The authors suggest mixing up examples, whether specimens, Dutch painters or macroeconomics principles, so you discriminate between types.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: True or false: Learners who achieve superior mastery from interleaved practice still tend to feel that blocked practice served them better.
questions.explain: The authors say they persist in that feeling, but studies show the feeling is illusory.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: Which of these steps does the author's advice on interleaving recommend?
options: Scatter a newly understood problem type throughout your practice
Mix in other subjects when you notice single-minded repetition
Work through a block of one problem type before testing yourself
Keep to the textbook's block order for the first month
questions.explain: The authors tell learners to alternate between problem types, mixing in other subjects and skills, rather than staying with the blocks of a textbook.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: Sort each practice plan as blocked or interleaved.

items.t: Solving a dozen spheroid-volume problems before any cone problems
Swinging at fifteen fastballs, then fifteen curveballs
Asking for random pitches in batting practice
Alternating between problems that need different solutions
Studying macroeconomics principles in a mixed order
Getting one specimen type down cold before the next

questions.explain: Blocked practice stays with one type until it feels mastered. Interleaved practice alternates, so you keep choosing the right solution.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: Explain the baseball example and what it shows about interleaved practice.
questions.a: A batter who swings at fifteen fastballs, then fifteen curveballs, then fifteen changeups performs better in practice than one who mixes pitches. But the batter who asks for random pitches builds his ability to decipher and respond to each pitch as it comes, and he becomes the better hitter. Interleaving improves the ability to discriminate between types and choose the right response.

questions.section: Interleave the Study of Different Problem Types
questions.q: Why does blocked practice feel better than interleaved practice, and what do the authors tell you to do about that feeling?
questions.a: Blocked practice feels and looks like better mastery as you go, while interrupting one type to practice another feels disruptive and counterproductive. The authors say learners keep feeling that blocked practice serves them better even when interleaving produces superior mastery, and that studies show the feeling is illusory. Knowing this, you can interleave anyway.

questions.q: Elaboration is the process of finding additional ____ of meaning in new material.
questions.explain: The authors say it includes relating the material to what you know, explaining it in your own words, or finding a metaphor or visual image.

questions.q: Generation is an attempt to answer a question or solve a problem before being shown the ____.
questions.explain: Even filling in a missing word yourself leads to better learning and memory than reading a complete text.

questions.q: Calibration means aligning your judgments of what you know with objective ____.
questions.explain: Quizzes and practice tests are the objective instruments students use so they are not carried off by illusions of mastery.

questions.q: The word mnemonic comes from the Greek word for ____.
questions.explain: Mnemonic devices are like mental file cabinets, giving you handy ways to store information and find it again.

questions.q: True or false: Mnemonic devices are tools for learning per se, according to the authors.
questions.explain: The authors say they are not tools for learning per se but for creating mental structures that make it easier to retrieve what you have learned.

questions.q: In the elaboration examples, what does a figure skater's rotation speeding up as her arms draw in help you grasp?
options: Conduction, with heat passing into your hands around a cup
Radiation, with the sun pooling in a room on a winter day
Convection, with cool air carrying you through city streets
Angular momentum, with her spin speeding up as her arms draw in
questions.explain: The authors pair physics principles with visual images: the skater for angular momentum, a hot cup for conduction, sunlight for radiation.

questions.q: What do airline pilots' flight instruments illustrate in the authors' discussion of calibration?
options: Memorizing checklists with a mnemonic so nothing is forgotten
Repeating a maneuver until it feels fluent and automatic
Learning by doing before being shown the solution
Using an objective instrument to correct perceptions that can mislead you
questions.explain: Pilots use instruments to know when their senses mislead them about, for example, whether the plane is level. Students use practice tests the same way.

questions.q: How did Mark Twain use mnemonics to teach his children the English monarchs?
options: He had them recite a rhyme like Old Elephants Have Musty Skin each day.
He staked out the reigns along his driveway and walked it with them.
He asked them to draw a large summary sheet for each reign in turn.
He quizzed them daily on one king and spaced the reviews monthly.
questions.explain: Twain used the winding driveway of his estate, adding images and storytelling. The rhyme mentioned is a Great Lakes mnemonic.

questions.q: A student looks at a practice test question, thinks Yup, I know that, and moves on without writing an answer. What problem do the authors warn about?
options: She may be giving in to the illusion of knowing instead of checking what she knows.
She is using elaboration too much and tying material to too many cues.
She is practicing generation, which gives answers before the question.
She is interleaving problem types without realizing it.
questions.explain: Calibration only works if you supply and check answers. Treat practice tests as tests.

questions.q: Which of these are forms of elaboration described by the authors?
options: Relating new material to what you already know
Explaining the material to someone else in your own words
Finding a metaphor or visual image for the material
Copying lecture slides verbatim into a notebook
questions.explain: The authors describe elaboration as finding layers of meaning, and they say copying slides is less fruitful than reflection.

questions.q: Which of these are named among the other effective study strategies?
options: Calibration
Reflection
Mnemonic devices
Massed practice
Blocked practice
questions.explain: Elaboration, generation, reflection, calibration and mnemonic devices are the others. Massed and blocked practice are the intuitive habits the authors argue against.

questions.q: Match each other study strategy to the authors' description.
pairs: Finding additional layers of meaning in new material
Trying to answer before being shown the answer
Reviewing what you learned and asking yourself questions
Checking your judgments of what you know against objective feedback
Mental file cabinets for storing and finding information
questions.explain: Each pairing restates the authors' own definition.

questions.q: Match each physics concept to the visual image the authors offer.
pairs: A figure skater spinning faster as her arms draw in
Warming your hands around a hot cup of cocoa
The sun pooling in the den on a wintry day
The solar system, with electrons as planets
questions.explain: These are examples of the powerful form of elaboration that finds a metaphor or visual image.

questions.q: Match each setting to how the authors say it uses a mnemonic or similar device.
pairs: Memory palaces for A-level essay exams
Reigns staked along the winding driveway
questions.explain: Each setting is an example the authors give of mnemonic devices: memory palaces, a driveway for monarchs, and a Great Lakes rhyme.

questions.q: Sort each example by whether it illustrates elaboration or generation.

items.t: Picturing a skater's rotation to grasp angular momentum
Explaining new material to a friend in your own words
Filling in a missing word rather than reading the full text
Solving a problem before the solution is taught
Trying to predict a reading's key ideas before reading it
Relating new material to your life outside class

questions.explain: Elaboration adds layers of meaning to material you have. Generation is an attempt to answer or solve before being shown.

questions.q: What is generation, and what examples does the author give?
questions.a: Generation is an attempt to answer a question or solve a problem before being shown the answer. Filling in a missing word yourself, experiential learning that starts with an unknown problem, predicting a reading's key ideas first, and working physics problems before class are examples. Wading into the unknown first makes you far more likely to learn and remember the solution.

questions.q: What is calibration, and why does it matter to answer the questions on your own practice tests?
questions.a: Calibration is aligning your judgments of what you know with objective feedback, to avoid the illusions of mastery that surprise learners at test time. If you glance at a question, think you know it and move on without writing an answer, you may be giving in to the illusion of knowing. Treat practice tests as tests, check your answers, and focus on the areas where you are weak.

questions.q: What are mnemonic devices for, and what are they not?
questions.a: Mnemonic devices are like mental file cabinets, giving handy ways to store information and find it again. They help you retrieve what you have learned and hold arbitrary information in memory. The authors say they are not tools for learning per se but for creating mental structures that make retrieval easier.

questions.q: What score did Michael Young earn on his first medical school exam, despite spending every available minute studying?
questions.explain: Young barely eked out a 65. That shock led him to look for a more effective way to study.

questions.q: What did Michael Young say he wanted when looking for a better way to study?
options: Advice from classmates who had premed backgrounds
A tutor to summarize the four hundred daily slides
Real data and research rather than someone's opinion
More hours in the day to reread the material
questions.explain: Young read empirical studies on learning, including the testing effect, because everybody has an opinion and he wanted real data.

questions.q: To meet the biology requirement for medical school, Michael Young took a ____ class at Columbus State.
questions.explain: It was the only biology course he could take there.

questions.q: True or false: After his poor first exam, Michael Young decided to spend more hours studying, which solved the problem.
questions.explain: Spending more time was not an option. He changed how he studied, using retrieval practice instead of rereading.

questions.q: Which of these did Michael Young adopt to improve his studying?
options: Testing himself on material before going back to look at it
Spacing retrieval practice and finding how much to space
Slowing down to find meaning, with visualization
Spending longer hours rereading all the slides
questions.explain: Young used retrieval practice, spacing and elaboration. Longer rereading was his old habit, which was not producing results.

questions.q: Match each of Michael Young's comments to its theme.
pairs: No time to rehearse every detail of four hundred slides
On making yourself answer the question
Test yourself first, then look back at the material
Longer waiting helps memory but lowers recall success
On slowing down to find the meaning
Visualizing the brain structure helps the dopamine fact stick
questions.explain: Each pairing summarizes one of the areas where Young adapted spaced retrieval and elaboration to medical school.

questions.q: Put these events from Michael Young's path into the order they happened.
items: Worked as a drug addiction counselor
Took a fishing class for biology
Crammed a month for the MCAT
Scored a 65 on his first exam
Rose to the high performers by second year
questions.explain: He came to medicine from psychology and counseling, patched together courses, crammed for the entrance test, and only then hit the wall that forced a new study method.

questions.q: Sort each of Young's habits as before or after he changed how he studied.

items.t: Reading the material passively
Hours of rereading all the material
Stopping to recall what he had just read
Checking his recall against the material
Visualizing the structure for dopamine
Spending every available minute studying coursework

questions.explain: Young was big on reading, which was all he knew how to do. His new approach added retrieval, checking and elaboration.

questions.q: How did Michael Young turn his grades around, and what did he find hardest?
questions.a: After barely scoring a 65 on his first exam, he read empirical research and became interested in the testing effect. He stopped rereading and made himself recall what he had just read, checked whether he was right, spaced his practice and used elaboration, such as visualizing a brain structure. The hardest part was trusting the process, since quizzing felt uncomfortable and slow.

questions.q: What led Stephen Madigan to ask Timothy Fellows about his study habits?
options: Fellows had failed the first exam and asked Madigan for help.
Fellows was getting 90 to 95 percent of the points on all class activities.
Fellows had majored in psychology and wanted to tutor others.
Fellows had questions about spaced retrieval practice by email.
questions.explain: Madigan noticed an outlier in his tough Psych 100 course three-quarters of the way through and took him aside.
