questions.q: True or false: Timothy Fellows always did the reading prior to a lecture.
questions.explain: Among his habits he did the reading before lectures and anticipated test questions as he read.

questions.q: Which of these were among Timothy Fellows's study habits?
options: Anticipating test questions and their answers as he read
Taking the professor's online practice test to find gaps
Spacing out his review over the duration of the course
Waiting until the week before the exam to start reviewing
questions.explain: Fellows used generation, self-testing and spacing. He did not cram.

questions.q: Match each of Timothy Fellows's habits to its purpose.
pairs: Discovers which concepts he does not know
Tests his retention of the reading
Finds terms he cannot recall and relearns them
questions.explain: Each habit is a form of self-testing or checking, and together they were spaced out over the whole course.

questions.q: Sort each of Fellows's habits as self-testing or preparing and organizing.

items.t: Anticipates test questions as he reads
Answers rhetorical questions in his head during lectures
Takes the online practice test
Reorganizes course information into a study guide
Copies bolded terms and definitions into a reading notebook
Does the reading before a lecture

questions.explain: The first three are ways of testing recall. The others build material, but all were spaced out through the course.

questions.q: What study habits did Timothy Fellows use, and what do they illustrate?
questions.a: Fellows did the reading before lectures, anticipated test questions as he read, answered rhetorical questions in his head during lectures, and relearned terms he could not recall. He took the online practice test to find gaps, posted key concepts above his bed and tested himself, and spaced his review over the course. They show doing what works and keeping at it, so practice is spaced and learning is embedded by exam time.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the learning strategies outlined for students are effective only for people in classroom settings.
questions.explain: They say these strategies are effective for anyone at any age, though lifelong learners apply them in less-structured settings.

questions.q: How does the authors' view of lifelong learners relate to their advice for students?
options: They need entirely different principles, since they are no longer in school.
They need no study strategies, since experience teaches them enough.
They should rely mainly on rereading, since they lack classroom quizzes.
They use the same principles, but in less structured settings than a classroom.
questions.explain: The student strategies are centered on classroom instruction, but lifelong learners use the same principles in a variety of less-structured settings.

questions.q: The authors call techniques such as generation and spaced practice ____, even if counterintuitive.
questions.explain: From birth we learn by experimentation, trial and error and recalling what we did last time, so many people discover these techniques on their own.

questions.q: Why does the chapter move from student tips to lifelong learners, and what links the two groups?
questions.a: The strategies outlined for students are effective for anyone at any age, but they are centered on classroom instruction. Lifelong learners use the same principles in less-structured settings, pursuing interests and careers that require continuous learning. The techniques are organic, even if counterintuitive, since from birth we learn through trial and error and recalling what we did before.

questions.q: Put the study strategy groups in the order the student tips present them.
items: Practice retrieving new learning
Space out your retrieval practice
Interleave different problem types
Other effective study strategies
questions.explain: The three keystone strategies come first, in that order, followed by other effective strategies such as elaboration and generation, and then the two student profiles.

questions.q: When the actor Nathaniel Fuller starts a new script, why does he highlight all of his lines?
options: To gauge how much he must learn and to sense how the lines and the back-and-forth work.
To mark them for repeated rereading until the words feel fluent and familiar to him on stage.
To pick out his hardest lines so that he can drill only those during the final week of study.
To flag the cues from other actors so that he can memorize those before learning his own.
questions.explain: Fuller's highlighting gives him a sense of workload and of the construction of the scene, which is different from students who highlight merely so they can reread. Rereading for fluency is the habit the authors warn against.

questions.q: Why does Nathaniel Fuller, once he reaches the end of a play, practice in reverse order from the last scene back toward the first?
options: Removing the story order stops him from learning lines by rote and forces him to rely on feelings alone.
It stitches less familiar material to more familiar material, deepening his mastery of the role.
Rehearsing the final scenes most often matters most, since the ending is where the audience judges a performance.
Varying the scene order keeps every scene from being repeated twice in a row, which he wants to avoid.
questions.explain: Fuller moves from the less familiar last scene to the more familiar one before it, and keeps reaching back. The point is to join new material to what he already knows, not to avoid repetition or favor the ending.

questions.q: True or false: Nathaniel Fuller keeps working on a role until he has every line perfect that day, because he fears that stopping early will let the lines fade.
questions.explain: Fuller stops when he reaches diminishing returns and returns the next day. Although he will not remember it then, he has faith that it will come back a little better the next time.

questions.q: Nathaniel Fuller says he needs to try his best to say a line without looking at it, and that he needs to have that ____ in order to make himself remember it.
questions.explain: Fuller deliberately makes recall difficult, because the effort of retrieving the line is what helps him remember it.

questions.q: The authors describe Nathaniel Fuller's learning process as a seamless blend of ____ difficulties: retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving, generation, and elaboration.
questions.explain: Desirable difficulties are the authors' term for challenges during learning that make it stronger and longer lasting, and Fuller's methods combine several of them.

questions.q: Put these steps of Nathaniel Fuller's script learning in the order he does them, from the start of a new script.
items: Highlights his lines in a binder to see how much he must learn
Covers a page and speaks his own line aloud from memory
Checks his accuracy and repeats the line if he got it wrong
Reveals the next passage and goes on
After reaching the end, practices in reverse order from the last scene
questions.explain: Fuller begins by highlighting his lines, then practices each page by speaking from memory and checking. When he reaches the end of the play, he works backward scene by scene.

questions.q: Match each of Nathaniel Fuller's practices to the learning idea it illustrates.
pairs: Speaking his line aloud from memory with the script covered
Coming back to a role the next day after stopping at diminishing returns
Examining the textures of words and figures of speech for meaning
questions.explain: Fuller's methods show retrieval practice (producing lines unaided), spacing (returning after a gap), and elaboration (adding layers of meaning to the language and character).

questions.q: How does Nathaniel Fuller use a palm-sized recorder to practice a role, and what kind of practice is this?
questions.a: Fuller records every line of the other actors in the play, voiced in character. He plays a line, pauses at his cue, speaks his own line from memory, and checks the script if he is unsure. This is a stepped-up form of retrieval practice, since he must produce his lines without the written text in front of him.

questions.q: Which of these does Nathaniel Fuller do while preparing to understudy a role?
options: Practices at home, imagining his living room as the stage and the blocking
Rereads his highlighted lines the night before he may go on
Waits until the blocking is final before learning any lines
Watches rehearsals from the back of the hall, walking through the blocking himself
questions.explain: Fuller practices with imagined blocking at home and then follows the real rehearsals from behind the seats, adapting his imaginary stage. He does not wait or rely on rereading.

questions.q: How does the writer John McPhee get past writer's block on a new subject?
options: He plans the whole piece in outline form first, so that no clumsy draft is ever needed at all.
He waits until he is clear about exactly what he wants to say, and then writes a clean version.
He writes his mother a letter about the subject, then deletes the whining and keeps the substance.
He talks the subject through with an editor, and then writes from the notes that the editor gives.
questions.explain: McPhee's letter lets him begin by blurting, and he then removes the Dear Mother and the complaints. The authors' point is that a rough draft has to exist before improvement can start.

questions.q: Priya is trying to learn a hard idea in economics. Rather than rereading the chapter, she writes a rough explanation in her own words and improves it over the next days. Which idea from the authors does this follow?
options: Rereading until the text feels fluent, since familiarity builds mastery of the underlying content.
Waiting until the idea is fully clear, since drafting early would lock in mistakes for good.
Passively reviewing slides, since seeing the whole topic quickly reveals how the ideas connect.
Like McPhee's rough first draft, an early clumsy attempt gets the mind working on the material.
questions.explain: McPhee says writing has not really begun until a draft exists, and the authors say learning works the same way. Rereading and passive slides do not engage the mind.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that you engage the mind in learning mainly by reading a text over and over or by passively watching slides.
questions.explain: They say the mind is engaged by making the effort to explain the material in your own words, connecting facts and relating them to what you know. Rereading and passive slides do not do this.

questions.q: John McPhee describes his first draft as an awful ____.
questions.explain: McPhee accepts that a first draft is rough, because only once a draft exists can the mind begin to improve it.

questions.q: The authors close the discussion of McPhee by telling learners to delete the whimpering and go wrestle the ____.
questions.explain: The bear is the subject McPhee wrote about, and the authors use it as a picture of struggling with unfamiliar material.

questions.q: Put the steps of John McPhee's process in the order the authors describe them.
items: Writes a letter to his mother about the subject
Deletes the whimpering and keeps just the subject
Treats the result as an awful first draft and puts it aside
On the drive home, his mind keeps working on the words
Thinks of a better way to say something
questions.explain: McPhee first blurts, then strips out the complaints, then sets the draft aside. His mind then keeps knitting at it and produces improvements.

questions.q: According to the authors, which of these engage the mind in learning and which do not?

items.t: Explaining the material in your own words
Relating the material to what you already know
Struggling with the puzzle before seeing the solution
Reading the text over and over
Passively watching slides
Pasting facts onto the surface of the brain

questions.explain: The authors say you engage the mind by making an effort to explain, connect, and make material vivid. Repeated reading and passive slides leave knowledge on the surface.

questions.q: How does John McPhee's awful blurting help explain the way learning works?
questions.a: Unfamiliar material feels clumsy and approximate at first, just like a rough first draft. But once you try to make sense of it in your own words, the mind starts to knit at the problem on its own and looks for parallels in your experience. The solution you reach is then embedded more deeply with prior knowledge than anything pasted on by slides.

questions.q: What does the authors' account of Captain Chesley Sullenberger show about the habit of reflection?
options: At its most powerful it engages the mind through generation, visualization, and mental rehearsal.
It consists mainly of taking stock of a personal experience, and nothing more is needed to learn.
It works best when drawn from personal experience, since observing others adds little of value.
It matters chiefly for pilots and surgeons, whose mistakes are costly enough to deserve study.
questions.explain: Sullenberger refined his understanding through training, experience, and close observation of others. The authors say reflection is more than taking stock of an experience.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' account, Captain Sullenberger analyzed the few available examples of commercial aircraft ditching and paid particular attention to pitch, speed, and level wings.
questions.explain: His study of ditching cases, focused on pitch, speed, and level wings, is one way he refined his understanding of flight.

questions.q: Match each person from the authors' earlier chapters to how they use reflection.
pairs: Devised a surgical repair for a delicate sinus structure at the back of the skull
Helped players learn playbooks and adjustments for the next game
Refined his understanding of flight and aircraft control over many years
questions.explain: Each person reflects on experience and asks how to improve, and the authors point to the results in their fields.

questions.q: Which of these does the authors' account of reflection include?
options: Repeating the same actions until they feel fluent
Highlighting your notes so that you can reread them later
Retrieval, asking what you did and how it worked
Mental rehearsal, imagining a change in what you do
Generation, asking how you could do it better next time
questions.explain: Reflection combines retrieval, generation, and imagery or mental rehearsal. Highlighting for rereading and fluent repetition are the habits the authors caution against.

questions.q: In the authors' account of the neurosurgeon Mike Ebersold, what does reflection involve, and what did it lead him to do?
questions.a: Reflection involves retrieval (what did I do and how did it work?) and generation (how could I do it better next time?), plus imagery and mental rehearsal. This habit led Ebersold to devise a surgical solution for repairing a delicate, flat sinus structure at the back of the skull that tears when it is tied off.

questions.q: How does the way the pianist Thelma Hunter learns a new score illustrate elaboration?
options: She plays it through from the first note to the last until it feels fluent and smooth to her.
She learns it physically, aurally, visually, and intellectually, giving the piece several layers of meaning.
She picks one sense, the sound, and drills it until the errors in that sense disappear.
She leaves the difficult passages for last so that the easy ones can build her confidence.
questions.explain: Hunter learns the piece in her fingering, in its sound, in the notes on the page, and in how she coaches herself through transitions. Multiple layers of meaning are the authors' picture of elaboration.

questions.q: Thelma Hunter sometimes sits down after a week away from a piece and plays it with a natural fingering she had not planned. What do the authors suggest may explain this?
options: Her time away made her forget the difficult passage, so that a simpler fingering came by chance.
She was copying a fingering she had seen in an earlier score, which she recalled without effort.
Her earlier effort at the keys may have set her mind searching memory for a more elegant solution.
Her age has made her hands favor easier fingerings, so that the music is now shaped by stamina.
questions.explain: The authors liken Hunter's effort at the keys to McPhee wrestling his bear: the struggle sets the mind to searching for something more fluent. The other options are not given by the book.

questions.q: Thelma Hunter visualizes the score and makes mental ____, such as telling herself up an octave at a certain point.
questions.explain: Hunter pictures the place on the sheet music and adds her own notes in her mind, a way of adding layers of meaning.

questions.q: Match each way Thelma Hunter learns a new score to what it involves.
pairs: In the notes on the score
In the way she coaches herself through transitions
questions.explain: Hunter gives the music several layers of meaning through different channels, and the authors say this strengthens learning and memory.

questions.q: Which of these does Thelma Hunter do when she works on a new piece?
options: Skips warming up, because she believes it wastes her stamina
Visualizes the score in her mind's eye
Slows down to work through difficult passages on a daily practice schedule
Says reminders aloud while practicing, such as going up an octave
Avoids thinking about a piece's structure, memorizing by feel alone
questions.explain: Hunter visualizes, talks herself through, and slows down for hard passages. Today she thinks about memorizing and does warm up, which she never used to do.

questions.q: How does Thelma Hunter's habit of thinking through a nearly memorized piece while driving resonate with McPhee's observations about writing?
questions.a: Away from the piano, Hunter thinks about the shape of the whole piece like a conductor and decides that a passage makes more sense if sped up. McPhee similarly found his mind still knitting at the words while driving home. In both cases the prior effort at the task keeps the mind working on it away from the task.

questions.q: In introducing their tips for teachers, the authors say they are leery of being too ____, because every teacher must find what is right in his or her classroom.
questions.explain: The authors still offer specifics, since they can help teachers adapt ideas in their own classrooms.

questions.section: Explain to Students How Learning Works
questions.q: Why do the authors say a teacher should explain to students how learning works?
options: Students otherwise leave every decision about reviewing each topic to the teacher's choice of schedule.
Students otherwise resist all quizzes, since quizzes feel too easy for most learners to take seriously.
Students otherwise cannot follow the research literature that they may later come across on their own.
Students hold myths and illusions that lead to poor choices about when and how to study.
questions.explain: The authors say it is the teacher's proper role to explain what empirical studies show so students can manage their own education.

questions.section: Explain to Students How Learning Works
questions.q: Among the ideas students need to understand, the authors say that when learning is easy, it is often ____ and soon forgotten.
questions.explain: Easy learning feels productive but is shallow, which is why the authors want students to see the value of desirable difficulties.

questions.section: Explain to Students How Learning Works
questions.q: Which of these ideas do the authors say teachers should help students understand?
options: Intellectual abilities are hardwired and effort cannot change the brain
Learning that feels easy is the most durable kind of learning
Setbacks often supply the information needed to adjust strategies
Wrestling with a new problem before seeing the solution helps learning
Some difficulties during learning make it stronger and better remembered
questions.explain: The authors say effortful learning changes the brain, easy learning is often superficial, and setbacks are informative. The two wrong options reverse these ideas.

questions.section: Explain to Students How Learning Works
questions.q: Why do the authors want students to understand that striving often results in setbacks?
questions.a: To surpass your current ability you must strive, and striving by its nature often brings setbacks. Those setbacks are signs of effort, not failure, and they give the information needed to adjust strategies and reach mastery. Students who know this are less likely to avoid intellectual risk.

questions.q: According to the authors, why do students gravitate to rereading, massed practice, and cramming?
options: They are generally not taught how to study and often get the wrong advice when they are.
Studies show these methods give the strongest long-term retention, so teachers recommend them.
Teachers require these methods so that grading can be consistent across a large class.
Students dislike self-testing only because they never see the correct answers afterward.
questions.explain: The authors say poor study habits stem from a lack of instruction or bad advice, and that effective strategies must be taught.

questions.q: Sort these study activities into those students gravitate to but that are far from optimal, and the effective strategies the authors recommend.

items.t: Rereading
Massed practice
Cramming
Self-quizzing from memory
Spaced retrieval practice
Interleaved practice

questions.explain: The authors name rereading, massed practice, and cramming as the common choices, and the chapter's three keystone strategies as the effective alternative.

questions.q: Which of these are activities that students often choose even though the authors call them far from optimal?
options: Massed practice
Rereading
Self-quizzing
Cramming
Spacing out review sessions
questions.explain: Students drift to rereading, massed practice, and cramming. Self-quizzing and spacing are the effective strategies.

questions.q: Why do the authors want teachers to help students stick with effective study strategies long enough to see their benefits?
questions.a: Students tend to drift toward rereading, massed practice, and cramming, so they need help to adopt better methods. The effective strategies may initially appear doubtful, because they feel harder, and students may give up before they see results. Sticking with them long enough lets students experience the benefits.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: According to the authors, when do students find classroom quizzing more acceptable?
options: When it comes as a surprise and the result carries heavy weight in the course grade.
When it is predictable and the stakes of any individual quiz are low.
When it is long and detailed so that it covers every topic since the term began.
When it comes only at the end of the term, so that earlier study time is left untouched.
questions.explain: The authors say predictable, low-stakes quizzing is easier for students to accept. Teachers, for their part, like it simple, quick, and free of makeup negotiations.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: Why should a teacher design quizzes and exercises to reach back to concepts covered earlier in the term?
options: Earlier topics then count for more of the grade than recent ones, which rewards early effort.
Quizzes then become hard to pass, which discourages students from missing a class.
Retrieval practice continues and learning becomes cumulative, building more complex mental models.
Students then need less new reading each week, because old material replaces the new.
questions.explain: Reaching back keeps retrieval going and ties ideas together, so understanding of relationships between ideas grows.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: A teacher wants quizzes that students and she herself will accept. Which plan best follows the authors' advice?
options: Rare surprise quizzes with high stakes, and makeups granted case by case after each absence.
Long weekly exams with high stakes, because they discourage students from skipping class.
Ungraded optional quizzes, because grade consequences take away the value of the practice.
Brief, predictable, low-stakes quizzes that count slightly toward the grade, with no makeups to negotiate.
questions.explain: The authors recommend low-stakes quizzes that carry some grade weight, and ground rules that keep them simple for the teacher.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: True or false: Students in classes where practice exercises count toward the course grade, even at very low stakes, learn better than students in classes where the same exercises carry no consequences.
questions.explain: The authors state this as a reason to make quizzing and practice exercises count, even for very low stakes.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: The authors advise making quizzing and practice exercises count toward the course grade, even for very low ____.
questions.explain: Low stakes keep quizzes acceptable to students, while a small grade consequence makes the practice more effective.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: The authors say to space, interleave, and vary topics so that students must ____ what they already know about each topic when shifting gears.
questions.explain: Switching between topics forces students to bring back what they know, which is a form of effortful retrieval.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: Which of these study tools do the authors suggest teachers create?
options: Open-note quizzes in which students look up every answer
Downloadable practice tests for reviewing and calibrating judgments
Writing exercises that ask students to reflect on past lessons
Exercises where students wrestle with a new kind of problem before class
Handouts that give complete solutions before class so students can read them
questions.explain: The suggested tools combine retrieval practice, generation, and elaboration. Handing out solutions or allowing lookup would remove the effort.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: Match each study tool the authors suggest to its purpose.
pairs: Wrestle with a new kind of problem before the solution is taught
Review material and calibrate judgments of what you know
Reflect on past lessons and relate them to other knowledge or life
Generate the key ideas of recent text or lecture material
questions.explain: These tools build retrieval practice, generation, and elaboration into classroom work.

questions.section: Create Desirable Difficulties in the Classroom
questions.q: Why do the authors say teachers should make quizzing count toward the course grade, even at very low stakes?
questions.a: Students in classes where practice exercises carry consequences for the course grade learn better than those in classes where the exercises are the same but carry no consequences. A small grade weight makes students take the practice seriously, and low stakes keep it acceptable to them.

questions.q: What should a teacher be up front about, according to the authors' advice to be transparent?
options: That desirable difficulties bring frustrations, and why persisting is worthwhile.
Which topics will appear on exams, so that students can focus their review on them alone.
How the grading formula is computed, so that students can work out the marks they need.
Which quizzes will be dropped, so that students know where they can safely cut back.
questions.explain: The authors want students to understand how and why desirable difficulties are built into lessons, and that they can be frustrating but worthwhile.

questions.q: Why do the authors recommend that teachers be transparent about desirable difficulties?
questions.a: Students need to understand how desirable difficulties have been built into the lessons and why. The strategies can be frustrating, so teachers should say so and explain why persisting is worthwhile. Michael Young's profile can show students the difficulties and eventual benefits.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Bloom's taxonomy classifies cognitive learning on ____ levels.
questions.explain: The levels run from knowledge at the most fundamental to evaluation at the most sophisticated.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Put the levels of Bloom's taxonomy in order from the most fundamental to the most sophisticated.
items: Knowledge
Comprehension
Application
Analysis
Synthesis
Evaluation
questions.explain: Wenderoth wants students to rise to the levels of synthesis and evaluation, the top levels of the taxonomy.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Match each level of Bloom's taxonomy to what it involves.
pairs: Understanding the underlying facts and ideas
Examining ideas and relationships to make inferences
Combining knowledge and ideas in new ways
questions.explain: These are five of the six levels the authors describe, with evaluation at the top.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: True or false: Wenderoth tells students whose textbooks are highlighted in four colors that this shows they have been studying in the most effective way.
questions.explain: She praises their effort but tells them any additional time spent rereading after the first pass was a waste. They should read a little and then test themselves.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: In Wenderoth's forest image, what happens when a student takes out the notes while trying to recall something?
options: The path to the memory is widened, because the notes show exactly where the memory lies.
The path to the memory is short-circuited, because someone has told the student the way.
A second path forms, since the notes add a new route to the same memory in the forest.
The memory fades faster, because the notes replace what the student already held in mind.
questions.explain: Wenderoth says the more times you make a path to a memory, the better the path becomes. Using the notes stops the search for the path.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Explain Wenderoth's forest image for memory and what it implies about looking at your notes.
questions.a: She tells students their brains are like a forest: the memory is somewhere in there, and the more times you make a path to it, the easier it is to find next time. As soon as you get your notes out, you short-circuit the path, because you are not exploring for it anymore. Someone has told you the way.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Which of these does Wenderoth do to get students to test themselves in class?
options: Throws out a question on what was just covered roughly every five minutes
Has students write three possible answers on the board and vote by raising fingers
Reads the correct answer aloud so students can compare it with their own
Lets students check their notes first so that nobody answers wrongly
Tells students not to look at notes but to think for a minute
questions.explain: These techniques make students retrieve and compare ideas before any answer is given.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Why does Wenderoth give students a new vocabulary, such as the illusion of knowing, for describing setbacks?
options: Students who use technical terms in their answers earn higher marks on her exams.
The terms replace the need to study, since naming an illusion removes it from the learner.
Blaming the test is a poor meeting ground, whereas naming the illusion lets her help.
The terms let her avoid discussing exam results with students who feel disappointed.
questions.explain: Students now come after a poor exam and say they have the illusion of knowing and ask how to get better. That is a problem she can work on.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Sort these features into Wenderoth's study groups and her testing groups.

items.t: The person who knows the most talks and the others listen
The emphasis is on memorizing things
Everyone wrestles with a question together
Textbooks stay closed
The emphasis is on exploration and understanding

questions.explain: Wenderoth turned study groups into testing groups to emphasize exploration and understanding.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: How does a Wenderoth testing group help one student explain a concept at the whiteboard?
questions.a: The group says which ideas they do not feel clear on, and one student goes to the whiteboard to try to explain the concept. As she struggles and puts up the pieces she knows, the rest of the group test her with questions whose answers lead her to the larger concept. Throughout, all textbooks remain closed.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: In Wenderoth's free recall exercise, students must sit for ____ minutes with a blank piece of paper each day.
questions.explain: She warns that it is uncomfortable, and they will run out of ideas after two minutes, but they must stick it out.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Put the steps of Wenderoth's end-of-day free recall exercise in order.
items: Sit with a blank sheet of paper
Write everything remembered from class for ten minutes
Check class notes to see what was remembered and forgotten
Focus on the material that was forgotten
Use the result to shape notes and questions for the next class
questions.explain: The exercise ends with students focusing on what they forgot and using it to guide the next class.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: What do students do in Wenderoth's free recall exercise, and what does she find it helps them do?
questions.a: Each day students sit for ten minutes with a blank piece of paper and write everything they can remember from class, even when it is uncomfortable. They then check their class notes to see what they remembered and forgot, and focus on what they forgot. Wenderoth finds this helps them pull learning forward and develop a more complex understanding of how the material interrelates.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: What are Wenderoth's weekly summary sheets, and which learning strategy do they promote?
questions.a: Every Monday students turn in a single sheet on which they illustrate the prior week's material in drawings annotated with key ideas, arrows, and graphs. They help students synthesize a week of information and see how systems are connected. This is a form of elaboration that adds layers of meaning.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Which of these did Wenderoth assign to her students?
options: A daily full read-through of the textbook with highlighting
Open-notes quizzes at the start of each class
Low-stakes learning paragraphs on some Fridays
A one-page illustrated summary sheet due every Monday
Ten minutes of free recall on a blank page at the end of each day
questions.explain: These three assignments promote retrieval, reflection, and elaboration. Rereading and highlighting are what she discourages.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Match each Wenderoth practice to its timing and form.
pairs: She throws out a question on what was just covered
Ten minutes of free recall on a blank sheet
Students turn in an illustrated summary sheet
Low-stakes learning paragraphs of five or six sentences
questions.explain: Each activity pushes students to retrieve, reflect, or elaborate, rather than to reread.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Match each Wenderoth technique to what it asks students to do.
pairs: Wrestle with a question together with textbooks closed
Write what they remember from class on a blank page
Illustrate the week's material with arrows and key ideas
Answer a question in five or six sentences, at low stakes
Find where their answers fell on the taxonomy
questions.explain: Together these techniques build retrieval, elaboration, and reflection.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: What does Wenderoth ask students to do when she returns tests along with her answer key organized by Bloom's taxonomy?
options: Compare their scores with classmates to see who earned the top marks at each taxonomy level.
Rewrite each missed answer from the key word for word so that it is fixed in memory.
Appeal any marked answers they believe belong at a higher level than the grader judged.
Identify where their answers fell on the taxonomy and what they need to know to reach a higher level.
questions.explain: The key gives a different answer for each level of the taxonomy, so students can see how far up they reached and what they would need to rise.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: What did Wenderoth and colleagues find when they compared high-structure with low-structure classes in a gateway biology course?
options: High-structure classes significantly reduced failure rates and narrowed the gap between students.
Low-structure classes with high-stakes exams gave better results at the higher levels of Bloom's taxonomy.
Both formats gave the same failure rates, but high-structure classes took far more instructor time.
High-structure classes helped the best prepared students most, and so widened the gap with their peers.
questions.explain: The high-structure format used daily and weekly low-stakes exercises. It also showed exam results at higher levels on Bloom's taxonomy.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: True or false: In Wenderoth's gateway biology experiments, high-structure classes raised student failure rates compared with low-structure classes.
questions.explain: High-structure classes significantly reduced failure rates and narrowed the gap between poorly prepared students and better prepared peers.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Sort these features into the low-structure and high-structure classes Wenderoth compared.

items.t: Traditional lecturing
High-stakes midterm and final exams
Daily and weekly low-stakes exercises
Constant practice in the analytical skills needed for exams

questions.explain: Low-structure classes rely on lecturing and a few big exams, whereas high-structure ones give constant low-stakes practice.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: Wenderoth's team teaches students a growth mindset, an idea from the work of Carol ____.
questions.explain: A growth mindset is the idea that learning is hard work and that struggle increases intellectual abilities.

questions.section: Mary Pat Wenderoth, Biology Professor, University of Washington
questions.q: How did Wenderoth and colleagues compare low-structure and high-structure classes, and what did they find?
questions.a: Low-structure classes used traditional lecturing and high-stakes midterm and final exams, while high-structure classes used daily and weekly low-stakes exercises for constant practice. High-structure classes in a gateway biology course significantly reduced failure rates and narrowed the gap between poorly and better prepared students, while showing exam results at higher levels on Bloom's taxonomy. Exercises that counted toward the grade, even at very low stakes, also gave higher success.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: West Point's instructional system, developed almost two hundred years ago, is called the ____ method.
questions.explain: It is named for Sylvanus Thayer, an early superintendent of the academy.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Which of these are part of the Thayer method at West Point?
options: Specific learning objectives for every course
One comprehensive exam at the end of each year
Long lectures covering the whole assigned reading
Responsibility for meeting the objectives placed on the student
Quizzing and recitation in every class meeting
questions.explain: The method sets objectives, puts responsibility on the student, and builds in quizzing and recitation. Matthews's courses have little or no lecturing.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Why does Matthews tell a student that reading every word of a chapter is not very efficient?
options: Cadets are expected to skim every chapter once and then depend on lectures for the content.
Cadets must zero in on what is essential, starting with questions and reading for the answers.
Every word is already covered in the class quiz, so reading adds nothing to what they know.
Reading counts for less than physical and military training in the way grades are computed.
questions.explain: The load is greater than the available hours, so cadets must focus on the essentials rather than slide their eyes over the words.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: What kind of questions do cadets tackle when they take to the boards in Matthews's courses?
options: Easier fact-recall questions than the daily quiz, so that every cadet can succeed at the board.
Questions on the learning objectives, which they must answer silently and alone at their desks.
Higher-order questions that require them to integrate ideas from the reading and apply them conceptually.
Open-ended questions on the instructor's lecture, which are graded on the quality of notes.
questions.explain: These board questions require more than the daily quiz does and give practice in retrieval, generation, and peer instruction.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Put the parts of a typical board day in Matthews's class in order.
items: Class opens with a quiz on the learning objectives
Groups go to the boards to answer a higher-order question
One student per group recites the group's answer
The group's work is critiqued
questions.explain: The day begins with the quiz and then moves to group work and recitation, followed by critique.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Match each West Point term to its meaning.
pairs: Objectives for every course, student responsibility, and quizzing and recitation daily
Groups at the blackboards collaborate on a question the professor gives
Pausing to check your bearing so that you stay on course
questions.explain: Each term describes how the academy keeps students focused and on course.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Matthews and Hunkler say that quizzing is a way of shooting an ____ in the classroom.
questions.explain: Shooting an azimuth means sighting a distant landmark and checking you are still on course, as quizzing checks that you are gaining mastery.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Explain how shooting an azimuth works in the wilderness and why the authors say quizzing is like it.
questions.a: You climb a tree or height of land and sight a distant landmark in your direction, note how many degrees it lies off due north, then descend and keep working toward it, pausing now and then to shoot another azimuth. Quizzing does the same in a classroom: it checks whether you are gaining the mastery you need to reach your goal.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: True or false: Matthews's class meetings focus mainly on specific facts rather than on the larger constructs underlying the matter at hand.
questions.explain: All class meetings focus on constructs, not specific facts, and the students work to understand and articulate the larger concepts.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: According to Roediger, for which students are methods with daily participation, like the Thayer method, especially helpful?
options: Students who are already the most capable and need little structure to succeed.
Students who arrive with strong premed coursework from earlier years of study.
Students who prefer to learn by listening to lectures and taking careful notes.
Students who are not prone to work hard on their own outside of class.
questions.explain: Roediger links this to Wenderoth's finding that high-structure classes help students who lack a history of effective learning habits.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: Sort these features into those that are part of Matthews's classes and those that are not.

items.t: An opening quiz on the learning objectives
Groups answering a question at the boards
A group's student reciting its answer to the class
Long stretches of lecturing
A focus on specific facts over larger constructs

questions.explain: There is little or no lecturing, and all meetings focus on constructs.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: What are the main features of the Thayer method used at West Point?
questions.a: It gives very specific learning objectives for every course, puts responsibility for meeting them on the student, and builds quizzing and recitation into every class meeting. It is a strong encouragement to keep at it for students who are not prone to work hard on their own.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 8 give specific practical advice when the earlier chapters did not?
options: Early readers urged the authors to get specific after the earlier chapters left conclusions to the reader.
The earlier chapters were already prescriptive, so this chapter only condenses their advice into lists.
The publisher required a closing chapter that would speak to a single audience of students.
New research findings appear for the first time in this chapter and needed practical tips.
questions.explain: The authors resisted becoming overtly prescriptive in the early chapters, then responded to readers who asked for practical advice.

questions.q: In the Tips for Teachers part of Chapter 8, what role do the profiles of Mary Pat Wenderoth and Michael Matthews play?
options: They introduce new research findings that were not covered in any of the earlier chapters.
They show how teachers are already putting the recommended strategies to work in real classrooms.
They warn teachers about strategies that fail in university and military settings.
They replace the recommendations by giving stories alone and no specific advice at all.
questions.explain: The authors say that brief descriptions follow of what some teachers are already doing, to help readers adapt the ideas.

questions.q: In what order does Chapter 8 address its audiences?
items: Students
Lifelong learners
Teachers
Trainers
questions.explain: The chapter begins with students, then lifelong learners, teachers, and finally trainers.

questions.q: In what order do the recommendations in the Tips for Teachers part appear?
items: Explain to students how learning works
Teach students how to study
Create desirable difficulties in the classroom
Be transparent
questions.explain: The recommendations lead from understanding to study skills, to classroom practice, and then to openness about the methods.

questions.q: True or false: The Tips for Lifelong Learners part applies the same strategies given to students, but in less-structured settings than classroom instruction.
questions.explain: The authors say the strategies are effective for anyone at any age, and lifelong learners use them in less-structured settings.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 8 tells readers to take the profile of the medical student Michael Young as a model for teachers, as the Be Transparent recommendation shows.
questions.explain: That recommendation suggests that teachers consider having students read Young's earlier profile in the chapter.

questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 8, Make It Stick, signal about where the chapter sits in the book?
questions.a: After seven chapters on the science of learning, the title signals a turn to practical advice on making learning last. The chapter draws on retrieval from Chapter 2, spacing and interleaving from Chapter 3, difficulties and elaboration from Chapter 4, and growth mindset from Chapter 7, and applies them for students, lifelong learners, teachers, and trainers.

questions.q: Match each earlier chapter to a person from it whom Chapter 8 revisits.
pairs: Mike Ebersold, who uses reflection in the operating room
Vince Dooley, who helped players learn playbooks by reflection
David Garman, who improves his undercover strategies
Anders Ericsson, whose research on deliberate practice Hunter's experience seems to show
questions.explain: Chapter 8 refers back to these earlier chapters as it shows how their ideas apply to real learners.

questions.section: Michael D. Matthews, Psychology Professor, U.S. Military Academy at West Point
questions.q: What did the cadet Kiley Hunkler do while preparing for the Medical College Admission Test, as an example of shooting her azimuth?
options: She memorized every fact for several months before attempting any practice test at all.
She reread each of the four course blocks until the wording felt entirely familiar to her.
She wrote her own learning objectives, took a practice test every three days, and adjusted.
She waited for the instructors to set her learning objectives, then studied them in order.
questions.explain: Hunkler created the objectives she judged most important, checked her progress with a practice test every three days, and focused on concepts rather than memorizing everything.

questions.q: Match each person to their field, as the chapter's tips for lifelong learners present them.
pairs: Actor at the Guthrie Theater who learns lines through retrieval practice
Writer who gets past writer's block with an awful first draft
Pianist who learns new scores through several layers of meaning
Pilot who landed US Airways Flight 1549 on the Hudson
questions.explain: Each person illustrates one of the strategies in the lifelong-learner part: retrieval, generation, elaboration, and reflection.

questions.q: Match each Tips for Teachers recommendation to its main advice.
pairs: Help students see why effortful learning is stronger and what setbacks tell them
Help students adopt effective strategies and stay with them long enough
Use frequent quizzing and tools built on retrieval, generation, and elaboration
Be up front about the frustrations and why persisting is worthwhile
questions.explain: These four recommendations open the teacher tips, before the profiles of teachers who use them.

questions.q: Sort these parts of Nathaniel Fuller's practice into retrieval practice and elaboration.

items.t: Covering his lines and speaking them aloud from memory
Hearing the other actors' lines on a recorder and speaking his own
Examining the textures of words and figures of speech for meaning
Discovering how the character carries himself and moves

questions.explain: Fuller produces lines unaided for retrieval, and adds layers of meaning through language and character for elaboration.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: In Kathleen McDermott’s course on human learning and memory, how is each daily quiz run?
options: Four questions on lecture or reading high points, at the end of class
Ten questions on the previous week’s reading, given at the start of each class
Two questions on that day’s lecture only, handed in at the following session
One long essay on the day’s topic, written at the end of each week
questions.explain: She gives a four-item quiz in the last three to five minutes of every class. Students who understood the material can get all four right, but they must think to do it.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: What does Kathleen McDermott give students in exchange for refusing to allow makeup quizzes?
options: The lowest exam score is replaced by the average of the quiz scores
Four quizzes may be dropped, and absences need not be justified
Each student may retake two failed quizzes during office hours
Only quizzes with a perfect score of four out of four are counted
questions.explain: The trade is four free drops across the semester: absences need no excuse, and in return no missed quizzes are made up. This keeps the system manageable for her and clear for students.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: Why does McDermott make her second midterm and final exam cumulative?
options: Cumulative exams allow her to drop the daily quizzes from the final grade
Cumulative exams reduce the number of items needed on each later test
Cumulative exams force students into spaced review, reinforcing learning
Cumulative exams compensate for the quiz scores that students are allowed to drop
questions.explain: The authors say cumulative exams reinforce learning by forcing spaced review of earlier material. They are not a substitute for the quizzes, which count for 20 percent of the grade.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: True or false: In McDermott’s course, the daily quizzes together count for 20 percent of a student’s grade.
questions.explain: The quizzes in totality count for 20 percent of the course grade; McDermott also gives two midterm exams and a final, the last two cumulative.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: McDermott lets students drop ____ quizzes across the semester, with no makeups allowed.
questions.explain: Four free absences are part of the clear ground rules she sets and repeats when students ask for makeups.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: Which of these are true of the daily quizzes in McDermott’s course?
options: Each has four items given in the last minutes of class
Students may drop four quizzes without justifying absences
A student with a legitimate excuse may take a makeup quiz
Items may cover earlier material that students have not fully grasped
questions.explain: The quiz is four items, four drops are allowed, and she may draw on past material students need to review. Makeups are refused even when students send excuses.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: Match each feature of McDermott’s course with its description.
pairs: Four items in the last three to five minutes of class
Four quizzes, with no explanation needed
Reinforce learning by requiring spaced review
questions.explain: These are the course details the authors give, from the four-item quiz to the cumulative midterm and final.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is part of McDermott’s quiz policy.

items.t: Gives a four-item quiz in the last minutes of class
Allows four dropped quizzes
Explains the research on the testing effect at the start of term
Draws on material from earlier in the course
Gives makeup quizzes for legitimate excuses
Requires students to justify each absence
Gives the quiz at the start of class

questions.explain: She sets out the ground rules and the research at the start, repeats that there are no makeups, and does not ask students to justify absences.

questions.section: Kathleen McDermott, Psychology Professor, Washington University at St. Louis
questions.q: Why does McDermott explain the research on the testing effect and set firm ground rules at the start of her course, and how do students feel by the end?
questions.a: She lays out the research on learning and explains why the quizzes help even if they do not feel helpful, then states clear rules: four free absences and no makeups. Students are unhappy at first, but by the end they say the quizzes helped them keep up and notice when they were getting off track. The rules keep things manageable for the professor and clear for the student.

questions.q: According to the authors, what has vertical alignment of the sciences curriculum in the Columbia, Illinois, district produced?
options: Less repetition of content, since each science topic is now taught only once
Fewer tests overall, since quizzes are being replaced by long writing tasks
Longer lessons, since each topic is covered in a single extended block
More spaced and interleaved instruction, since topics return in later years
questions.explain: Aligning the curriculum vertically means students meet a subject at several stages of school. The authors say the result is more spaced and interleaved instruction.

questions.q: True or false: The low-stakes quizzing project in Columbia, Illinois, has stayed within the middle school and has not reached the high school.
questions.explain: The project was extended into history and science classes in the district’s high school, where frequent retrieval practice is also used.

questions.q: In Columbia’s redesign, the sciences curriculum is being ____ aligned so that students are reexposed to a subject at various stages of school.
questions.explain: Vertical alignment brings students back to concepts such as the six basic machines in later grades, which spaces and interleaves the learning.

questions.q: Which of these changes is Columbia, Illinois, making as it redesigns its curriculum and tests?
options: Engaging students in more writing and analysis work
Aligning the sciences curriculum vertically so topics return in later grades
Dropping low-stakes quizzing as standards become more rigorous
Teaching each science topic once, in a single extended unit
questions.explain: The district aims at conceptual understanding, reasoning and problem solving, and is making tests more rigorous. Retrieval practice continues, and topics are revisited rather than taught once.

questions.q: Match each item from the Columbia, Illinois, story with its description.
pairs: Quizzing in a middle school, with teachers who saw good results adopting it
History and science classes in the district’s high school
Standards for college and career readiness by high school graduation
Students are reexposed to a subject at various stages of school
questions.explain: Each pair comes from the district’s story of quizzing, then curriculum redesign for higher-level skills.

questions.q: How is the Columbia, Illinois, school district using retrieval practice, and how is its curriculum redesign linked to spacing and interleaving?
questions.a: Teachers use regular low-stakes quizzing and other retrieval practice, first in a middle school and later in history and science classes in the high school, both to bolster learning and to show where instruction needs work. The district is also making its curriculum and tests more rigorous. Aligning the sciences curriculum vertically so students return to topics in later grades produces more spaced and interleaved instruction.

questions.q: What does the Qstream platform do for learners?
options: It sends periodic quizzes to mobile devices for spaced retrieval practice
It delivers recorded PowerPoint lectures to learners’ phones every month
It supplies thousands of crowdsourced practice questions and explanations
It matches learners with mentors for monthly social learning sessions
questions.explain: Qstream is based on the testing effect and helps trainers send periodic quizzes by mobile device. The crowdsourced question bank belongs to a different platform, Osmosis.

questions.q: What weakness of typical continuing education for licensed professionals does the chapter point out?
options: It is spread over many months, so participants forget the early lessons they were given
It is a compressed weekend of lectures lacking retrieval, spacing and interleaving
It relies on frequent quizzes but gives participants no feedback on their answers
It is taught by instructors who have not practiced in their own field recently
questions.explain: Training is typically squeezed into a weekend symposium with meals and PowerPoint lectures, so participants are lucky to retain much.

questions.q: True or false: Osmosis combines the testing effect, spacing and social networking, offering learners crowdsourced practice questions and explanations.
questions.explain: That is how the authors describe Osmosis, whose developers call the approach student-driven social learning.

questions.q: Qstream sends learners periodic quizzes via ____ devices to strengthen learning through spaced retrieval practice.
questions.explain: Qstream is one platform built on the testing effect; the quizzes arrive on mobile devices over time.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter suggest for a professional stuck with a weekend training format?
options: Use the presentation materials to quiz yourself on the key ideas
Schedule follow-up emails with retrieval questions every month or so
Re-read the slides on the trip home to fix them in memory
Ask the professional association to revamp its approach to training
questions.explain: The three suggestions are self-quizzing, scheduled follow-up questions, and asking the association to revamp training. Re-reading is not among them.

questions.q: Match each item from the in-service training discussion with its description.
pairs: A compressed weekend symposium with meals and PowerPoint lectures
Sends periodic quizzes to learners’ mobile devices
Offers crowdsourced practice questions and explanations
questions.explain: The authors contrast the usual weekend format with two platforms that apply the testing effect and spacing.

questions.q: Sort each item as a feature of typical in-service training or a remedy the authors suggest.

items.t: Compressed into a weekend symposium
Set at a hotel or resort
Structured around meals and PowerPoint lectures
Quiz yourself from the presentation materials
Schedule monthly follow-up emails with questions
Ask the professional association to revamp its training

questions.explain: The first three describe the usual format the authors criticize, and the last three are the steps they propose.

questions.q: Why does typical in-service training for professionals work poorly, and what can a participant do about it?
questions.a: Continuing education is usually compressed into a weekend symposium built around meals and PowerPoint lectures, so retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving are missing and participants retain little. A participant can use the presentation materials to quiz themselves, schedule follow-up emails with retrieval questions every month or so, and ask the professional association to revamp its training. Platforms such as Qstream and Osmosis show how spaced quizzing can be built in.

questions.q: Put the chapter’s four groups of tips in the order they appear.
items: Tips for Students
Tips for Lifelong Learners
Tips for Teachers
Tips for Trainers
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the learner’s own strategies to the classroom and finally to training outside school.

questions.q: What does Kathy Maixner see as her role when coaching clients?
options: Giving them proven solutions drawn from her many years of consulting work
Training their staff in sales scripts that she has already tested elsewhere
Helping them dig past symptoms to root causes and generate solutions
Auditing their finances and reporting what went wrong to the owners
questions.explain: She helps clients find the root causes of a problem, generate possible solutions and play out implications before committing, which fits the book’s learning principles.

questions.q: Why does Maixner have clients generate solutions rather than handing them the answer?
options: Clients accept an answer more readily when it appears to cost them nothing at all
Handing over answers would breach the terms of her usual consulting contract
Generated solutions are always cheaper to put into practice than her own
People who generate a solution travel the road to it and explore options
questions.explain: Maixner says that if you hand people the solution they need not explore how you got there, whereas those who generate it are the ones traveling down that road.

questions.q: True or false: Maixner uses role-playing so clients can generate solutions, try them out, get feedback and practice what works.
questions.explain: She simulates problems this way, which adds difficulties that make learning stronger and mirror what clients meet in the marketplace.

questions.q: Maixner helps clients dig past the symptoms of a problem to discover its ____ causes.
questions.explain: Finding root causes comes first, then generating solutions and playing out the implications of different strategies.

questions.q: Which of these does Maixner do in her coaching?
options: Uses role-playing to simulate problems
Gets clients to generate solutions and try them out
Hands clients a finished plan to follow step by step
Discusses options and implications before clients commit to a strategy
questions.explain: She has clients generate, test and discuss options. Handing over the solution is what she avoids.

questions.q: Match each item about Kathy Maixner with its description.
pairs: A Portland, Oregon, consulting shop on growth strategies and sales tactics
A company that added $21 million to annual revenue
Inner Gate Acupuncture, which needed a business management footing
Dig to root causes, generate solutions and play out the implications
questions.explain: The authors describe her firm, a big and a small client, and why her methods fit the book’s principles.

questions.q: How does Kathy Maixner’s coaching reflect the book’s learning principles?
questions.a: She helps clients dig past symptoms to root causes, then lets them generate possible solutions and play out the implications of different strategies before committing. Because the clients generate the answers instead of being handed them, they travel the road themselves. She also uses role-playing to simulate problems, with feedback and practice, which adds difficulties that make learning stronger and more like the marketplace.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the magazine-and-posterboard exercise at the start of Farmers’ new-agent training?
options: To picture personal success five years out, then work back to set metrics
To teach agents how to design advertising posters for their own agencies
To rank the products that agents will find easiest to sell in the first year
To show agents how the Farmers brand compares with rival insurers
questions.explain: The poster shows where the agent is headed, the metrics are the road map, and the skills learned in the following days are the tools for the journey.

questions.q: In Farmers’ get-acquainted exercise, which group learned the most about others, and why?
options: The red group, because it was told to meet as many people as possible
The green group, because it had a structure of topics to ask about
The blue group, because it was told to learn three specific things
All groups learned equally, because they all reconvened to share
questions.explain: Only the green group had a set of topics: family, prior occupation, recreation and what they enjoy. That structure later became the FORE tool.

questions.q: In Farmers’ 5-4-3-2-1 sales and marketing system, what does the number three stand for?
options: Three new business marketing initiatives every month
Three retention programs kept in place at all times
Three appointments scheduled every day
Three policies sold to each new customer on average
questions.explain: The three is appointments scheduled each day; two are kept, since prospects often reschedule. Marketing initiatives are the five, and policies per sale are two.

questions.q: Why do the authors call Farmers’ new-agent training an example of interleaving?
options: Each of the four topics is taught to completion on its own separate day
Agents alternate between lectures and breaks at fixed intervals each day
Agents switch between the two training campuses at the end of each week
Exercises cycle through four related topics, each adding meaning
questions.explain: The week keeps returning to sales, marketing systems, business planning and brand advocacy, so agents recall earlier learning and apply it in a new context.

questions.q: True or false: Farmers’ new-agent week is built mainly around PowerPoint lectures on product features.
questions.explain: The week is about learning from the bottom up through exercises and practice, with no PowerPoint lectures as such.

questions.q: In the Farmers acronym FORE, the letters stand for family, occupation, recreation, and ____.
accept: what he or she enjoys most
questions.explain: The icebreaker questions later become a tool for opening up a prospect’s needs.

questions.q: Farmers agents guessed that a direct mail campaign returns about 50 percent, but experienced agents said it is closer to ____ percent.
questions.explain: The sobering answer teaches agents which marketing strategies are likely to pay.

questions.q: Which of these are among the four areas of Farmers’ new-agent training?
options: Sales
Marketing systems
Business planning
Claims adjustment
Actuarial pricing
questions.explain: The four areas are sales, marketing systems, business planning and advocacy of the brand.

questions.q: Put the logic of Farmers’ opening poster exercise in order.
items: Illustrate personal success five years ahead on a poster
Work backward to set metrics for each year and month
Learn the skills needed to reach those metrics
questions.explain: The image shows where the agent is headed, the metrics are the road map, and the skills are the tools.

questions.q: Put the steps of Farmers’ 5-4-3-2-1 sales and marketing system in order.
items: Five new marketing initiatives every month
Four cross-marketing and four retention programs
Three appointments scheduled every day
Two appointments kept
One new customer sold two policies on average
questions.explain: The numbers count down from five to one, ending in one new customer sold two policies on average.

questions.q: Match each item in the Farmers training story with its description.
pairs: New business marketing initiatives every month
Cross-marketing and retention programs in place
New customer sold two policies on average
questions.explain: These are the pieces of the 5-4-3-2-1 structure.

questions.q: Match each group in Farmers’ get-acquainted exercise with its instruction.
pairs: Go meet people in the room
Ask about family, prior occupation, recreation and what they enjoy
questions.explain: The green group, with a structure, learned much more, and that structure became the FORE tool.

questions.q: Match each number in the Farmers story with what it describes.
pairs: Exclusive independent agents in the sales force
Yearly sales of policies and investment products
questions.explain: These facts describe the size of Farmers and its new-agent training.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is one of Farmers’ four training topics.
groups: One of the four training topics

items.t: Sales
Marketing systems
Business planning
Advocacy of the brand
Claims adjustment
Actuarial pricing
Legal compliance

questions.explain: The authors name sales, marketing systems, business planning and advocacy of the company’s values and brands.

questions.q: Explain how Farmers’ new-agent training week reflects generation, spaced practice and interleaving.
questions.a: Rather than lecturing, the week has agents ask what knowledge and skills they need, and exercises cycle through sales, marketing systems, business planning and brand advocacy again and again. Each return requires recalling earlier learning and applying it in a larger context, as with the icebreaker that becomes the FORE tool for prospects. Agents generate answers and practice by playing agent and customer.

questions.q: How does the get-acquainted exercise in Farmers’ training come back later in the week, and what does that show?
questions.a: The green group, which had a structure for talking to others, learned far more than the others. When sales comes up later, somebody recalls that exercise, and it becomes the FORE tool: family, occupation, recreation, enjoyment. It then also opens up the realms of a prospect’s life where insurance can help, so understanding deepens at each pivot between topics.

questions.q: What score must a Jiffy Lube employee reach on the e-learning exam to become eligible for on-the-job training?
options: 80 percent or better
70 percent or better
90 percent or better
100 percent on a second attempt
questions.explain: Employees who score 80 percent or better begin on-the-job practice with a written guide that breaks each service into steps.

questions.q: How does Jiffy Lube keep its technicians’ skills up to date?
options: Technicians retake the whole e-learning course every year
Technicians must recertify every two years
Supervisors re-sign each technician’s file every month
Technicians retrain only when a new car model is released
questions.explain: Recertification every two years keeps mastery current and adapts to operational and technical changes.

questions.q: True or false: At Jiffy Lube, an employee may begin working on customers’ cars once he or she passes the e-learning exam.
questions.explain: Passing the exam only makes the employee eligible to begin on-the-job training; no one may work on a customer’s car until certified proficient.

questions.q: Jiffy Lube’s Web-based learning platform is called Jiffy Lube ____.
questions.explain: Jiffy Lube University is an integrated suite of courses for franchisees’ employees.

questions.q: Jiffy Lube technicians must recertify every ____ years.
questions.explain: Recertification keeps their mastery up to snuff.

questions.q: Which of these are part of Jiffy Lube University’s approach?
options: Interactive e-learning with frequent quizzing and feedback
A virtual dashboard that shows each employee’s progress
Lectures at a central campus once a year
Recertification every two years
questions.explain: The program uses e-learning, a dashboard with an individualized learning plan, and recertification. It is Web-based rather than built on annual campus lectures.

questions.q: Put the steps of Jiffy Lube’s certification process in order.
items: Interactive e-learning with frequent quizzing
Score 80 percent or better on the exam
Practice on the job with a step-by-step guide
Supervisor rates performance on each step
Certification is recorded and signed by the supervisor
questions.explain: Certification starts with e-learning, moves to team-based practice with coaching, and ends with a record signed by the supervisor.

questions.q: Match each Jiffy Lube term with its description.
pairs: The Web-based learning platform for certification
An individualized learning plan to track progress
A Day in the Life of a Store Manager
A simulation game that gives managers feedback on their choices
Required every two years to keep mastery current
questions.explain: Each term is part of the training system the authors describe.

questions.q: Sort each Jiffy Lube training step by when it happens.

items.t: Interactive e-learning with frequent quizzing
Scoring 80 percent or better on the exam
Following a written guide that breaks the service into steps
Performing steps as a team with call and response
Supervisor rates performance on each step

questions.explain: The e-learning and exam come first; on-the-job practice follows under a coaching supervisor.

questions.q: How does Jiffy Lube University use quizzing, feedback and spaced and interleaved practice to train employees?
questions.a: Employees start with interactive e-learning that includes frequent quizzing and feedback, then train on the job following a step-by-step guide while a supervisor coaches and rates each step. They recertify every two years, move on to other jobs in the store, and track their progress on a dashboard. The authors describe these as active learning strategies, and turnover has dropped while customer satisfaction has risen.

questions.q: Why do workers at Renewal by Andersen’s double-hung line change jobs every two hours?
options: To keep workers from getting bored with the written standards of each job
To let crew leaders evaluate each worker on every task in a cell
To reduce repetitive stress injuries and broaden cross-training
To lower costs by reducing the number of workers required on the line
questions.explain: The authors add that frequent switching resembles interleaving, building understanding of the whole process and readiness for unexpected events.

questions.q: What happened after the Kaizen event on Andersen’s double-hung window line?
options: The line doubled production but shipments were paused for a month
Space needs fell by 40 percent but quality problems followed soon after
Managers redesigned the line alone and workers then learned new roles
After five months the plant met its stretch goals and halved costs
questions.explain: The plant met its goals of cutting the line’s space and doubling production, and the teams never missed a shipment or had a quality issue.

questions.q: True or false: At Andersen, a worker whose improvement idea is endorsed by management takes leave from production to help implement it.
questions.explain: That is how production workers teach managers: the worker who offered the idea helps implement the new standard.

questions.q: Switching between jobs every two hours at Andersen is likened by the authors to ____ the practice of different but related topics.
questions.explain: Frequent job switching builds an understanding of the integrated process.

questions.q: Kaizen is a Japanese term for ____.
questions.explain: It has been central to Toyota’s success and is used to create a culture of continuous improvement.

questions.q: Which of these were the work cells on the double-hung line at Cottage Grove?
options: Sash fabrication
Frame fabrication
Final assembly
Glass cutting
Shipping
