questions.explain: The line had three work cells, one each for sash fabrication, frame fabrication and final assembly.

questions.q: Put the sequence Rick Wynveen calls tell-show-do-review into order.
items: Tell
Show
Do
Review
questions.explain: New workers are paired with experienced workers, practice on the job, and receive feedback that brings performance in line with the written standard.

questions.q: Put the steps of Andersen’s Kaizen event in order.
items: Recruit a mixed design team
Team meets for a week to study the process
Team presents its plan to Wynveen
Each work station is asked what changes the plan needs
Line is rebuilt in two halves over two weekends
Fine-tuning generates two hundred more improvements
questions.explain: The team planned, the stations adapted the plan, and the line was rebuilt and then refined by workers’ suggestions.

questions.q: Match each Andersen term with its meaning.
pairs: Goals that need significant restructuring, not incremental improvement
A description of each step of a job, ensuring uniform quality
A management style of trust and willingness to talk
questions.explain: These ideas support the plant’s culture of continuous improvement.

questions.q: Sort each Andersen practice by the learning principle the authors link it to.

items.t: Workers change jobs every two hours
Cross-training across several related jobs
Team redesigns the line to meet a stretch goal
Workers diagnose why a team missed targets and redesign the process

questions.explain: Job rotation resembles interleaving, while workers solving problems themselves is generation.

questions.q: How do job rotation and written standards work at Renewal by Andersen, and why do the authors connect rotation to interleaving?
questions.a: Workers change jobs every two hours to cut repetitive stress injuries and broaden cross-training, while every job follows a written standard that describes each step so quality is uniform. The authors say switching between jobs is like interleaving related topics, because it builds understanding of the whole process and prepares workers for unexpected events. New employees learn by tell, show, do, review.

questions.q: How did the Kaizen event at Andersen illustrate learning by generation and by teaching, and what was the result?
questions.a: A mixed team, including five production workers, spent a week teaching each other about the process and devising a plan to cut the line’s space by 40 percent and double production. Workers and crew leaders at each station redesigned components, and testing and feedback produced two hundred more improvements. After five months the stretch goals were met and costs were cut in half, with no missed shipments.

questions.q: What does the author mean by a learning culture in the Andersen story?
questions.a: A learning culture places the responsibility for learning with the employees and empowers them to change the system. Problems become information rather than failures. Learning by solving problems (generation) and by teaching others (elaboration) becomes an engine for continuous improvement of individuals and of the production line.

questions.q: According to Erik Isaacman, why did Inner Gate’s rapid growth become a problem?
options: It covered up missing systems for costs, goals and management
It forced the partners to close the clinic for several months at a time
It brought in patients faster than clinicians could be trained to treat them
It reduced revenue because each new clinician cost more than they earned
questions.explain: Growth of 35 to 50 percent a year hid the lack of cost systems, clear goals and a management hierarchy, so the partners realized they did not know how to run a business.

questions.q: What did Maixner do in her coaching sessions with Erik and Oliver?
options: Wrote the operating manual and job descriptions herself and handed them over
Asked questions that exposed gaps, then left them to generate the systems
Took over day-to-day management of the clinic during its first year
Sent a trainer to lecture the clinicians on how to run a practice
questions.explain: Between frequent sessions the partners generated the infrastructure; she used generation, reflection, elaboration and rehearsal rather than giving them answers.

questions.q: The partners learned to raise insurance reimbursements from as little as ____ cents on the dollar.
questions.explain: Learning to ensure they were paid appropriately was one result of the coaching.

questions.q: Which of these did Erik and Oliver generate with Maixner’s coaching?
options: An operating manual
Job descriptions
A plan to sell the clinic
A uniform protocol for seeing a new patient
A merger with another clinic
questions.explain: They built an operating manual, job descriptions, financial goals, performance metrics and a protocol for a new patient’s first visit. Selling or merging were never part of it.

questions.q: Match each person in the Inner Gate story with their role.
pairs: Acupuncturist and co-founder who became a coach of his coworkers
Erik’s business partner in opening the clinic
Business coach and patient who offered to help
questions.explain: The story follows the partners and the coach who helped them put the clinic on a sound footing.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it was missing before the coaching or created during it.

items.t: Systems for managing costs
Clear goals
A management hierarchy
An operating manual
Job descriptions
Metrics for measuring clinicians’ performance
A protocol for a new patient’s first session

questions.explain: Growth had covered up what was missing, and the partners then generated these elements between coaching sessions.

questions.q: Put the events of the Inner Gate story in order.
items: The partners open the clinic in 2005
Growth of 35 to 50 percent a year hides missing systems
Maixner offers help and asks probing questions
The partners generate infrastructure between coaching sessions
Erik coaches clinicians with recorded role-play
The clinic supports four clinicians and eyes a second location
questions.explain: The story runs from growth and gaps through coaching to a solid, expanding practice.

questions.q: Why was Inner Gate Acupuncture struggling as a business, and how did Maixner’s coaching help?
questions.a: The clinic was succeeding therapeutically and growing 35 to 50 percent a year, but that growth covered up the lack of cost systems, clear goals and a management hierarchy. Maixner asked questions that exposed gaps, and between sessions the partners generated an operating manual, job descriptions, financial goals and metrics, and learned to secure proper insurance payments. The clinic ended up on sound footing.

questions.q: How does Erik Isaacman’s role-play training of clinicians apply the book’s learning principles?
questions.a: Erik trains clinicians with role-play: one plays the patient and the other the clinician, they raise objections, practice responses, and then switch roles. They record the sessions and listen for differences in how each responded. The authors call this learning through simulation, generation, testing, feedback and practice, and it makes Erik an effective coach and teacher of his coworkers.

questions.q: Why does the final chapter of Make It Stick consist of practical tips?
options: It adds new research findings that the earlier chapters had left out entirely
It replaces the earlier theory with a different method of teaching
Readers wanted specific advice, so it puts earlier ideas into practice
It reviews critics’ objections to the studies described in earlier chapters
questions.explain: The authors resisted being prescriptive in earlier chapters, but early readers urged them to get specific, so this chapter gives tips and stories of people already applying them.

questions.q: What do the stories of Farmers, Jiffy Lube and Andersen in the trainers’ section show about the book’s principles?
options: Workplace training needs a different set of principles from those used in school
Classroom techniques fail outside structured educational settings of any kind
Only large companies can afford to use the book’s learning principles
These principles work in workplaces as well as in classrooms
questions.explain: The section opens by saying trainers use the same principles as teachers in schools, in less structured and nonclassroom settings.

questions.q: True or false: In the closing remarks, the authors say the responsibility for education rests with each individual, and the responsibility for learning rests with institutions.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: responsibility for learning rests with every individual, while education and training rest with the institutions of society.

questions.q: In closing, the authors note that the book has been about learning, not about ____.
questions.explain: They say education raises difficult questions, but the techniques described can be used right now by learners, teachers and trainers.

questions.q: Why does the chapter move from tips for students to tips for teachers and then trainers, and what does that order suggest about the book’s message?
questions.a: It starts with what individual learners can do, then shows how teachers can build the same strategies into classrooms, and finally how trainers use them in workplaces and less structured settings. The sequence shows that the principles of retrieval, spacing, interleaving and generation apply wherever people learn. The authors close by saying the techniques cost nothing and need no structural reform.

questions.q: What distinction do the authors draw at the end of the book between learning and education, and why do the techniques still matter?
questions.a: Responsibility for learning rests with every individual, whereas responsibility for education and training rests with society’s institutions, which face hard questions about what to teach and how to measure outcomes. While those issues are worked out, the techniques in the book can be used right now by learners, teachers and trainers. They cost nothing, require no structural reform and promise real, long-lasting benefits.
